title: Preparation Checklist
text: Use this checklist while you prepare the explorables presentation. It restates the requirements of the syllabus as concrete checks. The presentation is worth 10% of the final grade.

title: Preparation Checklist
text:
Before the presentation

You have a partner and you work as a pair.
You chose your model one to two weeks before your presentation date.
You know which of the two explorables sessions you present in (five pairs per session).
You can explain the model in your own words without reading from the explorable’s page.

title: Preparation Checklist
text:
Content

What is modelled. You name the real system and the quantities the model tracks.
Assumptions. You list the simplifications of the model explicitly.
Your own contribution. You add an extension, a test or a criticism of your own.

title: Preparation Checklist
text:
Timing

Your presentation fits in ten minutes. Rehearse it with a timer.

title: Preparation Checklist
text:
Assessment criteria
The syllabus asks you to explain what is modelled, state the assumptions, and add an extension, test or criticism of your own, within ten minutes. The syllabus lists no further criteria, so prepare against these three content items and the time limit.







NoteExercise



Pick one explorable from Complexity Explorables that you do not plan to present. Write one sentence for each content item: what is modelled, one assumption, and one extension, test or criticism.








TipSolution





There is no single answer. A good answer is specific. For example, for a model of flocking: the model represents birds as points that align with neighbours within a fixed radius; one assumption is that every bird sees all neighbours within that radius, with no blind angle; one test is to vary the noise level and check whether the order parameter drops as the noise grows (Vicsek et al. 1995). Compare with the Vicsek model in Module 2.

title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Nagel and Schreckenberg (1992).
Recommended: Boccara (2010), Chapter 6.
Guide to the paper: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did reports what the paper defines, measures and finds, and checks its numbers by simulation.
Nagel and Schreckenberg proposed a cellular automaton for single-lane freeway traffic (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). The road is a ring of \(L\) cells. Each cell is empty or holds one car. Each car \(n\) has a position \(x_n\) and an integer speed \(v_n \in \{0, 1, \ldots, v_{\max}\}\), measured in cells per time step. The model is agent-based: every car carries its own state and reacts to the car in front.

title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
text:
From cellular automata to agents
In an elementary cellular automaton every cell follows the same binary rule. The traffic model keeps discrete time and a one-dimensional road, but enriches the state (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992; Wilensky and Rand 2015):

Occupied cells correspond to cars.
Each car stores a speed.
The update depends on the gap ahead and on a random slowdown.

The update is still local. It is more expressive, because agents now carry internal state.
Why call this agent-based if the road is still a grid? Because each occupied cell corresponds to an individual car with its own speed. You write the update from the point of view of each car and its local environment, not as an equation for a global density field.
The road is periodic: the first and last cells are neighbours. This removes boundary effects and makes the congestion dynamics easier to interpret. The page Boundary Conditions shows what an open edge does to Rule 184.

title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
text:
The four rules
Let \(d_n\) be the number of empty cells between car \(n\) and the car ahead. At every time step, all cars apply the following rules in this order, in parallel (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992):

Acceleration. \(v_n \leftarrow \min(v_n + 1,\ v_{\max})\).
Braking. \(v_n \leftarrow \min(v_n,\ d_n)\).
Randomization. With probability \(p\), \(v_n \leftarrow \max(v_n - 1,\ 0)\).
Motion. \(x_n \leftarrow x_n + v_n\).

Rule 2 guarantees that cars never collide. Cars never overtake, so their order on the ring never changes. The number of cars is conserved on the ring, and the density is \(\rho = N/L\).
The paper words the first rule as a condition: a car with \(v < v_{\max}\) accelerates only if the distance to the next car, counted as the difference of site indices, is larger than \(v + 1\). This gives the same new speed as the two-line form above. We checked it on 20 000 random configurations with shared random numbers (see What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did). The paper also allows open boundaries and uses them in its bottleneck experiment.

title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
section: The role of the randomization step
text:
The role of the randomization step
Without rule 3 (\(p = 0\)) the model is deterministic. From a random start it reaches a stationary state with flow
\[
q(\rho) = \min\big(\rho\, v_{\max},\ 1 - \rho\big),
\]
so every car moves at \(v_{\max}\) for \(\rho < 1/(v_{\max}+1)\) and jams only appear above that density (Chowdhury et al. 2000). In the jammed regime the stationary pattern of cars is shifted one cell backwards per time step, against the traffic, as the paper observes (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). In our simulations (\(v_{\max} = 5\), \(p = 0\), \(\rho = 0.3\), \(0.4\) and \(0.5\)) the occupancy after each step was exactly the previous occupancy shifted by one cell to the left. In free flow the pattern instead moves forward with the cars.
With \(p > 0\) three things change (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992; Chowdhury et al. 2000):

drivers fluctuate in speed, even on an empty road;
a car that brakes randomly forces the car behind to brake, which can start a jam in free traffic, with no external cause;
jams move backwards, against the direction of traffic.

With \(v_{\max} = 1\) and \(p = 0\) the model reduces to the elementary Rule 184 (Chowdhury et al. 2000).








Figure 1: Space-time diagrams on a ring of 200 cells at density 0.15, v_max = 5. Left: p = 0, all cars move freely after a transient. Right: p = 0.3, jams form spontaneously and travel backwards. Cars move to the right; time runs downward.

title: The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model
text:
Scales
In the original interpretation one cell corresponds to 7.5 m, the space a car occupies in a jam, and one time step to about 1 s. Then \(v_{\max} = 5\) corresponds to \(5 \times 7.5\) m/s \(= 135\) km/h. The paper fixes the time step differently: free traffic moves at \(4.5\) cells per step, which is \(v_{\max} - p\) for \(p = 0.5\) (the value of \(p\) is inferred, see What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did), and this should correspond to about 120 km/h. Then one step lasts \(7.5 \times 4.5 / (120/3.6) \approx 1\) s (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992).






NoteExercise



Why must the braking rule come before the randomization rule? What could go wrong if you apply randomization first and braking second?








TipSolution





Let \(v'\) be the speed after acceleration. If randomization comes first, a car whose gap is smaller than \(v'\) is slowed down to \(v' - 1 \ge d_n\) and then braked to \(d_n\) anyway, so the random slowdown has no effect on it. Fluctuations then only act on cars with at least \(v'\) empty cells ahead. In the original order the random slowdown acts after braking, on every moving car, including cars that follow closely. This is what lets one random slowdown propagate backwards as a jam. The effect is large. On a ring of 500 cells with \(v_{\max} = 5\) and \(p = 0.3\) we measured the flow for both orders (random start, 2000 burn-in steps, 4000 steps averaged, one seed):

At \(\rho = 0.1\) cars rarely brake and the orders agree. At higher density the swapped order has a much higher flow. Test it yourself: swap the two rules in your code and compare the space-time diagrams.









NoteExercise



Show that for \(v_{\max} = 1\) and \(p = 0\) the model is the elementary Rule 184 with cars moving to the right.








TipSolution





With \(v_{\max} = 1\), a car has speed 1 after acceleration, and braking sets it to 0 only if the next cell is occupied. So a car moves exactly when the cell ahead is empty. Write the neighbourhood as (left, centre, right). A cell is occupied in the next step if (a) it is occupied and the cell to its right is occupied, since the car cannot move, or (b) it is empty and the cell to its left is occupied, since that car moves in. This gives the new states \(1,0,1,1,1,0,0,0\) for the neighbourhoods \(111,110,101,100,011,010,001,000\), which read \(10111000_2 = 184\). A numerical check on 200 random rings of 50 cells found that one step of nasch_step() with \(v_{\max} = 1\) and \(p = 0\) equals one step of Rule 184 every time.

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Nagel and Schreckenberg (1992), Section 3 and Figures 4 to 6.
Guide to the paper: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did.
The fundamental diagram is the relation between traffic density and traffic flow in the stationary state. It is the main macroscopic observable of a traffic model and the one you compare with road measurements (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992; Chowdhury et al. 2000).

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text:
Density, flow and speed
On a ring of \(L\) cells with \(N\) cars:
\[
\rho = \frac{N}{L}, \qquad
\bar v = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N v_n, \qquad
q = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{n=1}^N v_n = \rho\, \bar v .
\]
The flow \(q\) is the number of cars that pass a fixed point per time step, averaged over the ring. In simulations you average \(q\) over time after discarding a burn-in period.

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text:
Free flow and congested branches

Free flow. At low density cars rarely interact. Each car moves at about \(v_{\max} - p\) on average, so \(q \approx \rho\,(v_{\max} - p)\) grows linearly with \(\rho\) (Chowdhury et al. 2000).
Congested branch. At high density the gaps limit the speeds and \(q\) decreases with \(\rho\). At \(\rho = 1\) nothing moves.
Maximum flow. Between the two branches the flow reaches a maximum, the capacity of the road. Randomization lowers the capacity and moves it to lower density.

For \(p = 0\) the diagram is the exact triangle \(q = \min(\rho\, v_{\max},\ 1 - \rho)\) with its maximum at \(\rho = 1/(v_{\max} + 1)\) (Chowdhury et al. 2000).








Figure 1: Simulated fundamental diagram (ring of 400 cells, v_max = 5, 400 steps after 200 burn-in steps, random initial positions). The dashed line is the exact result for p = 0. Left: flow. Right: mean speed.





The simulation for \(p = 0\) lies on the exact triangle, which validates the code. For \(p > 0\) the peak is lower and rounded.

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text:
What the paper measured
Nagel and Schreckenberg obtained the diagram on a ring of \(10^4\) cells with \(v_{\max} = 5\) (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). They started from random positions at rest and discarded \(10L\) steps. Each dot in their Figure 4 averages the flow over only 100 steps, so that the scatter can be compared with detector data on real roads (their Figure 5). The line averages over \(10^6\) steps. They report that the flow changes from laminar to jammed near \(\rho \approx 0.08\), that the position and form of the maximum depend on the system size, and that this dependence is absent without randomization. The maximum flow in their open-road experiment and on the ring is about \(0.32\) to \(0.30\) cars per step. Real freeway data put the maximum at roughly twice that density, and at about \(2000\) vehicles per hour and lane, which is \(0.56\) vehicles per second.
We reproduced these features with \(p = 0.5\), a value that the text does not state and that we inferred from the mean free speed of \(4.5\) cells per step quoted in the paper. The maximum lies at \(\rho \approx 0.08\) to \(0.10\) with \(q \approx 0.32\) on a ring of \(10^4\) cells. On a ring of 100 cells the maximum is higher, about \(0.43\) at \(\rho = 0.10\), and for \(p = 0\) the flow on rings of 100, 1000 and \(10^4\) cells is identical. The figure above uses a ring of 400 cells, so for \(p > 0\) the exact height of its peak depends on that choice. The page What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did contains the code and the figure.

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text:
Explore the ring road
The figure below runs the four Nagel-Schreckenberg rules in parallel on a ring of 200 cells. Measure q at this ρ repeats the procedure behind Figure 1: a ring of 400 cells, random start at rest, 200 burn-in steps and an average over the next 400.


Set \(p = 0\) and \(\rho = 0.15\). After the transient, what is the mean speed? Now set \(\rho = 0.25\): why do some cars stay stopped for ever?
Keep \(\rho = 0.15\) and switch on \(p = 0.3\). Do jams appear without any bottleneck? In which direction do they move in the space-time diagram?
Press Sweep all densities with \(p = 0\) and compare the dots with the dashed exact result. Then repeat with \(p = 0.3\): where is the maximum flow now, and how high is it?
With \(p = 0\), change \(v_{\max}\). How does the density of maximum flow move? Compare with \(\rho^* = 1/(v_{\max} + 1)\).



Build this in Python. In the lab you write the code behind this figure: Traffic Model for the update rule and the space-time diagram, and Flow and Congestion for the fundamental diagram.

title: The Fundamental Diagram
text:
Empirical evidence: jams without bottlenecks
Sugiyama and co-workers asked 22 drivers to drive around a circular track of 230 m, starting from a uniform configuration. A stop-and-go wave formed spontaneously and travelled backwards, with no bottleneck on the track (Sugiyama et al. 2008). They interpret the jam as a collective instability of free flow that appears when the density exceeds a critical value.
This is the phenomenon that the randomization step produces in the Nagel-Schreckenberg model: jams on a homogeneous ring, triggered by fluctuations. The experiment does not test the specific rules of the model. It shows that a model of homogeneous traffic on a ring must be able to produce such jams.






NoteExercise



Use the free-flow approximation \(q \approx \rho (v_{\max} - p)\) and the congested branch \(q \approx 1 - \rho\) of the deterministic model to estimate where the maximum flow occurs for \(v_{\max} = 5\) and \(p = 0.3\). Compare with the figure.








TipSolution





The two lines cross at \(\rho (v_{\max} - p) = 1 - \rho\), so \(\rho^* = 1/(v_{\max} - p + 1) = 1/5.7 \approx 0.175\) and \(q^* \approx 0.82\). This is a poor estimate for the stochastic model. In simulations on a ring of 400 cells (600 steps, 200 burn-in) the flow for \(p = 0.3\) rises along the free-flow line up to \(\rho \approx 0.10\) and then stays near \(0.46\) to \(0.49\), with a maximum of about \(0.49\) near \(\rho \approx 0.12\). The sampling noise is about \(0.02\). So the maximum is at a lower density than the crossing and its height is about 40 per cent lower. The same happens for the case in the paper, \(p = 0.5\): the crossing gives \(\rho^* \approx 0.18\) and \(q^* \approx 0.82\), while the simulated maximum is \(q \approx 0.32\) near \(\rho \approx 0.08\). Jams form before the free-flow branch reaches the line \(1 - \rho\), and the congested branch lies below \(1 - \rho\), because stopped cars restart with a delay. The crossing of the two straight lines is therefore only an upper bound on the maximum flow.

title: Module 6: Explorables and Discrete Models
text:
This module has two parts. First, you present an interactive model in pairs, the explorables session. Then you switch from continuous fields to fully discrete systems: time, space and state all take discrete values. You study elementary cellular automata, the Game of Life and the Nagel-Schreckenberg model of traffic flow (Wolfram 1983; Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992).

Session Structure
Sessions 27-28: Explorables (double session)
Explorables Presentations Preparation Checklist
Session 29: Modelling with cellular automata
Cellular Automata Wolfram Classes Special Rules and Theorems
Session 30: Laboratory, cellular automata
1D Cellular Automata Space-Time Diagrams Rule Exploration Boundary Conditions Game of Life Random Soups Practice: Cellular Automata
Session 31: Modelling traffic flow and congestion
The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model The Fundamental Diagram What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did From Cars to a Continuum
Session 32: Laboratory, traffic models
Traffic Model Flow and Congestion Traffic Extensions Practice: Traffic


Learning Goals

Explain a published model to your peers, state its assumptions and add an extension, test or criticism of your own.
Encode an elementary cellular automaton rule as an 8-entry lookup table and simulate it with synchronous updates.
Build and interpret space-time diagrams, and compare how rule choice and initial condition affect long-run behaviour.
Classify space-time diagrams with the four Wolfram classes and discuss the limits of that classification.
Explain how boundary conditions and finite lattice size shape long-run behaviour.
Implement the Game of Life and identify still lifes, oscillators and gliders.
Represent traffic with occupancy and speed arrays, and implement the Nagel-Schreckenberg rules.
Measure density and flow, estimate the fundamental diagram, and explain how local agent behaviour creates stop-and-go waves and jams.
Read the original traffic paper critically: state what it defines, measures and concludes, and reproduce its main numbers by simulation.
Relate the discrete traffic model to a continuum description through conservation of cars and kinematic waves, and compare it with the social force model of Module 2.
Decide which model extensions change the fundamental diagram qualitatively.








References

Nagel, Kai, and Michael Schreckenberg. 1992. “A Cellular Automaton Model for Freeway Traffic.” Journal de Physique I 2 (12): 2221–29. https://doi.org/10.1051/jp1:1992277.


Wolfram, Stephen. 1983. “Statistical Mechanics of Cellular Automata.” Reviews of Modern Physics 55 (3): 601–44. https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.55.601.

title: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Nagel and Schreckenberg (1992), the whole paper (nine pages). Concentrate on Sections 2 to 5 and on Figures 4 to 6.
This page reports what the original paper defines, measures and concludes, and checks each number against our own simulations. Read the paper first and use this page as a guide, not as a substitute. The rules themselves are on the page The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model.

title: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did
text:
The claim of the paper
Nagel and Schreckenberg ask whether a Boolean, fully discrete model can reproduce the transition from laminar traffic to start-stop waves that appears when the vehicle density increases (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). They argue that it can: a stochastic cellular automaton shows this transition, and analytical results are available for special cases. The authors also report that, with an open road and a bottleneck, the simulated system reaches a state of its own accord, and they note a resemblance to self-organised criticality. They leave a quantitative treatment of this state, and of the case \(v_{\max} > 1\), to later work.

title: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did
section: The model as the paper defines it
text:
The model as the paper defines it
The paper allows open or periodic boundaries. Each vehicle has an integer velocity between \(0\) and \(v_{\max}\), and one update consists of four steps carried out in parallel (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992):

Acceleration. If \(v < v_{\max}\) and the distance to the next car ahead is larger than \(v + 1\), then \(v \to v + 1\).
Slowing down. If the next car is at distance \(j \le v\) sites, then \(v \to j - 1\).
Randomization. With probability \(p\), a car with \(v > 0\) reduces its speed by one.
Motion. Each car advances \(v\) sites.

Here “distance” is the difference between site indices, so the number of empty cells in between is the distance minus one. The paper’s acceleration step carries the condition on the distance, while the page The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model writes \(v \leftarrow \min(v+1, v_{\max})\) followed by \(v \leftarrow \min(v, d)\) with \(d\) the number of empty cells. The two forms give the same new speed. The chunk below confirms this on 20 000 random configurations, with the same random numbers in both versions.

import numpy as np
from amlab.cellular_automata.traffic_models import gaps_ahead

L, vmax = 60, 5
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
agree = True
for _ in range(20_000):
    n = rng.integers(1, 40)
    x = np.sort(rng.choice(L, n, replace=False))
    gap = gaps_ahead(x, L)
    v = np.minimum(rng.integers(0, vmax + 1, n), gap)      # a legal state
    rand = rng.random(n) < 0.4                              # shared random draws
    dist = gap + 1                                          # paper: difference of site indices
    v_paper = np.where((v < vmax) & (dist > v + 1), v + 1, v)
    v_paper = np.minimum(v_paper, dist - 1)
    v_paper = np.where(rand & (v_paper > 0), v_paper - 1, v_paper)
    v_page = np.minimum(np.minimum(v + 1, vmax), gap)
    v_page = np.where(rand & (v_page > 0), v_page - 1, v_page)
    agree &= np.array_equal(v_paper, v_page)
print("The two formulations agree:", agree)

The two formulations agree: True


The paper stresses that step 3 is essential. Without it the dynamics is deterministic, and every initial configuration quickly reaches a stationary pattern that moves backwards, against the traffic, by one site per time step (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). In our simulations of the jammed regime (\(\rho > 1/(v_{\max}+1)\), \(p = 0\), \(v_{\max}=5\)), the occupancy pattern was shifted by exactly one site to the left in every step, for \(\rho = 0.3\), \(0.4\) and \(0.5\). This statement therefore holds in the congested phase. In free flow (\(\rho < 1/(v_{\max}+1)\)) the stationary pattern moves forward with the cars instead.

title: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did
section: How the paper measures the flow
text:
How the paper measures the flow
The paper measures the flow in the way a road detector does. It starts from random positions with all speeds equal to zero, discards the first \(t_0 = 10 L\) steps, and then records the time-averaged occupancy and the time-averaged number of cars that pass a fixed pair of neighbouring sites (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). For a ring of \(L\) cells the flow measured at a fixed site equals \(\sum_n v_n / L\) on average, which is the definition on the page The Fundamental Diagram. Figure 4 of the paper uses \(L = 10^4\). Its dots are averages over 100 steps and can be compared with real detector data (Figure 5), and its line is an average over \(10^6\) steps.






NoteWhich value of \(p\)?



The captions and the text I read do not state the value of \(p\) for Figures 4 and 6. Two details point to \(p = 0.5\): the paper calls \(4.5\) sites per step the mean speed in free traffic, which equals \(v_{\max} - p\) for \(v_{\max} = 5\) (see the scale argument below), and the data-file label printed inside Figure 6 reads V5/p.5/.... Our simulations at \(p = 0.5\) reproduce the numbers quoted in the paper, which supports this reading. The value of \(p\) is nevertheless inferred, not quoted.










Figure 1: Reproduction of the closed-system experiment of the paper (v_max = 5, p = 0.5, random start at rest, burn-in 10 L steps, ring of 1000 cells). Left: flow against density. Dots are averages over 100 steps, three per density, and the line is the average over 20 000 steps. Right: flow near the maximum for rings of 100, 400 and 1600 cells, and for p = 0 (dashed) on the ring of 100 cells. The maximum depends on the system size for p = 0.5 but not for p = 0.





The paper reports that the change from laminar to jammed flow takes place near \(\rho \approx 0.08\), that the position and shape of the maximum of \(q(\rho)\) depend on the system size when \(p > 0\), and that simulations without randomization show no such dependence (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). It adds that it is not clear from the plots where an exact transition point lies. Our simulations show the same three features. For \(p = 0.5\) the maximum is at \(\rho \approx 0.08\) to \(0.10\) with \(q \approx 0.32\) on large rings (a ring of \(10^4\) cells, checked separately, gives \(q = 0.316\), \(0.321\) and \(0.321\) at \(\rho = 0.08\), \(0.09\) and \(0.10\)), the right panel of Figure 1 shows a higher maximum on short rings, and the \(p = 0\) curve does not move.

title: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did
text:
The exactly solvable case \(v_{\max} = 1\)
For \(v_{\max} = 1\) the acceleration step is trivial, because every car reaches speed 1 in one step, so each car only asks whether the next site is free and whether it is randomly stopped. The paper treats random sequential update in continuous time, where a car at site \(i\) jumps to \(i + 1\) at rate \(1 - p\) if that site is free (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). In that case the factor \(1-p\) only rescales time, all values of \(p < 1\) share the same stationary distribution, every configuration with a given number of cars is equally likely, and the flow is
\[
q(\rho) = \rho\,(1 - \rho),
\tag{1}\]
the probability that a car has a free site in front of it (Equation 7 of the paper). The paper adds that the parallel update gives a different function that is also symmetric about \(\rho = 1/2\).
The chunk below checks both statements numerically. The random sequential update is run with hop probability \(1 - p\) per attempt, so that the measured flow in hops per site per sweep is \((1-p)\rho(1-\rho)\), which is Equation 1 with the time axis rescaled by \(1-p\). The parallel update is run with the course code, and the parallel flow at \(\rho\) and \(1 - \rho\) is compared.

import numpy as np
from amlab.cellular_automata.traffic_models import mean_flow


def random_sequential_flow(rho, p, length=400, sweeps=1500, burn_in=300, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    occ = np.zeros(length, dtype=bool)
    occ[rng.choice(length, int(round(rho * length)), replace=False)] = True
    hops = 0
    for s in range(sweeps):
        for i in rng.integers(0, length, length):
            j = (i + 1) % length
            if occ[i] and not occ[j] and rng.random() < 1 - p:
                occ[i], occ[j] = False, True
                hops += s >= burn_in
    return hops / (length * (sweeps - burn_in))


p = 0.5
for rho in (0.2, 0.5):
    print(f"random sequential, rho = {rho}: q = {random_sequential_flow(rho, p):.3f},"
          f"  (1-p) rho (1-rho) = {(1 - p) * rho * (1 - rho):.3f}")

for rho in (0.2, 0.3, 0.4):
    q1 = mean_flow(2000, int(rho * 2000), 6000, 2000, vmax=1, p=p, seed=2)
    q2 = mean_flow(2000, int((1 - rho) * 2000), 6000, 2000, vmax=1, p=p, seed=2)
    print(f"parallel update, v_max = 1: q({rho}) = {q1:.3f}, q({1 - rho:.1f}) = {q2:.3f}")

random sequential, rho = 0.2: q = 0.080,  (1-p) rho (1-rho) = 0.080
random sequential, rho = 0.5: q = 0.127,  (1-p) rho (1-rho) = 0.125
parallel update, v_max = 1: q(0.2) = 0.088, q(0.8) = 0.088
parallel update, v_max = 1: q(0.3) = 0.119, q(0.7) = 0.119
parallel update, v_max = 1: q(0.4) = 0.139, q(0.6) = 0.140


The run gave \(q = 0.080\) and \(0.127\) for the random sequential update, against the predictions \(0.080\) and \(0.125\), and equal flows at \(\rho\) and \(1-\rho\) for the parallel update, up to sampling noise of about 0.002 (for example \(0.119\) at \(\rho = 0.3\) and \(0.7\)).

title: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did
section: The open road with a bottleneck
text:
The open road with a bottleneck
In Section 4 the paper changes only the boundaries. A car with speed \(0\) is placed on the first site whenever that site is empty, which models a saturated wider road that feeds a single lane, and every car that reaches the last six sites is deleted (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). After relaxation the paper reports a density \(\langle\rho_c\rangle = 0.069 \pm 0.002\) and a flow \(\langle q_c\rangle = 0.304 \pm 0.001\), from rings of up to \(10^4\) sites and runs of up to \(5 \times 10^6\) steps. Figure 6 shows that this self-organised state lies at a lower flow than the maximum of the closed system for \(v_{\max} = 5\), while for \(v_{\max} = 1\) the open system drives itself to the maximum flow at \(\rho = 1/2\).
The paper does not say in which order the update and the boundary operations are applied. The code below applies them after the update, which is one reasonable choice.

import numpy as np


def bottleneck(length=2000, steps=150_000, burn_in=30_000, vmax=5, p=0.5, seed=0):
    """Open road: inject a car with v = 0 when cell 0 is empty, delete cars in the last 6 cells."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = np.array([], dtype=int)
    v = np.array([], dtype=int)
    left, right = length // 4, 3 * length // 4        # measure the density in the middle half
    n_out, occupied, n_obs = 0, 0.0, 0
    for t in range(steps):
        if x.size == 0 or x[0] > 0:
            x = np.concatenate(([0], x))
            v = np.concatenate(([0], v))
        gap = np.append(np.diff(x) - 1, 10**6)         # the front car sees a free road
        v = np.minimum(np.minimum(v + 1, vmax), gap)
        v = np.where(rng.random(x.size) < p, np.maximum(v - 1, 0), v)
        x = x + v
        gone = x >= length - 6
        if t >= burn_in:
            n_out += gone.sum()
            occupied += ((x >= left) & (x < right)).sum() / (right - left)
            n_obs += 1
        x, v = x[~gone], v[~gone]
    return occupied / n_obs, n_out / (steps - burn_in)


rho_c, q_c = bottleneck()
print(f"density {rho_c:.3f}, flow {q_c:.3f}")

density 0.069, flow 0.306


The chunk gives a density of \(0.069\) and a flow of about \(0.306\). Two longer runs with different seeds (\(3 \times 10^5\) steps on the same ring of 2000 sites) gave densities \(0.0688\) and \(0.0685\) and flows \(0.3041\) and \(0.3042\). All of these agree with the values of the paper, which are \(0.069 \pm 0.002\) and \(0.304 \pm 0.001\). For comparison, the closed ring at \(p = 0.5\) reaches \(q \approx 0.32\) at its maximum (previous section), so the bottleneck state indeed lies below the maximum flow.

title: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did
section: The scale argument and the comparison with real traffic
text:
The scale argument and the comparison with real traffic
Section 5 fixes the units in four ways and finds that they agree in order of magnitude (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992).

Length and mean speed. A car occupies about 7.5 m in a complete jam, so one site is 7.5 m. Free traffic with \(4.5\) sites per step should correspond to about 120 km/h, which gives a time step of about 1 s.
Position of the maximum. Real measurements put the maximum of the flow at about 30 vehicles per kilometre and lane, which is \(0.225\) vehicles per 7.5 m. This is about twice the position of the maximum in the simulation.
Capacity. A freeway lane carries about 2000 vehicles per hour, which is \(0.56\) vehicles per second. The simulated maximum of \(0.32\) vehicles per step then suggests a time step of about \(0.5\) s.
Speed of the backward wave. Start-stop waves travel backwards at about 15 km/h, or 4.2 m/s. With a maximum capacity of about \(0.3\) cars per step, the paper takes \(0.3\) sites, that is \(2.25\) m, per step as the speed of the backward wave.

The paper concludes that the parameters of a discrete model are rather rigid once one accepts one car per site in a jam. The comparison is deliberately rough. Figure 5 shows measured flow in vehicles per hour against occupancy in per cent. The caption gives the units of occupancy as “cars per hour”, which is evidently a misprint.






NoteExercise



Redo the four scale estimates with the numbers quoted in the paper. Which of them reproduces the value that the paper prints?








TipSolution






\(7.5 \times 4.5 / (120/3.6) = 33.75 / 33.3 = 1.01\) s. (2) The position of the maximum is not a time estimate. \(0.225 / 0.08 \approx 2.8\), so the model maximum is lower in density by a factor of 2 to 3, which the paper rounds to “about 2”. (3) \(0.32 / 0.56 = 0.57\) s, printed as about 0.5 s. (4) \(2.25 / 4.2 = 0.54\) s, whereas the paper prints “about 0.7 seconds” and describes it as lying between the first and the third estimate. The ratio is 0.54 s, which is almost the same as the third estimate, so the printed value is not consistent with the quoted inputs. The conclusion that a time step corresponds to roughly one second, within a factor of two, is not affected. Check also that \(135\) km/h for \(v_{\max} = 5\) and \(7.5\) m per cell is the speed of a car at the maximum speed, whereas the paper’s 120 km/h refers to the mean speed \(v_{\max} - p = 4.5\).

title: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did
text:
Queueing picture of a jam
At the end of Section 5 the paper offers a remark that goes beyond the numbers (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). A jam of a given length gains a car at its rear with some probability per step and loses one at its front with another probability per step. Because the departure rate of one jam fixes the arrival rate at the next, all clusters behave like queues at the critical point where the two rates coincide. The authors suggest that start-stop waves may be a queueing phenomenon in which only the formation of the jam is dynamical. This is a conjecture of the paper. It is not tested there.






NoteExercise



Measure the back-travelling speed of the jams in your own simulation for \(v_{\max} = 5\) and \(p = 0.5\) on a ring of 2000 cells at \(\rho = 0.2\), \(0.3\) and \(0.4\). Record the positions of the cars with \(v = 0\) at every step, correlate the pattern at time \(t\) with that at \(t + 20\) for shifts between \(-60\) and \(+10\) cells, and take the shift with the largest correlation divided by \(20\). Compare with the number \(0.3\) that the paper uses.








TipSolution





Our measurement, with the pattern of stopped cars correlated over a lag of 20 steps and two seeds, gave \(-0.35\) to \(-0.40\) sites per step, with the same value for both seeds at each density. The magnitude is close to the \(0.3\) used in the paper, but the paper’s value is an estimate from the maximum capacity, not a measurement of jams. The two numbers need not coincide, and with the lag, grid and averaging we used, the measured speed has a resolution of about \(0.05\) sites per step. The page From Cars to a Continuum compares the jam speed with the slope of the fundamental diagram.

title: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did
section: What the paper does not do
text:
What the paper does not do

It does not fit \(p\) or \(v_{\max}\) to data. It argues that \(v_{\max} = 5\) is the realistic choice “for reasons stated below”, and then fixes the scales.
It does not locate the transition point. It states that the position and form of the maximum depend on the system size.
It states the result for \(v_{\max} > 1\) in terms of a mean-field treatment to be reported elsewhere, and its Reference 12 is announced as “in preparation”.
It does not investigate lane changes. They are announced as a topic for later investigations. The page Traffic Extensions gives some of the later work.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
This is ungraded practice. It collects the cellular automata lab into one short study that you can use to check your understanding: encode the rule, update the row synchronously, build a space-time diagram, and compare outcomes across experiments (Wolfram 1983).
You can follow the guide here:
1D Cellular Automata Space-Time Diagrams Rule Exploration Boundary Conditions Game of Life Random Soups

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Goals
The practice checks three skills:

Translate a rule number into a working local update.
Simulate repeated synchronous updates on a one-dimensional lattice.
Interpret how rule choice, initial condition and boundary shape the global pattern.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Core tasks

Implement apply_rule() and a reusable simulate_ca() function.
Reproduce a space-time diagram for Rule 30 starting from a single occupied cell at the centre.
Compare at least three rules from the set {30, 90, 110, 184} using the same initial condition.
For one chosen rule, compare two different initial conditions, one single-seed row and one random row.
Write a short paragraph that explains which features are controlled by the rule and which depend strongly on the initial condition.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Questions to answer

Which rule in your experiments produced the most regular pattern?
Which rule was most sensitive to the initial condition? Support your answer with the Hamming distance after a single flip.
Did you find one rule that already looks like transport or directed motion? Explain why.







TipOptional extensions




Implement periodic boundary conditions and compare the result with fixed-zero edges.
Add a stochastic flip rule, for example flipping a cell with small probability after each update.
Track the density of occupied cells over time for one rule and interpret the trend.
Add interactivity to the initial row, either in a notebook or with the reference script.
Find a Game of Life pattern of at most 5 cells that grows for more than 100 generations before it settles.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Tips

Test apply_rule() on a short row before you run a long simulation.
Print the rule table once so you know which output corresponds to each neighbourhood.
Keep the first experiments small enough that you can inspect the pattern visually.
Reuse the same plotting code when you compare rules so the differences are easier to see.

Reference code: amlab/cellular_automata/cellular.py, amlab/cellular_automata/elementary.py and amlab/cellular_automata/life.py.

title: Practice: Cellular Automata
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



On a ring of 100 cells, you run Rule 30 for 1000 steps and see no repetition. A classmate concludes that Rule 30 is aperiodic on this ring. Is the conclusion correct?








TipSolution





No. A ring of 100 cells has \(2^{100}\) configurations, so every orbit is eventually periodic. The period can be far longer than 1000 steps, which is why you see no repetition. What you observe is a long transient or a long cycle of a finite system, not true aperiodicity.

title: Boundary Conditions
text: Every simulation runs on a finite lattice, so you must decide what the edge cells see. This page compares periodic and fixed boundaries and shows how the finite size shapes the long-run behaviour. The reference code is amlab/cellular_automata/elementary.py.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



Before you code, answer two questions. On a ring of \(N\) cells there are \(2^N\) possible rows. What does this imply for the long-run behaviour of any rule? Which rule, 90 or 184, will be affected more by fixed-zero edges?








TipSolution





After at most \(2^N\) steps some row must repeat, and from then on the evolution cycles. So every orbit on a ring is eventually periodic, whatever the rule. Both rules change once the pattern reaches the edges, but Rule 184 changes qualitatively: it conserves the number of 1s on a ring, and fixed-zero edges let the 1s leave at the right end, so the road empties. The experiments below show both effects.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Implementation
With periodic boundaries the left neighbour of cell 0 is cell \(N-1\). np.roll gives both neighbours of every cell in one line, and the three bits give the index into the rule table.






NoteExercise



Complete step() so that it supports periodic and fixed-zero boundaries.
def step(state, rule, boundary="periodic"):
    table = np.array([(rule >> n) & 1 for n in range(8)])  # entry n: output for neighbourhood n
    if boundary == "periodic":
        left, right = # TODO: use np.roll
    else:
        padded = # TODO: add one ghost cell with value 0 at each end
        left, right = padded[:-2], padded[2:]
    return table[4 * left + 2 * state + right]








TipSolution





def step(state, rule, boundary="periodic"):
    table = np.array([(rule >> n) & 1 for n in range(8)])
    if boundary == "periodic":
        left, right = np.roll(state, 1), np.roll(state, -1)
    else:
        padded = np.concatenate(([0], state, [0]))
        left, right = padded[:-2], padded[2:]
    return table[4 * left + 2 * state + right]
This is step_eca() in the reference module.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Validation
Far from the edges, the two boundary choices must give the same rows. Check it on a wide lattice where the pattern never reaches the edges:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import simulate_eca, single_seed, random_row, transient_and_period

a = simulate_eca(single_seed(201), 30, 80, boundary="periodic")
b = simulate_eca(single_seed(201), 30, 80, boundary="fixed")
print("Identical while the pattern is far from the edges:", np.array_equal(a, b))

Identical while the pattern is far from the edges: True

title: Boundary Conditions
section: Experiment: patterns that reach the edge
text:
Experiment: patterns that reach the edge








Figure 1: Rule 90 from a single seed on 41 cells for 120 steps. Left: periodic, the two fronts meet on the other side of the ring. Right: fixed zero edges.













Figure 2: Number of occupied cells under Rule 184, from the same random row of 100 cells with density 0.4.





With fixed-zero edges, Rule 184 moves particles out through the right edge and brings in nothing at the left, so the road empties. With periodic edges the count is conserved. For a traffic model the boundary decides whether you model a closed ring road or an open road segment.

title: Boundary Conditions
section: Experiment: every orbit on a ring is periodic
text:
Experiment: every orbit on a ring is periodic
A ring of \(N\) cells has \(2^N\) configurations. After at most \(2^N\) steps some row must repeat, and from then on the evolution cycles. transient_and_period() records every row until the first repeat.








Figure 3: Period of the orbit that starts from a single seed on a ring of N cells. Logarithmic vertical axis. The dashed line is the bound 2^N.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Interpretation

Any finite simulation is eventually periodic. For Rule 30 the period grows quickly with \(N\), so on a lattice of a few hundred cells you never see the repeat. The class 3 behaviour you observe is a transient of a finite system.
Rule 90 has short periods, and for some sizes the seed dies out completely. Find the sizes where the period is 1 in the output of transient_and_period().
A boundary is part of the model. Report it together with the rule and the lattice size.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Limitations

The period depends on the initial row, not only on the rule and \(N\). The figure uses a single seed.
Storing every row limits transient_and_period() to rings of about 20 cells.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Optional extension






NoteExercise



Optional. Replace the ghost value 0 by 1, or use reflecting edges (the ghost copies the edge cell). Track the number of occupied cells for Rules 184, 90 and 30. Which rules change their long-run behaviour?








TipSolution





Rule 184 is the rule that changes most. With ghost value 1 the left ghost feeds new 1s into the lattice, the right ghost blocks the exit, and the row fills up completely. With reflecting edges no 1 can leave or enter, so the count is conserved and all 1s pile up at the right end as one jam. Rules 90 and 30 keep an irregular pattern whose number of occupied cells fluctuates from step to step, for every boundary choice. The single values printed below are snapshots of these fluctuations, not steady states.

from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import rule_table, step_eca


def step_reflect(state, rule):
    table = rule_table(rule)
    padded = np.concatenate((state[:1], state, state[-1:]))
    return table[4 * padded[:-2] + 2 * state + padded[2:]]


updates = {
    "ghost 0": lambda s, r: step_eca(s, r, boundary="fixed", fixed_value=0),
    "ghost 1": lambda s, r: step_eca(s, r, boundary="fixed", fixed_value=1),
    "reflecting": step_reflect,
}
row = random_row(100, 0.4, seed=2)
for rule in (184, 90, 30):
    for name, update in updates.items():
        state = row.copy()
        for t in range(300):
            state = update(state, rule)
        print(f"Rule {rule:3d}, {name:10s}: {int(state.sum()):3d} occupied cells after 300 steps")

Rule 184, ghost 0   :   0 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule 184, ghost 1   : 100 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule 184, reflecting:  40 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  90, ghost 0   :  47 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  90, ghost 1   :  47 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  90, reflecting:  50 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  30, ghost 0   :  50 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  30, ghost 1   :  49 occupied cells after 300 steps
Rule  30, reflecting:  35 occupied cells after 300 steps

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
This is ungraded practice. You now have the core ingredients of an agent-based traffic model: local update rules, a reproducible simulator, a space-time diagram, and macroscopic observables such as density and flow (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992; Wilensky and Rand 2015). This page combines them into one short traffic study.
You can follow the guide here:
Traffic Model Flow and Congestion Traffic Extensions

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Goals
The practice checks three skills:

Build a correct agent-based traffic simulator.
Connect microscopic update rules with macroscopic observables.
Explain when and why congestion appears.

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Core tasks

Implement initialize_road(), step(), and simulate() for the Nagel-Schreckenberg model.
Produce space-time diagrams for at least three densities: one low-density regime, one intermediate regime, and one congested regime.
Estimate the fundamental diagram \(q(\rho)\) using at least 10 density values and a burn-in period before you average the flow.
Validate the result for p_slow = 0 against \(q = \min(\rho\, v_{\max},\ 1 - \rho)\).
Compare the flow-density curve for at least two values of p_slow, and describe where the maximum flow occurs and how the onset of congestion changes when p_slow increases.

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Questions to answer

At what density does free flow begin to break down in your experiments?
Does higher random slowdown mostly change the peak flow, the jam onset, or both?
Which figure best explains the transition from microscopic rules to macroscopic congestion?







TipOptional extensions




Add sliders for density, p_slow, or vmax.
Compare random initial conditions with a localized dense cluster of cars.
Introduce a small fraction of slow vehicles and study the effect on the flow curve.
Replace the periodic road by open boundaries with inflow and outflow.

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Tips

Test one update step on a short road before you launch long runs.
Fix the seed when you debug.
Discard an initial burn-in window when you estimate stationary flow.
Keep the plotting code separate from the simulation code so repeated experiments stay simple.

Reference code: amlab/cellular_automata/traffic.py and amlab/cellular_automata/traffic_models.py.

title: Practice: Traffic
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



On a ring road you measure the same density twice and get two clearly different mean flows. Your code has no bug. Name one model feature from this page that can explain it.








TipSolution





A slow-to-start rule (\(p_0 > p\)). It creates a density range with a metastable high-flow state and a jammed state, so the flow depends on the initial condition and not only on the density (Barlović et al. 1998). A run that is too short, so that the burn-in has not removed the transient, can give the same symptom.

title: Flow and Congestion
text: Once the simulator works, the next step is to extract macroscopic observables. In traffic modelling the most important one is the fundamental diagram, the relationship between density and average flow (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). The theory is on the page The Fundamental Diagram, and the measurement protocol of the paper is described on What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



Sketch \(q(\rho)\) for p_slow = 0 before you run anything. Where is the maximum? How should the curve change for p_slow = 0.3?








TipSolution





For p_slow = 0 the curve is the triangle \(q = \min(5\rho,\ 1 - \rho)\). It rises with slope \(v_{\max} = 5\), peaks at \(\rho = 1/6 \approx 0.17\) with \(q = 5/6 \approx 0.83\), and falls linearly to \(q = 0\) at \(\rho = 1\). For p_slow = 0.3 the free-flow slope drops to about \(v_{\max} - p = 4.7\), the peak is rounded and much lower, about \(q \approx 0.49\) near \(\rho \approx 0.12\) on a ring of 400 cells (the sampling noise near the maximum is about \(0.02\)), and the congested branch lies below \(1 - \rho\). Compare with the figure on The Fundamental Diagram.











Figure 1: Estimated fundamental diagram for two slowdown probabilities.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Measure density and flow
Two standard macroscopic quantities are
\[
\rho = \frac{N_{\mathrm{cars}}}{L},
\qquad
q(t) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i \in \mathrm{cars}} v_i(t).
\]
Here \(\rho\) is the density and \(q(t)\) is the instantaneous flow, measured as the mean number of cells traveled per road cell and per time step.
To estimate stationary behavior, average \(q(t)\) after a burn-in window.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Record flow during one run
The simplest extension of the simulator is to track the flow after each update.
def simulate_with_flow(steps, length, density, vmax, p_slow, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    occupied, speeds = initialize_road(length=length, density=density, vmax=vmax, rng=rng)

    flow_history = np.zeros(steps)
    flow_history[0] = speeds[occupied].sum() / length

    for t in range(1, steps):
        occupied, speeds = step(
            occupied,
            speeds,
            vmax=vmax,
            p_slow=p_slow,
            rng=rng,
        )
        flow_history[t] = speeds[occupied].sum() / length

    return flow_history

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Sweep the density
Now repeat the experiment for many densities.
densities = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19)
mean_flows = []

for density in densities:
    flow_history = simulate_with_flow(
        steps=300,
        length=100,
        density=density,
        vmax=5,
        p_slow=0.3,
        seed=7,
    )
    mean_flows.append(flow_history[100:].mean())
Plotting mean_flows against densities gives the fundamental diagram.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Validation
For p_slow = 0 the stationary flow is \(q = \min(\rho\, v_{\max},\ 1 - \rho)\) (Chowdhury et al. 2000). Compare your sweep with this line before you trust the curves for p_slow > 0.

# initialize_road() draws the occupancy at random, so measure the actual density
actual = np.array([
    initialize_road(length=100, density=d, vmax=5, rng=np.random.default_rng(7))[0].mean()
    for d in densities
])
exact = np.minimum(actual * 5, 1 - actual)
sim = np.array([simulate_with_flow(density=d, p_slow=0.0, seed=7)[burn_in:].mean() for d in densities])
print("Largest deviation from the exact p = 0 result:", np.round(np.abs(sim - exact).max(), 3))

Largest deviation from the exact p = 0 result: 0.0


Use the measured density \(N/L\), not the target value: on a road of 100 cells the random initialization can differ from the target by several cars.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Compare slowdown probabilities
The most informative parameter to vary is p_slow.

At small density, cars rarely interact and the flow grows roughly linearly with density.
At intermediate density, the flow reaches a maximum.
At high density, braking dominates and the flow drops because congestion limits motion.

Increasing p_slow usually lowers the peak flow and shifts the congested regime earlier.






NotePractical tip



Use several seeds if you want smoother curves. For example, estimate the mean flow for each density with 5 to 10 trials and then average the stationary values.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Interpretation

A space-time diagram in a free-flow regime and one in a congested regime show the microscopic picture.
The flow-density curve shows the macroscopic picture: where the maximum flow occurs and how noise changes it.

title: Flow and Congestion
text:
Limitations

initialize_road() draws the occupancy at random, so the number of cars fluctuates around density * length. Use the measured density \(N/L\) on the horizontal axis for precise work.
One seed per density gives noisy curves near the maximum.

title: From Cars to a Continuum
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: the introduction and Section 3 of Nagel and Schreckenberg (1992).
Related pages of the course: Social Force Model and Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door in Module 2.
The Nagel-Schreckenberg model describes every car. Traffic engineers often describe the road with a density field instead. The introduction of the paper recalls that fluid-dynamical approaches to traffic have existed since the 1950s, and that methods of nonlinear dynamics applied to them stressed the notion of a phase transition from laminar flow to start-stop waves (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). In its conclusion, the paper argues that the discrete model contains the transition from laminar to start-stop traffic of the fluid approach and keeps more elements of individual behaviour. This page connects the two descriptions, and then compares the traffic automaton with the continuous social force model that you met in Module 2.

title: From Cars to a Continuum
section: Conservation of cars and kinematic waves
text:
Conservation of cars and kinematic waves
On a ring no car enters or leaves, so the number of cars is conserved. For a density \(\rho(x,t)\) averaged over a few cells and the corresponding flow \(q(x,t)\), conservation reads
\[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial q}{\partial x} = 0 .
\tag{1}\]
This statement is exact for the number of cars. It is not yet a closed model. A closure assumes that the flow adjusts at once to the local density, \(q = Q(\rho)\), where \(Q\) is the fundamental diagram of the page The Fundamental Diagram. This is an approximation: it ignores the time that cars need to accelerate and the fluctuations of the random slowdown. With the closure, Equation 1 becomes \(\partial_t \rho + Q'(\rho)\,\partial_x \rho = 0\), so a small disturbance of density travels with the speed
\[
c(\rho) = Q'(\rho) .
\tag{2}\]
For the deterministic model, \(Q(\rho) = \min(\rho\, v_{\max},\ 1 - \rho)\), so \(c = v_{\max}\) in free flow and \(c = -1\) in the congested phase. In free flow a disturbance moves with the cars. In the congested phase it moves backwards by one cell per step, against the traffic. The claim of the paper that the deterministic stationary pattern moves backwards by one site per step is exactly this statement (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992).








Figure 1: Left: space-time diagram of the deterministic model (v_max = 5, p = 0, ring of 100 cells, density 0.3, cars move to the right, time runs downward) after the transient. The dashed line moves one cell to the left per step and stays on an occupied cell: the pattern is carried backwards at the kinematic speed c = -1. Right: flow Q against density for p = 0 (exact) and p = 0.5 (simulation, ring of 1000 cells), with straight lines whose slope is the kinematic speed at density 0.3 for p = 0 (-1) and the fitted slope for p = 0.5 (about -0.30).





For \(p = 0.5\) the slope of \(Q\) on the congested branch is still negative, so jams again travel backwards. A straight-line fit through simulated flows on a ring of 2000 cells at \(\rho = 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40\) gives \(Q' \approx -0.30\), and the free-flow branch has slope \(v_{\max} - p = 4.5\) (a flow of \(0.09\) at \(\rho = 0.02\)). A direct measurement of the speed of the back-travelling pattern of stopped cars gave \(-0.35\) at \(\rho = 0.2\) and \(-0.40\) at \(\rho = 0.3\) and \(0.4\). Both are of the same order and have the same sign, but they are not equal. The local slope of \(Q\) varies between \(-0.25\) and \(-0.34\) over this range, the closure ignores the internal structure of a jam, and the measurement has a resolution of about \(0.05\) cells per step. We do not claim that Equation 2 predicts the jam speed of the stochastic model quantitatively.






NoteExercise




Use Equation 2 to find the kinematic speed of the deterministic model with \(v_{\max} = 3\) at \(\rho = 0.1\) and at \(\rho = 0.5\). (b) Check the second value by simulation: start from random positions on a ring of 100 cells, run 500 steps, and find the shift \(s\) for which the occupancy after the next step equals the previous occupancy shifted by \(s\) cells.









TipSolution






The density of maximum flow is \(1/(v_{\max}+1) = 0.25\). At \(\rho = 0.1\) the flow is \(3\rho\), so \(c = 3\). At \(\rho = 0.5\) it is \(1 - \rho\), so \(c = -1\).
The code below returns the shift \(-1\) in every step, which means that the pattern moves one cell to the left.


import numpy as np
from amlab.cellular_automata.traffic_models import nasch_step, ring_initial

L, vmax = 100, 3
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x, v = ring_initial(L, 50, "random", vmax, rng)
for _ in range(500):
    x, v = nasch_step(x, v, L, vmax, 0.0, None, rng)
before = np.zeros(L, dtype=int); before[x] = 1
x, v = nasch_step(x, v, L, vmax, 0.0, None, rng)
after = np.zeros(L, dtype=int); after[x] = 1
print([s for s in range(-L // 2, L // 2) if np.array_equal(np.roll(before, s), after)])

[-1]

title: From Cars to a Continuum
section: Two ways to model crowds and traffic
text:
Two ways to model crowds and traffic
The traffic automaton and the social force model of Module 2 are both models of agents that obstruct each other, and both produce jams. They differ in nearly every modelling choice. Table 1 lists the choices as defined on the pages of the course and in the paper.



Table 1: Modelling choices of the traffic automaton and of the social force model.











Nagel-Schreckenberg automaton
Social force model with contact forces




Space
one-dimensional lattice of cells
continuous plane


Time
discrete steps, synchronous update
continuous time, integrated with a small time step


State of an agent
cell and integer speed
position and velocity vectors, disc radius and mass


Interaction
the gap to the car ahead
repulsion and, in contact, a body force and friction


Randomness
slowdown with probability \(p\)
random initial placement of the pedestrians


Where jams come from
random slowdowns, also on a homogeneous ring
the door as a bottleneck and the arches that form there


Main observable
flow against density
flow through the door and evacuation time






The rows on the social force model follow the page Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door. The two models answer different questions. The automaton is built for the density-flow relation of a lane of identical cars, while the social force model is built for geometry: walls, doors and the shape of the room. A one-dimensional automaton has no way to represent an arch across a door, and a social force model of a ring road would be a costly way to obtain the fundamental diagram that the automaton gives cheaply.






NoteExercise



For each question, say whether you would use the traffic automaton, the social force model, or a continuum equation such as Equation 1, and give one reason. (i) How many cars per hour can one lane of a freeway carry? (ii) How long does it take to evacuate a lecture hall through two doors? (iii) How fast does the tail of a jam move upstream over several kilometres of road?








TipSolution






The automaton. The fundamental diagram is its main output and it needs only cars on a lane. (ii) The social force model. The question is set by the geometry of the doors and by contact between bodies, which a lane model does not have. (iii) The continuum equation. Over several kilometres the individual cars do not matter and the kinematic speed of Equation 2 is the relevant quantity, with \(Q\) taken from measurements or from the automaton.

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
On the page 1D Cellular Automata you wrote apply_rule() and simulate_ca(). Here you test them against an exact result and use them to draw space-time diagrams.
The chunks on this page use the reference apply_rule(). Replace it by your own version to test your code.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from amlab.cellular_automata.cellular import apply_rule

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
Validation
Rule 90 has an exact solution: from a single seed, row \(t\) is Pascal’s triangle modulo 2 (see Special Rules). Use it as a test. The chunk below runs the check with the reference apply_rule.

from math import comb


def simulate_ca(initial_state, rule_number, steps):
    rule_bin = np.array([int(bit) for bit in f"{rule_number:08b}"])
    grid = np.zeros((steps, len(initial_state)), dtype=int)
    grid[0] = initial_state
    for t in range(1, steps):
        grid[t] = apply_rule(grid[t - 1], rule_bin)
    return grid


width, steps = 81, 40
seed_row = np.zeros(width, dtype=int)
seed_row[width // 2] = 1
g = simulate_ca(seed_row, 90, steps)
ok = all(g[t, width // 2 - t + 2 * k] == comb(t, k) % 2 for t in range(steps) for k in range(t + 1))
print("Rule 90 matches Pascal's triangle mod 2:", ok)

Rule 90 matches Pascal's triangle mod 2: True


Keep the lattice wider than \(2 \times\) steps so the pattern never reaches the edges during the test.

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
Experiment: the space-time diagram
iterations = 80
grid_size = 121

initial_state = np.zeros(grid_size, dtype=int)
initial_state[grid_size // 2] = 1

grid = simulate_ca(initial_state, rule_number=30, steps=iterations)

plt.imshow(grid, cmap="binary", interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
plt.xlabel("Cell index")
plt.ylabel("Time")
plt.show()

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
Interpretation

Compare the diagram with your prediction on 1D Cellular Automata: the growth speed and the broken symmetry.
Do you see long diagonal structures, nested triangles, or irregular texture? Rule 30 shows all three: a regular left edge, triangles of many sizes and an irregular right part.







NoteExercise



Add a second occupied cell at grid_size // 2 - 5 in the first row. Count, at every time step, the number of cells in which the two runs differ. Does the effect of the change stay local or spread through the whole diagram?








TipSolution





The difference spreads. It starts at 1 cell and grows to about 50 cells after 60 steps, roughly one new cell per step. Rule 30 is sensitive to small changes in the initial row.

changed = np.zeros(121, dtype=int)
changed[60] = 1
changed[55] = 1
single = np.zeros(121, dtype=int)
single[60] = 1

diff = (simulate_ca(single, 30, 60) != simulate_ca(changed, 30, 60)).sum(axis=1)
print("Differing cells at t = 0, 10, 30, 59:", diff[[0, 10, 30, 59]])

Differing cells at t = 0, 10, 30, 59: [ 1 11 30 51]

title: Space-Time Diagrams
text:
Limitations

The loop in apply_rule() is slow for large lattices. The vectorized version in amlab/cellular_automata/elementary.py computes all neighbourhood indices at once.
Fixed-zero edges are a modelling choice. Once the pattern reaches them, the result depends on the edges.







TipOptional extension: interactive initial row



The script amlab/cellular_automata/cellular.py lets you click on the first row, toggle cells, and recompute the automaton immediately. Run it locally, not in the notes:
from amlab.cellular_automata.cellular import main

main(rule_number=30, grid_size=101, iterations=50)

title: Fixed Points and Stability
text: A one-dimensional model \(\dot x = f(x)\) is fully described by the graph of \(f\). This page applies that idea to the budworm model \(f(x) = rx(1 - x/k) - x^2/(1+x^2)\) from The Spruce Budworm Model (Strogatz 2024, chap. 2 and Section 3.7).

title: Fixed Points and Stability
text:
Fixed points
A fixed point (equilibrium) \(x^*\) satisfies \(f(x^*) = 0\). For the budworm, \(x^* = 0\) is always a fixed point. The others satisfy
\[
r\left(1 - \frac{x}{k}\right) = \frac{x}{1 + x^2}.
\tag{1}\]
The left side is the per capita growth rate, a straight line with intercepts \(r\) and \(k\). The right side is the per capita predation rate. Fixed points are the intersections of the two curves, and there can be one, two or three of them (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.7; Ludwig et al. 1978, fig. 1).








Figure 1: Graphical solution of the fixed point equation for k = 10. Small r gives one intersection (refuge), intermediate r gives three, large r gives one (outbreak).

title: Fixed Points and Stability
text:
Linear stability
Write \(x = x^* + \eta\) with \(\eta\) small. A Taylor expansion gives \(\dot\eta \approx f'(x^*)\,\eta\), so the perturbation grows or decays like \(e^{f'(x^*)t}\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 2.4).

\(f'(x^*) < 0\): the fixed point is stable.
\(f'(x^*) > 0\): the fixed point is unstable.
\(f'(x^*) = 0\): linearization is inconclusive; this happens at a bifurcation.

The time scale of the decay or growth is \(1/|f'(x^*)|\). For the budworm,
\[
f'(x) = r\left(1 - \frac{2x}{k}\right) - \frac{2x}{(1 + x^2)^2}.
\]
At \(x^* = 0\), \(f'(0) = r > 0\), so the zero state is always unstable. A small budworm population always grows, because predation vanishes faster than growth as \(x \to 0\) (Ludwig et al. 1978, 317).

title: Fixed Points and Stability
text:
The phase line
You can read stability directly from the sign of \(f\): the flow moves right where \(f > 0\) and left where \(f < 0\). Figure 2 shows the rate for \(r = 0.5\) and \(k = 10\).








Figure 2: Rate dx/dt against x for r = 0.5, k = 10. Blue: stable fixed points. Red: unstable fixed point. The green dashed line marks x = 1.





The positive fixed points for these values can be computed exactly, since Equation 1 is a cubic in \(x\).

from amlab.odes_1d.budworm_analysis import budworm_equilibria, budworm_slope

x_star = budworm_equilibria(r=0.5, k=10.0)
for x in x_star:
    s = budworm_slope(x, 0.5, 10.0)
    print(f"x* = {x:.3f}, f'(x*) = {s:+.3f}, {'stable' if s < 0 else 'unstable'}")

x* = 0.683, f'(x*) = -0.203, stable
x* = 2.000, f'(x*) = +0.140, unstable
x* = 7.317, f'(x*) = -0.237, stable








NoteExercise



Show that the middle fixed point for \(r = 0.5\), \(k = 10\) is exactly \(x^* = 2\).








TipSolution





Substitute \(x = 2\) in Equation 1: the left side is \(0.5(1 - 0.2) = 0.4\) and the right side is \(2/5 = 0.4\). The other roots of the cubic \(-(r/k)x^3 + rx^2 - (1 + r/k)x + r = 0\) are \(4 \pm \sqrt{11} \approx 0.683\) and \(7.317\).

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
The Lorenz attractor is deterministic, but long-term prediction is still limited because nearby trajectories diverge over time (Lorenz 1963; Strogatz 2024). This is sensitivity to initial conditions. On the attractor the separation grows on average like \(e^{\lambda t}\), with a largest Lyapunov exponent \(\lambda \approx 0.9\) for the standard parameters (Strogatz 2024, sec. 9.3).
Figure 1: Two nearby Lorenz trajectories and their separation over time.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
Explore sensitive dependence
The figure runs the same computation as the code on this page: forward Euler with \(dt = 0.01\) for 3000 steps, run A from \((0, 1, 1.05)\) and run B from the same point with \(z\) increased by \(\delta\).


With \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), when are the two runs 1 apart? Before that time, can you tell them apart in the left panel?
Make \(\delta\) a thousand times smaller, \(10^{-8}\). How much later do the runs separate? What does a thousandfold better measurement buy you?
Compare the red curve with the dashed slope \(\lambda \approx 0.9\). Why does the separation stop growing at around 10 to 30?
Set \(r = 10\). What happens to the separation now, and where do both runs end? Check against \(C^\pm = \bigl(\pm\sqrt{b(r-1)}, \pm\sqrt{b(r-1)}, r - 1\bigr)\).



Build this in Python. In the lab you write lorenz() and simulate_lorenz() with forward Euler, run two nearby initial conditions and plot their separation, which is exactly this figure: Practice: Lorenz System. The code on the rest of this page is your starting point.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
Compare two nearby initial conditions
To test sensitivity, keep the parameters fixed and change only the initial state by a tiny amount.
initial_state_a = (0.0, 1.0, 1.05)
initial_state_b = (0.0, 1.0, 1.05001)

trajectory_a = simulate_lorenz(initial_state=initial_state_a, dt=0.01, num_steps=3000)
trajectory_b = simulate_lorenz(initial_state=initial_state_b, dt=0.01, num_steps=3000)
At first, the two runs are nearly indistinguishable. Later, they separate enough that their detailed future motion no longer matches.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
Measure the separation
The most direct diagnostic is the Euclidean distance between the two trajectories at each time step:
\[
d_n = \left\|\mathbf{x}_n^{(1)} - \mathbf{x}_n^{(2)}\right\|.
\]
separation = np.linalg.norm(trajectory_a - trajectory_b, axis=1)
times = 0.01 * np.arange(len(separation))

plt.semilogy(times, separation)
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Separation")
plt.show()
If the separation grows rapidly from a tiny initial perturbation, then the predictability horizon is short even though the equations themselves are deterministic.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
What chaos means here
In this context, chaos does not mean that the model is random.

The update rule is fixed.
The same initial condition gives the same trajectory.
Small errors in the initial state can still lead to very different long-run outcomes.

This is why deterministic chaos matters in modeling. Exact equations do not guarantee exact long-term forecasts.

title: Sensitivity and Chaos
text:
Parameter variation
The parameter r strongly influences the geometry of the trajectories. A useful first comparison is to simulate one run with a smaller value such as r=10 and another with the standard value r=28.
trajectory_low_r = simulate_lorenz(dt=0.01, num_steps=3000, r=10)
trajectory_standard = simulate_lorenz(dt=0.01, num_steps=3000, r=28)
That comparison helps separate two ideas:

sensitivity to initial conditions at fixed parameters,
and qualitative changes driven by the parameter regime.

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
NoteReading




Recommended: Strogatz (2024), Chapter 1.
Course material: Syllabus and How the Course Works.
A mathematical model is a deliberate simplification of a real system. You keep a few variables and a few rules that you believe control the behaviour you care about, and you discard the rest. The model then lets you reason about the system with the tools of mathematics and computation.

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
Variables, parameters and rules
Most models in this course have three parts.

State variables describe the system at a given time: a population \(x(t)\), the fractions \(S, I, R\) of an epidemic, two chemical concentrations.
Parameters are numbers that stay fixed during one experiment: a growth rate, a carrying capacity, a transmission rate.
Rules say how the state changes. In Part I of the course the rules are ordinary differential equations \(\dot{\mathbf x} = \mathbf f(\mathbf x; \theta)\) (Strogatz 2024).

The same structure reappears later with random rules (Module 3), spatial rules (Module 4), networks (Module 5) and discrete rules (Module 6).

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
All models are wrong
George Box wrote that “since all models are wrong the scientist cannot obtain a ‘correct’ one by excessive elaboration” (Box 1976, 792). A few years later he titled a section “All models are wrong but some are useful” (Box 1979, 202). The point is practical. You cannot make a model true by adding detail, so you should ask whether it is useful for a stated purpose.
Two consequences follow.

A model that fits the data well can still be useless, for example when it has so many parameters that it would fit any data.
A model that gets the numbers wrong can still be useful, for example when it correctly predicts that a system has two stable states.

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
Parsimony
Box also argued for parsimonious models: use the fewest parameters that still capture the effect you study (Box 1976). Each extra parameter must be estimated, and each one makes it harder to see which mechanism produces the behaviour.
The spruce budworm model is a good example. Ludwig, Jones and Holling reduced a detailed forest simulation to three differential equations, and a single equation for the fast variable already explains the outbreak pattern (Ludwig et al. 1978). They state that their conclusions depend on the qualitative shape of the terms, not on their exact form (Ludwig et al. 1978, 317).

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
section: When is a model good enough?
text:
When is a model good enough?
There is no general rule, but you can ask the same questions every time.

Purpose: what question should the model answer? Explanation, prediction and control need different levels of detail.
Assumptions: can you list them? Which one is the weakest?
Sensitivity: does the conclusion survive small changes in the parameters and in the form of the terms?
Data: does the model reproduce the observations it was not fitted to?
Limits: does it give the right answer in simple limiting cases you already understand?







NoteExercise



Take the logistic model \(\dot N = rN(1 - N/K)\) for a population. List three assumptions it makes about the real population. For each one, name a situation where it fails.








TipSolution





Possible answers:

The population is large enough to treat \(N\) as a continuous variable. It fails for small or endangered populations, where random births and deaths matter.
The per capita growth rate decreases linearly with \(N\). It fails when individuals need a minimum density to reproduce (Allee effect).
\(r\) and \(K\) are constant. They fail when food supply or climate changes on the same time scale as the population.

title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
text:
Next
The next page turns these questions into a workflow you will use in every session.

title: Predicting the Peak
text: Given the data up to today, can you predict when the epidemic curve will peak? Castro, Ares, Cuesta and Manrubia argue that during the expansion phase you cannot: the time of the turning point cannot be determined with certainty before it is reached, there is only a short horizon for reliable prediction, and this persists even in error-free synthetic data (Castro et al. 2020). They reach this conclusion with an SIR model extended by confinement and a Bayesian fit to COVID-19 data from Spain. Here you reproduce the main effect with the plain SIR model.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Prediction
Before you run the experiment, write down how many days of data you think you need to predict the peak day within \(\pm 3\) days, for an epidemic that peaks around day 55.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Implementation
For each cut-off day \(T\):

take the first \(T\) days of the data;
fit \(\beta\), \(\gamma\), \(I(0)\) and \(N\) with fit_sir_incidence(..., fit_population=True);
simulate the fitted model forward and record the day of maximum incidence.

To see the spread caused by noise, repeat this for ten synthetic epidemics with the same true parameters and different noise seeds.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from amlab.epidemics import fit_sir_incidence, sir_incidence, synthetic_sir_cases

N = 1e6
horizon = np.arange(1, 301)
true_peak = sir_incidence(horizon, 0.3, 0.1, 1e-5, N).argmax() + 1
cutoffs = [30, 40, 50, 60, 70]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for T in cutoffs:
    peaks = []
    for seed in range(10):
        d, c = synthetic_sir_cases(seed=seed)
        f = fit_sir_incidence(d[:T], c[:T], population=N, fit_population=True)
        peaks.append(sir_incidence(horizon, f["beta"], f["gamma"], f["i0"], f["population"]).argmax() + 1)
    ax.plot([T] * len(peaks), peaks, "o", color="tab:blue", alpha=0.6)
    print(f"T = {T}: predicted peaks from {min(peaks)} to {max(peaks)}")
ax.axhline(true_peak, color="k", ls="--", label=f"true peak (day {true_peak})")
ax.plot(cutoffs, cutoffs, ":", color="gray", label="today")
ax.set_xlabel("Days of data used (T)")
ax.set_ylabel("Predicted peak day")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

T = 30: predicted peaks from 33 to 69
T = 40: predicted peaks from 43 to 74
T = 50: predicted peaks from 51 to 65
T = 60: predicted peaks from 54 to 58
T = 70: predicted peaks from 55 to 57








Figure 1: Predicted peak day against the number of days of data used in the fit, for ten synthetic SIR epidemics (R0 = 3) with different noise. The dashed line is the true peak of the expected incidence.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Validation
After the peak (\(T = 60\) and \(T = 70\)) the predictions cluster around the true peak. This confirms that the fitting code works when the data contain enough information.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Interpretation
Before the peak, the predictions spread over several weeks, even though the model is exactly right and only the reporting noise differs. The reason is the identifiability problem from Fitting an Epidemic to Data: the rising part of the curve fixes \(\beta - \gamma\) but not \(R_0\) or \(N\), and the peak time depends on those. Castro et al. show that this sensitivity is a property of exponential growth, and conclude that forecasts should be given as probabilities of different outcomes, not as a single date (Castro et al. 2020).

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Limitations

The model used for the fit is the model that generated the data. With real data the model is also wrong, which adds uncertainty.
Least squares with ten noise realizations is a rough substitute for a proper uncertainty analysis such as the Bayesian fit of Castro et al. (2020).







TipOptional extension



If you have real incidence data, save them as data/epidemic/cases.csv (schema in data/epidemic/README.md) and repeat the experiment with a moving cut-off. Compare the predicted peaks with the observed one.

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



Two groups fit an SIR model to the first 30 days of an outbreak. Group A reports “\(R_0 = 2.9\), peak on day 57”. Group B reports “\(R_0\) between 2 and 200, peak between day 40 and day 70”. Which report is more useful, and why?








TipSolution





Group B’s report is more useful. With only early data, the fit determines the growth rate but not \(R_0\) or the peak time. A single number hides this uncertainty and invites decisions based on false precision. A range, or better a probability distribution, states honestly what the data support (Castro et al. 2020).

title: Predicting the Peak
text:
Next
The next topic is two-dimensional systems, starting with Linear Systems in the Plane.

title: Excitability
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2024), Section 7.5 on relaxation oscillators.
Recommended: Ellner and Guckenheimer (2006), chapter on neural and excitable dynamics.
A system is excitable if it has a stable rest state, small perturbations decay back to rest, and perturbations above a threshold produce a large excursion before the system returns to rest.
