Nerve cells behave this way: a small current injection changes the membrane potential slightly, while a larger one triggers an action potential (Hodgkin and Huxley 1952; Strogatz 2024).

title: Excitability
text:
Background: the Hodgkin-Huxley model
Hodgkin and Huxley described the membrane potential \(V\) of the squid giant axon with four ODEs: one for \(V\) and three for gating variables \(m\), \(h\), \(n\) that control the sodium and potassium conductances (Hodgkin and Huxley 1952):
\[
C\dot V = I - \bar g_{\text{Na}} m^3 h (V - V_{\text{Na}}) - \bar g_{\text{K}} n^4 (V - V_{\text{K}}) - g_L (V - V_L),
\]
with each gating variable relaxing to a voltage-dependent steady state. The model reproduced the shape and speed of the action potential measured in experiments. Hodgkin and Huxley shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with John Eccles, for discoveries on the ionic mechanisms of excitation and inhibition in nerve cell membranes.
Four variables are hard to analyse geometrically. The two-variable models of this page keep the essential structure and can be studied in the phase plane (FitzHugh 1961; Morris and Lecar 1981).

title: Excitability
text:
The ingredients

A fast variable (membrane potential) with an S-shaped, or cubic, nullcline. The middle branch has positive feedback: a small depolarization opens channels that depolarize further.
A slow recovery variable that eventually pulls the fast variable back.
A separation of time scales: the fast variable changes much faster than the slow one, so trajectories jump quickly between the outer branches of the cubic nullcline and drift slowly along them (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.5).

The threshold is not a sharp number in general. In FitzHugh’s analysis it is a narrow band in the phase plane near the middle branch of the cubic nullcline (“quasi-threshold”) (FitzHugh 1961).








Figure 1: FitzHugh-Nagumo model at rest (I_app = 0, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 0.5, epsilon = 0.01). Initial kicks v(0) of 0.05 and 0.11 decay; kicks of 0.2 and 0.3 produce a full spike before returning to rest.





The response is all or nothing: the spikes started from \(v(0) = 0.2\) and \(0.3\) have almost the same height, far above the size of the kick.






NoteExercise



In Figure 1 the rest state is \((v, w) = (0, 0)\). Use the Jacobian to show that it is stable.








TipSolution





With \(f(v) = v(1-v)(v - \alpha)\), \(f'(0) = -\alpha\). The Jacobian at the origin is \(\begin{pmatrix} -\alpha/\epsilon & -1/\epsilon \\ 1 & -\gamma \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -10 & -100 \\ 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}\), with \(\tau = -10.5 < 0\) and \(\Delta = 5 + 100 > 0\). The origin is stable. Excitability is a global property: it cannot be seen in the linearization.

title: Budworm and Forest: Fast and Slow
text: With the forest fixed, an outbreak never ends. Ludwig, Jones and Holling let the forest change on its own, slower time scale and obtained the outbreak and collapse cycle from three differential equations (Ludwig et al. 1978). This page summarizes their model. All equations and parameter values come from that paper.

title: Budworm and Forest: Fast and Slow
text:
Time scales
Ludwig et al. estimate that the budworm density can change several hundredfold in a few years, so its characteristic time is of the order of months. Trees need 7 to 10 years to replace their foliage and live 100 to 150 years (Ludwig et al. 1978, 316). The budworm is the fast variable; the forest is slow.

title: Budworm and Forest: Fast and Slow
section: From a parameter to a variable: a two-variable slow-fast model
text:
From a parameter to a variable: a two-variable slow-fast model
The budworm equation of The Spruce Budworm Model contains the parameter \(k\), which measures the foliage available to the insect. There the forest is an external input that the modeller turns up and down. Ecologically this is not possible: forest condition is not independent of the budworm population, because feeding removes foliage and the forest regrows. The one-dimensional model is better read as the fast subsystem of a larger system in which \(k\) becomes a slowly changing variable \(S\).
Write \(S(t)\) for the available foliage in the units of \(k\). The budworm density \(x\) and the forest \(S\) then obey
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dx}{d\tau} &= r x\left(1 - \frac{x}{S}\right) - \frac{x^2}{1 + x^2},\\
\frac{dS}{d\tau} &= \varepsilon\,\bigl[\,G(S) - H(x, S)\,\bigr], \qquad 0 < \varepsilon \ll 1 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
The small number \(\varepsilon\) says that the forest changes much more slowly than the insect. \(G(S)\) is forest regrowth without budworms and \(H(x, S)\) is the foliage lost to feeding. The page does not fix the form of \(H\), because the assumptions about how insects damage trees are ecological choices. Four are reasonable:








Defoliation \(H(x, S)\)
Assumption
Comment




\(a\,x\)
Each larva eats at a constant rate.
Simplest. Needs bounded forest growth so that \(S\) stays positive.


\(a\,x\,S\)
Feeding is proportional to the foliage present.
Defoliation vanishes as \(S \to 0\) and the forest feeds back strongly on the insect.


\(a\,S\,\dfrac{x}{1 + x}\)
Feeding saturates at high larval density.
Crowding or limited feeding time, as in many consumer-resource models.


\(a\,S\,\dfrac{x^2}{1 + x^2}\)
Holling type III, like the predation term.
Little defoliation at low density (refuge), strong during an outbreak.




The geometry: hysteresis becomes a cycle
For fixed \(S\), the equilibria of the fast equation form the S-shaped curve of the hysteresis diagram: a lower branch (refuge), an upper branch (outbreak) and an unstable middle branch. This curve is called the critical manifold. Because \(\varepsilon\) is small, \(x\) relaxes quickly to a stable branch and then follows it while \(S\) drifts slowly. When \(S\) reaches a fold, the branch the system sits on disappears and \(x\) jumps to the other branch. The hysteresis loop of the one-dimensional model has become a relaxation oscillation in time, a mechanism you will meet again in Relaxation Oscillations.
Figure 1 shows this for the simplest choice, \(G(S) = S\,(1 - S/S_{\max})\) and \(H = a\,x\). The parameter values are chosen for the demonstration and are not fitted to data: \(r = 0.55\), \(\varepsilon = 0.02\), \(S_{\max} = 30\), \(a = 2\).








Figure 1: Slow-fast budworm and forest model with H = a x. Left: the critical manifold (stable branches blue, unstable red) and the trajectory, which follows the lower branch while the forest grows, jumps up at the fold, follows the upper branch while the forest is defoliated, and jumps down. Right: the same trajectory in time. Units are dimensionless.





Read the cycle as an endogenous outbreak, one that needs no external forcing:

The forest recovers slowly and \(S\) increases while the budworm stays at the refuge level.
\(S\) crosses the fold at which the refuge disappears.
The budworm jumps to the outbreak level.
Defoliation \(H\) now exceeds regrowth and \(S\) falls.
\(S\) drops below the fold at which the outbreak branch disappears and the population collapses.
The forest recovers and the cycle repeats.

The oscillation is asymmetric, with a fast rise and a slow recovery, which is the geometry of a relaxation oscillation. The geometry of the original bifurcation diagram is unchanged; what changes is its interpretation, because hysteresis is now part of the dynamics instead of a property of a parameter sweep.






NoteThe form of \(H\) matters for the outcome, not for the geometry



All four defoliation forms share the same critical manifold, but a cycle needs two things: the forest must be able to grow past the fold where the refuge disappears, and feeding during an outbreak must push \(S\) below the fold where the outbreak disappears. If feeding is too weak the system settles to a steady state, and if it is too strong the forest never grows enough to reach the first fold. With \(r = 0.55\), \(\varepsilon = 0.02\) and \(G = S(1 - S/30)\), we integrated the model from \(x = 0.5\), \(S = 3\) and found:

The three-variable model of Ludwig et al. below is a more detailed version of this idea, with a separate variable for the condition of the trees.

title: Budworm and Forest: Fast and Slow
text:
The three-variable model
The state is the budworm density \(B\) (larvae per acre), the total branch surface area \(S\) (branches per acre) and an “energy reserve” \(E\) that measures the condition of the trees, with maximum \(K_E = 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dB}{dt} &= r_B B\left(1 - \frac{B}{K' S}\right) - \beta\,\frac{B^2}{(\alpha' S)^2 + B^2},\\
\frac{dS}{dt} &= r_S S\left(1 - \frac{S}{K_S}\,\frac{K_E}{E}\right),\\
\frac{dE}{dt} &= r_E E\left(1 - \frac{E}{K_E}\right) - P\,\frac{B}{S}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
This is eqns (3), (10) and (11) of Ludwig et al. (1978) with the carrying capacity \(K_B = K'S\) and the half-saturation density \(\alpha = \alpha' S\) both proportional to branch area (eqns 13 and 14). The budworm equation is the model of The Spruce Budworm Model; its dimensionless groups become
\[
R = \frac{\alpha' r_B}{\beta}\,S, \qquad Q = \frac{K'}{\alpha'} ,
\]
so \(Q\) is fixed and \(R\) grows with the forest (Ludwig et al. 1978, eqn 15).

title: Budworm and Forest: Fast and Slow
text:
The outbreak cycle
Ludwig et al. describe the cycle qualitatively (Ludwig et al. 1978, 322–23):

A young forest has small \(S\), so \(R\) is small and the budworm stays at the refuge level, controlled by predators.
As the forest grows, \(R\) increases until it crosses the upper fold of the \((Q, R)\) diagram. The refuge disappears and the budworm jumps to the outbreak level.
During the outbreak, consumption \(PB/S\) exceeds the recovery of \(E\) when \(M = PK'/(r_E K_E) > 1/4\), so \(E\) and then \(S\) decline.
The smaller forest lowers \(R\) below the lower fold and the outbreak collapses.

Figure 2 integrates Equation 2 with the Level III parameter values of the paper (\(r_B = 1.52\), \(K' = 335\), \(\beta = 43\,200\), \(\alpha' = 1.11\), \(r_S = 0.095\), \(K_S = 25\,440\), \(r_E = 0.92\), \(P = 0.00195\)), which give \(Q \approx 302\) and \(M \approx 0.71\) (Ludwig et al. 1978, Table 1 and p. 328).








Figure 2: One outbreak in the Ludwig, Jones and Holling model with Level III parameters, from a young forest (S = 0.1 K_S). B/S is larvae per branch; S is relative branch area. The integration stops when E falls to 0.05, where the model stops being valid.





The budworm stays low for about three decades while the forest grows, then rises by more than two orders of magnitude within a few years, and the energy reserve collapses. Ludwig et al. state that with realistic parameter values the outbreak leads to a collapse of the forest, and show one outbreak cycle in their Fig. 5 (Ludwig et al. 1978, 324 and 328). The exact timing in Figure 2 depends on the initial state chosen here.

title: Budworm and Forest: Fast and Slow
text:
Limitations

With these parameters \(E\) becomes negative after the outbreak. Ludwig et al. note that the model then describes one cohort of trees and must be restarted with a young forest, or modified for small \(E\) (their eqns 20 to 22) (Ludwig et al. 1978, 324).
The model is continuous in time, while the insect has one generation per year.
Birds, parasites and weather are summarized in two predation parameters.

title: Budworm and Forest: Fast and Slow
text:
Management
Ludwig et al. point out that if budworm densities are partially controlled, for example by spraying, the forest may stay at an equilibrium with high budworm, foliage and branch area. They link this to the “perpetual outbreak” observed in New Brunswick after insecticide spraying (Ludwig et al. 1978, 322–23). Keeping the budworm below the outbreak level also keeps the forest in the state where the next outbreak is possible.

title: Budworm and Forest: Fast and Slow
text:
Evidence from real outbreaks
Slow-fast models predict long quiet phases punctuated by abrupt outbreaks and collapses. Forest insects are one of the few cases where long records exist to compare with this prediction.
Larch budmoth in the Alps. The larch budmoth (Zeiraphera diniana) periodically defoliates larch, which leaves a growth reduction in the tree rings. From 47 513 wood-density measurements, Esper et al. reconstructed outbreaks over 1173 years and found remarkably regular peaks, on average every 9.3 years (Esper et al. 2007). Büntgen et al. later compiled more than 5000 tree-ring series from the Alps and the Tatra Mountains and found cyclic outbreaks recurring about every 8 to 9 years at the site level between AD 1700 and 2000 (Büntgen et al. 2009). Both studies also report a change in recent decades. The regular peaks stopped after 1981 in the first reconstruction, and the second finds that synchronized Alpine-wide defoliation has ceased even though local cycles persisted. Esper et al. relate this to exceptional regional warmth, so the regularity of the cycle is not guaranteed to continue.
Spruce budworm. Ludwig et al. calibrate their model to an outbreak period of about 40 years (Ludwig et al. 1978). Unlike the larch budmoth, outbreaks of the spruce budworm are not strictly periodic, with variable amplitude and spacing. Noise, spatial heterogeneity and climate are natural explanations for this variability, and a slow-fast mechanism does not require exact periodicity.
Other forest Lepidoptera. Population cycles are common in forest moths, including the forest tent caterpillar and the gypsy moth, and the review of Myers and Cory covers what is known about their mechanisms (Myers and Cory 2013).






WarningThe mechanism is still debated



The agreement between the cycle shape and the data does not prove that a slow-fast host-resource mechanism causes the cycles. Myers and Cory report that delayed density-dependent parasitism and reduced fecundity at peak density are common influences on forest Lepidoptera, that induced plant defences give inconsistent results, and that the hypothesis that sunspots explain cycles is rejected (Myers and Cory 2013). The model on this page is one candidate mechanism, and it is useful because it is simple enough to analyse completely.








NoteExercise



Using the Level III values, compute \(R\) for a mature forest (\(S = K_S\)). Is it above the value \(1/2\) needed for outbreaks when \(Q\) is large?








TipSolution





\(R = \alpha' r_B K_S / \beta = 1.11 \times 1.52 \times 25\,440 / 43\,200 \approx 0.99 > 1/2\). A mature forest is past the fold, so it cannot hold the budworm at the refuge level. The outbreak starts once \(S\) exceeds roughly half of \(K_S\).

ImportantCore activity



This page and the next two form the core activity of the first laboratory: implement the budworm model, integrate it, and wrap it in a Streamlit app.
You will implement the dimensionless budworm model from The Spruce Budworm Model (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.7):
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = rx\left(1 - \frac{x}{k}\right) - \frac{x^2}{1 + x^2}.
\tag{1}\]
The first term is logistic growth. The second term is predation by birds, with a saturating functional response.

There are three positive equilibria, \(x_a \approx 0.68\), \(x_b = 2\) and \(x_c \approx 7.32\), plus the unstable state \(x = 0\). The slope \(f'(x^*)\) is negative at \(x_a\) and \(x_c\) (stable) and positive at \(x_b\) (unstable). The validation at the end of this page checks these values.

def spruce_budworm(t: float, x: float, r: float = 0.5, k: float = 10) -> float:
    """Dimensionless spruce budworm model (Strogatz, Section 3.7)."""
    return r * x * (1 - x / k) - x**2 / (1 + x**2)

Figure 1 shows the expected output.










Figure 1: Rate plot of the budworm model for r = 0.5, k = 10. Stable equilibria in blue, unstable in red, current population as a green dashed line.











TipHint






Use np.linspace to create the grid of \(x\) values.
np.diff(np.sign(dxdt)) is nonzero exactly where the sign changes between two grid points.
An equilibrium \(x^*\) is a value where \(dx/dt = 0\). It is stable if small perturbations decay back to \(x^*\), and unstable if they grow.
A fixed point is stable if \(dx/dt\) decreases as you pass through it. So if dxdt[i+1] < 0 at a crossing, the curve goes from positive to negative and the equilibrium is stable.










TipSolution





This follows plot_spruce_budworm_rate in amlab/odes_1d/spruce_budworm.py.
def plot_spruce_budworm_rate(x_t: float, r: float = 0.5, k: float = 10):
    """Plot dx/dt against x, mark the equilibria and the current state x_t."""
    x = np.linspace(0, k, 1000)
    dxdt = spruce_budworm(0, x, r, k)

    mask_zerocross = np.diff(np.sign(dxdt)).astype(bool)
    is_stable = np.where(mask_zerocross & (dxdt[1:] < 0))[0]
    is_unstable = np.where(mask_zerocross & (dxdt[1:] > 0))[0]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
    ax.plot(x, dxdt)
    ax.axhline(0, color="red", lw=1)
    ax.scatter(x[is_stable], np.zeros(len(is_stable)), color="blue", zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(x[is_unstable], np.zeros(len(is_unstable)), color="red", zorder=3)
    ax.axvline(x_t, color="green", lw=1, linestyle="--")
    ax.set_xlabel("Budworm population")
    ax.set_ylabel("Rate of change")
    ax.set_title("Spruce budworm rate of change")
    ax.grid()
    return fig, ax

title: Linear Systems in the Plane
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2024), Chapter 5, Sections 6.1-6.2, Chapter 7 and Section 8.2.
Recommended: Epstein and Pojman (1998).
In one dimension a trajectory can only move monotonically towards a fixed point or away from it. In two dimensions it can also rotate, and sustained oscillations become possible. The first step is to understand linear systems, because near a fixed point every smooth system looks linear (Strogatz 2024, chap. 5).

title: Linear Systems in the Plane
text:
Eigenvalues from trace and determinant
Consider \(\dot{\mathbf x} = A\mathbf x\) with \(A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\). Let
\[
\tau = \operatorname{tr} A = a + d, \qquad \Delta = \det A = ad - bc .
\]
The eigenvalues are the roots of \(\lambda^2 - \tau\lambda + \Delta = 0\):
\[
\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{\tau \pm \sqrt{\tau^2 - 4\Delta}}{2}, \qquad \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \tau, \quad \lambda_1\lambda_2 = \Delta .
\tag{1}\]
Solutions are combinations of \(e^{\lambda_1 t}\) and \(e^{\lambda_2 t}\), so the signs and the type (real or complex) of the eigenvalues decide the phase portrait (Strogatz 2024, sec. 5.2).

title: Linear Systems in the Plane
text:
Classification

\(\Delta < 0\): real eigenvalues of opposite sign. Saddle point.
\(\Delta > 0\) and \(\tau^2 > 4\Delta\): real eigenvalues of the same sign. Node, stable if \(\tau < 0\) and unstable if \(\tau > 0\).
\(\Delta > 0\) and \(\tau^2 < 4\Delta\): complex eigenvalues \(\tau/2 \pm i\omega\). Spiral, stable if \(\tau < 0\) and unstable if \(\tau > 0\). The frequency is \(\omega = \sqrt{4\Delta - \tau^2}/2\).
\(\Delta > 0\) and \(\tau = 0\): purely imaginary eigenvalues. Center, with closed orbits.
\(\Delta = 0\): at least one zero eigenvalue. Non-isolated fixed points.









Figure 1: Classification of fixed points of linear systems in the (trace, determinant) plane. The parabola is tau^2 = 4 Delta.













Figure 2: Phase portraits of four linear systems: saddle, stable node, stable spiral and center.

title: Linear Systems in the Plane
text:
From linear to nonlinear
For a nonlinear system, the Jacobian at a fixed point plays the role of \(A\). The linear classification carries over to the nonlinear system for saddles, nodes and spirals. Centers and the borderline cases on \(\Delta = 0\) or \(\tau^2 = 4\Delta\) can change type under nonlinear terms (Strogatz 2024, sec. 6.3).

title: Linear Systems in the Plane
text:
Worked example: species in competition
Rabbits \(x\) and sheep \(y\) compete for the same grass (Strogatz 2024, sec. 6.4):
\[
\dot x = x(3 - x - b\,y), \qquad \dot y = y(2 - c\,x - y),
\]
with \(b = 2\) and \(c = 1\) in Strogatz’s example. Each species grows logistically on its own, and \(b\) and \(c\) measure how strongly each one is harmed by the other. The fixed points are \((0, 0)\), \((3, 0)\), \((0, 2)\) and, when it lies in the positive quadrant, a coexistence point where the two slanted nullclines cross. Classify each one with the Jacobian, then check your answer in the figure.


With \(b = 2\) and \(c = 1\), click a few starting points. Which species survives? What decides it?
Use the readout to classify the four fixed points. Which one is the saddle, and which curve through it separates the two outcomes?
Set \(b = c = 0.5\). A coexistence point appears in the positive quadrant. Where is it, and is it stable?
Set \(b = 0.8\) and \(c = 1\). Who wins now, from any start with both species present?

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
The FitzHugh-Nagumo model is a two-variable simplification of the Hodgkin-Huxley equations that keeps excitability and spiking (FitzHugh 1961; Nagumo et al. 1962). The version used in this course is
\[\begin{aligned}
\epsilon \dot v &= f(v) - w + I_{\text{app}}, \\
\dot w &= v - \gamma w,
\end{aligned} \tag{1}\]
with the cubic
\[
f(v) = v (1 - v)(v - \alpha), \qquad 0 < \alpha < 1 .
\]
\(v\) is the fast variable (membrane potential), \(w\) the slow recovery variable, \(I_{\text{app}}\) an applied current, and \(\epsilon \ll 1\) sets the separation of time scales.

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
Nullclines and geometry
\[
\dot v = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; w = f(v) + I_{\text{app}},
\qquad
\dot w = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; w = \frac{v}{\gamma}.
\]
The cubic \(v\)-nullcline and the straight \(w\)-nullcline organize the flow. Away from the cubic, \(\dot v\) is of order \(1/\epsilon\), so trajectories move almost horizontally. Near the outer branches of the cubic they drift slowly (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.5).

If the nullclines cross on an outer branch of the cubic, the fixed point is stable and the system is excitable (see Excitability).
If they cross on the middle branch, the fixed point is unstable and the system produces a relaxation oscillation.

Increasing \(I_{\text{app}}\) shifts the cubic upwards and moves the crossing from the left branch to the middle branch.








Figure 1: FitzHugh-Nagumo phase planes for alpha = 0.1, gamma = 0.5, epsilon = 0.01. Left: I_app = 0, excitable; one trajectory starting at v = 0.2 makes a single excursion. Right: I_app = 0.5, oscillatory; the trajectory settles on a limit cycle.

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
Explore excitability and spiking
The figure uses the same parameters as Figure 1: \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\gamma = 0.5\). Click in the phase plane to set \((v(0), w(0))\).


With \(I_{\text{app}} = 0\), click at \((v, w) = (0.05, 0)\) and then at \((0.2, 0)\). Only one of them fires a spike. Where is the threshold, roughly?

def fitzhugh_nagumo(t, vw, i_app=0.5, gamma=0.5, alpha=0.1, epsilon=0.01):
    v, w = vw
    fv = v * (1 - v) * (v - alpha)
    dvdt = (fv - w + i_app) / epsilon
    dwdt = v - gamma * w
    return np.array([dvdt, dwdt])

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
Time series
Follow the CDIMA pipeline again: solve trajectories, inspect the phase plane, compute nullclines, and then animate the motion. Figure 2 shows the fast variable \(v(t)\) in the oscillatory regime.








Figure 2: Time series v(t) of the FitzHugh-Nagumo system for I_app = 0.5, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 0.5, epsilon = 0.01, starting at (v, w) = (0.3, 0). Each spike is a fast jump followed by a slow recovery.





The time trace and the phase plane explain the same phenomenon from two viewpoints.

Some initial conditions return directly to equilibrium.
Others produce a large transient spike before recovery.
In the oscillatory regime, every initial condition ends on the same limit cycle.

title: FitzHugh-Nagumo Model
text:
Interpret the parameters

Smaller \(\epsilon\) makes the jumps faster relative to the slow drift.
\(I_{\text{app}}\) moves the system between rest, excitability and repetitive firing.
\(\gamma\) and \(\alpha\) change the slope of the \(w\)-nullcline and the position of the cubic, and therefore where the nullclines intersect.







NoteExercise



For \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\gamma = 0.5\), find the fixed point for \(I_{\text{app}} = 0\) and show that it is the only one.








TipSolution





Fixed points satisfy \(v/\gamma = f(v)\), that is \(2v = v(1-v)(v - 0.1)\). One root is \(v = 0\). The others solve \((1 - v)(v - 0.1) = 2\), i.e. \(v^2 - 1.1v + 2.1 = 0\), whose discriminant \(1.21 - 8.4\) is negative. So \((0, 0)\) is the only fixed point.









NoteExercise



Change the initial condition and \(I_{\text{app}}\) and watch how the time series changes. Use \(I_{\text{app}} = 0\) and \(I_{\text{app}} = 0.5\), and start from \((v, w) = (0.05, 0)\) and \((0.3, 0)\). Connect what you see to the nullclines in Figure 1.








TipSolution





For \(I_{\text{app}} = 0\) the fixed point \((0, 0)\) sits on the left branch of the cubic. The start at \(v = 0.05\) lies left of the middle branch and decays straight back to rest. The start at \(v = 0.3\) lies right of the middle branch, so \(v\) jumps to the right branch, drifts up, jumps back and returns to rest: one spike. For \(I_{\text{app}} = 0.5\) the crossing is on the middle branch, and both starts end on the same limit cycle with repeated spikes.

for i_app in [0.0, 0.5]:
    for v0 in [0.05, 0.3]:
        s = solve_ivp(fitzhugh_nagumo, (0, 4), [v0, 0.0], args=(i_app, gamma, alpha, eps), max_step=0.002)
        late = s.t > 2
        print(f"I_app = {i_app}, v0 = {v0}: max v = {s.y[0].max():.2f}, "
              f"range of v for t > 2 = {np.ptp(s.y[0][late]):.2f}")

title: Morris-Lecar Model
text: Morris and Lecar built a model of the voltage oscillations of the barnacle giant muscle fiber, with two non-inactivating conductances: an excitatory calcium current and a potassium recovery current (Morris and Lecar 1981). Unlike FitzHugh-Nagumo, every term has a physiological meaning.

title: Morris-Lecar Model
text:
The equations
With membrane potential \(V\) and the fraction \(n\) of open potassium channels,
\[
\begin{aligned}
C\dot V &= I_{\text{app}} - g_{\text{Ca}}\, m_\infty(V)(V - V_{\text{Ca}}) - g_{\text{K}}\, n\,(V - V_{\text{K}}) - g_L (V - V_L),\\
\dot n &= \phi\,\frac{n_\infty(V) - n}{\tau_n(V)},
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
\[
m_\infty(V) = \tfrac12\left[1 + \tanh\frac{V - V_1}{V_2}\right],\quad
n_\infty(V) = \tfrac12\left[1 + \tanh\frac{V - V_3}{V_4}\right],\quad
\tau_n(V) = \operatorname{sech}\frac{V - V_3}{2V_4}.
\]
The calcium activation \(m\) is assumed instantaneous, \(m = m_\infty(V)\), which reduces the model to two variables (Morris and Lecar 1981). This is the form given by Lecar in Scholarpedia, with the rate constant written as \(\phi\).
amlab/odes_2d/morris_lecar.py implements Equation 1 with default values \(C = 20\), \(g_{\text{Ca}} = 4\), \(g_{\text{K}} = 8\), \(g_L = 2\) (conductances in mS/cm², capacitance in µF/cm²), \(V_{\text{Ca}} = 120\), \(V_{\text{K}} = -84\), \(V_L = -60\), \(V_1 = -1.2\), \(V_2 = 18\), \(V_3 = 2\), \(V_4 = 30\) (all in mV) and \(\phi = 0.04\). The results below are for these values.








Figure 1: Morris-Lecar model with the amlab default parameters. Left: V(t) for three applied currents, starting at V = -60 mV, n = 0. Right: phase plane for I_app = 150 with the V-nullcline (blue), the n-nullcline (red) and the limit cycle.

title: Morris-Lecar Model
text:
What the simulations show
With these parameters:

for small currents (\(I_{\text{app}} = 60\)) the model rests at a stable fixed point;
for intermediate currents (\(I_{\text{app}} = 150\)) it fires periodically;
for large currents (\(I_{\text{app}} = 260\)) the membrane stays depolarized at a new stable fixed point.

The rest state loses stability through a pair of complex eigenvalues, a Hopf bifurcation. You can locate it with the numerical Jacobian of CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point:

from scipy.optimize import brentq, fsolve


def max_real_eigenvalue(i_app, h=1e-6):
    fp = fsolve(lambda y: morris_lecar(0, y, i_app), [-30.0, 0.1])
    jac = np.zeros((2, 2))
    for j in range(2):
        e = np.zeros(2)
        e[j] = h
        jac[:, j] = (morris_lecar(0, fp + e, i_app) - morris_lecar(0, fp - e, i_app)) / (2 * h)
    return np.linalg.eigvals(jac).real.max()


print(f"Lower Hopf point: I_app = {brentq(max_real_eigenvalue, 90, 110):.1f}")
print(f"Upper Hopf point: I_app = {brentq(max_real_eigenvalue, 220, 240):.1f}")

Lower Hopf point: I_app = 101.8
Upper Hopf point: I_app = 235.1


Simulations started far from rest already oscillate for \(I_{\text{app}} \approx 96\), below the lower Hopf point near 101.8. In that range a stable rest state and a stable limit cycle coexist, which indicates a subcritical Hopf bifurcation for this parameter set. Other parameter sets make the Morris-Lecar model start firing through a saddle-node bifurcation instead, at arbitrarily low frequency; this is why it is used to compare different classes of neural excitability (Ellner and Guckenheimer 2006).






NoteExercise



Derive the \(V\)-nullcline shown in Figure 1 from Equation 1.








TipSolution





Set \(\dot V = 0\) and solve for \(n\): \(n = \dfrac{I_{\text{app}} - g_{\text{Ca}} m_\infty(V)(V - V_{\text{Ca}}) - g_L(V - V_L)}{g_{\text{K}}(V - V_{\text{K}})}\). The \(n\)-nullcline is \(n = n_\infty(V)\).









TipOptional extension



Run python amlab/odes_2d/morris_lecar.py for the interactive version, then find the smallest current at which the model fires when you start from the rest state and when you start from \(V = 20\) mV.

title: Animations and Interactivity
text:
This page summarizes the core Matplotlib pattern we use to animate trajectories in the phase plane, and how to restart an animation when the user changes parameters or initial conditions (Hunter 2007; Virtanen et al. 2020).
If you get stuck, compare with the complete CDIMA animation in the repository.

title: Animations and Interactivity
text:
What you need

scipy.integrate.solve_ivp computes the trajectory; the state now has two components.
matplotlib.pyplot plots trajectories, nullclines, fixed points and time traces.
matplotlib.animation updates the plot frame by frame, in the phase plane and in time.
matplotlib.backend_bases gives you the event system, so a click in the phase plane can set a new initial condition and restart the simulation.

Why scripts instead of Streamlit here? The most direct interactive behaviour comes from Matplotlib animations and click events, and those are simpler to prototype in standalone scripts than in a Streamlit app.

title: Animations and Interactivity
text:
Minimal Animation Template
import matplotlib.animation as animation
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ...
# Your code to compute trajectories, nullclines, fixed point...
# Example: sol = solve_ivp(...)
# ...

# Open a new figure (white canvas)
fig = plt.figure()
ax = plt.gca()  # get current axis

# Initialize the line object for animation on the phase plane
(plot_trajectory,) = ax.plot([], [], lw=2)
# This trajectory would be x-y for the
# phase plane of the CDIMA and Van der Pol models, and v-w for the FitzHugh-Nagumo model


def animate(frame: int, xy: tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]):
    """Update function called once per frame."""
    # unpack the solution (x(t), y(t)) or (v(t), w(t))
    x, y = xy
    # update the line data to show the trajectory up to the current frame
    plot_trajectory.set_data(x[:frame], y[:frame])
    # return the updated artist (line) for blitting
    return (plot_trajectory,)


# The animation object that will run the animation
ani = animation.FuncAnimation(
    fig,
    animate,
    fargs=(sol.y,),
    frames=len(sol.t),
    interval=1,  # delay between frames in milliseconds
    blit=True,  # redraw only the updated artists for efficiency
)

What Happens in an Animation?
The animation function is called once per frame:

frame (or i) is the frame index (0, 1, 2, …).
xy is the data to plot (here, the solution sol.y returned by solve_ivp).
the function must update the artists (lines, points, text, etc.).
it must return an iterable with the updated artists when blit=True. This tells Matplotlib which parts of the plot to redraw for the next frame, improving performance.



The Animation Function in Detail
Template:
def animate_function(i: int, *args):
    # update plot elements
    return (artist1, artist2, ...)
In our case, the second input argument is the solution from solve_ivp. Updating a line is typically done with:
line.set_data(x, y)
This replaces the line coordinates by the new points \((x,y)\).


Creating the Animation (FuncAnimation)
import matplotlib.animation as animation

ani = animation.FuncAnimation(
    fig,
    function,
    fargs=(sol.y,),
    interval=1,
    blit=True,
)
Arguments:

fig: the Matplotlib figure to animate
function: the callback that updates plot elements on each frame
fargs: extra arguments passed to function (everything except the frame index)
interval: delay between frames (milliseconds)
blit: if True, redraws only the updated artists (faster). When using blit=True, your animation function must return the artists that were updated.

title: Animations and Interactivity
text:
Interactivity: Restarting the Animation
When the user clicks (new initial condition) or changes a parameter, a common pattern is:
ani.event_source.stop()          # stop the current animation
ani.frame_seq = ani.new_frame_seq()  # reset frame generator
ani._args = (xy, ...)            # replace animation inputs (like new fargs)
ani.event_source.start()         # start again
This is the mechanism used in the interactive scripts: recompute solve_ivp(...), update nullclines/fixed point, then restart the animation with the new data.

title: Animations and Interactivity
text:
Mouse Clicks
Matplotlib figures can react to user input via the event system. A common pattern is to capture clicks in a specific axis and use the click position as a new initial condition.






NoteExercise



Complete mouse_click so that a click in the phase plane ax1 restarts the animation from the clicked point. You will need to stop the current animation, clear it, update the initial condition, and start over (see the previous section).
from matplotlib.backend_bases import MouseEvent


def mouse_click(event: MouseEvent):
    # Check if the mouse click happens in the axis "ax1"
    if event.inaxes == ax1:
        # Get the position of the mouse click on the axis
        x0 = event.xdata
        y0 = event.ydata
    else:
        return

    # This part of the code should update the plot.
    # Use the animation functions we have learnt:
    # 1) stop the current animation
    # 2) clear/reset it
    # 3) recompute the solution (and nullclines/fixed point if needed)
    # 4) set new animation arguments
    # 5) start again


# Make the figure aware of user clicks.
# Whenever the user clicks, we run the function "mouse_click".
fig.canvas.mpl_connect("button_press_event", mouse_click)








TipSolution





This assumes fig, ax1, ani, the model cdima, the parameters a, b, t_span and t_eval are defined as in the template above. update_simulation in amlab/odes_2d/cdima.py is the full version, which also updates nullclines and the fixed point.
def mouse_click(event: MouseEvent):
    if event.inaxes != ax1:
        return
    x0, y0 = event.xdata, event.ydata

    sol = solve_ivp(cdima, t_span, [x0, y0], args=(a, b), t_eval=t_eval)

    ani.event_source.stop()
    ani.frame_seq = ani.new_frame_seq()
    ani._args = (sol.y,)
    ani.event_source.start()


fig.canvas.mpl_connect("button_press_event", mouse_click)

text:
Validation
Run the reference script and click in the phase plane. Each click should restart the animation from the clicked point, and the trajectory should follow the direction of the vector field.
python amlab/odes_2d/cdima.py

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
TipOptional extension



This page is optional. It applies the CDIMA pipeline to a second oscillator. It returns in Relaxation Oscillations.
The Van der Pol oscillator, introduced by van der Pol for electrical circuits with triodes (Pol 1926), is a prototypical nonlinear system that exhibits self-sustained oscillations. For a wide range of initial conditions, trajectories converge to a stable limit cycle.
In the form we will use in this course, the system is written as (Strogatz 2024, 7.5):
\[\begin{aligned}
\dot x &= \mu\,(y - f(x)) \\
\dot y &= -\frac{x}{\mu}
\end{aligned} \tag{1}\]
where \(\mu>0\) controls the strength of the nonlinearity (and the fast-slow character for large \(\mu\)), and
\[
f(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - x.
\tag{2}\]

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
Nullclines and Fixed Point
The nullclines are especially simple in this model:
\[
\dot x = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad y = \frac{x^3}{3} - x,
\qquad
\dot y = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x = 0.
\]
They intersect at the origin, so \((0,0)\) is the equilibrium point. For the parameter regime used on this page, the main long-run object of interest is not the equilibrium itself, but the attracting limit cycle around it.








Figure 1: Phase plane of the Van der Pol system with mu = 3. Trajectories are shown for different initial conditions (IC as x-y, marked black). Generated with scipy.integrate.solve_ivp() and matplotlib.

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
Implement the Vector Field






NoteExercise



Complete the Van der Pol vector field Equation 1.
def van_der_pol(t, xy, mu=1.0):
    x, y = xy
    dxdt = # TODO
    dydt = # TODO
    return np.array([dxdt, dydt])








TipSolution





def van_der_pol(t, xy, mu=1.0):
    x, y = xy
    fx = x**3 / 3 - x
    dxdt = mu * (y - fx)
    dydt = -x / mu
    return np.array([dxdt, dydt])



Follow the same pipeline as in CDIMA: Phase Plane: define the right-hand side, solve the initial value problem, compute nullclines, and then animate the resulting trajectory.

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
The Stable Limit Cycle
For every \(\mu > 0\) the Van der Pol system has a unique, stable limit cycle; this follows from Liénard’s theorem (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.4).






NoteExercise



Plot this limit cycle as an \(x(t)\) against \(t\) plot for \(\mu = 3\) and the initial condition \((2, -2)\), and verify that it matches the phase plane trajectories. Figure 2 shows the expected result.








TipSolution





sol = solve_ivp(van_der_pol, [0, 40], (2, -2), args=(3,), t_eval=np.linspace(0, 40, 4000))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0])
ax.set_xlabel("Time (t)")
ax.set_ylabel("x(t)")
plt.show()
The maximum of \(x(t)\) is close to 2, the largest \(|x|\) on the closed orbit in Figure 1.











Figure 2: Time series of x(t) for the Van der Pol system with mu = 3 and IC: (2, -2). Generated with scipy.integrate.solve_ivp() and matplotlib.

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
The Role of \(\mu\)
The amplitude and period of the limit cycle depend on \(\mu\).

For smaller \(\mu\), the oscillation looks smoother and less sharply separated into time scales.
For larger \(\mu\), the motion develops a clear slow-fast structure.
The trajectory spends long intervals drifting near the cubic nullcline, then jumps rapidly between branches.

This is the characteristic relaxation-oscillation picture.

title: Van der Pol Oscillator
text:
What to Look For

Different initial conditions approach the same closed orbit.
The transient depends on the initial state, but the long-run behavior does not.
The time trace \(x(t)\) reflects the same slow-fast pattern you see in the phase plane.







NoteExercise



Play with the parameter \(\mu\) (try 0.5, 1, 3 and 10) to see how it changes the shape of the limit cycle, its amplitude, its period and the transient dynamics.








TipSolution





The amplitude of \(x\) stays close to 2 for every \(\mu\). The period grows with \(\mu\): about 6.4 for \(\mu = 0.5\) and 19 for \(\mu = 10\). For large \(\mu\) it approaches \((3 - 2\ln 2)\mu\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.5). Small \(\mu\) gives a nearly sinusoidal oscillation; large \(\mu\) gives slow drifts along the cubic nullcline and fast jumps between its branches.

for mu_test in [0.5, 1, 3, 10]:
    t_end = 40 + 30 * mu_test
    s = solve_ivp(van_der_pol, (0, t_end), [2, -2], args=(mu_test,),
                  t_eval=np.linspace(0, t_end, 200001), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-11)
    late = s.t > t_end / 2
    x_late, t_late = s.y[0][late], s.t[late]
    up = np.where((x_late[:-1] < 0) & (x_late[1:] >= 0))[0]
    print(f"mu = {mu_test}: amplitude {x_late.max():.2f}, period {np.diff(t_late[up]).mean():.2f}, "
          f"(3 - 2 ln 2) mu = {(3 - 2 * np.log(2)) * mu_test:.2f}")

mu = 0.5: amplitude 2.00, period 6.38, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = 0.81
mu = 1: amplitude 2.01, period 6.66, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = 1.61
mu = 3: amplitude 2.02, period 8.86, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = 4.84
mu = 10: amplitude 2.01, period 19.08, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = 16.14

title: Practice: Lorenz System
text:
This is ungraded practice on the optional Lorenz material. You now have the full workflow for a first chaos experiment: define the Lorenz vector field, integrate the trajectory numerically, visualize the attractor in three dimensions, and compare nearby initial conditions (Lorenz 1963; Strogatz 2024).
You can follow the guide here:
Lorenz Attractor Sensitivity and Chaos

title: Practice: Lorenz System
Practice: Lorenz System
text:
Tasks

title: Practice: Lorenz System
text:
Short discussion
Write a short paragraph that answers:

For how long do the nearby trajectories remain visually close?
Does the system appear random, periodic, or something in between? Explain.
What role does the parameter r seem to play in the shape or complexity of the trajectory?







TipOptional extension




Replace Euler’s method by a higher-order integrator and compare the trajectories.

title: Practice: Lorenz System
text:
Tips

Start with a small dt, such as 0.01, before you vary parameters.
Use the same dt and number of steps when you compare two trajectories.
Plot the separation on a logarithmic vertical axis if the early growth is hard to see.
Keep the parameter comparison focused. Two or three values are enough if you interpret them well.

title: Budworm: a Streamlit App
text: With the functions from Budworm: the Model in Code and Budworm: Integration and Time Series, you can build an interactive app in which a slider changes a parameter and the plots update immediately. See the Streamlit documentation.

title: Budworm: a Streamlit App
text:
Setup
Streamlit runs on your own machine, not in Google Colab. Follow the instructions in the README of the course repository to set up your environment.
Create a script spruce_budworm_app.py. Either import your functions from a module (for example spruce_budworm_model.py) or paste them into the script. A separate module is better practice. Run the app with
streamlit run spruce_budworm_app.py

title: Budworm: a Streamlit App
Budworm: a Streamlit App
text:
Interactive features

Display the differential equation with the current parameter values.
Show the rate plot from the rate plot section and the time series from the time series section.
Add an “Evolve” button that continues the simulation and updates the plots.
Store the time and population arrays in st.session_state. Streamlit reruns the whole script on every interaction, so anything not stored there is reset.

title: Budworm: a Streamlit App
text:
Layout
import numpy as np
import streamlit as st

from your_module import (
    evolve_spruce_budworm,
    plot_spruce_budworm,
    plot_spruce_budworm_rate,
)

st.title("Spruce Budworm Population Dynamics")

r = st.sidebar.slider("Intrinsic growth rate (r)", 0.0, 1.0, 0.5)
k = st.sidebar.slider("Carrying capacity (k)", 0.1, 10.0, 10.0)
x0 = k / 10

# Initialize session state on the first run
if "sbw_x" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["sbw_t"] = np.array([0.0])
    st.session_state["sbw_x"] = np.array([x0])

t_eval = st.sidebar.slider("Time", 1, 100, 10)
button = st.sidebar.button("Evolve")

t = st.session_state["sbw_t"]
x = st.session_state["sbw_x"]

if button:
    t, x = evolve_spruce_budworm(t, x, r=r, k=k, t_eval=t_eval)
    st.session_state["sbw_t"] = t
    st.session_state["sbw_x"] = x

fig1, ax1 = plot_spruce_budworm_rate(x[-1], r=r, k=k)
st.pyplot(fig1)
fig2, ax2 = plot_spruce_budworm(t, x)
st.pyplot(fig2)

title: Budworm: a Streamlit App
text:
Validation

With \(r = 0.5\), \(k = 10\) and \(x_0 = 1\), pressing “Evolve” several times should bring the population to about 0.68.
The green line on the rate plot should always sit where the time series ends.







TipOptional extension




Add a reset button that clears st.session_state.

Animate the population dynamics.
Let \(k\) drift slowly in time and plot \(x\) against \(k\) to see the hysteresis loop of Hysteresis.

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
TipOptional extension



This page and Sensitivity and Chaos are extra material, not part of the core syllabus. They extend the planar systems to three dimensions, where the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem no longer applies and chaos becomes possible (Strogatz 2024, chap. 9).
The Lorenz system is one of the standard examples where a smooth deterministic ODE produces irregular long-term behavior (Lorenz 1963; Strogatz 2024).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot x &= s (y - x), \\
\dot y &= r x - y - x z, \\
\dot z &= x y - b z.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
For the classical Lorenz attractor, the standard parameter choice is
\[
s = 10,
\qquad
r = 28,
\qquad
b = \frac{8}{3}.
\]
Figure 1: Lorenz attractor trajectory (Euler integration).

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
From ODEs to chaos
The earlier sessions studied phase portraits, fixed points and oscillations. The Lorenz system keeps the same ingredients, a deterministic vector field and a time-stepping scheme, but adds a new phenomenon:

trajectories remain bounded;
the system is fully deterministic;
long-term prediction still becomes difficult because nearby initial conditions diverge.

This is the core idea behind deterministic chaos.






Note



The Lorenz attractor is bounded but not periodic. A trajectory keeps moving forever without settling into a fixed point or a simple closed orbit.

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
Implement the vector field
The right-hand side takes one point \((x,y,z)\) and returns the instantaneous velocity in phase space.






NoteExercise



Complete the Lorenz vector field Equation 1.
def lorenz(xyz, s=10.0, r=28.0, b=8.0 / 3.0):
    x, y, z = xyz
    x_dot = # TODO
    y_dot = # TODO
    z_dot = # TODO
    return np.array([x_dot, y_dot, z_dot])








TipSolution





def lorenz(xyz, s=10.0, r=28.0, b=8.0 / 3.0):
    x, y, z = xyz
    x_dot = s * (y - x)
    y_dot = r * x - y - x * z
    z_dot = x * y - b * z
    return np.array([x_dot, y_dot, z_dot])

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
Fixed points
Setting the right-hand side equal to zero gives the equilibrium points.
For \(r > 1\), the Lorenz system has three fixed points (Strogatz 2024, sec. 9.2):
\[
(0,0,0),
\qquad
\left(\sqrt{b(r-1)}, \sqrt{b(r-1)}, r-1\right),
\qquad
\left(-\sqrt{b(r-1)}, -\sqrt{b(r-1)}, r-1\right).
\]
For \(s = 10\), \(b = 8/3\) the two nonzero fixed points lose stability in a subcritical Hopf bifurcation at \(r = s(s + b + 3)/(s - b - 1) \approx 24.74\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 9.2). At \(r = 28\) no fixed point is stable, and trajectories keep circling around the two lobes of the attractor.

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
Simulate with Euler
Forward Euler updates the state by
\[
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n + \Delta t\, f(\mathbf{x}_n).
\]
In code, that becomes a simple loop over time steps. Euler is only first-order accurate. It is used here because it is simple enough that you see how time stepping turns a continuous ODE into a computable trajectory. Use solve_ivp for quantitative work.
def simulate_lorenz(initial_state=(0.0, 1.0, 1.05), dt=0.01, num_steps=10000):
    xyzs = np.empty((num_steps + 1, 3))
    xyzs[0] = initial_state

    for i in range(num_steps):
        xyzs[i + 1] = xyzs[i] + lorenz(xyzs[i]) * dt

    return xyzs

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
What to look for

The trajectory stays in a bounded region of phase space.
It alternates between two lobes instead of converging to one point.
The geometry looks structured, but the switching times are hard to predict over long intervals.







NoteExercise



Change \(r\) to 0.5, 10, 20 and 28, keeping \(s = 10\), \(b = 8/3\) and the initial condition \((0, 1, 1.05)\). Where does the trajectory end up? Then change the initial condition at \(r = 28\).








TipSolution





For \(r = 0.5 < 1\) the origin is the only fixed point and the trajectory decays to it. For \(r = 10\) and \(r = 20\) it settles on one of the two nonzero fixed points \(\bigl(\pm\sqrt{b(r-1)}, \pm\sqrt{b(r-1)}, r-1\bigr)\). For \(r = 28\) it never settles and keeps switching between the lobes. A new initial condition at \(r = 28\) gives a different path on the same attractor.

from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp


def lorenz_rhs(t, u, r, s=10.0, b=8.0 / 3.0):
    x, y, z = u
    return [s * (y - x), r * x - y - x * z, x * y - b * z]


for r in [0.5, 10, 20, 28]:
    end = solve_ivp(lorenz_rhs, (0, 200), [0.0, 1.0, 1.05], args=(r,), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12).y[:, -1]
    c = np.sqrt(8 / 3 * (r - 1)) if r > 1 else 0.0
    print(f"r = {r}: state at t = 200 = {np.round(end, 2)}, sqrt(b(r-1)) = {c:.2f}")

r = 0.5: state at t = 200 = [ 0. -0.  0.], sqrt(b(r-1)) = 0.00
r = 10: state at t = 200 = [4.9 4.9 9. ], sqrt(b(r-1)) = 4.90
r = 20: state at t = 200 = [-7.12 -7.12 19.  ], sqrt(b(r-1)) = 7.12
r = 28: state at t = 200 = [-4.32  0.53 28.89], sqrt(b(r-1)) = 8.49





Reference code: amlab/extra/lorenz_attractor.py.

title: Practice: Planar Systems
text:
This is ungraded practice. You will build a Matplotlib animation for one planar ODE model (Strogatz 2024; Hunter 2007). The goal is to connect the geometry of the phase plane with the time evolution of the solution.
You can use these pages as guides:
CDIMA: Phase Plane Van der Pol Oscillator FitzHugh-Nagumo Model Animations and Interactivity

title: Practice: Planar Systems
text:
Goals
Your work should show that you can:

simulate a two-dimensional ODE correctly;
visualize the model in the phase plane and in time;
interpret nullclines, equilibria, and transient or oscillatory behaviour.

title: Bistable Switches
text: A bistable switch is a system with two stable states and a threshold between them. You met one in Bistability for the budworm. In cell biology, switches let a cell make a lasting decision from a transient signal. Gardner, Cantor and Collins built one from two genes that repress each other, and predicted the conditions for bistability with a two-variable model (Gardner et al. 2000).

title: Bistable Switches
text:
The toggle switch
Let \(u\) and \(v\) be the concentrations of two repressor proteins. Each one represses the promoter of the other:
\[
\dot u = \frac{\alpha_1}{1 + v^{\beta}} - u, \qquad
\dot v = \frac{\alpha_2}{1 + u^{\gamma}} - v .
\tag{1}\]
\(\alpha_1, \alpha_2\) are the effective synthesis rates, \(\beta, \gamma\) describe the cooperativity of repression, and the \(-u\), \(-v\) terms are degradation and dilution (Gardner et al. 2000).

title: Bistable Switches
text:
Geometry of the switch
The nullclines are \(u = \alpha_1/(1 + v^\beta)\) and \(v = \alpha_2/(1 + u^\gamma)\). When repression is cooperative (\(\beta, \gamma > 1\)) and the two synthesis rates are balanced and large enough, the nullclines cross three times: two stable states (one gene on, the other off) and a saddle between them. The stable manifold of the saddle separates the two basins (Gardner et al. 2000).








Figure 1: Toggle switch with alpha1 = alpha2 = 10 and beta = gamma = 2. Nullclines (blue: du/dt = 0, red: dv/dt = 0) cross three times. Trajectories from different initial conditions end in one of the two stable states (black dots); the open dot is the saddle.

title: Bistable Switches
section: Why it works as a memory
text:
Why it works as a memory
A transient signal that pushes the state across the separatrix, for example an inducer that temporarily inactivates one repressor, flips the switch. When the signal is removed, the system stays in the new state. Gardner et al. showed this experimentally in Escherichia coli: the toggle switched between states in response to transient chemical or thermal induction and kept its state afterwards (Gardner et al. 2000).
The same structure appears in the budworm: two stable states, a threshold, and hysteresis when a parameter changes slowly (Hysteresis).






NoteExercise



Take \(\beta = \gamma = 1\) (no cooperativity) and \(\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \alpha\). Show that the symmetric fixed point \(u = v\) is the only fixed point with \(u = v\) and find it.








TipSolution





With \(u = v\): \(u = \alpha/(1 + u)\), so \(u^2 + u - \alpha = 0\) and \(u = (-1 + \sqrt{1 + 4\alpha})/2\), the only positive root. For \(\beta = \gamma = 1\) the nullclines are hyperbolas that cross only once, so this fixed point is the only one and there is no bistability. Cooperativity is needed for the switch (Gardner et al. 2000).

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text: This page continues CDIMA: Nullclines and Fixed Points. You decide the stability of the fixed point from the Jacobian and check the Hopf condition \(b_c = 3a/5 - 25/a\) from Hopf Bifurcation (Strogatz 2024, sec. 8.3).

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



For \(a = 10\), which of \(b = 3\) and \(b = 4\) gives a stable fixed point? What should the eigenvalues look like at \(b = 3.5\)?








TipSolution





\(b_c = 3 \cdot 10/5 - 25/10 = 3.5\). The fixed point is stable for \(b > b_c\), so \(b = 4\) gives a stable spiral and \(b = 3\) an unstable one. At \(b = b_c\) the eigenvalues are a purely imaginary pair: the real part crosses zero while the imaginary part stays nonzero.

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Implementation: the Jacobian
The Jacobian collects the partial derivatives of the right-hand side:
\[
J =
\begin{bmatrix}
\partial f/\partial x & \partial f/\partial y \\
\partial g/\partial x & \partial g/\partial y
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
As in one dimension, a stable equilibrium attracts nearby trajectories and an unstable one repels them. In two dimensions the eigenvalues of \(J\) at the fixed point decide which. You can compute \(J\) analytically or numerically. The numerical route uses central differences and works for any model.






NoteExercise



Complete the central difference Jacobian. Column \(j\) is the derivative of the right-hand side with respect to variable \(j\).
def numerical_jacobian(func, point, args, h=1e-6):
    jac = np.zeros((2, 2))
    for j in range(2):
        e = np.zeros(2)
        e[j] = h
        jac[:, j] = # TODO: (f(point + e) - f(point - e)) / (2h)
    return jac








TipSolution





def numerical_jacobian(func, point, args, h=1e-6):
    jac = np.zeros((2, 2))
    for j in range(2):
        e = np.zeros(2)
        e[j] = h
        jac[:, j] = (np.asarray(func(0, point + e, *args))
                     - np.asarray(func(0, point - e, *args))) / (2 * h)
    return jac
amlab.odes_2d.cdima_analysis.numerical_jacobian is the reference version for CDIMA.



Then compute the eigenvalues with np.linalg.eigvals:

both real parts negative: stable (node or spiral);
at least one real part positive: unstable.

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Validation
Compare the numerical Jacobian with the analytical one and check where the real part of the eigenvalues changes sign.

import numpy as np

from amlab.odes_2d.cdima_analysis import (
    cdima_jacobian,
    hopf_b,
    locate_hopf_numerically,
    numerical_jacobian,
)

a = 10.0
for b in [3.0, 3.5, 4.0]:
    ev = np.linalg.eigvals(numerical_jacobian(a, b))
    diff = np.max(np.abs(numerical_jacobian(a, b) - cdima_jacobian(a, b)))
    print(f"b = {b}: eigenvalues {np.round(ev, 4)}, |J_num - J_exact| = {diff:.1e}")

for a in [8.0, 10.0, 15.0]:
    print(f"a = {a}: numerical Hopf b = {locate_hopf_numerically(a):.4f}, formula 3a/5 - 25/a = {hopf_b(a):.4f}")

b = 3.5: eigenvalues [-0.+2.6458j -0.-2.6458j], |J_num - J_exact| = 4.9e-10
b = 4.0: eigenvalues [-0.1+2.8267j -0.1-2.8267j], |J_num - J_exact| = 4.9e-10
a = 8.0: numerical Hopf b = 1.6750, formula 3a/5 - 25/a = 1.6750
a = 10.0: numerical Hopf b = 3.5000, formula 3a/5 - 25/a = 3.5000

At \(b = 3.5\) the eigenvalues are \(\pm i\sqrt 7 \approx \pm 2.6458i\), as predicted, and the numerical Hopf point agrees with the formula to the accuracy of the root finder.

Experiment

Run the phase plane from CDIMA: Phase Plane with \(a = 10\) and \(b = 4, 3.6, 3.4, 3\). Where does the limit cycle appear? How does its size change as \(b\) decreases below \(b_c\)?

for b in [4.0, 3.6, 3.4, 3.0]:
    print(f"b = {b}: amplitude of x after transients = {limit_cycle_amplitude(10.0, b, t_end=400.0):.3f}")

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Interpretation
For \(b > b_c\) the fixed point is a stable spiral and the reaction settles to constant concentrations. For \(b < b_c\) it is an unstable spiral surrounded by a stable limit cycle: the concentrations oscillate. The formula gives the whole stability boundary in the \((a, b)\) plane. Note that \(b_c > 0\) requires \(a > \sqrt{125/3} \approx 6.45\); for smaller \(a\) the fixed point is stable for every \(b > 0\).

title: CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point
text:
Limitations
The linear analysis says nothing about the size of the limit cycle, nor whether the Hopf bifurcation is supercritical. You answered those questions with simulations in Hopf Bifurcation.

title: Hopf Bifurcation
text: In a Hopf bifurcation a fixed point changes stability because a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues crosses the imaginary axis. A limit cycle appears or disappears at the same time. It is the standard way in which an oscillation is born as a parameter varies (Strogatz 2024, sec. 8.2).

title: Hopf Bifurcation
text:
Normal forms
In polar coordinates, the prototype of a supercritical Hopf bifurcation is
\[
\dot r = \mu r - r^3, \qquad \dot\theta = \omega + b r^2 .
\tag{1}\]

\(\mu < 0\): the origin is a stable spiral.
\(\mu > 0\): the origin is an unstable spiral, surrounded by a stable limit cycle of radius \(r = \sqrt{\mu}\).

The eigenvalues at the origin are \(\lambda = \mu \pm i\omega\). Near the bifurcation the amplitude grows like \(\sqrt{\mu}\) and the period is close to \(2\pi/\omega\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 8.2).
In the subcritical case the cubic term is destabilizing, for example \(\dot r = \mu r + r^3 - r^5\). An unstable cycle shrinks onto the fixed point as \(\mu \to 0^-\). At \(\mu = 0\) the state jumps to a distant, large-amplitude attractor, and the oscillation persists when you decrease \(\mu\) again: another form of hysteresis (Strogatz 2024, sec. 8.2).
The linearization only tells you that eigenvalues cross the axis. Whether the bifurcation is supercritical or subcritical depends on the nonlinear terms. In practice you often decide it numerically, by checking whether a small limit cycle appears on the unstable side (Strogatz 2024, sec. 8.2).

title: Hopf Bifurcation
text:
Worked example: the CDIMA reaction
The chlorine dioxide-iodine-malonic acid reaction oscillates in a stirred reactor. Lengyel and Epstein proposed a two-variable model for it (Lengyel and Epstein 1991); in dimensionless form (Strogatz 2024, sec. 8.3)
\[
\dot x = a - x - \frac{4xy}{1 + x^2}, \qquad \dot y = b x\left(1 - \frac{y}{1 + x^2}\right),
\tag{2}\]
where \(x\) and \(y\) are the dimensionless concentrations of I\(^-\) and ClO\(_2^-\) and \(a, b > 0\).
Fixed point. The \(y\)-nullcline (for \(x > 0\)) is \(y = 1 + x^2\). Substituting in \(\dot x = 0\) gives \(a - 5x = 0\), so the unique fixed point is
\[
x^* = \frac{a}{5}, \qquad y^* = 1 + (x^*)^2 .
\]
Jacobian. At the fixed point,
\[
J = \frac{1}{1 + (x^*)^2}\begin{pmatrix} 3(x^*)^2 - 5 & -4x^* \\ 2b(x^*)^2 & -bx^* \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Delta = \frac{5bx^*}{1 + (x^*)^2} > 0, \qquad \tau = \frac{3(x^*)^2 - 5 - bx^*}{1 + (x^*)^2}.
\]
Since \(\Delta > 0\), the fixed point is never a saddle. It is unstable when \(\tau > 0\), that is when
\[
b < b_c = \frac{3a}{5} - \frac{25}{a} .
\tag{3}\]
This is the condition in Strogatz (2024), Section 8.3. At \(b = b_c\) the eigenvalues are \(\pm i\omega\) with \(\omega^2 = \Delta\). For \(b < b_c\), Strogatz constructs a trapping region and applies the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem to prove that a closed orbit exists.








Figure 1: Amplitude of the CDIMA oscillation in x for a = 10, from long simulations. The Hopf point is b_c = 3.5. The dashed curve is proportional to sqrt(b_c - b), fitted at the point closest to b_c.





The amplitude goes to zero continuously as \(b \to b_c\), close to the \(\sqrt{b_c - b}\) law. This is the signature of a supercritical Hopf bifurcation for these parameters. In the lab you will check Equation 3 with a numerical Jacobian (CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point).

title: Hopf Bifurcation
text:
Explore the Hopf bifurcation
The figure integrates Equation 2 from the same initial conditions as the lab, \((0, 3)\), \((0, 1.5)\) and \((2, 0)\), with \(a = 10\) and \(b = 4\).


At \(b = 4\) the trajectories spiral into the fixed point \((2, 5)\). Lower \(b\) slowly. At which value does the readout change, and what do the trajectories approach instead?
Compare the size of the cycle at \(b = 3.4\) and at \(b = 2\). Does the oscillation appear with a finite amplitude or does it grow from zero?
Set \(b = 3.6\), just on the stable side. Why does the time series take so long to settle? Look at \(\operatorname{tr} J\) in the readout.
Change \(a\) to 8. Check the new Hopf point against \(b_c = 3a/5 - 25/a\).



Build this in Python. In the lab you write the code behind this figure and find the Hopf point numerically: CDIMA: Phase Plane for the trajectories and CDIMA: Stability and the Hopf Point for the numerical Jacobian.







NoteExercise



For \(a = 10\), compute \(b_c\) and the period of small oscillations near the bifurcation.








TipSolution





\(b_c = 6 - 2.5 = 3.5\) and \(x^* = 2\). Then \(\omega^2 = \Delta = 5 \cdot 3.5 \cdot 2 / 5 = 7\), so \(\omega = \sqrt 7 \approx 2.65\) and the period is \(T \approx 2\pi/\sqrt 7 \approx 2.37\) dimensionless time units.

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text: You now estimate \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) from a time series of daily new cases. This is your first parameter estimation problem of the course.

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
The data
amlab.epidemics.load_cases() reads data/epidemic/cases.csv with columns date,new_cases (see data/epidemic/README.md). If the file does not exist, it returns synthetic data and prints a warning: a deterministic SIR epidemic with \(R_0 = 3\) (\(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\) per day) in a population of one million, with random reporting noise and a fixed seed. The figures on this page use the synthetic data unless you add a real file. With synthetic data you know the true parameters, so you can check whether the fit recovers them.

import numpy as np

from amlab.epidemics import load_cases

days, cases, synthetic = load_cases()
print("Synthetic data:", synthetic, "| days:", len(days), "| total cases:", int(cases.sum()))

Synthetic data: True | days: 120 | total cases: 945521

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
The observation model
The SIR model predicts fractions. The data are counts of new infections per day. The expected number of new cases on day \(d\) is
\[
\mu_d = N\,\bigl(S(d-1) - S(d)\bigr),
\]
the number of people who left the susceptible class during that day. sir_incidence(days, beta, gamma, i0, N) computes \(\mu_d\).

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



Before fitting, estimate the growth rate from the early data by eye: on a log scale, the rising part of the curve is roughly a straight line with slope \(\beta - \gamma\). What slope do you expect for the synthetic data?








TipSolution





The synthetic data use \(\beta = 0.3\) and \(\gamma = 0.1\), so the slope of \(\ln c_d\) is \(\beta - \gamma = 0.2\) per day: cases double about every \(\ln 2 / 0.2 \approx 3.5\) days. A straight-line fit to the first weeks gives a value close to this.

early = (days >= 5) & (days <= 30) & (cases > 0)
slope = np.polyfit(days[early], np.log(cases[early]), 1)[0]
print(f"slope of log(cases) for days 5 to 30: {slope:.3f} per day")

slope of log(cases) for days 5 to 30: 0.200 per day

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Implementation
Least squares chooses the parameters that minimize \(\sum_d (\sqrt{\mu_d} - \sqrt{c_d})^2\), where \(c_d\) are the observed counts. The square root reduces the weight of the large counts near the peak, since count noise grows with the mean.






NoteExercise



Complete the residual function for a population of \(N = 10^6\). Here i0 is the initial infected fraction.
from scipy.optimize import least_squares

def residuals(log_params):
    beta, gamma, i0 = np.exp(log_params)   # log scale keeps parameters positive
    model = # TODO: sir_incidence(...)
    return # TODO: sqrt(model) - sqrt(cases)

result = least_squares(residuals, np.log([0.25, 0.12, 1e-5]))








TipSolution





amlab.epidemics.fit_sir_incidence implements exactly this, with bounds on each parameter. It takes the initial number of infected people in the guess instead of the fraction.

from scipy.optimize import least_squares

from amlab.epidemics import sir_incidence


def residuals(log_params):
    beta, gamma, i0 = np.exp(log_params)
    model = sir_incidence(days, beta, gamma, i0, 1e6)
    # clip tiny negative values produced by the ODE solver
    return np.sqrt(np.clip(model, 0, None)) - np.sqrt(cases)


result = least_squares(residuals, np.log([0.25, 0.12, 1e-5]))
beta_hat, gamma_hat, i0_hat = np.exp(result.x)
print(f"beta = {beta_hat:.3f}, gamma = {gamma_hat:.3f}, i0 = {i0_hat:.1e}")

beta = 0.303, gamma = 0.103, i0 = 9.2e-06

N = 1e6
fit = fit_sir_incidence(days, cases, population=N)
print(f"beta = {fit['beta']:.3f}, gamma = {fit['gamma']:.3f}, R0 = {fit['r0']:.2f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.plot(days, cases, ".", color="gray", label="data")
ax.plot(days, sir_incidence(days, fit["beta"], fit["gamma"], fit["i0"], N), "tab:red", label="SIR fit")
ax.set_xlabel("Day")
ax.set_ylabel("New cases")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Validation
With the full curve, the fit should recover values close to \(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\). Check the residuals: they should look like noise, with no systematic pattern before or after the peak.

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Experiment: identifiability
A parameter is identifiable if the data determine it. Now treat the population size \(N\) as unknown too (fit_population=True); in a real epidemic you rarely know how many people can actually be reached. Fit only the first \(T\) days for several values of \(T\).

print(" T   beta-gamma    R0          N")
for T in [20, 30, 40, 60, 90, 120]:
    f = fit_sir_incidence(days[:T], cases[:T], population=N, fit_population=True)
    print(f"{T:3d}   {f['beta'] - f['gamma']:.3f}      {f['r0']:8.2f}   {f['population']:.3g}")

 T   beta-gamma    R0          N
 20   0.220          3.79   7.37e+06
 30   0.189          2.94   1.46e+06
 40   0.209        143.16   2.25e+05
 60   0.204        205.26   8.18e+05
 90   0.201          2.83   1.01e+06
120   0.200          2.94   1e+06


The growth rate \(\beta - \gamma\) is close to the true 0.2 for every \(T\). \(R_0\) and \(N\) are not: before and around the peak (near day 55), the fit can return values far from the truth, including very large \(R_0\) with a small \(N\), and these fits have a lower cost than the true parameters. During exponential growth \(I(t) \approx I(0)e^{(\beta-\gamma)t}\), so very different combinations of \(\beta\), \(\gamma\) and \(N\) produce almost the same curve. Only the decline of the epidemic pins them down.

title: Fitting an Epidemic to Data
text:
Limitations

The fit assumes the SIR model is correct. Real outbreaks involve interventions that change \(\beta\) in time.
Reported cases are a variable, unknown fraction of true infections.
Least squares gives a point estimate. Quantifying uncertainty needs bootstrap or Bayesian methods, as in Castro et al. (2020).

title: Stylized Facts of Returns
text: A stylized fact is a statistical property that appears in many markets, instruments and periods. Cont (2001) lists eleven. Any model of prices should reproduce at least the first few. This page quotes the ones you test in the lab.

title: Stylized Facts of Returns
section: The facts you test in the lab
text:
The facts you test in the lab
From Cont (2001, sec. 2):

Absence of autocorrelations. Linear autocorrelations of returns are often insignificant, except at very small intraday time scales (about 20 minutes).
Heavy tails. The unconditional distribution of returns has a power-law or Pareto-like tail, with a tail index that is finite, higher than two and less than five for most data sets. This excludes both the normal distribution and stable laws with infinite variance.
Aggregational Gaussianity. As the time scale \(\Delta t\) of the returns grows, their distribution looks more and more normal. The shape of the distribution is therefore not the same at different time scales.
Volatility clustering. Measures of volatility have positive autocorrelation over several days: large changes tend to be followed by large changes, of either sign.
Slow decay of autocorrelation in absolute returns. The autocorrelation of \(|r_t|\) decays roughly as a power law of the lag with an exponent between 0.2 and 0.4.

The list also contains gain/loss asymmetry, intermittency, conditional heavy tails, the leverage effect, volume/volatility correlation and asymmetry in time scales (Cont 2001).

title: Stylized Facts of Returns
section: What this does to the random walk model
text:
What this does to the random walk model
The first fact supports the random walk hypothesis of Returns and Efficient Markets. The others reject its strong form. Uncorrelated is not the same as independent: \(|r_t|\) is predictable from \(|r_{t-1}|\) even when \(r_t\) is not predictable from \(r_{t-1}\) (Cont 2001). The heavy-tail fact also rejects Mandelbrot’s stable model with \(\alpha < 2\) (Mandelbrot 1963) for the far tail, since a tail index above two means finite variance.

title: Stylized Facts of Returns
section: A model that reproduces some of them
text:
A model that reproduces some of them
The ARCH model of Engle (1982) and its generalization GARCH(1,1) by Bollerslev (1986) let the variance depend on the past:
\[
r_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad \sigma_t^2 = \omega + a\, r_{t-1}^2 + b\, \sigma_{t-1}^2 ,
\tag{1}\]
with \(z_t\) independent, zero mean and unit variance, and \(a + b < 1\) for a finite unconditional variance \(\omega / (1 - a - b)\). A large return raises tomorrow’s variance, which produces volatility clustering while \(r_t\) stays uncorrelated. See also Mantegna and Stanley (2000, chap. 10).
The figure compares i.i.d. Gaussian returns with a GARCH(1,1) series with Student-t innovations, the synthetic fallback of the lab (amlab.finance.synthetic_garch_prices). The GARCH series is built to show these facts, so the figure illustrates the definitions; it is not evidence about markets.








Figure 1: Top: 2000 days of i.i.d. Gaussian returns and of a synthetic GARCH(1,1) series with the same unconditional standard deviation (1% per day). Bottom: autocorrelation of \(r_t\) and of \(|r_t|\) for the GARCH series. The dashed band is \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n}\).











NoteExercise



Compute the excess kurtosis (scipy.stats.kurtosis) of the Gaussian and GARCH returns above. Then shuffle the GARCH returns in time with rng.permutation and recompute the autocorrelation of \(|r_t|\) at lag 1. Which property survives the shuffle, and which one disappears?








TipSolution






from scipy import stats

shuffled = rng.permutation(r_garch)
print(f"excess kurtosis, Gaussian: {stats.kurtosis(r_iid):.2f}")
print(f"excess kurtosis, GARCH:    {stats.kurtosis(r_garch):.2f}")
print(f"lag-1 ACF of |r|, GARCH:    {autocorrelation(np.abs(r_garch), 1)[1]:.3f}")
print(f"lag-1 ACF of |r|, shuffled: {autocorrelation(np.abs(shuffled), 1)[1]:.3f}")

excess kurtosis, Gaussian: 0.07
excess kurtosis, GARCH:    11.97
lag-1 ACF of |r|, GARCH:    0.166
lag-1 ACF of |r|, shuffled: -0.014


Shuffling keeps the distribution, so the fat tails (large kurtosis) survive. It destroys the time order, so volatility clustering disappears. Heavy tails and clustering are separate facts, and a model can have one without the other.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Newman (2005).
Recommended: Mantegna and Stanley (2000), Chapters 3 and 4.
In The Diffusion Equation the position of a walker became Gaussian after many steps. The central limit theorem (CLT) says this happens for sums of almost any independent steps, provided their variance is finite. This page is about what happens when that proviso fails.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
Statement
Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) be independent and identically distributed with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2 > 0\). Let \(S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n\). Then, for every real \(z\),
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \Pr\left( \frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma \sqrt{n}} \le z \right) = \Phi(z),
\tag{1}\]
where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (Gnedenko and Kolmogorov 1954). The width of \(S_n\) grows as \(\sqrt{n}\), the same scaling as the random walk.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
Assumptions

Independence. Strongly correlated terms can change both the scaling and the limit.
Identical distribution. Versions for non-identical terms exist (Lindeberg conditions), but no single term may dominate the sum (Gnedenko and Kolmogorov 1954).
Finite variance. This is the assumption that matters on this page. If \(\Pr(|X| > x)\) decays like \(x^{-\alpha}\) with \(0 < \alpha < 2\), the variance is infinite and the limit is not Gaussian (Gnedenko and Kolmogorov 1954; Mantegna and Stanley 2000).

The theorem says nothing about how fast convergence happens. The tails of the distribution converge last.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text:
A simulated check
Exponential variables are skewed, far from Gaussian. The figure standardizes sums of \(n\) of them and compares them with the standard normal density.








Figure 1: Histograms of \((S_n - n)/\sqrt{n}\) for sums of \(n\) exponential variables with mean 1 and variance 1 (20000 samples each). The curve is the standard normal density.











NoteExercise



Repeat the experiment with Student-t variables with 3 degrees of freedom (finite variance \(3\)) and with 1.5 degrees of freedom (infinite variance). Use rng.standard_t. For \(n = 100\), compare the fraction of standardized sums with \(|z| > 3\) to the Gaussian value \(0.0027\). For the second case, standardize by the sample standard deviation of the sums.








TipSolution






rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 100
for df in [3.0, 1.5]:
    s = rng.standard_t(df, size=(20000, n)).sum(axis=1)
    z_s = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
    print(f"df = {df}: fraction |z| > 3 is {np.mean(np.abs(z_s) > 3):.4f}")

df = 3.0: fraction |z| > 3 is 0.0050
df = 1.5: fraction |z| > 3 is 0.0016


With 3 degrees of freedom the fraction is of the same order as the Gaussian value but still larger. The CLT holds, but the tails converge slowly. With 1.5 degrees of freedom the sample standard deviation is dominated by a few huge values; the rescaled sums pile up near zero and do not approach the normal law as \(n\) grows. The next pages explain why.

title: Loading Prices and Computing Returns
text: In this laboratory you test the random walk model of Returns and Efficient Markets on a daily price series. The lab has five pages: this one (returns and autocorrelation), Normality Tests, Calibrated KS Test, Tail Exponent and Scaling of Returns in Data.

title: Loading Prices and Computing Returns
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



Before you run any code, write down your answers:

What order of magnitude do you expect for the standard deviation of daily log returns of a stock index: 0.01 %, 1 % or 10 %?
If the market is weak-form efficient, what should the autocorrelation of \(r_t\) at lag 1 be?
Should the autocorrelation of \(|r_t|\) at lag 1 be zero too?









TipSolution






About 1 %. A typical stock index moves by roughly one percent on an ordinary day.
Close to zero. A clear linear correlation would let you forecast tomorrow’s return from today’s.
No. Efficiency says nothing about the size of the moves. Large moves tend to follow large moves (volatility clustering), so the autocorrelation of \(|r_t|\) is positive (Cont 2001). You check both answers below.

Experiment: autocorrelation of returns and absolute returns
Under the null hypothesis of i.i.d. returns, sample autocorrelations are approximately normal with standard deviation \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so values outside \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n}\) are unusual.






NoteExercise



Complete the function below. Then compute the sample autocorrelation of \(r_t\) and of \(|r_t|\) for lags 1 to 50 and plot both with the \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n}\) band.
def autocorrelation(x, max_lag):
    """Sample autocorrelation at lags 0..max_lag."""
    x = x - x.mean()
    # TODO: for each lag k, compute sum(x[:-k] * x[k:]) / sum(x * x)
    return ...








TipSolution





Lag 0 needs care, because x[:-0] is empty. Slice with x[: x.size - k] instead.
def autocorrelation(x, max_lag):
    """Sample autocorrelation at lags 0..max_lag."""
    x = x - x.mean()
    return np.array([np.sum(x[: x.size - k] * x[k:]) / np.sum(x * x) for k in range(max_lag + 1)])

title: Loading Prices and Computing Returns
text:
Interpretation
Compare with your predictions. For market data Cont (2001) reports insignificant linear autocorrelation of daily returns and a positive, slowly decaying autocorrelation of absolute returns. If your plot shows the same pattern, the returns are close to uncorrelated but they are not independent. The strong form of the random walk hypothesis, i.i.d. returns, fails.

title: Loading Prices and Computing Returns
text:
Limitations

The \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n}\) band assumes i.i.d. data. With volatility clustering the true spread of the sample autocorrelation of \(r_t\) is wider, so a few crossings are not strong evidence (Cont 2001).
Closing prices that are not adjusted for dividends and splits create artificial jumps. Check the source of the frozen file.
Weekends and holidays are skipped, so a “daily” return sometimes covers three or more calendar days.
