title: Calibrated KS Test
text:
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test compares a whole distribution function with a model. Used naively with estimated parameters it gives wrong p-values. On this page you see why and build a version calibrated by simulation. You continue from Normality Tests.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

from amlab.finance import load_prices, log_returns

r = log_returns(load_prices()["close"])

WARNING: data/finance/prices.csv not found. Using a SYNTHETIC GARCH(1,1) series with Student-t innovations (seed 2026). These are not market data. See data/finance/README.md.

title: Calibrated KS Test
section: Why the plain KS test is not valid here
text:
Why the plain KS test is not valid here
The KS statistic is the largest distance between the empirical CDF \(F_n\) and a model CDF \(F\):
\[
D = \sup_x |F_n(x) - F(x)| .
\]
Kolmogorov’s null distribution of \(D\), which scipy.stats.kstest uses for its p-value, assumes that \(F\) is fixed before you see the data. Here you do not know \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\); you estimate them from the same returns. The fitted normal is then pulled towards the data, so \(D\) is systematically smaller than under a fixed \(F\). The standard p-values are too large and the test rejects too rarely (Lilliefors 1967). Clauset et al. (2009, footnote 7) make the same point for power-law fits, where \(x_{\min}\) and \(\alpha\) are estimated from the data, and compute a Monte Carlo p-value for that reason; see Fitting Power Laws Properly.
Lilliefors (1967) obtained the correct null distribution by Monte Carlo. The same idea is a parametric bootstrap (Efron 1979): simulate many normal samples of size \(n\), estimate \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) on each one, recompute \(D\), and compare the observed \(D\) with that simulated distribution. Because the normal is a location-scale family, the null distribution of \(D\) with estimated parameters does not depend on the true \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), so you can simulate from \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\).

title: Calibrated KS Test
section: Core activity: a bootstrap-calibrated KS test

Core activity: a bootstrap-calibrated KS test

    # TODO: estimate mu and sigma (ddof=1) and call stats.kstest(x, "norm", args=(mu, sigma))
    return ...

    d_obs = ks_stat_normal(x)
    # TODO: for n_boot repetitions, draw a standard normal sample of len(x)
    #       and store ks_stat_normal of it
    d_boot = ...
    # TODO: p-value = (1 + number of d_boot >= d_obs) / (n_boot + 1)
    return d_obs, ...








TipSolution






def ks_stat_normal(x):
    """KS distance between x and the normal fitted to x."""
    return stats.kstest(x, "norm", args=(x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1))).statistic


def ks_normal_bootstrap(x, n_boot, rng):
    d_obs = ks_stat_normal(x)
    d_boot = np.array([ks_stat_normal(rng.standard_normal(x.size)) for _ in range(n_boot)])
    return d_obs, (1 + np.sum(d_boot >= d_obs)) / (n_boot + 1)


rng = np.random.default_rng(18)
d_obs, p_boot = ks_normal_bootstrap(r, n_boot=300, rng=rng)
p_naive = stats.kstest(r, "norm", args=(r.mean(), r.std(ddof=1))).pvalue
print(f"D = {d_obs:.4f}; naive p = {p_naive:.2e}; bootstrap p = {p_boot:.4f}")

D = 0.0760; naive p = 1.42e-25; bootstrap p = 0.0033


With 300 bootstrap samples the smallest possible p-value is \(1/301 \approx 0.003\). A result at that floor means “smaller than 0.003”. When the departure from normality is this large, both versions reject; the validation below shows where they differ. The function is also available as amlab.finance.ks_normal_bootstrap.

title: Calibrated KS Test
section: Validation: the test on data that are normal
text:
Validation: the test on data that are normal
A valid test at level 5 % rejects 5 % of truly normal samples. Check both versions on 500 normal samples of size 200. The null distribution of \(D\) is the same for all of them, so you simulate it once.

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
m = 200
d_null = np.array([ks_stat_normal(rng.standard_normal(m)) for _ in range(1000)])
p_naive, p_boot = [], []
for _ in range(500):
    x = rng.normal(3.0, 2.0, m)
    d = ks_stat_normal(x)
    p_naive.append(stats.kstest(x, "norm", args=(x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1))).pvalue)
    p_boot.append((1 + np.sum(d_null >= d)) / (d_null.size + 1))
p_naive, p_boot = np.array(p_naive), np.array(p_boot)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.hist([p_naive, p_boot], bins=10, range=(0, 1), label=["naive", "bootstrap"])
ax.set_xlabel("p-value")
ax.set_ylabel("count")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"rejection rate at 5%: naive {np.mean(p_naive < 0.05):.3f}, bootstrap {np.mean(p_boot < 0.05):.3f}")







Figure 1: p-values of the naive KS test (parameters estimated, standard p-value) and of the bootstrap-calibrated test on 500 samples that really are normal. A valid test gives uniformly distributed p-values.





rejection rate at 5%: naive 0.000, bootstrap 0.048


The naive p-values pile up near 1 and almost never fall below 0.05. The bootstrap version rejects close to 5 % of the time, as it should.

title: Calibrated KS Test
text:
Interpretation
The Q-Q plot, the Jarque-Bera test and the KS test ask the same question: are the returns consistent with an i.i.d. normal sample? For market data the answer is usually a clear no, because of the heavy tails you see in the Q-Q plot (Cont 2001).

title: Calibrated KS Test
text:
Limitations

Every test here assumes i.i.d. data. Returns with volatility clustering are not i.i.d., so the bootstrap null distribution is only approximate.
With thousands of observations any test rejects even small departures from normality. Rejection says nothing about whether the departure matters for your purpose.
The Jarque-Bera test depends on moments that may not exist for heavy tails.

title: Calibrated KS Test
text:
Optional extension






NoteExercise



Fit a Student-t distribution to the returns with stats.t.fit(r) and adapt the bootstrap KS test to it. The t family has a shape parameter, so the null distribution now depends on it: simulate from the fitted t and refit all three parameters on every bootstrap sample. Keep n_boot small (about 100) because stats.t.fit is slow.








TipSolution





The structure is the same as for the normal. Only the fit and the simulation change. A large p-value means the fitted t is consistent with the data at the level of the KS test. It does not remove the i.i.d. assumption.
def ks_stat_t(x):
    """KS distance between x and the Student-t fitted to x."""
    params = stats.t.fit(x)
    return stats.kstest(x, "t", args=params).statistic, params


def ks_t_bootstrap(x, n_boot, rng):
    d_obs, params = ks_stat_t(x)
    d_boot = np.array([
        ks_stat_t(stats.t.rvs(*params, size=x.size, random_state=rng))[0]
        for _ in range(n_boot)
    ])
    return d_obs, params, (1 + np.sum(d_boot >= d_obs)) / (n_boot + 1)


d_t, params_t, p_t = ks_t_bootstrap(r, n_boot=100, rng=np.random.default_rng(19))
print(f"fitted nu = {params_t[0]:.2f}; D = {d_t:.4f}; bootstrap p = {p_t:.3f}")

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Mantegna and Stanley (1995), the whole letter (four pages). Note that the letter analyses intraday S&P 500 index differences, not daily returns.
In Scaling of Returns you saw the prediction \(p_{\Delta t}(0) \propto \Delta t^{-1/\alpha}\) and the result \(\alpha \approx 1.4\) of Mantegna and Stanley (1995) for minute data. Here you aggregate daily returns over longer horizons and test how the distribution changes with \(\Delta t\).
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

from amlab.finance import load_prices, log_returns

r = log_returns(load_prices()["close"])
r = r - r.mean()
horizons = np.array([1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100])

WARNING: data/finance/prices.csv not found. Using a SYNTHETIC GARCH(1,1) series with Student-t innovations (seed 2026). These are not market data. See data/finance/README.md.

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



For each model below, predict how the standard deviation of \(r(\Delta t)\) and its excess kurtosis change with \(\Delta t\):

i.i.d. Gaussian returns;
i.i.d. returns with finite variance but fat tails;
returns that are uncorrelated but show volatility clustering.









TipSolution





In all three cases the standard deviation grows as \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\), because the variances of uncorrelated terms add. The kurtosis tells the models apart:

i.i.d. Gaussian: the excess kurtosis is 0 at every horizon.
i.i.d. with fat tails (finite fourth moment): it starts positive and falls as \(K_1 / \Delta t\).
Volatility clustering: it starts positive and falls more slowly than \(K_1 / \Delta t\), because days in a calm or a turbulent period are not independent.

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Core activity: aggregate the returns
The log return over \(\Delta t\) days is the sum of \(\Delta t\) daily log returns. Use non-overlapping blocks, so that different aggregated returns do not share days.






NoteExercise



Complete aggregate_returns. Then compute the standard deviation, the excess kurtosis and the density at zero of \(r(\Delta t)\) for every horizon in horizons.
def aggregate_returns(r, horizon):
    """Sum r over non-overlapping blocks of length horizon."""
    m = # TODO: number of complete blocks
    # TODO: reshape r[: m * horizon] to (m, horizon) and sum along axis 1
    return ...








TipSolution






def aggregate_returns(r, horizon):
    """Sum r over non-overlapping blocks of length horizon."""
    m = r.size // horizon
    return r[: m * horizon].reshape(m, horizon).sum(axis=1)


def p_zero(x):
    """Density at 0, estimated in a window of one tenth of the IQR."""
    q75, q25 = np.percentile(x, [75, 25])
    eps = 0.1 * (q75 - q25)
    return np.mean(np.abs(x) < eps / 2) / eps


def scaling_table(r):
    """Standard deviation, excess kurtosis and p(0) at every horizon."""
    rows = []
    for h in horizons:
        x = aggregate_returns(r, h)
        rows.append((x.std(), stats.kurtosis(x), p_zero(x)))
    return np.array(rows)


table = scaling_table(r)
for h, (sd, kurt, p0) in zip(horizons, table):
    print(f"dt = {h:3d}: blocks {r.size // h:5d}, std {sd:.4f}, kurtosis {kurt:6.2f}, p(0) {p0:7.2f}")

dt =   1: blocks  5000, std 0.0091, kurtosis  11.97, p(0)   59.46
dt =   2: blocks  2500, std 0.0127, kurtosis   8.86, p(0)   45.14
dt =   5: blocks  1000, std 0.0206, kurtosis   4.24, p(0)   24.77
dt =  10: blocks   500, std 0.0294, kurtosis   5.64, p(0)   16.92
dt =  20: blocks   250, std 0.0396, kurtosis   1.31, p(0)   12.45
dt =  50: blocks   100, std 0.0697, kurtosis   1.03, p(0)    6.05
dt = 100: blocks    50, std 0.0913, kurtosis  -0.58, p(0)    3.37

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Validation: a shuffled series
Shuffling the returns in time keeps their distribution and destroys all dependence. The shuffled series is i.i.d. with the same fat tails. For it, the standard deviation must grow as \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) and, when the fourth moment is finite, the excess kurtosis of a sum of \(\Delta t\) i.i.d. terms is the one-day value divided by \(\Delta t\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(32)
table_shuffled = scaling_table(rng.permutation(r))
slope_sd = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons), np.log(table_shuffled[:, 0]), 1)[0]
print(f"shuffled: slope of log std vs log dt = {slope_sd:.3f} (theory 0.5)")
slope_p0_shuffled = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons), np.log(table_shuffled[:, 2]), 1)[0]
print(f"shuffled: slope of log p(0) vs log dt = {slope_p0_shuffled:.3f} (about -0.5 for i.i.d. returns with finite variance)")

shuffled: slope of log std vs log dt = 0.497 (theory 0.5)
shuffled: slope of log p(0) vs log dt = -0.498 (about -0.5 for i.i.d. returns with finite variance)

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Experiment: three scaling plots

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.5))
for tab, label, marker in [(table, "original", "o"), (table_shuffled, "shuffled", "s")]:
    axes[0].loglog(horizons, tab[:, 0], marker, label=label)
    axes[1].semilogx(horizons, tab[:, 1], marker, label=label)
    axes[2].loglog(horizons, tab[:, 2], marker, label=label)
axes[0].loglog(horizons, table[0, 0] * np.sqrt(horizons), "k-", lw=0.8)
axes[1].semilogx(horizons, table[0, 1] / horizons, "k-", lw=0.8)
axes[2].loglog(horizons, table[0, 2] / np.sqrt(horizons), "k-", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("std of $r(\\Delta t)$")
axes[1].set_ylabel("excess kurtosis")
axes[2].set_ylabel("$p_{\\Delta t}(0)$")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("$\\Delta t$ (days)")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

slope_p0 = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons), np.log(table[:, 2]), 1)[0]
print(f"p(0) slope, original data: {slope_p0:.3f}  ->  effective alpha = {-1 / slope_p0:.2f}")







Figure 1: Scaling with the horizon \(\Delta t\) for the original and the shuffled returns. Left: standard deviation, with slope 1/2. Centre: excess kurtosis, with the i.i.d. prediction \(K_1/\Delta t\). Right: density at zero, with slope \(-1/2\).





p(0) slope, original data: -0.616  ->  effective alpha = 1.62

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Interpretation

The standard deviation grows close to \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) because daily returns are nearly uncorrelated. This is the part of the random walk model that survives.
The excess kurtosis falls with \(\Delta t\): the distribution becomes more Gaussian at longer horizons, which is the aggregational Gaussianity of Cont (2001). If it falls more slowly for the original data than for the shuffled data, the difference comes from volatility clustering, since that is the only thing the shuffle removed.
Mantegna and Stanley (1995) also simulated a GARCH(1,1) process with parameters chosen to mimic their one-minute distribution. Its \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) has a slope of \(-0.531 \pm 0.025\), hence an effective \(\alpha \approx 1.88\), far from the value 1.40 of their data. Compare this with the effective \(\alpha\) that you obtain for the original and for the shuffled series: the shuffled series should give the Gaussian benchmark of about \(-0.5\).
The effective \(\alpha\) from \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) tells you whether the centre of the distribution rescales like a Lévy law or like a Gaussian over these horizons. Mantegna and Stanley (1995) found \(\alpha \approx 1.4\) for horizons of 1 to 1000 minutes on the S&P 500; daily and longer horizons are a different regime.

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Limitations

At \(\Delta t = 100\) days a 20-year series gives only about 50 blocks. The kurtosis and \(p(0)\) at long horizons are very noisy. Report them with that caveat or use overlapping blocks and account for the dependence they introduce.
The sample kurtosis is unreliable for heavy tails (Cont 2001). Use it to compare series, not as a precise value.
The \(p(0)\) estimate depends on the window width. Try a few widths and check that your conclusion does not change.

Repeat with \(\Delta t^{1/1.4}\) and compare which rescaling collapses the centre better, as in Mantegna and Stanley (1995).

Loop over the two exponents and draw one panel for each. Judge the collapse near zero, not in the tails, where the long horizons have few points.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5), sharey=True)
for ax, alpha in zip(axes, [2.0, 1.4]):

        dens, edges = np.histogram(x, bins=40, density=True)
        ax.semilogy(0.5 * (edges[1:] + edges[:-1]), dens, ".-", label=f"dt = {h}")

title: Scaling of Returns in Data
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



Suppose that on the same daily series the \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) method gives an effective \(\alpha\) below 2 while the Hill estimator of Tail Exponent gives about 3. Is that a contradiction?








TipSolution





No. The two methods look at different parts of the distribution. The Hill estimator measures the far tail of one-day returns. The \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) method measures how the height of the centre changes under aggregation, which depends on the whole distribution and on the dependence between days. Mantegna and Stanley (1995) found a similar combination for intraday S&P 500 data: a Lévy-like centre with \(\alpha \approx 1.4\) and tails that fall off approximately exponentially, faster than a Lévy law, so the variance is finite. (They did not fit a power-law tail with exponent 3; that value comes from later work on individual stocks (Gopikrishnan et al. 1998).) The truncated Lévy flight of Mantegna and Stanley (1994) is one model with both properties.

title: Lévy Flights
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Viswanathan et al. (1999).
Recommended: Metzler and Klafter (2000), for the mathematics of Lévy flights and walks.
A Lévy flight is a random walk whose step lengths have a power-law distribution with infinite variance. The walk is dominated by rare long jumps, and it spreads faster than ordinary diffusion.

title: Lévy Flights
text:
The model
In the plane, draw each step with a uniformly random direction and a length \(\ell\) with density
\[
p(\ell) \propto \ell^{-\mu}, \qquad \ell \ge \ell_{\min},
\]
the parametrization used by Viswanathan et al. (1999). Three regimes follow from Power Laws and Stable Distributions:

\(\mu \le 1\): the density cannot be normalized.
\(1 < \mu < 3\): the step variance is infinite. The position after \(n\) steps is a sum in the domain of attraction of a stable law with index \(\alpha = \mu - 1\), so its typical size grows as \(n^{1/\alpha} = n^{1/(\mu - 1)}\). This is faster than \(n^{1/2}\).
\(\mu > 3\): the variance is finite, the CLT applies, and you recover normal diffusion.

The mean squared displacement of a Lévy flight is infinite at every time, because a single step already has infinite variance. You measure the spreading with a quantile, such as the median distance, instead. Models that give each jump a finite speed, called Lévy walks, have a finite MSD growing as \(t^{\gamma}\) with \(\gamma > 1\) (superdiffusion) (Metzler and Klafter 2000).

title: Lévy Flights
text:
Trajectories








Figure 1: Two planar walks of 2000 steps with \(\ell_{\min} = 1\). Left: \(\mu = 10\), finite variance, a Brownian-like path. Right: \(\mu = 2\), a Lévy flight made of clusters of short steps joined by rare long jumps. Note the different axis scales.

title: Lévy Flights
text:
Why it matters
Viswanathan et al. (1999) asked which flight-length distribution makes a searcher most efficient when it detects targets only within a short distance and the targets are placed at random. The efficiency has a maximum at \(\mu \approx 2\) only if targets are sparse and can be visited again (non-destructive foraging). If a target disappears once it has been found, the efficiency keeps improving as \(\mu \to 1\), and if targets are dense the exponent has no significant effect. The comparison of the paper with flight data on bumble-bees, albatrosses, deer and amoebae is qualitative: the exponents are read from published histograms. The page Lévy Foraging reproduces the argument and a simulation. Metzler and Klafter (2000) review the mathematics of anomalous diffusion, including Lévy flights and walks. In finance, Mandelbrot (1963) proposed that price changes are stable with \(\alpha < 2\), which makes the logarithm of the price a one-dimensional Lévy flight. You test that idea in Modelling Financial Markets.






NoteExercise



Simulate 1000 flights of 1000 steps for \(\mu = 2.5\) and for \(\mu = 10\). Compute the median distance from the origin at each step and fit the exponent \(\nu\) in \(\text{median} \propto n^{\nu}\) over \(n \in [10, 1000]\). Compare with \(1/(\mu - 1)\) and \(1/2\).








TipSolution






rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n = np.arange(10, 1001)
for mu, theory in [(2.5, 1 / 1.5), (10.0, 0.5)]:
    paths = np.array([levy_flight_2d(1000, mu=mu, rng=rng) for _ in range(1000)])
    med = np.median(np.linalg.norm(paths, axis=2), axis=0)
    nu = np.polyfit(np.log(n), np.log(med[n]), 1)[0]
    print(f"mu = {mu:4}: nu = {nu:.3f}, theory {theory:.3f}")

mu =  2.5: nu = 0.677, theory 0.667
mu = 10.0: nu = 0.501, theory 0.500


The Lévy flight spreads with \(\nu \approx 2/3\), the finite-variance walk with \(\nu \approx 1/2\). Convergence to the asymptotic exponent is slow, so expect a small deviation at these sizes.

title: Power Laws
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Clauset et al. (2009), Sections 1 to 3 and Box 1.
Recommended: Newman (2005). The tests of Sections 4 and 5 of the first paper are the subject of Fitting Power Laws Properly.
A distribution has a fat (heavy) tail when large values are much more likely than under a Gaussian. The simplest example is the power law. This page follows Newman (2005) and Clauset et al. (2009).

title: Power Laws
text:
Definition
A continuous power law has density
\[
p(x) = \frac{\alpha - 1}{x_{\min}} \left( \frac{x}{x_{\min}} \right)^{-\alpha}, \qquad x \ge x_{\min},
\tag{1}\]
with \(\alpha > 1\) so that it can be normalized. Its complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF) is also a power law, with exponent one less:
\[
P(X \ge x) = \left( \frac{x}{x_{\min}} \right)^{-(\alpha - 1)} .
\tag{2}\]
The mean is finite only if \(\alpha > 2\) and the variance only if \(\alpha > 3\) (Newman 2005). For \(1 < \alpha \le 3\) the sample variance never settles, however much data you collect.

title: Power Laws
section: Pareto, Zipf and the same law
text:
Pareto, Zipf and the same law
Pareto’s law is a statement about the CCDF: the fraction of people with wealth above \(x\) decays as a power of \(x\). Zipf’s law is a statement about ranks: the \(r\)-th most frequent word appears with frequency proportional to \(r^{-s}\). A rank plot is the CCDF with the axes swapped, so both are power laws for the same data (Newman 2005).

title: Power Laws
text:
Log-log plots and their pitfalls
On log-log axes Equation 1 is a straight line with slope \(-\alpha\). That suggests fitting a line by least squares. Clauset et al. (2009) show that this is a poor estimator:

A histogram with linear bins has very few counts in the tail, and its logarithm is noisy and biased. For 10000 continuous samples with \(\alpha = 2.5\) and \(x_{\min} = 1\), Clauset et al. (2009) obtain \(1.39 \pm 0.05\) from a least-squares fit to a histogram with constant-width bins and \(1.19 \pm 0.02\) with logarithmic bins, against \(2.50 \pm 0.02\) from maximum likelihood (their Table 3.1).
The least-squares fit has no valid error estimate. The noise in the logarithm of a count is not Gaussian, and for a fit to a cumulative distribution neighbouring points are strongly correlated. The error bar of a biased fit therefore gives no warning that the estimate is wrong.
A straight-looking stretch does not prove a power law, and a high \(r^2\) is no evidence either. Clauset et al. (2009) show small samples from a power law, a log-normal and an exponential distribution that all look roughly straight on log-log axes (their Fig. 4.1a).

A least-squares fit to the CCDF built without binning (a rank-frequency plot) does much better than a histogram fit. For the same continuous data it gives \(2.4869 \pm 0.0003\). The paper still recommends maximum likelihood, because the least-squares error bars are not valid and the CCDF fit is biased for integer data (2.570 against a true value of 2.5). Plot the CCDF, which needs no binning, and estimate \(\alpha\) by maximum likelihood.








Figure 1: The same 5000 samples of a power law with \(\alpha = 2.5\) and \(x_{\min} = 1\). Left: histogram with linear bins on log-log axes. Right: empirical CCDF, with the exact CCDF \(x^{-1.5}\) as a dashed line.

title: Power Laws
text:
The maximum likelihood estimator
Given \(n\) observations \(x_i \ge x_{\min}\), the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\alpha\) is
\[
\hat{\alpha} = 1 + n \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \frac{x_i}{x_{\min}} \right]^{-1},
\qquad
\sigma_{\hat{\alpha}} = \frac{\hat{\alpha} - 1}{\sqrt{n}},
\tag{3}\]
(Newman 2005; Clauset et al. 2009). The estimator is unbiased only asymptotically. Its bias decays as \(1/n\), and the authors give \(n \gtrsim 50\) as a rule of thumb for an estimate accurate to about 1 %. In practice \(x_{\min}\) is unknown, and it matters. If it is too low, the fit includes data that do not follow the power law and \(\hat{\alpha}\) is biased. If it is too high, data are thrown away and the error grows. Clauset et al. (2009) choose \(x_{\min}\) by minimizing the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the data above \(x_{\min}\) and the fitted law. They then test the fit with a bootstrap p-value and compare the power law with alternative distributions (their Box 1). Fitting Power Laws Properly implements this procedure. You meet the same estimator again as the Hill estimator in the lab. For integer data the estimator has to change: the paper gives an approximation that replaces \(x_{\min}\) by \(x_{\min} - 1/2\) inside the logarithm, accurate to about 1 % for \(x_{\min} \gtrsim 6\).

alpha_hat, err = mle_power_law_exponent(x, xmin=1.0)
print(f"MLE: alpha = {alpha_hat:.3f} +/- {err:.3f}  (true 2.5)")

MLE: alpha = 2.503 +/- 0.021  (true 2.5)








NoteExercise



Estimate \(\alpha\) by a least-squares line through the log-log histogram of the left panel (use only bins with counts). Repeat for 200 independent samples of size 5000 and compare the mean and spread of the least-squares and MLE estimates.








TipSolution






rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
ls, ml = [], []
for _ in range(200):
    s = sample_pareto(5000, 2.5, 1.0, rng)
    c, e = np.histogram(s, bins=200)
    m = 0.5 * (e[1:] + e[:-1])
    keep = c > 0
    ls.append(-np.polyfit(np.log(m[keep]), np.log(c[keep]), 1)[0])
    ml.append(mle_power_law_exponent(s, 1.0)[0])
print(f"least squares: {np.mean(ls):.3f} +/- {np.std(ls):.3f}")
print(f"MLE:           {np.mean(ml):.3f} +/- {np.std(ml):.3f}")

least squares: 1.599 +/- 0.171
MLE:           2.499 +/- 0.020


The least-squares estimate is strongly biased (about 1.6 with a spread of 0.17 in this run) because the sparse tail bins, many with a single count, flatten the line. The MLE is centred on 2.50 with a spread of 0.02, close to \((\alpha - 1)/\sqrt{n} \approx 0.021\).

title: Fitting Power Laws Properly
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Clauset et al. (2009), Sections 1 to 5 and Box 1.
Recommended: Newman (2005).
Power Laws explained why a straight line on a log-log plot is a weak argument and gave the maximum likelihood estimator for a known \(x_{\min}\). In practice \(x_{\min}\) is unknown, and a fitted exponent says nothing about whether the power law is a good model. On this page you implement the complete procedure of Clauset et al. (2009) on synthetic data whose true distribution you know. You then know what a correct answer looks like before you apply the procedure to returns in the Tail Exponent lab.

title: Fitting Power Laws Properly
text:
The recipe
Clauset et al. (2009) summarise their method in three steps (their Box 1).

Fit. Estimate \(\alpha\) by maximum likelihood for every candidate \(x_{\min}\) and choose the \(x_{\min}\) that minimizes the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the data above \(x_{\min}\) and the fitted power law.
Test the fit. Compute a p-value for the power-law hypothesis with a Monte Carlo procedure. The authors treat the power law as ruled out if \(p \le 0.1\) and as plausible if \(p > 0.1\). A large \(p\) does not prove the power law, and with few data a large \(p\) is easy to obtain.
Compare alternatives. Compare the power law with other distributions (log-normal, exponential, stretched exponential, power law with cutoff) through a log-likelihood ratio and its significance.

The limits of each step matter as much as the steps. The maximum likelihood estimate is unbiased only for large samples, and the authors suggest that \(n \gtrsim 50\) tail observations give a reasonably reliable estimate. Their KS-based choice of \(x_{\min}\) worked well in their tests once roughly 1000 or more observations lay above \(x_{\min}\), and it is a procedure with no performance guarantee (Clauset et al. 2009, sec. 3.2 to 3.4).

title: Fitting Power Laws Properly
text:
Step 1: choosing \(x_{\min}\)
Take an assumed \(x_{\min}\) that is too low, and the fit includes data that do not follow the power law, so \(\hat{\alpha}\) is biased. Take it too high, and you discard legitimate data, so the statistical error grows. The figure shows both effects for a sample that follows a power law above \(x_{\min} = 5\) and has an exponential body below.

import time

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import optimize, special


def sample_power_law(n, alpha, xmin, rng):
    """Inverse-transform samples of p(x) = (alpha - 1) / xmin * (x / xmin)^(-alpha), x >= xmin."""
    return xmin * (1.0 - rng.random(n)) ** (-1.0 / (alpha - 1.0))


def sample_with_body(n, alpha, xmin, rng, share_tail=0.4, scale=2.0):
    """Power law above xmin, exponential body (scale `scale`) truncated at xmin below."""
    k = rng.binomial(n, share_tail)
    u = rng.random(n - k)
    body = -scale * np.log(1.0 - u * (1.0 - np.exp(-xmin / scale)))
    return np.concatenate([sample_power_law(k, alpha, xmin, rng), body])


def ks_distance(tail, xmin, alpha):
    """KS distance between the empirical CDF of `tail` and the fitted power law."""
    xs = np.sort(tail)
    n = xs.size
    model = 1.0 - (xs / xmin) ** (1.0 - alpha)
    return max((np.arange(1, n + 1) / n - model).max(), (model - np.arange(n) / n).max())


def fit_at(x, xmin):
    """MLE of alpha and KS distance for the data with x >= xmin."""
    tail = x[x >= xmin]
    alpha = 1.0 + tail.size / np.sum(np.log(tail / xmin))
    return alpha, ks_distance(tail, xmin, alpha)


def fit_power_law(x, n_tail_min=50, max_candidates=100):
    """Maximum likelihood fit with xmin chosen by minimizing the KS distance.

    Candidates are data values that leave at least `n_tail_min` points above;
    for speed at most `max_candidates` of them are scanned (a coarse grid of
    quantiles). Clauset et al. scan every observed value.
    """
    x = np.sort(np.asarray(x, dtype=float))
    pool = np.unique(x[: x.size - n_tail_min])
    if pool.size > max_candidates:
        pool = np.unique(np.quantile(pool, np.linspace(0, 1, max_candidates)))
    best = None
    for xm in pool:
        alpha, d = fit_at(x, xm)
        if best is None or d < best["D"]:
            best = {"xmin": xm, "alpha": alpha, "D": d, "n_tail": int(np.sum(x >= xm))}
    best["se"] = (best["alpha"] - 1.0) / np.sqrt(best["n_tail"])
    return best


rng = np.random.default_rng(2009)
x = sample_with_body(2000, 2.5, 5.0, rng)
scan = np.logspace(np.log10(0.5), np.log10(60), 60)
alphas, dists = np.array([fit_at(x, xm) for xm in scan]).T
chosen = fit_power_law(x)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
axes[0].semilogx(scan, alphas, "o-", ms=3)
axes[0].axhline(2.5, color="k", ls="--", lw=0.8)
axes[0].axvline(5.0, color="k", ls="--", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\hat{\alpha}$")
axes[1].loglog(scan, dists, "o-", ms=3)
axes[1].axvline(chosen["xmin"], color="C3", ls=":")
axes[1].set_ylabel("KS distance $D$")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("assumed $x_{\\min}$")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"KS choice: xmin = {chosen['xmin']:.2f}, alpha = {chosen['alpha']:.3f} +/- {chosen['se']:.3f} "
      f"(n_tail = {chosen['n_tail']}; true values 5 and 2.5)")







Figure 1: Left: maximum likelihood estimate of \(\alpha\) against the assumed \(x_{\min}\) for 2000 samples that follow a power law with \(\alpha = 2.5\) above \(x_{\min} = 5\) and an exponential body below (dashed lines: true values). Right: KS distance between the data above the assumed \(x_{\min}\) and the fitted power law. The vertical dotted line marks the \(x_{\min}\) with the smallest distance.





KS choice: xmin = 5.03, alpha = 2.512 +/- 0.054 (n_tail = 779; true values 5 and 2.5)


The estimate \(\hat{\alpha}\) drifts away from the true value below \(x_{\min} = 5\) and becomes noisy above it, which is the behaviour described by Clauset et al. (2009) in their Fig. 3.3. The KS distance is smallest close to the true \(x_{\min}\). The selected value is not exact, because the scan uses a coarse grid and the sample is finite.

title: Fitting Power Laws Properly
text:
Step 2: a goodness-of-fit p-value
The KS distance \(D\) of the fit measures how far the data are from the fitted power law, but its distribution under the null hypothesis is unknown, because \(x_{\min}\) and \(\alpha\) were estimated from the same data. This is the same problem as with the normal fit in Calibrated KS Test, and Clauset et al. (2009, footnote 7) give it as the reason for a Monte Carlo p-value. The procedure is:

Generate a synthetic data set of the same size. Draw each value from the fitted power law above \(\hat{x}_{\min}\) with probability \(n_{\text{tail}}/n\). Otherwise resample one of the observed values below \(\hat{x}_{\min}\). This keeps the non-power-law body of the data.
Fit the synthetic set from scratch, including its own \(x_{\min}\), and record its KS distance.
The p-value is the fraction of synthetic distances at least as large as the observed one.

The authors’ rule of thumb is that a p-value accurate to \(\epsilon\) needs at least \(\tfrac{1}{4}\epsilon^{-2}\) synthetic sets. For \(\epsilon = 0.01\) this is 2500. The code below uses 200 to keep the page fast, so its p-values are accurate to about \(\pm 0.035\).

def gof_p_value(x, fit, n_boot, rng):
    """Semiparametric bootstrap p-value (Clauset et al. 2009, Section 4.1)."""
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    body = x[x < fit["xmin"]]
    share = fit["n_tail"] / x.size
    d_boot = np.empty(n_boot)
    for b in range(n_boot):
        k = rng.binomial(x.size, share)
        synthetic = np.concatenate([sample_power_law(k, fit["alpha"], fit["xmin"], rng),
                                    rng.choice(body, x.size - k)])
        d_boot[b] = fit_power_law(synthetic)["D"]  # refit xmin and alpha every time
    return np.mean(d_boot >= fit["D"])


print(f"synthetic sets needed for epsilon = 0.01: {0.25 / 0.01**2:.0f}")
print(f"accuracy of p with 200 sets: {np.sqrt(0.25 / 200):.3f}")

synthetic sets needed for epsilon = 0.01: 2500
accuracy of p with 200 sets: 0.035

title: Fitting Power Laws Properly
text:
Step 3: alternatives
A good fit of the power law does not exclude that another distribution fits as well. For two models with densities \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) fitted to the same tail data, the log-likelihood ratio is
\[
R = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \ln p_1(x_i) - \ln p_2(x_i) \right].
\tag{1}\]
\(R > 0\) favours model 1. Because \(R\) fluctuates from sample to sample, its sign is only trustworthy if \(R\) is significantly different from zero. Clauset et al. (2009) (Appendix C, following Vuong) approximate the fluctuations of \(R\) by a normal law with variance \(n\sigma^2\), where \(\sigma^2\) is the variance of the pointwise differences. The p-value is
\[
p = \operatorname{erfc}\!\left( \frac{|R|}{\sqrt{2n}\,\sigma} \right).
\tag{2}\]
If \(p\) is small, say below 0.1, the sign of \(R\) is reliable. If \(p\) is large the data do not discriminate between the two models, and the authors point out that this is itself a useful answer. This version of the test is for non-nested models. For a power law against a power law with cutoff, which are nested, the paper describes a modified test that this page does not implement.
All models are fitted on the tail \(x \ge \hat{x}_{\min}\) only, so each density is normalized on that range.

def tail_log_likelihoods(tail, xmin, alpha):
    """Pointwise log-likelihoods of power law, truncated log-normal and shifted exponential."""
    ll_power = np.log((alpha - 1.0) / xmin) - alpha * np.log(tail / xmin)
    lam = 1.0 / np.mean(tail - xmin)
    ll_exp = np.log(lam) - lam * (tail - xmin)
    lx = np.log(tail)

    def log_normal_ll(p):
        mu, s = p[0], np.exp(p[1])
        mass = 0.5 * special.erfc((np.log(xmin) - mu) / (s * np.sqrt(2.0)))
        return -lx - np.log(s * np.sqrt(2.0 * np.pi)) - (lx - mu) ** 2 / (2 * s**2) - np.log(mass)

    res = optimize.minimize(lambda p: -log_normal_ll(p).sum(),
                            [lx.mean(), np.log(lx.std())], method="Nelder-Mead")
    return ll_power, log_normal_ll(res.x), ll_exp


def vuong(ll_a, ll_b):
    """Log-likelihood ratio R of Eq. (llr) and its p-value, Eq. (vuong)."""
    d = ll_a - ll_b
    return d.sum(), special.erfc(abs(d.sum()) / (np.sqrt(2 * d.size) * d.std()))

title: Fitting Power Laws Properly
text:
Three test cases
You now apply all three steps to three samples with known truth: a power law above 5 with an exponential body, a log-normal sample of 2000 values, and a log-normal sample of 50000 values. The log-normal has parameters \(\mu = 0.3\) and \(\sigma = 2\), the values Clauset et al. (2009) use to show that a log-normal looks straight on a log-log plot over a wide range.

rng = np.random.default_rng(2009)
samples = {
    "power law above 5,\nexponential body (n = 2000)": sample_with_body(2000, 2.5, 5.0, rng),
    "log-normal (n = 2000)": rng.lognormal(0.3, 2.0, 2000),
    "log-normal (n = 50000)": rng.lognormal(0.3, 2.0, 50000),
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4), sharey=True)
t0 = time.time()
for ax, (name, x) in zip(axes, samples.items()):
    fit = fit_power_law(x)
    p_fit = gof_p_value(x, fit, n_boot=200, rng=rng)
    tail = x[x >= fit["xmin"]]
    ll_power, ll_lognormal, ll_exp = tail_log_likelihoods(tail, fit["xmin"], fit["alpha"])
    r_ln, p_ln = vuong(ll_power, ll_lognormal)
    r_ex, p_ex = vuong(ll_power, ll_exp)
    print(name.replace("\n", " "))
    print(f"  xmin = {fit['xmin']:.1f}, alpha = {fit['alpha']:.2f} +/- {fit['se']:.2f}, "
          f"n_tail = {fit['n_tail']}, goodness-of-fit p = {p_fit:.2f}")
    print(f"  power law vs log-normal:  R = {r_ln:7.2f}, p = {p_ln:.3f}")
    print(f"  power law vs exponential: R = {r_ex:7.1f}, p = {p_ex:.1e}")

    xs = np.sort(x)
    ax.loglog(xs, 1.0 - np.arange(xs.size) / xs.size, ".", ms=2)
    grid = np.logspace(np.log10(fit["xmin"]), np.log10(xs[-1]), 50)
    ax.loglog(grid, fit["n_tail"] / x.size * (grid / fit["xmin"]) ** (1.0 - fit["alpha"]), "k--")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$P(X \geq x)$")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Figure 2: Empirical CCDFs (dots) and maximum likelihood power laws above the selected \(x_{\min}\) (dashed lines) for the three synthetic samples. The log-normal curves bend downwards beyond the fitted line, but only a large sample makes this bend statistically visible.





Read the output as the paper recommends. For the true power law the goodness-of-fit p-value is above 0.1 and the exponential is rejected with a huge \(R\). The log-normal cannot be told apart from the power law: its \(p\) is large, so the data do not choose between the two. For the log-normal sample of 2000 values the outcome depends on the draw. In 30 repeated draws (60 synthetic sets each) the power law was rejected at the 0.1 level in about half of the runs, so a non-rejection in a single run, which is common at this sample size, proves nothing. This is the warning of the paper that a large p-value does not establish a power law. For the large sample the power law is rejected, and the likelihood ratio favours the log-normal significantly.






NoteExercise



Apply the three steps to the absolute log returns of the lab series, a = np.abs(r - r.mean()). Report \(\hat{x}_{\min}\), \(\hat{\alpha}\), the number of observations above \(\hat{x}_{\min}\), the goodness-of-fit p-value, and the likelihood-ratio results against the log-normal and exponential. Convert \(\hat{\alpha}\) to the tail index of \(\Pr(|r| > x)\) and compare it with the Hill estimate of Tail Exponent. Which assumption of the method do volatility clustering and the synthetic fallback series put at risk?








TipSolution





The density exponent \(\hat{\alpha}\) and the tail index \(\alpha_{\text{tail}}\) of \(\Pr(|r| > x) \sim x^{-\alpha_{\text{tail}}}\) are related by \(\alpha_{\text{tail}} = \hat{\alpha} - 1\).

from amlab.finance import load_prices, log_returns

r = log_returns(load_prices()["close"])
a = np.abs(r - r.mean())
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

fit = fit_power_law(a, n_tail_min=100)
p_fit = gof_p_value(a, fit, n_boot=100, rng=rng)
tail = a[a >= fit["xmin"]]
ll_power, ll_lognormal, ll_exp = tail_log_likelihoods(tail, fit["xmin"], fit["alpha"])
print(f"xmin = {fit['xmin']:.4f}, alpha = {fit['alpha']:.2f} +/- {fit['se']:.2f}, "
      f"tail index = {fit['alpha'] - 1:.2f}, n_tail = {fit['n_tail']}, p = {p_fit:.2f}")
for name, ll in [("log-normal", ll_lognormal), ("exponential", ll_exp)]:
    R, p = vuong(ll_power, ll)
    print(f"power law vs {name}: R = {R:.2f}, p = {p:.3f}")

If \(p \le 0.1\), the power law is rejected for this range. Otherwise it is plausible, which is a weaker statement than “the tail is a power law”. For the likelihood ratios, a positive \(R\) with a small \(p\) favours the power law, a negative \(R\) with a small \(p\) favours the alternative, and a large \(p\) means that the data cannot decide. Both the bootstrap and the Vuong test assume independent observations. Volatility clustering makes the effective number of independent observations smaller than \(n_{\text{tail}}\), so the p-values are optimistic. If the series is the synthetic fallback of the lab, the result describes a GARCH simulation and not a market.

title: Fitting Power Laws Properly
text:
Limits of the method

The three steps assume that the tail observations are independent and identically distributed. Return series are not, so treat p-values as indicative.
The p-value is a tool for ruling a model out. Even a non-rejection is compatible with many other distributions, and the log-likelihood ratio can only compare the candidates you chose.
The authors scan every observed value as a candidate for \(x_{\min}\). The code above scans at most 100 quantiles of the data, which is faster and slightly coarser.
The code handles continuous data. For integer data Clauset et al. (2009) give a different (discrete) maximum likelihood estimator and an approximation that replaces \(x_{\min}\) by \(x_{\min} - \tfrac{1}{2}\) in the estimator of Power Laws, which they report to be accurate to about 1 % for \(x_{\min} \gtrsim 6\). Applying the continuous estimator to integer data is not recommended.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text: The mean squared displacement (MSD) measures how far a random walker spreads. It is the standard quantity you compute from tracked particles, cells or animals.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text:
Definition
For an ensemble of walkers that start at the origin,
\[
\mathrm{MSD}(t) = \langle |\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{x}(0)|^2 \rangle ,
\]
where \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) is the average over walkers. For the unbiased 1D lattice walk you found \(\langle x^2(n) \rangle = n\delta^2\) in The Random Walk.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text:
Diffusive scaling
A walker that takes one step every \(\tau\) seconds has made \(n = t/\tau\) steps at time \(t\). Then \(\langle x^2 \rangle = (t/\tau)\,\delta^2\). Berg (1993, Eqs. 1.9 to 1.11) defines the diffusion coefficient
\[
D = \frac{\delta^2}{2\tau}
\tag{1}\]
and obtains
\[
\langle x^2(t) \rangle = 2Dt .
\tag{2}\]
Motions along different axes are independent, so each coordinate contributes \(2Dt\). In \(d\) dimensions
\[
\langle r^2(t) \rangle = 2dDt ,
\tag{3}\]
which gives \(4Dt\) in the plane and \(6Dt\) in space (Berg 1993, Eqs. 1.13 and 1.14). The root-mean-square distance grows as \(\sqrt{t}\). To go twice as far, a diffusing particle needs four times as long.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text:
A simulated check
The figure uses 2000 planar walkers with independent Gaussian steps of standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\) per coordinate and \(\tau = 1\). Each coordinate has step variance \(\sigma^2\), so \(D = \sigma^2 / (2\tau) = 1/2\) and Equation 3 predicts \(\mathrm{MSD} = 4Dt = 2t\).








Figure 1: Simulated MSD of 2000 planar Gaussian walkers (dots) and the prediction \(4Dt\) with \(D = 1/2\) (line). On log-log axes a slope of 1 is the signature of normal diffusion.

title: Mean Squared Displacement
text:
Anomalous diffusion
Many experiments find \(\mathrm{MSD} \propto t^{\gamma}\) with \(\gamma \neq 1\). The case \(\gamma < 1\) is subdiffusion and \(\gamma > 1\) is superdiffusion (Metzler and Klafter 2000). Such behaviour requires that one of the random walk assumptions fails: steps are correlated, waiting times have no finite mean, or step lengths have no finite variance. You see the last case in Lévy flights.






NoteExercise



Estimate \(D\) from the simulation by fitting a straight line to \(\mathrm{MSD}(t)\) through the origin. How close is your estimate to \(1/2\)? Then fit the exponent \(\gamma\) as the slope of \(\log \mathrm{MSD}\) against \(\log t\).








TipSolution





The least-squares slope through the origin is \(\sum t\,\mathrm{MSD} / \sum t^2\), and \(D\) is that slope divided by \(2d = 4\).

slope = np.sum(t * msd) / np.sum(t**2)
gamma = np.polyfit(np.log(t[1:]), np.log(msd[1:]), 1)[0]
print(f"D estimate: {slope / 4:.3f}  (theory 0.5)")
print(f"exponent gamma: {gamma:.3f}  (theory 1)")

exponent gamma: 1.007  (theory 1)

title: Lévy Foraging
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Viswanathan et al. (1999), the whole letter (four pages).
Recommended: Metzler and Klafter (2000), for the mathematics of Lévy flights and walks.
Lévy Flights showed that step lengths with density \(\ell^{-\mu}\) and \(1 < \mu < 3\) spread faster than Brownian motion. This page asks whether such a walk is also a good way to search. Viswanathan et al. (1999) posed the question for a forager that looks for randomly placed targets, and the answer depends on a detail that is easy to overlook: what happens to a target after it has been found.

title: Lévy Foraging
text:
What the paper does
The model is deliberately simple. Targets are placed at random with mean spacing \(\lambda\), and the forager can detect a target only within a “direct vision” distance \(r_v\). The forager follows two rules.

If a target lies within \(r_v\), move straight to the nearest one.
Otherwise draw a direction at random and a flight length \(\ell\) from \(P(\ell) \propto \ell^{-\mu}\) with \(1 < \mu \le 3\), and fly towards that point, stopping early if a target comes within \(r_v\) on the way.

Foraging is destructive if a target disappears once it has been found, and non-destructive if it can be visited again, because it regenerates or because the forager returns to a patch. The search efficiency is the number of targets found per unit distance travelled,
\[
\eta = \frac{1}{\langle \ell \rangle\, N},
\tag{1}\]
where \(\langle \ell \rangle\) is the mean flight length and \(N\) is the mean number of flights between two successive targets (Viswanathan et al. 1999, Eq. 3). Long flights make \(\langle \ell \rangle\) large. Short flights make \(N\) large, because the forager keeps searching the same neighbourhood. An optimum can only exist if these two effects balance.
The paper’s mean-field argument treats all inter-target distances as equal to \(\lambda\), so that a flight longer than \(\lambda\) is counted as having length \(\lambda\): it ends at the next target. It then uses two scaling laws for the number of flights, \(N_d \sim (\lambda/r_v)^{\mu - 1}\) for destructive foraging and \(N_n \sim (\lambda/r_v)^{(\mu - 1)/2}\) for non-destructive foraging. The second one is smaller because a forager can revisit the site it has just left, which is cheap for a walker that stays close to it. The paper reports three regimes.

Dense targets (\(\lambda \lesssim r_v\)): \(\langle \ell \rangle \approx \lambda\) and \(N \approx 1\), so \(\eta\) does not depend on \(\mu\).
Sparse targets, destructive foraging: \(\eta\) has no maximum, and smaller \(\mu\) is always better. The forager should move almost in straight lines (\(\mu \to 1\)).
Sparse targets, non-destructive foraging: \(\eta\) is maximal at \(\mu_{\text{opt}} = 2 - \delta\), where the paper gives \(\delta \approx 1/[\ln(\lambda/r_v)]^2\). When \(\lambda/r_v\) is large but not known precisely, \(\mu \approx 2\) is the robust choice.

So “the optimum is \(\mu = 2\)” is a statement about sparse, revisitable targets only. The paper also notes that non-destructive foraging is the more realistic case, because food often sits in patches that regenerate, and that simulations of destructive foraging on patchy and fractal target sets gave results consistent with the non-destructive case on uniformly spread targets.

title: Lévy Foraging
text:
The mean-field curve
Equation (2) of the paper gives the mean flight length when flights longer than \(\lambda\) are counted as \(\lambda\) (I checked the closed form against numerical integration of \(\ell\,\ell^{-\mu}\)):
\[
\langle \ell \rangle = \frac{\mu - 1}{2 - \mu}\, r_v^{\mu - 1} \left( \lambda^{2 - \mu} - r_v^{2 - \mu} \right) + r_v^{\mu - 1} \lambda^{2 - \mu}.
\tag{2}\]
Combining it with \(N_n = (\lambda / r_v)^{(\mu-1)/2}\) in Equation 1 gives the efficiency curve of the figure.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def mean_flight(mu, lam, rv=1.0):
    """Mean flight length, Eq. (forage-meanl), with the cutoff at lam."""
    mu = np.asarray(mu, dtype=float)
    a = np.where(np.abs(2.0 - mu) < 1e-9, 1e-9, 2.0 - mu)  # avoids 0/0 at mu = 2
    return (mu - 1.0) * rv ** (mu - 1.0) * ((lam**a - rv**a) / a + lam**a / (mu - 1.0))


def efficiency_mean_field(mu, lam, rv=1.0):
    """eta = 1 / (N_n <l>) with N_n = (lam / rv)^((mu - 1) / 2)."""
    return 1.0 / ((lam / rv) ** ((np.asarray(mu) - 1.0) / 2.0) * mean_flight(mu, lam, rv))


mus = np.linspace(1.05, 3.0, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
for lam in [1e2, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5]:
    y = lam * efficiency_mean_field(mus, lam)
    ax.plot(mus, y / y.max(), label=rf"$\lambda/r_v = 10^{{{int(np.log10(lam))}}}$")
ax.set_xlabel(r"Lévy exponent $\mu$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\lambda\eta$, divided by its maximum")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Mean-field efficiency \(\lambda\eta\) of non-destructive foraging against the Lévy exponent \(\mu\) for four values of \(\lambda/r_v\), each curve divided by its maximum. The maximum approaches \(\mu = 2\) from below as targets become sparser.





The location of the maximum approaches 2 only logarithmically in \(\lambda/r_v\).

for lam in [1e2, 1e3, 1e4, 1e6, 1e9]:
    mu_opt = mus[np.argmax(efficiency_mean_field(mus, lam))]
    delta = 2.0 - mu_opt
    print(f"lambda/r_v = {lam:7.0e}: mu_opt = {mu_opt:.3f}, "
          f"delta = {delta:.4f}, delta * ln(lambda/r_v)^2 = {delta * np.log(lam)**2:.2f}")

lambda/r_v =   1e+02: mu_opt = 1.817, delta = 0.1827, delta * ln(lambda/r_v)^2 = 3.87
lambda/r_v =   1e+03: mu_opt = 1.910, delta = 0.0898, delta * ln(lambda/r_v)^2 = 4.29
lambda/r_v =   1e+04: mu_opt = 1.944, delta = 0.0556, delta * ln(lambda/r_v)^2 = 4.72
lambda/r_v =   1e+06: mu_opt = 1.974, delta = 0.0263, delta * ln(lambda/r_v)^2 = 5.02
lambda/r_v =   1e+09: mu_opt = 1.988, delta = 0.0117, delta * ln(lambda/r_v)^2 = 5.00


The offset \(\delta\) does scale like \(1/[\ln(\lambda/r_v)]^2\), as the paper states, but with a prefactor between about 4 and 5 for these formulas and not 1. The statement in the paper is an order-of-magnitude one.

title: Lévy Foraging
text:
A simulation
The simulation below follows the two rules on a ring, with some choices of my own that the paper does not specify.

Successive targets are separated by a gap drawn uniformly from \((\lambda/2, 3\lambda/2)\). Uniformly random positions would create pairs of targets closer than \(r_v\), and a non-destructive forager would then bounce between them at almost no cost and inflate \(\eta\).
Flight lengths are drawn from \(P(\ell) \propto \ell^{-\mu}\) with \(\ell \ge r_v\) and truncated at the ring length.
The target the forager stands on is ignored when it chooses its next move. A later return to a target counts as a new find in the non-destructive case, as in the paper’s model.


from bisect import bisect_right


def forage(mu, lam, destructive, n_found, rng, rv=1.0, n_targets=2000):
    """Targets found per unit distance for a 1D forager on a ring."""
    gaps = rng.uniform(0.5 * lam, 1.5 * lam, n_targets)
    t = np.cumsum(gaps).tolist()
    L = float(gaps.sum())
    x = rng.random() * L
    skip, found, dist = None, 0, 0.0
    while found < n_found:
        n = len(t)
        i = bisect_right(t, x)
        ahead = next(t[(i + j) % n] for j in range(3) if t[(i + j) % n] != skip)
        behind = next(t[(i - 1 - j) % n] for j in range(3) if t[(i - 1 - j) % n] != skip)
        da, db = (ahead - x) % L, (x - behind) % L
        hit = None
        if min(da, db) <= rv:  # rule 1: a target in direct vision
            hit, step = (ahead, da) if da <= db else (behind, db)
        else:  # rule 2: a new random flight
            length = min(rv * (1.0 - rng.random()) ** (-1.0 / (mu - 1.0)), L)
            if rng.random() < 0.5:
                if da - rv <= length:
                    hit, step = ahead, da
                else:
                    x, step = (x + length) % L, length
            else:
                if db - rv <= length:
                    hit, step = behind, db
                else:
                    x, step = (x - length) % L, length
        dist += step
        skip = hit
        if hit is not None:
            x = hit
            found += 1
            if destructive:
                t.remove(hit)
    return found / dist

Destructive foraging with a large \(\mu\) needs about \(\lambda^{\mu - 1}\) flights per target, so the destructive runs use a shorter grid and fewer targets.

mu_grid = np.round(np.arange(1.2, 3.01, 0.2), 1)
short_grid = mu_grid[mu_grid <= 2.4]
settings = [  # (lambda / r_v, destructive, mu values, targets per run, runs)
    (3, False, mu_grid, 300, 16), (3, True, short_grid, 100, 8),
    (100, False, mu_grid, 300, 16), (100, True, short_grid, 100, 8),
    (1000, False, mu_grid, 300, 16),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.4))
best = {}
for lam, destructive, grid, n_found, reps in settings:
    ax = axes[[3, 100, 1000].index(lam)]
    eta = []
    for mu in grid:
        rng = np.random.default_rng(1000 * lam + int(10 * mu) + 7 * destructive)
        eta.append(lam * np.mean([forage(mu, lam, destructive, n_found, rng) for _ in range(reps)]))
    label = "destructive" if destructive else "non-destructive"
    ax.semilogy(grid, eta, "s-" if destructive else "o-", ms=4, label=label)
    ax.set_title(rf"$\lambda/r_v = {lam}$")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"Lévy exponent $\mu$")
    best[(lam, label)] = grid[int(np.argmax(eta))]
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\lambda\,\eta$")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

for (lam, label), mu in best.items():
    if lam >= 100:
        print(f"lambda/r_v = {lam:4d}, {label:15s}: best mu on the grid = {mu:.1f}")







Figure 2: Simulated search efficiency \(\lambda\eta\) of a one-dimensional forager against the Lévy exponent \(\mu\), on a logarithmic vertical axis. Left: dense targets, \(\lambda/r_v = 3\), where \(\eta\) hardly depends on \(\mu\). Centre and right: sparse targets, \(\lambda/r_v = 100\) and \(1000\). For sparse targets non-destructive foraging has a maximum near \(\mu = 2\), and destructive foraging (shown for \(\mu \le 2.4\)) does not improve with \(\mu\). Each point averages independent runs.





lambda/r_v =  100, non-destructive: best mu on the grid = 1.8
lambda/r_v =  100, destructive    : best mu on the grid = 1.2
lambda/r_v = 1000, non-destructive: best mu on the grid = 2.2


The non-destructive curves for sparse targets are broad maxima around \(\mu \approx 2\), with the peak a little below 2 for \(\lambda/r_v = 100\), as the mean-field curve predicts. Destructive foraging is far less efficient at the same \(\lambda\) and gets worse as \(\mu\) grows, and for dense targets nothing depends on \(\mu\). The qualitative picture of the paper is reproduced; the exact location of the maximum is blurred by statistical noise and by the model details listed above.






NoteExercise




Use efficiency_mean_field to find \(\mu_{\text{opt}}\) for \(\lambda/r_v = 10^2, 10^4, 10^8\) and compare with \(2 - 1/[\ln(\lambda/r_v)]^2\). (b) With forage, estimate \(\lambda\eta\) for \(\lambda/r_v = 100\) at \(\mu = 2\) using ring sizes of 500 and 4000 targets. Is the result sensitive to the size of the ring?









TipSolution






fine = np.linspace(1.05, 3.0, 4000)
for lam in [1e2, 1e4, 1e8]:
    mu_opt = fine[np.argmax(efficiency_mean_field(fine, lam))]
    print(f"lambda/r_v = {lam:6.0e}: mu_opt = {mu_opt:.3f}, 2 - 1/ln^2 = {2 - 1 / np.log(lam)**2:.3f}")

for n_targets in [500, 4000]:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
    eta = np.mean([forage(2.0, 100, False, 300, rng, n_targets=n_targets) for _ in range(16)])
    print(f"{n_targets:5d} targets: lambda*eta = {100 * eta:.2f}")

lambda/r_v =  1e+02: mu_opt = 1.818, 2 - 1/ln^2 = 1.953
lambda/r_v =  1e+04: mu_opt = 1.945, 2 - 1/ln^2 = 1.988
lambda/r_v =  1e+08: mu_opt = 1.985, 2 - 1/ln^2 = 1.997
  500 targets: lambda*eta = 1.82
 4000 targets: lambda*eta = 1.70


The prefactor-free formula \(2 - 1/\ln^2\) overshoots the mean-field optimum: the two agree only in the limit of enormous \(\lambda/r_v\). The simulated efficiency agrees within about 10 % for both ring sizes, as long as the ring contains many more targets than a forager finds in one run.

title: Lévy Foraging
section: What the paper does not show
text:
What the paper does not show

The analytical results rest on a mean-field estimate that assumes equal distances between targets. The paper also assumes a finite cutoff on the flight length, which makes the flight distribution a truncated Lévy distribution. Such a walk converges to Gaussian behaviour only after a very large number of steps, and without a cutoff the mean flight length diverges for \(\mu \le 2\) (Viswanathan et al. 1999).
The comparison with data uses published flight-length or foraging-time histograms for bumble-bees, wandering albatrosses and deer, and a published range of \(2 \le \mu \le 2.5\) for amoebae. The bee data are reported with \(\mu \approx 2\) at low nectar concentration and \(\mu \approx 3.5\) at higher concentration, where long flights become rare and the model predicts no advantage for Lévy flights. The exponents are read from double-logarithmic plots of digitised histograms, and the letter reports neither a fitting method nor uncertainties. Given the pitfalls of that practice (see Power Laws and Fitting Power Laws Properly), treat these exponents as consistent with \(\mu \approx 2\) and not as precise estimates.
Short-range correlations in flight directions and lengths can change the width of \(P(\ell)\) but not \(\mu\), according to the authors, so learning and short-term memory do not alter the long-distance result. This is an argument in the paper and is not tested here.

title: SIS Initial State
SIS Initial State
text:
Initialize States
Store the state of each individual directly on the graph as a node attribute called state.
For example, start with everyone susceptible: create the attribute “state” and set it to “S” for all nodes:

nx.set_node_attributes(G, "S", "state")

print("Node 0:", G.nodes[0])  # node attributes are stored in a dictionary

Node 0: {'state': 'S'}


To infect node 20:

node_20 = G.nodes[20]
node_20["state"] = "I"

print("Node 20:", G.nodes[20])  # now node 20 has state "I"

Node 20: {'state': 'I'}


Alternatively, use a dictionary to set the states of multiple nodes at once:

# Infect nodes 20, 35, and 50
# The rest will be susceptible by default
state_dict = {node: "I" if node in [20, 35, 50] else "S" for node in G.nodes()}
nx.set_node_attributes(G, state_dict, "state")

print("Node 20:", G.nodes[20])  # node 20 is infected
print("Node 21:", G.nodes[21])  # node 21 is susceptible

Node 20: {'state': 'I'}
Node 21: {'state': 'S'}

TipSolution





The optional rng argument lets a whole simulation share one generator; you will need it on the next page.

def initialize_state(G, initial_infected=5, seed=SEED, rng=None):
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    # Start everyone susceptible
    nx.set_node_attributes(G, "S", "state")

    # Infect a random subset
    infected = rng.choice(list(G.nodes()), size=initial_infected, replace=False)
    for node in infected:
        G.nodes[node]["state"] = "I"

    return G




Always validate your functions. Here, check that the number of infected nodes is correct:

initialize_state(G, initial_infected=initial_infected, seed=SEED)
print(
    "Initially infected:",
    sum(G.nodes[node]["state"] == "I" for node in G.nodes()),
)

Initially infected: 5

text:
NoteToolkit page



This page is self-study material for the network labs. It continues NetworkX Basics.
The first chunk rebuilds the country graph of the previous page, with four nodes and a population attribute.
import networkx as nx

G = nx.Graph()
G.add_node("Spain", population=47_000_000)
G.add_node("Portugal", population=10_000_000)
G.add_node("France", population=67_000_000)
G.add_node("Italy", population=60_000_000)

title: Edges and Weights
text:
Edges (Links)
Edges represent the connections between nodes in a graph. To add edges to the graph, you can use the add_edge(<node1>, <node2>) method. This will create an undirected edge between node1 and node2 (you refer to nodes by their IDs). You can see the list of edges in the graph using the edges() method.

# Add edges between the nodes (neighboring countries)
G.add_edge("Spain", "Portugal")
G.add_edge("Spain", "France")
# Show the edges in the graph
print(G.edges())

[('Spain', 'Portugal'), ('Spain', 'France')]


Because you are working on an undirected graph, the connection between two nodes does not have a direction. However, you can also create directed graphs where the edges have a direction (from one node to another) using DiGraph() instead of Graph(). In a directed graph, you use add_edge(<source>, <target>) to specify the direction of the edge.

Edge Attributes
Just like nodes, edges can also have attributes, such as weight, which might represent the strength of the connection. For example, in a social network, an edge might represent a friendship between two people, and the weight could represent how close they are.
You can add attributes to an edge by accessing it through G.edges[<node1>, <node2>] and assigning values to the attributes. For example, add a “distance” (between capitals) attribute to represent the distance between the countries:

# Add distance attribute to the edges
G.edges["Spain", "Portugal"]["distance"] = 600  # distance in kilometers
G.edges["Spain", "France"]["distance"] = 1000  # distance in kilometers

# Show the edges with their attributes
distance = nx.get_edge_attributes(G, 'distance')
for edge, dist in distance.items():
    print(f"{edge}: {dist} km")

('Spain', 'Portugal'): 600 km
('Spain', 'France'): 1000 km


Using get_edge_attributes(<graph>, <attribute>), you can retrieve the distance attribute for all edges in the graph as a dictionary.
Again, you can also add attributes to an edge at the same time as you create it using the add_edge() method with keyword arguments. For example:

# Add a new edge with attributes
G.add_edge("France", "Italy", distance=800)

# Show the edges with their attributes
distance = nx.get_edge_attributes(G, 'distance')
for edge, dist in distance.items():
    print(f"{edge}: {dist} km")

('Spain', 'Portugal'): 600 km
('Spain', 'France'): 1000 km
('France', 'Italy'): 800 km




Adding Nodes and Edges Together
You can also add nodes and edges together using the add_edge() method. If you add an edge between two nodes that do not exist in the graph, networkx will automatically create those nodes. For example:

# Add an edge between two nodes that do not exist
G.add_edge("USA", "Canada", distance=3000)
G.add_edge("Netherlands", "Germany", distance=500)
G.add_edge("Germany", "France", distance=900)

# Add the population attribute for the new nodes separately
G.nodes["USA"]["population"] = 331_000_000
G.nodes["Canada"]["population"] = 38_000_000
G.nodes["Netherlands"]["population"] = 17_000_000
G.nodes["Germany"]["population"] = 83_000_000

# Show the nodes and edges in the graph
print("Nodes:", G.nodes())
print("Edges:", G.edges())

Nodes: ['Spain', 'Portugal', 'France', 'Italy', 'USA', 'Canada', 'Netherlands', 'Germany']
Edges: [('Spain', 'Portugal'), ('Spain', 'France'), ('France', 'Italy'), ('France', 'Germany'), ('USA', 'Canada'), ('Netherlands', 'Germany')]




Weighted Edges
The most common edge attribute is weight, which represents the strength of the connection between two nodes. For example, in a social network, the weight of an edge could represent how close two people are. In a transportation network, the weight could represent the distance or travel time between two locations.
Weight is so common that networkx has a special method to add weighted edges: add_weighted_edges_from(). This method takes a list of tuples, where each tuple contains the source node, target node, and weight of the edge. For example:

# Initialize a directed graph
D_contracts = nx.DiGraph()

# Add weighted edges (contracts between companies with the amount of money as weight)
# Disclaimer: weights are made up
weighted_edges = [
    ("OpenAI", "Microsoft", 100_000_000),
    ("OpenAI", "Oracle", 50_000_000),
    ("Microsoft", "Nvidia", 20_000_000),
    ("Oracle", "Nvidia", 10_000_000),
    ("Nvidia", "OpenAI", 5_000_000),
]
D_contracts.add_weighted_edges_from(weighted_edges)

# Show the edges with their weights
weights = nx.get_edge_attributes(D_contracts, 'weight')
for edge, weight in weights.items():
    print(f"{edge}: ${weight}")

('OpenAI', 'Microsoft'): $100000000
('OpenAI', 'Oracle'): $50000000
('Microsoft', 'Nvidia'): $20000000
('Oracle', 'Nvidia'): $10000000
('Nvidia', 'OpenAI'): $5000000

title: Drawing Attributes
text:
Visualizing Attributes

Node Attributes
You can also visualize the attributes of nodes and edges by using different colors or sizes. For example, you can color the nodes based on their population attribute:

# Get the population attribute for each node
population = nx.get_node_attributes(G, 'population')
# Draw the graph with node sizes proportional to population
node_sizes = [population[node] / 1_000_000 for node in G.nodes()]  # scale down for visualization

pos = nx.circular_layout(G)

nx.draw(
    G,
    pos=pos,
    with_labels=True,
    node_color='lightblue',
    edge_color='gray',
    node_size=node_sizes,  # size of the nodes (vertices) proportional to population
    font_size=12,
    )
plt.show()














TipWhat happens if a node is missing an attribute?





In this case, the population dictionary will not have an entry for that node, and trying to access it will raise a KeyError. To avoid this, you can use the get() method of the dictionary, which lets you specify a default value if the key is not found. For example:

# Add a new node without the population attribute
G.add_edge("Denmark", "Germany", distance=400)
# Get the population attribute for each node, using 0 as default if not found
population = nx.get_node_attributes(G, 'population')
# Draw the graph with node sizes proportional to population
node_sizes = [population.get(node, 0) / 1_000_000 for node in G.nodes()]  # scale down for visualization

pos = nx.circular_layout(G)

nx.draw(
    G,
    pos=pos,
    with_labels=True,
    node_color='lightblue',
    edge_color='gray',
    node_size=node_sizes,  # size of the nodes (vertices) proportional to population
    font_size=12,
    )
plt.show()

















NoteExercise



Add a new attribute to the nodes, called “visited”, which is a boolean that indicates whether you have visited that country or not. Then, visualize the graph by coloring the nodes differently based on whether you have visited them or not: use blue for visited countries and red for unvisited countries.
G.nodes["Spain"]["visited"] = True
# TODO: set "visited" for the other countries

visited = nx.get_node_attributes(G, "visited")
node_colors = # TODO: one colour per node, "blue" if visited, else "red"
nx.draw(G, pos=nx.circular_layout(G), with_labels=True, node_color=node_colors)
plt.show()








TipSolution





Nodes without the attribute (here Netherlands, Germany and Denmark) count as not visited, thanks to visited.get(node, False).

# Add the "visited" attribute to the nodes
G.nodes["Spain"]["visited"] = True
G.nodes["Portugal"]["visited"] = True
G.nodes["France"]["visited"] = True
G.nodes["Italy"]["visited"] = True
G.nodes["USA"]["visited"] = False
G.nodes["Canada"]["visited"] = True

# Get the "visited" attribute for each node
visited = nx.get_node_attributes(G, 'visited')
# Define node colors based on the "visited" attribute
node_colors = ['blue' if visited.get(node, False) else 'red' for node in G.nodes()]

pos = nx.circular_layout(G)

# Draw the graph with node colors based on the "visited" attribute
nx.draw(
    G,
    pos=pos,
    with_labels=True,
    node_color=node_colors,  # color of the nodes based on "visited" attribute
    edge_color='gray',
    node_size=2000,
    font_size=12,
    )
plt.show()













Edge Attributes
You can also visualize edge attributes by showing them as labels on the edges. For example, you can show the distance attribute on the edges:

# Get the distance attribute for each edge
distance = nx.get_edge_attributes(G, 'distance')
# Draw the graph
pos = nx.circular_layout(G)
nx.draw(
    G,
    pos=pos,
    with_labels=True,
    node_color='lightblue',
    edge_color='gray',
    node_size=2000,
    font_size=12,
    )
# Draw edge labels for the distance attribute
nx.draw_networkx_edge_labels(G, pos, edge_labels=distance)
plt.show()
