title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Pastor-Satorras et al. (2015), Sections IV.B (degree-based mean field), V.A (SIS) and V.B (SIR).
Recommended: Newman (2002).
What the review states: For the SIS model, the degree-based mean-field theory gives the threshold \(\lambda_c = \langle k \rangle / \langle k^2 \rangle\) (their Eq. 28), which tends to zero for degree exponents \(2 < \gamma \le 3\) in the limit of infinite size. For SIR, the mapping to bond percolation gives for tree-like uncorrelated networks the exact threshold in transmissibility \(T_c = \langle k \rangle / (\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle)\) (their Eq. 60), and for exponentially distributed infectious periods, where the mean transmissibility is \(\lambda/(1+\lambda)\), the threshold in the rate ratio \(\lambda_c = \langle k \rangle / (\langle k^2 \rangle - 2\langle k \rangle)\) (their Eq. 62). The expression \(\langle k \rangle / (\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle)\) also appears in their Eq. 53 as a threshold in \(\lambda\) from a modified degree-based mean field, which they call an approximation of the exact result. They warn that the individual-based mean-field threshold \(1/\Lambda_1\), applied to SIR, is qualitatively wrong for \(\gamma > 3\).
In the well-mixed SIS model of Compartmental Models, an infection persists only if \(R_0 > 1\). On a network, the corresponding condition depends on the degree distribution. This page derives it and states exactly when the threshold vanishes.

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
Setup
Use the continuous-time SIS model: each S-I edge transmits at rate \(\beta\) and each infected node recovers at rate \(\mu\). The spreading rate is \(\lambda = \beta/\mu\). In the discrete-time simulations of SIS Simulation, \(\lambda \approx \beta/\mu\) when both probabilities are small.

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
Homogeneous mean field
If every node had exactly \(\langle k \rangle\) neighbours, the infected density \(\rho\) would obey \(\dot\rho = -\rho + \lambda\langle k \rangle \rho(1-\rho)\) (time in units of \(1/\mu\)). The threshold is \(\lambda_c = 1/\langle k \rangle\) (Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015).

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
Heterogeneous mean field
Now group nodes by degree. Let \(\rho_k\) be the fraction of infected nodes among nodes of degree \(k\). Assume an uncorrelated network: an edge leads to a node of degree \(k'\) with probability \(k' p_{k'}/\langle k \rangle\). Then (Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani 2001; Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015)
\[
\frac{d\rho_k}{dt} = -\rho_k + \lambda k (1 - \rho_k)\,\Theta, \qquad \Theta = \frac{1}{\langle k \rangle}\sum_{k'} k' p_{k'} \rho_{k'} .
\]
Linearize around \(\rho_k = 0\). Multiply by \(k p_k / \langle k \rangle\) and sum over \(k\): \(\dot\Theta = \left(\lambda \langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle - 1\right)\Theta\). The disease-free state becomes unstable when
\[
\lambda > \lambda_c = \frac{\langle k \rangle}{\langle k^2 \rangle}.
\]
For a Poisson degree distribution, \(\langle k^2 \rangle = \langle k \rangle^2 + \langle k \rangle\) and \(\lambda_c = 1/(\langle k \rangle + 1)\), close to the homogeneous result. For SIR the analogous result is a critical transmissibility \(T_c = \langle k \rangle / (\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle)\) (Newman 2002). Note that this is a threshold in the transmissibility \(T\), the probability that an infected node transmits to a given neighbour before recovering, and not in the rate ratio \(\lambda\). With exponentially distributed infectious periods \(T = \lambda/(1+\lambda)\), so \(T_c = 1/(\kappa - 1)\) with \(\kappa = \langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle\) corresponds to \(\lambda_c = 1/(\kappa - 2) = \langle k \rangle / (\langle k^2 \rangle - 2\langle k \rangle)\) (Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015, Eq. 62). For a Poisson graph with \(\langle k \rangle = 6\) this gives \(T_c = 1/6\) and \(\lambda_c = 1/5\). SIR as Bond Percolation derives the relation.

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
When does the threshold vanish?
For a scale-free distribution \(p_k \sim k^{-\gamma}\) with \(2 < \gamma \le 3\), \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) diverges as \(N \to \infty\), so \(\lambda_c \to 0\) (Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani 2001). Read this result with its assumptions:

It is an asymptotic result for an idealized infinite scale-free network with \(2 < \gamma \le 3\).
It relies on the heterogeneous mean-field approximation, which ignores degree correlations and the fixed structure of the contacts.
Every finite network has a largest degree \(k_{\max}\), so \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) is finite and the threshold is small but nonzero (Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani 2002). For the Barabási-Albert model, \(\langle k^2 \rangle \approx m(m+1)\ln N\) (see Preferential Attachment), so the formula gives \(\lambda_c \approx 2/\big((m+1)\ln N\big)\), which decreases only logarithmically with \(N\).
Other approximations give other finite-size thresholds. The quenched mean-field theory, which keeps the full adjacency matrix, predicts \(\lambda_c = 1/\Lambda_{\max}\), where \(\Lambda_{\max}\) is the largest eigenvalue of \(A\) (Castellano and Pastor-Satorras 2010; Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015).

Figure 1 computes both predictions on generated graphs.








Figure 1: Epidemic threshold predictions against network size for Barabási-Albert (m = 3) and Erdős-Rényi graphs with the same mean degree. Solid: heterogeneous mean field /<k^2>. Dashed: quenched mean field 1/Lambda_max. One graph per size.





BA HMF: [0.079 0.076 0.062 0.054 0.051]
ER HMF: [0.141 0.144 0.143 0.143 0.143]


For the ER graphs the threshold stays near \(1/(\langle k \rangle + 1) = 1/7 \approx 0.14\). For the BA graphs it decreases slowly with \(N\) but stays well above zero at every size you can simulate.

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
Spread it yourself
The simulation uses the discrete-time update of the lab: a susceptible node with \(m\) infected neighbours is infected with probability \(1 - (1-\beta)^m\), and an infected node recovers with probability \(\mu\). Both networks have mean degree close to 6, as in Figure 1. Vaccinated nodes start immune.


Choose SIS, keep \(\mu = 0.1\) and set \(\beta = 0.015\), so \(\lambda = 0.15\). Run several times on the Barabási–Albert graph, then on the Erdős–Rényi graph. On which network does the infection survive? Compare \(\lambda\) with \(\langle k \rangle / \langle k^2 \rangle\) in the readout.
Back to SIR with \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\mu = 0.1\) on the Barabási–Albert graph. Vaccinate 10% of the nodes at random, then 10% of the hubs first. How much smaller is the final epidemic?
Press Compare strategies over g on each network. Why does vaccinating hubs help so much more on the Barabási–Albert graph than on the Erdős–Rényi graph?
Acquaintance vaccination uses only local information. Where does its curve fall between the other two, and why does a random neighbour tend to be a hub?



Build this in Python. In the lab you write the code behind this figure: SIR Simulation and Vaccination Strategies. You will code the synchronous SIS/SIR update on a NetworkX graph, run it on generated and real networks, and compare random, acquaintance and targeted immunization.







NoteExercise



A BA network with \(m = 3\) has \(N = 10^9\) nodes. Estimate \(\lambda_c\) from the heterogeneous mean-field formula. Compare it with an ER graph with the same mean degree.








TipSolution





\(\lambda_c \approx 2/\big((m+1)\ln N\big) = 2/(4 \times 20.7) \approx 0.024\). The ER graph gives \(\lambda_c = 1/(\langle k \rangle + 1) = 1/7 \approx 0.14\) at any size. Even for a network the size of a large country the BA threshold is small but clearly positive.

title: Epidemic Threshold
text:
Optional extension






NoteExercise



Use amlab.networks_spreading.run_sis_fast on a BA graph with \(N = 2000\). Fix \(\mu = 0.05\), vary \(\beta\), and plot the long-time prevalence against \(\lambda = \beta/\mu\). Locate the value of \(\lambda\) where the prevalence leaves zero and compare it with both predictions.








TipSolution





Start from 50 infected nodes, run 1000 steps and average the last 200 steps over 3 runs.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
from amlab.networks_spreading import run_sis_fast

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(2000, 3, seed=7)
mu = 0.05
lams = np.linspace(0.02, 0.2, 10)
prevalence = [
    np.mean([run_sis_fast(G, lam * mu, mu, steps=1000, initial_infected=50, rng=rng)[-200:].mean() for _ in range(3)])
    for lam in lams
]
k = np.array([d for _, d in G.degree()], dtype=float)
plt.plot(lams, prevalence, "o-")
plt.axvline(k.mean() / (k**2).mean(), color="grey", ls=":", label="<k>/<k²>")
plt.xlabel(r"$\lambda = \beta/\mu$")
plt.ylabel("long-time prevalence")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
For this graph both predictions give \(\lambda_c \approx 0.059\). The simulated prevalence is still zero at \(\lambda = 0.08\) and becomes positive between \(0.08\) and \(0.10\). The mean-field theories ignore dynamical correlations: a newly infected node cannot pass the infection back to the neighbour that infected it while that neighbour is still infected, so part of the infection attempts are wasted and the true threshold is higher. On a finite graph, fluctuations also end outbreaks that are just above threshold within the simulated time.



See also: SIR as Bond Percolation, which derives the threshold from the transmissibility of the epidemic.

title: Module 5: Complex Networks
text:
This module replaces the well-mixed populations of Modules 1 and 2 by networks: who interacts with whom is now given by a graph. You will measure the structure of networks, build the classical models of network growth, and study three processes whose outcome depends on that structure: percolation under node removal, cascades of overload failures, and epidemic spreading (Newman 2003; Newman 2018). The code uses networkx (Hagberg et al. 2008). Reusable functions are in amlab/networks_cascades/ and amlab/networks_spreading/.

Session Structure
Session 23: Networks: fundamental concepts
Network Concepts Robustness and Percolation PageRank
Toolkit (self-study before the labs):
NetworkX Basics Edges and Weights Drawing Graphs Drawing Attributes Graphs from Edge Lists Paths and Components Paths in Directed Graphs Degree and Clustering Centrality in NetworkX
Session 24: Laboratory: cascading failures in power grids
The Iberian Blackout The Motter-Lai Model Cascade Simulation Swing Equation
Session 25: Models of network growth
Erdős-Rényi Random Graphs Small-World Networks Preferential Attachment Comparing Graph Models Scaling of Path Length and Clustering Triadic Closure (Holme-Kim) The Configuration Model
Session 26: Laboratory: spreading processes on networks
SIS Model on Networks SIS Initial State SIS Simulation Comparing Networks under SIS SIR on Networks SIR Simulation Epidemic Threshold SIR as Bond Percolation Vaccination Strategies Metapopulation Epidemics
Practice: Real Networks Practice: Flights and Other Networks Practice: Propagation



Learning Goals
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

Represent a real system as a graph and load network data with networkx.
Compute and interpret degree distributions, path lengths, clustering, centrality and communities.
Apply the Molloy-Reed criterion to predict when a network keeps a giant component under random failure, and explain why targeted attacks are more damaging on heterogeneous networks.
Implement the Motter-Lai cascade model, validate it, and explain what it leaves out compared with a real power grid event.
Generate Erdős-Rényi, Watts-Strogatz and Barabási-Albert networks and relate their properties to the model rules.
Simulate SIS and SIR on networks with reproducible seeds, derive the threshold \(\lambda_c = \langle k \rangle / \langle k^2 \rangle\), and state the assumptions behind the vanishing threshold of scale-free networks.
Compare random, targeted and acquaintance vaccination.
Compute PageRank by power iteration and explain the role of the damping factor and of dangling nodes.
Explain how path length and clustering scale with network size in the ER, WS and BA models, and how triadic closure raises clustering in growing networks.
Build configuration-model graphs and degree-preserving null models, and relate SIR to bond percolation through the transmissibility.
Simulate an epidemic on a network of patches linked by mobility and distinguish its effect on arrival time from its effect on final size.








References

Hagberg, Aric A., Daniel A. Schult, and Pieter J. Swart. 2008. “Exploring Network Structure, Dynamics, and Function Using NetworkX.” Proceedings of the 7th Python in Science Conference (SciPy 2008), 11–15.


Newman, M. E. J. 2003. “The Structure and Function of Complex Networks.” SIAM Review 45 (2): 167–256. https://doi.org/10.1137/S003614450342480.


Newman, Mark. 2018. Networks. 2nd ed. Oxford University Press.

title: NetworkX Basics
text:
NoteToolkit page



This page is self-study material for the network labs. Work through it before the network labs.
A graph models pairwise relations between objects. It consists of nodes (also called vertices) and edges (also called links) that connect pairs of nodes (Newman 2018).
This page shows how to build graphs with the networkx library (Hagberg et al. 2008). NetworkX is a Python package for the creation, manipulation and study of the structure, dynamics and functions of complex networks. The examples follow A First Course in Network Science (Menczer et al. 2020); see the book’s GitHub repository. The folder references/networkx_indiana of this repository has the matching notebooks. You will learn to:
First, import the library:
Now initialize an empty graph:
G = nx.Graph()

print(G)

Graph with 0 nodes and 0 edges
G is now an empty undirected graph. The next sections add nodes and edges to it.

title: NetworkX Basics
text:
Nodes (Vertices)
Nodes represent the entities in a graph. They can be anything: people in a social network, airports in a flight network, or web pages in the internet.
To add nodes, use the add_node(<id>) method. The <id> can be any hashable Python object. You can see the list of nodes in the graph using the nodes() method.

# Add three nodes to the graph
G.add_node("Spain")
G.add_node("Portugal")
G.add_node("France")

# Show the nodes in the graph
print(G.nodes())

['Spain', 'Portugal', 'France']








TipWhat does “hashable” mean?





In Python, a hashable object is an object that has a hash value that remains constant during its lifetime. This means that the object can be used as a key in a dictionary or as an element in a set. Examples of hashable objects include integers, strings, and tuples (as long as they contain only hashable types). Lists and dictionaries are not hashable because they are mutable (their contents can change).




Node Attributes
Each node can have attributes that provide additional information about it. For example, in a social network, a node might represent a person and have attributes like name, age, or location.
NetworkX stores attributes on nodes. Think of G.nodes as a dictionary where the keys are the node IDs and the values are dictionaries of attributes. You can add attributes to a node by accessing it through G.nodes[<id>] and assigning values to the attributes.
For example, add a “population” attribute to the country nodes:

# Add population attribute to the nodes
G.nodes["Spain"]["population"] = 47_000_000
G.nodes["Portugal"]["population"] = 10_000_000
G.nodes["France"]["population"] = 67_000_000

# Show the nodes with their attributes
population = nx.get_node_attributes(G, 'population')
for node, pop in population.items():
    print(f"{node}: {pop} inhabitants")

Spain: 47000000 inhabitants
Portugal: 10000000 inhabitants
France: 67000000 inhabitants

title: Comparing Networks under SIS
text:
Interpretation






NoteExercise



Compare Figure 1 with your prediction on SIS Model on Networks:

Which network type sustains infection longer at the same \((\beta, \mu)\)?
Do hubs (scale-free) make persistence easier? Why?
How does clustering (small-world) change local outbreaks vs global spread?
If you increase \(N\) but keep average degree similar, what do you expect to happen?









TipSolution






The scale-free graph. At \(\beta = 0.02\) it keeps close to 20% of its nodes infected, the random graph a few percent and the small-world graph almost none.
Yes. A hub has many neighbours, so it is reinfected soon after it recovers, and while infected it exposes many susceptible nodes. This is why the threshold \(\langle k \rangle / \langle k^2 \rangle\) of Epidemic Threshold is lower on heterogeneous networks.
In the small-world graph most neighbours of an infected node are also neighbours of each other. Many infection attempts hit nodes that are already infected, and the outbreak stays local for longer. Only the few rewired shortcuts carry it across the ring.
With 5 initial infected nodes, a larger \(N\) starts from a smaller infected fraction, so the curves take longer to rise. The long-time prevalence depends on the threshold. For the random and small-world graphs the threshold does not depend on \(N\) at fixed mean degree. For the Barabási-Albert graph \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) grows like \(\ln N\), so its threshold decreases slowly and persistence becomes easier.

title: Comparing Networks under SIS
text:
Limitations

Time is discrete and all nodes update at once. The continuous-time SIS model used in the theory of Epidemic Threshold has rates instead of probabilities; for small \(\beta\) and \(\mu\) the two are close.
The contact network is static. Real contacts change over time.
Every node has the same \(\beta\) and \(\mu\).
With \(N = 150\) and 12 runs the curves are noisy, and on a finite network SIS always dies out eventually, although this can take extremely long above the threshold.

TipSolution





def node_loads(G):
    return nx.betweenness_centrality(G, normalized=False)


def run_cascade(G, trigger, alpha, tol=1e-9):
    loads0 = node_loads(G)
    capacity = {v: (1 + alpha) * load for v, load in loads0.items()}
    H = G.copy()
    H.remove_node(trigger)
    while True:
        loads = node_loads(H)
        overloaded = [v for v, load in loads.items() if load > capacity[v] + tol]
        if not overloaded:
            break
        H.remove_nodes_from(overloaded)
    largest = max(nx.connected_components(H), key=len) if len(H) else set()
    return len(largest) / G.number_of_nodes()
The small tolerance tol protects the test load > capacity from rounding errors: with \(\alpha = 0\) an unchanged load must not count as an overload.

text:
Validation
Check your code on cases with a known answer before you trust any plot. The chunk below uses the amlab version; run the same checks on yours.

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

from amlab.networks_cascades import run_cascade, select_trigger, cascade_curve

# A cycle has equal loads everywhere. Removing one node turns it into a path.
C = nx.cycle_graph(12)
print("cycle, alpha = 10:", run_cascade(C, 0, alpha=10).G_ratio, "expected", 11 / 12)

# The centre of a star carries every shortest path.
S = nx.star_graph(10)
print("star, centre removed:", run_cascade(S, 0, alpha=1).G_ratio, "expected", 1 / 11)

# Very large alpha: only the trigger is lost on a well-connected graph.
G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(100, 3, seed=1)
r = run_cascade(G, select_trigger(G, "load"), alpha=100)
print("BA, alpha = 100: failed per step", r.failed_per_step)

Explain the output for the cycle with \(\alpha = 10\). Then predict what happens on the same cycle with \(\alpha = 0\) and check it.

After the removal the cycle becomes a path of 11 nodes. Loads grow near the middle of the path, but with \(\alpha = 10\) no node exceeds its capacity, so \(G = 11/12\). Interpretation






NoteExercise



Compare Figure 1 with your predictions:

For which graph and which trigger does the cascade stay small at small \(\alpha\)?
How large must \(\alpha\) be before the highest-load trigger stops causing a large cascade on the BA graph?
Motter and Lai found that heterogeneous networks are fragile to load-based attacks (Motter and Lai 2002). Does your plot agree? With a single graph realization of 150 nodes, which features of the curves would you trust and which not?









TipSolution






No combination keeps the cascade small at \(\alpha = 0\): every curve starts well below 1. Random triggers recover first: \(G\) is close to 1 from about \(\alpha = 0.25\) on both graphs.
On the BA graph the highest-load trigger still destroys a large part of the network at \(\alpha = 0.5\), and \(G\) stays below 0.9 up to \(\alpha = 1\). On the ER graph the same trigger stops causing large cascades near \(\alpha = 0.4\) to \(0.5\).
Yes: the gap between random and load-based triggers is much larger and lasts much longer on the BA graph, as Motter and Lai found. Trust this qualitative gap. Do not trust the exact values of \(\alpha\) or the small bumps: one graph of 150 nodes and 5 random trials give noisy curves.

title: Cascade Simulation
text:
Limitations

Load follows shortest paths. Electric power follows Kirchhoff’s laws and spreads over all parallel paths.
The model has no time: the redistribution is instantaneous. Schäfer et al. (2018) show that transient dynamics of a few seconds matter for real grid cascades.
Every node has the same relative margin \(\alpha\). Real equipment has heterogeneous limits and protection settings.
A node fails deterministically as soon as \(L_i > C_i\).
A single BA graph with \(N = 150\) gives noisy curves. Average over several graphs before you draw conclusions.







TipOptional extension




Average the curves over 10 graph realizations and add error bars.
Replace the trigger “highest load” with “highest degree” (select_trigger(G, "degree")). Do the two rankings give the same cascade?
Load a real network from data/ (for example the USA flights graph) and repeat the sweep on its largest component. Use nx.betweenness_centrality(G, k=..., seed=...) if the exact computation is too slow.

title: Erdős-Rényi Random Graphs
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory for the session: Watts and Strogatz (1998); Barabasi and Albert (1999) (see the Reading boxes of the next two pages).
For this page: Newman (2003), Section 4.1 (Poisson random graphs).
Recommended: Newman (2018); Newman (2003), Sections 6 and 7.
Real networks have short paths, high clustering and, often, hubs (Newman 2003). This page builds three models that reproduce some of these features. The first one is the simplest random graph: it serves as the null model against which you compare the others.

title: Erdős-Rényi Random Graphs
text:
The model
In the Gilbert model \(G(N, p)\) every pair of nodes is joined independently with probability \(p\) (Gilbert 1959). The closely related Erdős-Rényi model \(G(N, E)\) picks a graph uniformly among all graphs with exactly \(E\) edges (Erdos and Renyi 1959). For large \(N\) the two behave the same, and both go by the name “random graph”.
Let \(c = (N-1)p\) be the mean degree. Key properties, for large \(N\) with \(c\) fixed (Newman 2003, sec. 4.1; Newman 2018):

The degree distribution is binomial and tends to a Poisson distribution, \(p_k = e^{-c} c^k / k!\). So \(\langle k^2 \rangle = c^2 + c\).
The clustering coefficient is \(C = p = c/(N-1)\), which tends to zero as \(N\) grows.
A giant component exists if and only if \(c > 1\). This agrees with the Molloy-Reed criterion of Robustness and Percolation: \(\kappa = \langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle = c + 1 > 2\).
The fraction \(S\) of nodes in the giant component solves \(S = 1 - e^{-cS}\).
The typical distance grows like \(\ell \approx \ln N / \ln c\).

The same results can be written with \(\langle k \rangle = p(N-1)\) in place of \(c\), calling the average path length \(L\) and using \(p(k)\) for the degree distribution:
\[
p(k) = \binom{N-1}{k} p^k (1-p)^{N-1-k} \approx e^{-\langle k \rangle}\frac{\langle k \rangle^k}{k!}, \qquad L \sim \frac{\log N}{\log \langle k \rangle}, \qquad C = p \approx \frac{\langle k \rangle}{N}.
\]
Two remarks complete this summary. First, for large mean degree the Poisson distribution is approximately Gaussian with mean and variance \(\langle k \rangle\) (Stirling’s formula for \(k!\)), so the degree distribution of a random graph is narrow, without hubs. A direct comparison gives a largest pointwise difference between the Poisson and the Gaussian densities of 0.021 at \(\langle k \rangle = 5\) (the peak of the Poisson is 0.176) and 0.0019 at \(\langle k \rangle = 50\) (peak 0.056). Second, the formula for \(L\) is an estimate that holds for \(\langle k \rangle > 1\), where a giant component exists; Scaling of Path Length and Clustering tests it numerically. In the summary table, the random graph gets a tick for short paths, and crosses for clustering and for hubs.

title: Erdős-Rényi Random Graphs
text:
Implementation
NetworkX provides nx.erdos_renyi_graph(n, p) for \(G(N,p)\) and nx.gnm_random_graph(n, m) for \(G(N,E)\). The algorithm behind \(G(N,p)\) is short:

Select a pair of nodes \(i\) and \(j\).
Draw a random number \(r\) in \([0, 1)\). If \(r < p\), add the edge \((i, j)\).
Repeat for all pairs.


import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

SEED = 7

G_random = nx.erdos_renyi_graph(n=80, p=0.06, seed=SEED)
pos = nx.spring_layout(G_random, seed=SEED)
nx.draw(G_random, pos=pos, node_size=60, node_color="lightgray", edge_color="gray")
plt.title("Erdős-Rényi random graph, N = 80, p = 0.06")
plt.show()

k = np.array([d for _, d in G_random.degree()])
print(f"<k> = {k.mean():.2f} (expected {(80 - 1) * 0.06:.2f})")
print(f"C = {nx.average_clustering(G_random):.3f} (expected p = 0.06)")
print(f"components = {nx.number_connected_components(G_random)}")

C = 0.078 (expected p = 0.06)
components = 1

In \(G(N, E)\) you fix the number of edges instead of an edge probability. In NetworkX:

nx.gnm_random_graph(n, m) implements \(G(N, E)\) with \(E = m\);
nx.erdos_renyi_graph(n, p) (alias nx.gnp_random_graph) implements \(G(N, p)\).




With \(N = 80\) and \(E = 180\) the mean degree is \(2E/N = 4.5\), close to the \(4.74\) of \(G(80, 0.06)\). The degree histogram has the same binomial shape.

k_gnm = [d for _, d in G_gnm.degree()]

title: Erdős-Rényi Random Graphs
text:
The giant component
Figure 1 compares simulated graphs with the self-consistency equation \(S = 1 - e^{-cS}\).








Figure 1: Fraction of nodes in the largest component of G(N, p) with N = 2000 (dots, one graph per value) and the theoretical giant component S = 1 - exp(-cS) (line).





Near \(c = 1\) the finite graph has a largest component of size \(o(N)\) that is still visible, so the dots do not drop exactly to zero.






NoteExercise



Watts and Strogatz measured \(C = 0.79\) in the collaboration network of film actors, against \(C = 0.00027\) for a random graph of the same size and mean degree (Watts and Strogatz 1998, Table 1). Estimate \(C\) for a random graph with \(N = 10^6\) people and mean degree \(c = 100\). What does this say about random graphs as models of social networks?








TipSolution





\(C = c/(N-1) \approx 10^{-4}\). A random graph has almost no triangles, so it cannot reproduce the clustering of social networks. It does reproduce short paths: \(\ell \approx \ln 10^6 / \ln 100 = 3\). The small-world model keeps both.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani (2002).
Recommended: Pastor-Satorras et al. (2015), Section VI.A (efficient immunization protocols).
What the paper did and found: Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani study the SIS model with a fraction \(g\) of immunized nodes. In the degree-based mean field, uniform immunization is eradicating when \(1 - g_c = \lambda_c/\lambda\) (their Eq. 16), so a network with \(\langle k^2 \rangle \to \infty\) needs \(g_c = 1\). For targeted immunization of the nodes with the highest degree in the Barabási-Albert model, a continuum calculation gives the approximation \(g_c \simeq \exp(-2/(m\lambda))\) (their Eq. 28), exponentially small in \(1/\lambda\). They conclude that scale-free networks require strategies that use the connectivity hierarchy.
A check of the approximation: solving their threshold condition (Eq. 25) numerically with the continuum degree distribution \(2m^2/k^3\) for \(m = 3\) gives \(g_c = 0.041, 0.139, 0.402\) at \(\lambda = 0.2, 0.3, 0.5\), against \(0.036, 0.108, 0.264\) from the closed form. The exponential formula is a small-\(\lambda\) approximation: it is 13% low at \(\lambda = 0.2\) and 34% low at \(\lambda = 0.5\). The page below simulates SIR, not SIS, so compare the ordering of the strategies, not the values of \(g_c\).
You have a limited number of vaccine doses. Which nodes should get them? On a heterogeneous network the answer matters much more than on a well-mixed population.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Three strategies

Random immunization. Vaccinate a fraction \(g\) of nodes chosen uniformly at random. In the heterogeneous mean-field picture this rescales the spreading rate to \(\lambda(1-g)\), so the epidemic stops when \(g > g_c = 1 - \lambda_c/\lambda\). For an infinite scale-free network with \(2 < \gamma \le 3\), \(\lambda_c \to 0\) and therefore \(g_c \to 1\): random vaccination would have to reach almost everyone (Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani 2002).
Targeted immunization. Vaccinate the nodes with the highest degree. Removing hubs cuts \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) sharply, and a small fraction \(g\) is enough to restore a finite threshold (Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani 2002). This needs the degree of every node, which you rarely know for a real population.
Acquaintance immunization. Pick a random node and vaccinate one of its random neighbours. A random neighbour has degree \(k\) with probability \(k p_k / \langle k \rangle\), so the method favours hubs without any global knowledge (Cohen et al. 2003).

The three selection rules are in amlab.networks_spreading.






ImportantCore activity



Implement acquaintance immunization, then compare the final SIR epidemic size under the three strategies on a Barabási-Albert graph.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



Rank the three strategies by the final epidemic size you expect at \(g = 0.1\). Where do you expect acquaintance immunization to fall?








TipSolution





Targeted immunization should give the smallest epidemic and random immunization the largest. Acquaintance immunization should fall in between: it reaches hubs more often than random selection, but less reliably than a list of the highest degrees. Figure 1 below confirms this ranking.

title: Vaccination Strategies
Vaccination Strategies
text:
Validation
Check the mean degree of the vaccinated nodes. Random selection should match the network mean up to sampling noise (with 100 nodes and a broad degree distribution, the noise is about \(\pm 0.6\)). Acquaintance selection should give a clearly higher value, and targeted selection the highest.

for name, chosen in [

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Experiment
Figure 1 runs the discrete-time SIR model (\(\beta = 0.05\), \(\mu = 0.1\), 5 initial infected nodes) for each strategy and each coverage \(g\).








Figure 1: Mean final epidemic size (fraction of all nodes ever infected) against vaccination coverage g on a Barabási-Albert graph (N = 1000, m = 3). 20 runs per point.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Interpretation






NoteExercise



Read Figure 1 and answer:

How large must \(g\) be for each strategy to reduce the final size below 5%?
Acquaintance immunization uses only local information. How close does it get to the targeted strategy?
Is random vaccination useless on this network? Compare with the asymptotic statement \(g_c \to 1\) and remember that this graph is finite.









TipSolution






Targeted immunization needs \(g = 0.1\) (final size about 3%). Acquaintance immunization needs between \(g = 0.25\) and \(g = 0.3\). Random immunization never gets below 5% in the plotted range: at \(g = 0.3\) the final size is still about 40%.
It needs about two and a half to three times as many doses as the targeted strategy for the same effect, but it is far better than random selection at every coverage.
No. The final size falls steadily with \(g\), from about 73% to about 40% at \(g = 0.3\). On a finite graph \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) is finite, so \(g_c\) is below 1. It is still large, so random vaccination is the most expensive way to stop the epidemic.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Limitations

The graph is a model network with \(N = 1000\), not a real contact network.
Vaccination is perfect and permanent, and every vaccinated node is removed from the spreading process.
Targeted immunization assumes you know every degree exactly.
20 runs per point leave visible noise, especially near the threshold.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Optional extension






NoteExercise




Repeat the experiment on an Erdős-Rényi graph with the same mean degree. Does the choice of strategy still matter?
Target by betweenness instead of degree. Compare with the Motter-Lai trigger choice in Cascade Simulation.









TipSolution





Reuse G, rng, gs and strategies from the page. Swap the graph for an ER graph with \(p = 6/(N-1)\), and add a betweenness strategy.
G_er = nx.erdos_renyi_graph(1000, 6 / 999, seed=SEED)


def betweenness_ranking(G):
    """Nodes sorted by decreasing betweenness (approximate, 200 sources)."""
    bc = nx.betweenness_centrality(G, k=200, seed=SEED)
    return sorted(bc, key=bc.get, reverse=True)


for graph, label in [(G, "BA"), (G_er, "ER")]:
    ranking = betweenness_ranking(graph)
    selectors = {
        "random": lambda g: random_immunization(graph, g, rng),
        "acquaintance": lambda g: acquaintance_immunization(graph, g, rng),
        "targeted": lambda g: targeted_immunization(graph, g),
        "betweenness": lambda g: ranking[: int(round(g * graph.number_of_nodes()))],
    }
    for name, select in selectors.items():
        sizes = [
            np.mean([run_sir_fast(graph, 0.05, 0.1, initial_infected=5, immune=select(g), rng=rng) for _ in range(20)])
            for g in gs
        ]
        print(label, name, np.round(sizes, 2))

On the ER graph the strategies are much closer. The degrees are nearly all similar, so there are no hubs to target. Targeted immunization still wins, but it needs \(g \approx 0.25\) to push the final size to about 5%, against \(g = 0.1\) on the BA graph. Acquaintance immunization is barely better than random selection.
On the BA graph the betweenness ranking performs almost as well as the degree ranking, because the hubs are also the nodes with the largest betweenness. The same overlap explains why the highest-load and highest-degree triggers give the same cascade on the BA graph of Cascade Simulation. On the ER graph degree and betweenness rankings differ more, and the degree ranking is the better choice here.

title: Vaccination Strategies
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



A health agency cannot map the contact network but can ask people to name one contact. Which strategy from this page can it implement, and why does it work better than vaccinating the people it first reaches?








TipSolution





Acquaintance immunization. It vaccinates the named contacts, not the people first reached. A named contact is a random neighbour, and random neighbours have degree \(k\) with probability proportional to \(k p_k\), so they are more often hubs (Cohen et al. 2003). Vaccinating hubs lowers \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) and raises the epidemic threshold.



See also: SIR as Bond Percolation for the site-bond immunization threshold \(g_c = 1 - 1/R_0\).

title: SIR on Networks
text:
The SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) model adds permanent immunity to SIS: once a node recovers, it cannot be infected again (Kermack and McKendrick 1927; Keeling and Rohani 2008). You met its ODE version in Compartmental Models. On a network, the final size of an SIR outbreak is closely related to bond percolation, and the mapping is exact when every infected node stays infectious for the same time (Newman 2002). This links the page to Robustness and Percolation.
This page reuses the graph models and node attributes of the SIS pages and focuses on what is new:

title: SIR on Networks
text:
What is the SIR Model?

States: Each node can be Susceptible (S), Infected (I), or Recovered (R).
Transitions:

\(S \to I\): a susceptible node becomes infected through infected neighbors.
\(I \to R\): an infected node recovers and becomes permanently immune.

Permanent immunity: \(R\) is an absorbing state (once recovered, always recovered).


Discrete-Time Update Rule
You simulate in discrete time steps \(t = 0, 1, 2, \dots\).
If a susceptible node has \(m\) infected neighbors, use the same “independent trials” rule as SIS (Keeling and Rohani 2008):
\[
\mathbb{P}(S \to I) = 1 - (1 - \beta)^m.
\]
If a node is infected, it recovers with probability:
\[
\mathbb{P}(I \to R) = \mu.
\]
Recovered nodes stay recovered:
\[
\mathbb{P}(R \to R) = 1.
\]






TipWhat changes compared to SIS?





In SIS, \(I \to S\) (you become susceptible again). In SIR, \(I \to R\) (you become immune). That single change alters the long-term behaviour.





Related Rumor Model
If you want one extra reference beyond SIR, a classical rumor counterpart is the Daley-Kendall model (Ignorant -> Spreader -> Stifler), where spreaders become stiflers after contact with spreaders/stiflers (Daley and Kendall 1965).

title: SIR on Networks
text:
Absorbing States
On a finite graph with \(\mu > 0\), the process reaches a time \(T\) such that there are no infected nodes (\(I(T)=0\)), and after that nothing can ever change (Keeling and Rohani 2008; Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015).
Each node can become infected at most once (because \(R\) is permanent), so there can be at most \(N\) infection events. Since recovery happens with positive probability, infections cannot persist forever.
This means SIR always ends in a “frozen” configuration containing only \(S\) and \(R\) nodes.

title: Metapopulation Epidemics
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Arenas et al. (2020), Section II.B (social contacts and mobility among patches, Eqs. 12 to 19).
Recommended: the same paper, Section III (effective reproduction number), and Barbeito et al. (2023) for the statistical counterpart (effect of restrictions on transmission in Spain).
Background: SIR Extensions (Module 1), mobility matrix, and The Final Size of an Epidemic.
So far in this module the nodes of the network were individuals. A network can also connect populations: cities, regions or countries, each with its own epidemic, linked by the movement of people. This is a metapopulation model. In the menu of extensions of SIR Extensions it is the row “a single population” replaced by “patches coupled by a mobility matrix”. The mobility network does for whole populations what the contact network did for individuals: it decides where and when the infection arrives.

title: Metapopulation Epidemics
text:
The model
Consider \(n\) patches, labelled \(k = 1, \dots, n\), each with an SIR epidemic of its own, and a mobility matrix \(m_{k\ell}\) that gives the rate at which individuals move from patch \(k\) to patch \(\ell\). For patch \(k\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot S_k &= -\beta_k S_k I_k + \sum_{\ell \neq k}\big(m_{\ell k} S_\ell - m_{k\ell} S_k\big), \\
\dot I_k &= \beta_k S_k I_k - \gamma_k I_k + \sum_{\ell \neq k}\big(m_{\ell k} I_\ell - m_{k\ell} I_k\big), \\
\dot R_k &= \gamma_k I_k + \sum_{\ell \neq k}\big(m_{\ell k} R_\ell - m_{k\ell} R_k\big).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
Susceptible, infected and recovered people all move with the same rates. The new behaviours are importation and exportation of cases and staggered regional waves, and a travel restriction is simply a change of the parameters in \(m\).
To connect with the rest of the module, we take all patches to be identical (\(\beta_k = \beta\), \(\gamma_k = \gamma\)) and the patches to form a graph with adjacency matrix \(A\). Each individual leaves along each link of its patch at the same rate \(\sigma\), so \(m_{k\ell} = \sigma A_{k\ell}\). Then the sums in Equation 1 become
\[
\sum_{\ell}\big(m_{\ell k} X_\ell - m_{k\ell} X_k\big) = \sigma \sum_\ell A_{k\ell}(X_\ell - X_k) = -\sigma\,(L X)_k,
\qquad L = D - A,
\tag{2}\]
where \(D\) is the diagonal matrix of degrees and \(L\) is the graph Laplacian. The symmetric rates keep a uniform population uniform, so we can normalise each patch population to 1 and read \(S_k, I_k, R_k\) as fractions. Mobility acts as diffusion on the graph, and the epidemic in each patch as a reaction term.

title: Metapopulation Epidemics
section: Where and when does the epidemic arrive?
text:
Where and when does the epidemic arrive?
We start an outbreak in patch 0 (a fraction \(10^{-3}\) of its population infected) and use \(\beta = 0.3\) and \(\gamma = 0.1\) per day, so that \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma = 3\) in every patch, the value quoted by Arenas et al. (2020) for COVID-19. The arrival time of a patch is the first time at which its infected fraction exceeds \(10^{-4}\). We compare three graphs of \(n = 60\) patches with the same mean degree (about 4): a ring lattice in which each patch is joined to its 4 nearest neighbours, the same lattice with 10% of its links rewired (small-world, Small-World Networks), and a Barabási-Albert graph (Preferential Attachment).

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

SEED = 7
beta, gamma = 0.3, 0.1


def simulate_patches(G, sigma, t_max=400, seed_patch=0, i0=1e-3, thr=1e-4):
    """Integrate the metapopulation SIR on the graph G of patches.

    Returns the arrival time of every patch, the solution and the population of every patch over time.
    """
    n = G.number_of_nodes()
    A = nx.to_numpy_array(G, nodelist=range(n))
    Lap = np.diag(A.sum(axis=1)) - A

    def rhs(t, y):
        S, I, R = y[:n], y[n:2 * n], y[2 * n:]
        return np.concatenate([-beta * S * I - sigma * Lap @ S,
                               beta * S * I - gamma * I - sigma * Lap @ I,
                               gamma * I - sigma * Lap @ R])

    y0 = np.concatenate([np.ones(n), np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n)])
    y0[seed_patch] -= i0
    y0[n + seed_patch] = i0
    t = np.linspace(0, t_max, 4001)
    sol = solve_ivp(rhs, (0, t_max), y0, t_eval=t, rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-12, method="LSODA")
    I = sol.y[n:2 * n]
    arrival = np.array([t[np.argmax(I[k] > thr)] if (I[k] > thr).any() else np.nan for k in range(n)])
    population = sol.y[:n] + sol.y[n:2 * n] + sol.y[2 * n:]
    return arrival, sol, population


n_patches = 60
patch_graphs = {
    "ring lattice": nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n_patches, 4, 0.0, seed=1),
    "small-world (p = 0.1)": nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n_patches, 4, 0.1, seed=1),
    "Barabási-Albert (m = 2)": nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n_patches, 2, seed=1),
}
sigma = 0.01
arrival = {}
print(f"{'patch graph':<26}{'<k>':>5}{'mean arrival':>14}{'last arrival':>14}{'Spearman(arrival, distance)':>29}{'max |N_k - 1|':>15}")
for name, G in patch_graphs.items():
    arr, sol, pop = simulate_patches(G, sigma)
    arrival[name] = arr
    dist = nx.single_source_shortest_path_length(G, 0)
    d = np.array([dist[k] for k in range(n_patches)])
    k_mean = 2 * G.number_of_edges() / n_patches
    print(f"{name:<26}{k_mean:>5.1f}{np.nanmean(arr):>14.1f}{np.nanmax(arr):>14.1f}"
          f"{spearmanr(d, arr)[0]:>29.3f}{np.abs(pop - 1).max():>15.1e}")

patch graph                 <k>  mean arrival  last arrival  Spearman(arrival, distance)  max |N_k - 1|
ring lattice                4.0          59.5         117.6                        0.998        2.6e-15
small-world (p = 0.1)       4.0          35.5          61.3                        0.986        1.3e-15
Barabási-Albert (m = 2)     3.9          13.7          26.5                        0.916        3.3e-15


The last column is a check of the implementation: the population of every patch stays equal to 1 up to the integration error, as Equation 2 predicts for symmetric rates. The Spearman correlation between the arrival time and the number of links separating a patch from the seed is above 0.9 for all three graphs, so the arrival order is essentially the order of distance on the mobility network. The scale of the times, however, depends strongly on the topology: shortcuts and hubs bring the infection to every patch much earlier.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
for (name, G), marker in zip(patch_graphs.items(), "osD"):
    dist = nx.single_source_shortest_path_length(G, 0)
    d = np.array([dist[k] for k in range(n_patches)])
    axes[0].plot(d + 0.08 * (marker == "s") - 0.08 * (marker == "D"), arrival[name], marker, ms=4, alpha=0.7, label=name)
axes[0].set_xlabel("graph distance from the seed patch")
axes[0].set_ylabel("arrival time (days)")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)

sigmas = np.array([0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1])
for (name, G), marker in zip(patch_graphs.items(), "osD"):
    axes[1].semilogx(sigmas, [np.nanmean(simulate_patches(G, s, t_max=600)[0]) for s in sigmas], marker + "-", ms=4, label=name)
axes[1].set_xlabel(r"mobility rate $\sigma$ per link (per day)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("mean arrival time (days)")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Metapopulation SIR on three graphs of 60 patches (R0 = 3 in every patch, mobility rate sigma per link). Left: arrival time of the infection in each patch (first time the infected fraction exceeds 1e-4) against its graph distance from the seed patch, for sigma = 0.01 per day. Right: mean arrival time over the patches against the mobility rate sigma. The time grows when mobility is restricted, with a slope that depends on the topology.











NoteExercise 1: hub or leaf



On the Barabási-Albert graph of patches, start the outbreak in the patch of largest degree and then in a patch of smallest degree. Compare the mean arrival times. What does this say about the importance of the place where an epidemic starts?








TipSolution





G = patch_graphs["Barabási-Albert (m = 2)"]
degs = dict(G.degree())
for label, seed_patch in [("hub", max(degs, key=degs.get)), ("leaf", min(degs, key=degs.get))]:
    arr = simulate_patches(G, 0.01, seed_patch=seed_patch)[0]
    print(label, degs[seed_patch], round(np.nanmean(arr), 1))
The seed in the hub reaches the other patches sooner than the seed in a leaf, since from the hub every other patch is a few links away and from a leaf the infection must first reach a hub; see the printed values. This is the same asymmetry between hubs and ordinary nodes that Vaccination Strategies uses to design immunization.

title: Metapopulation Epidemics
text:
A discrete-time mobility model
Arenas et al. (2020) use a different formalism, the microscopic Markov chain approach, in discrete time with one step per day. We keep its mobility ingredients and drop its age groups, ten compartments and density-dependent contacts, and use an SIR model. Each patch \(i\) has \(n_i\) residents. A fraction \(p\) of them (“degree of mobility”) commute, and a commuter from \(i\) chooses patch \(j\) with probability \(R_{ij}\); here \(R_{ij} = A_{ij}/k_i\). The effective mobility matrix is \(M_{ji} = (1-p)\delta_{ji} + p R_{ji}\), the fraction of the residents of \(j\) who are present in \(i\), and the effective population of patch \(i\) during the day is \(\tilde n_i = \sum_j M_{ji} n_j\) (Arenas et al. 2020, Eqs. 16 and 17). With \(\rho^I_j\) the infected fraction of the residents of \(j\), a susceptible who is in patch \(i\) is exposed to \(\sum_j M_{ji} n_j \rho_j^I / \tilde n_i\) infected people per unit of the contacts it makes, so it is infected with probability
\[
P_i = 1 - (1-\beta_c)^{\bar k\, X_i}, \qquad X_i = \frac{\sum_j M_{ji}\, n_j\, \rho^I_j}{\tilde n_i},
\tag{3}\]
where \(\beta_c\) is the probability of infection per contact and \(\bar k\) the number of contacts. A resident of \(i\) is infected with probability
\[
\Pi_i = (1-p)\,P_i + p\sum_j R_{ij}\,P_j,
\tag{4}\]
the first term for contagion in the home patch and the second for contagion in the patches visited (Arenas et al. 2020, Eq. 12). Then \(\rho^S_i \leftarrow (1 - \Pi_i)\rho^S_i\), and the infected fraction gains \(\Pi_i\rho^S_i\) and loses \(\mu\rho^I_i\) per step.

def simulate_mmca(G, p, beta_c=0.03, k_bar=10, mu=0.1, t_max=300, seed_patch=0, i0=1e-3, thr=1e-4):
    """Reduced Markov-chain metapopulation SIR with equal patch populations (n_j = 1)."""
    n = G.number_of_nodes()
    A = nx.to_numpy_array(G, nodelist=range(n))
    R = A / A.sum(axis=1)[:, None]
    M = (1 - p) * np.eye(n) + p * R              # M[j, i]: fraction of residents of j present in i
    n_eff = M.sum(axis=0)                        # effective populations
    rS, rI, rR = np.ones(n), np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n)
    rS[seed_patch] -= i0
    rI[seed_patch] = i0
    arrival, totals = np.full(n, np.nan), []
    for t in range(1, t_max + 1):
        X = (M.T @ rI) / n_eff
        P = 1 - (1 - beta_c) ** (k_bar * X)
        Pi = (1 - p) * P + p * R @ P
        new = Pi * rS
        rS, rI, rR = rS - new, rI + new - mu * rI, rR + mu * rI
        totals.append(rS + rI + rR)
        arrival[np.isnan(arrival) & (rI > thr)] = t
    return arrival, np.array(totals), n_eff


G_sw = patch_graphs["small-world (p = 0.1)"]
arr_mmca, totals, n_eff = simulate_mmca(G_sw, 0.1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8))
axes[0].plot(arrival["small-world (p = 0.1)"], arr_mmca, "o", ms=4)
lim = [0, max(np.nanmax(arr_mmca), np.nanmax(arrival["small-world (p = 0.1)"])) + 3]
axes[0].plot(lim, lim, "k--", lw=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("arrival time, continuous-time model (days)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("arrival time, discrete-time model (days)")

G_ba = patch_graphs["Barabási-Albert (m = 2)"]
_, _, n_eff_ba = simulate_mmca(G_ba, 0.1)
deg_ba = np.array([G_ba.degree(k) for k in range(n_patches)])
axes[1].plot(deg_ba, n_eff_ba, "o", ms=4)
axes[1].axhline(1, color="k", ls="--", lw=1)
axes[1].set_xlabel("degree of the patch")
axes[1].set_ylabel("effective population $\\tilde n_i$ (residents = 1)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"sum of effective populations = {n_eff_ba.sum():.6f} (total population = {n_patches}); "
      f"range of n_eff on the BA graph: {n_eff_ba.min():.2f} to {n_eff_ba.max():.2f}")
print(f"max |N_k - 1| over time = {np.abs(totals - 1).max():.1e}")
print(f"Spearman correlation of the two arrival times (small-world graph): "
      f"{spearmanr(arrival['small-world (p = 0.1)'], arr_mmca)[0]:.3f}")
print("patches never reached with p = 0:", int(np.isnan(simulate_mmca(G_sw, 0.0)[0]).sum()), "of", n_patches)







Figure 2: Discrete-time mobility model (reduced from Arenas et al.). Left: arrival time in each patch of the 60-patch small-world graph, discrete-time model with p = 0.1 against the continuous-time model with sigma = 0.01 (same seed, same threshold); the dashed line is the identity. Right: effective population of each patch of the Barabási-Albert graph against its degree: patches with more links receive more commuters than they send.





sum of effective populations = 60.000000 (total population = 60); range of n_eff on the BA graph: 0.92 to 1.40
max |N_k - 1| over time = 1.4e-15
Spearman correlation of the two arrival times (small-world graph): 0.995
patches never reached with p = 0: 59 of 60


Three checks support the implementation. The total population is conserved to rounding error. The effective populations add up to the total population, as they must, but individual patches differ: on the Barabási-Albert graph the busiest patch hosts about 1.4 times its residents at the time of contact. Finally, with \(p = 0\) there is no mobility and 59 of the 60 patches are never reached. The arrival times of the discrete-time model agree with those of the continuous-time model on the same graph, although the two parameter sets were chosen only to give similar growth rates and not fitted to each other; what the two share is the mobility network.

title: Metapopulation Epidemics
section: Restricting mobility: what changes and what does not
text:
Restricting mobility: what changes and what does not
A restriction of travel reduces \(\sigma\) in the continuous model or \(p\) in the discrete one. Figure 1 shows its effect on the arrival time. What it does not change is the epidemic inside each patch. The table reports, for three values of \(\sigma\) on the small-world graph, the delay and the final size of the epidemic in the patches, to be compared with the final size relation \(z = 1 - e^{-R_0 z}\) of The Final Size of an Epidemic.

from scipy.optimize import brentq

z_th = brentq(lambda z: z - 1 + np.exp(-(beta / gamma) * z), 1e-9, 1.0)
print(f"final size relation for R0 = {beta / gamma:.0f}: z = {z_th:.4f}")
print(f"{'sigma':>8}{'mean arrival':>14}{'delay vs sigma = 0.01':>24}{'mean final size':>17}{'min final size':>16}")
base = np.nanmean(arrival["small-world (p = 0.1)"])
for s in (0.1, 0.01, 0.001):
    arr, sol, _ = simulate_patches(G_sw, s, t_max=1500)
    final = sol.y[2 * n_patches:, -1]
    print(f"{s:>8}{np.nanmean(arr):>14.1f}{np.nanmean(arr) - base:>24.1f}{final.mean():>17.4f}{final.min():>16.4f}")

final size relation for R0 = 3: z = 0.9405
   sigma  mean arrival   delay vs sigma = 0.01  mean final size  min final size
     0.1          15.5                   -20.0           0.9385          0.9385
    0.01          35.6                     0.1           0.9350          0.9348
   0.001          70.1                    34.6           0.9370          0.9358


Restricting mobility by a factor of ten delays the arrival by weeks but leaves the final size in each patch at 0.935 to 0.939, within 0.6% of the value 0.9405 of an isolated population with \(R_0 = 3\). This is a statement about the model in which each patch has \(R_0 > 1\) by itself: mobility only decides when the patches are infected, and only measures that reduce transmission inside the patches (smaller \(\beta\)) change the final size. Arenas et al. (2020) derive the effective reproduction number of the whole system as a function of the mobility and confinement parameters, which is the quantity that decides whether an epidemic is suppressed. The statistical analysis of Barbeito et al. (2023) looks at the same question from the data side: an increase of one standard deviation in the overall stringency index over nine fields of activity was associated with a 22% lower growth of the 7-day cumulative incidence over the following week in Spain between September 2020 and May 2021 (relative risk 0.78). Among single fields, culture and leisure and social distancing showed the largest effects, although culture and leisure was no longer significant in a model with fewer fields.






NoteExercise 2: what mobility restrictions cannot do



Explain with the final size relation why restricting mobility on this model cannot reduce the final size, and name the parameter that would. For which value of \(R_0\) inside the patches would mobility restrictions determine whether the epidemic occurs?








TipSolution





Within a patch the final size solves \(z = 1 - e^{-R_0 z}\) in the limit of weak coupling, a relation that does not contain \(\sigma\). Restricting mobility only postpones the moment at which the patches start their own epidemics. The parameters that change \(z\) are those that change \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma\), such as contact reduction or vaccination. If \(R_0 < 1\) inside every patch, an epidemic in one patch dies out locally and mobility has no influence on whether the epidemic occurs. For \(R_0\) slightly above 1, the delay is not the main effect: the epidemic is slow in each patch, and the importation of cases matters for whether it takes off.

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani (2001).
Recommended: Pastor-Satorras et al. (2015); Newman (2002).
In Module 1 you wrote the SIS model as an ODE for a well-mixed population. Here every individual is a node, and infection travels only along edges (Keeling and Rohani 2008; Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015). You will implement SIS on networks with NetworkX and measure how network structure (random, small-world, scale-free) changes the spread.

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
What is the SIS Model?

States: each node is Susceptible (S) or Infected (I).
Transitions:

\(S \to I\): infection through contacts (controlled by \(\beta\)).
\(I \to S\): recovery (controlled by \(\mu\)).

No permanent immunity: recovered nodes can be reinfected.


Discrete-Time Update Rule
You simulate in discrete time steps \(t = 0, 1, 2, \dots\).
A susceptible node with \(m\) infected neighbors becomes infected with probability (Keeling and Rohani 2008):
\[
\mathbb{P}(S \to I) = 1 - (1 - \beta)^m.
\]






TipWhy \(1 - (1-\beta)^m\)?





If each infected neighbor independently infects you with probability \(\beta\), then the probability you avoid infection from all \(m\) neighbors is \((1-\beta)^m\). So the probability of at least one successful infection is \(1-(1-\beta)^m\).



On the other hand, if a node is infected, it recovers with probability:
\[
\mathbb{P}(I \to S) = \mu.
\]

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
Prediction
You will compare random (Erdős-Rényi), small-world (Watts-Strogatz) and scale-free (Barabási-Albert) graphs. Try sizes such as \(N \in \{50, 100, 300\}\), run 10 to 30 repetitions for each case and plot the average infected fraction over time.






NoteExercise



Answer these questions before you write any code:

Take a random graph and a scale-free graph with the same \(N\) and the same mean degree. With the same \((\beta, \mu)\), which one do you expect to sustain more infection?
What should happen to the infected fraction when \(\beta = 0\)?









TipSolution






The scale-free graph. Its hubs have many neighbours, so they are infected early and often, and each infected hub exposes many susceptible nodes. In the language of Epidemic Threshold, its larger \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) lowers the threshold.
Nobody can be infected, so the infected nodes only recover. Each one stays infected with probability \(1 - \mu\) per step, and the expected number of infected nodes decays as \(I(0)(1-\mu)^t\). You will use this case to validate your code.

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
Imports and Parameters

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

These are the parameters you can tune:

SEED = 7

# Model parameters
beta = 0.20  # infection probability per infected neighbor (per step)
mu = 0.10    # recovery probability (per step)

# Simulation parameters
steps = 120  # number of time steps to simulate
initial_infected = 5  # should always be < N
N = 100  # number of nodes in the graph







NoteAbout SEED (why you fix it)



There are two sources of randomness in this activity:

the graph you generate (e.g., which edges appear in Erdős-Rényi), and
the stochastic SIS dynamics (who gets infected / recovers at each step).

You fix SEED so results are reproducible: rerunning the page gives the same plots, which makes debugging and reporting possible.
When you run many repetitions, you use SEED + r so repetition r is a different random trial (new graph + new random infection events) but still reproducible. If you reused the same SEED in every repetition, you would repeat the same realization and your “average over runs” would be meaningless.

title: SIS Model on Networks
text:
Choose a Network
You will compare several models. Start by picking one. The three models are described in Erdős-Rényi Random Graphs, Small-World Networks and Preferential Attachment.

The update is synchronous: compute all changes from the old state, then apply them.

TipHint





Loop through all nodes and their neighbours with G.nodes() and G.neighbors(node). Use a random number generator such as np.random.default_rng() for the probabilistic transitions.









TipSolution






def step_sis(G, beta, mu, rng=None):
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng()

    # Retrieve current states of all nodes
    current = {node: G.nodes[node]["state"] for node in G.nodes()}
    new_state = current.copy()  # start with the same state for synchronous update
    # Loop through all nodes to compute new states
    for node in G.nodes():
        if current[node] == "S":
            # Count infected neighbors
            m = sum(1 for nbr in G.neighbors(node) if current[nbr] == "I")
            if m > 0:
                # Compute infection probability
                p_infect = 1 - (1 - beta) ** m
                if rng.random() < p_infect:
                    new_state[node] = "I"
        else:  # current[node] == "I"
            if rng.random() < mu:
                new_state[node] = "S"
    nx.set_node_attributes(G, new_state, "state")
    return G

TipSolution





Copy the graph so that the original stays untouched, and let one seeded generator control all the randomness of a run.

def run_sis(G, beta, mu, steps=100, initial_infected=5, seed=SEED):
    # Copy the graph to avoid mutating the original
    H = G.copy()

    # One seeded RNG controls all randomness for this run
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    # Initialize states
    initialize_state(H, initial_infected=initial_infected, seed=seed, rng=rng)
    # Count initial number of infected nodes and initialize the list
    infected_counts = [sum(H.nodes[node]["state"] == "I" for node in H.nodes())]
    # Apply SIS steps and record infected counts
    for _ in range(steps):
        step_sis(H, beta=beta, mu=mu, rng=rng)
        infected_counts.append(sum(H.nodes[node]["state"] == "I" for node in H.nodes()))
    return infected_counts

title: Scaling of Path Length and Clustering
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Watts and Strogatz (1998), the first two pages (definition of \(L(p)\) and \(C(p)\), and the regime \(n \gg k \gg \ln n \gg 1\)).
Recommended: Newman (2003), Section 3.1 (small-world effect), Section 4.1 (random graph), Section 6 (small-world model) and Section 7.2 (Barabási-Albert model).
Each model is summarised by three columns: the average path length \(L\), the clustering \(C\) and the degree distribution \(p(k)\). Entries such as “\(L \sim \log N\)” or “\(C \approx \langle k \rangle / N\)” are statements about how a quantity changes with the size \(N\) of the network. A single graph cannot confirm them. This page measures \(L\) and \(C\) for graphs of increasing size, compares the measurements with the formulas of the lecture, and states where the formulas hold only asymptotically.

title: Scaling of Path Length and Clustering
text:
Definitions
For a connected graph with \(N\) nodes the average path length is
\[
L = \frac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i \neq j} d(i,j),
\tag{1}\]
where \(d(i,j)\) is the length of the shortest path between \(i\) and \(j\). A network is called small-world if \(L\) grows like \(\log N\) or more slowly. The average clustering is \(C = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i C_i\) with \(C_i = 2E_i/\big(k_i(k_i-1)\big)\), where \(E_i\) is the number of edges among the neighbours of node \(i\) (Watts and Strogatz 1998). A real network is considered clustered when \(C \gg C_{\text{random}}\), the value of a random graph with the same \(N\) and \(\langle k \rangle\).

title: Scaling of Path Length and Clustering
text:
Theoretical predictions



Model
\(L\)
\(C\)
Source of the formula




Erdős-Rényi
\(\ln N / \ln \langle k \rangle\)
\(\langle k \rangle / N\)
\(\langle k \rangle^{\ell} \sim N\); \(C = p\)


Watts-Strogatz, \(p = 0\)
\(\approx N / (2k)\)
\(3(k-2) / \big(4(k-1)\big)\)
ring lattice


Watts-Strogatz, \(p > 0\)
\(\sim \ln N\) for \(N\) large enough

shortcuts; see Small-World Networks


Barabási-Albert
smaller than ER

The Erdős-Rényi estimate follows from counting: the number of nodes at distance \(\ell\) from a given node grows like \(\langle k \rangle^{\ell}\), so the whole graph is reached when \(\langle k \rangle^{\ell} \sim N\) (Newman 2003, sec. 4.1). For the ring lattice, Watts and Strogatz (1998) give \(L \approx n/2k\) and \(C \to 3/4\) as \(k\) grows. In the Watts-Strogatz entry \(k\) is the full degree of the ring lattice, as in nx.watts_strogatz_graph.

title: Scaling of Path Length and Clustering
text:
Measurement
Computing \(L\) exactly needs a shortest-path search from every node. The helper below averages the distances from at most 300 randomly chosen source nodes, which is exact for \(N \le 300\) and, in a test at \(N = 3200\) with five different source samples, deviated from the exact value by at most 1.5%. It works on the largest connected component. All graphs have mean degree 6 (\(k = 6\) for Watts-Strogatz, \(m = 3\) for Barabási-Albert and for the clustered variant introduced in Triadic Closure). Each point is an average over 3 graphs.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import shortest_path

SEED = 7


def avg_path_length(G, n_src=300, seed=0):
    """Average distance in the largest component, from at most n_src random sources."""
    H = G.subgraph(max(nx.connected_components(G), key=len))
    nodes = list(H)
    A = nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(H, nodelist=nodes, format="csr")
    # SciPy's csgraph routines require int32 CSR index buffers in this environment.
    A.indices = A.indices.astype(np.int32)
    A.indptr = A.indptr.astype(np.int32)
    n = len(nodes)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    src = np.arange(n, dtype=np.int32) if n <= n_src else rng.choice(n, n_src, replace=False).astype(np.int32)
    D = shortest_path(A, unweighted=True, indices=src)
    return D.sum() / (len(src) * (n - 1))


generators = {
    "ER": lambda N, s: nx.fast_gnp_random_graph(N, 6 / (N - 1), seed=s),
    "WS p=1": lambda N, s: nx.watts_strogatz_graph(N, 6, 1.0, seed=s),
    "WS p=0.1": lambda N, s: nx.watts_strogatz_graph(N, 6, 0.1, seed=s),
    "WS p=0.01": lambda N, s: nx.watts_strogatz_graph(N, 6, 0.01, seed=s),
    "WS p=0": lambda N, s: nx.watts_strogatz_graph(N, 6, 0.0, seed=s),
    "BA": lambda N, s: nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N, 3, seed=s),
    "HK": lambda N, s: nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(N, 3, 0.5, seed=s),
}
Ns = np.array([100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, 6400])
L = {name: [] for name in generators}
C = {name: [] for name in generators}
for name, gen in generators.items():
    for N in Ns:
        graphs = [gen(int(N), SEED + r) for r in range(3)]
        L[name].append(np.mean([avg_path_length(G, seed=r) for r, G in enumerate(graphs)]))
        C[name].append(np.mean([nx.average_clustering(G) for G in graphs]))
    L[name], C[name] = np.array(L[name]), np.array(C[name])
print("done:", list(generators))

axes[0].legend()

print("mean increase of L per doubling of N (N >= 400):")
for name in ["ER", "WS p=1", "WS p=0.1", "BA", "HK"]:
    print(f"  {name:>8}: {doubling(L[name]):.2f}")
print(f"  ln 2 / ln 6 = {np.log(2) / np.log(6):.2f} (ER formula)")
print("L - ln N / ln 6 for ER:", np.round(L["ER"] - np.log(Ns) / np.log(6), 2))







Figure 1: Average path length L against the number of nodes N (logarithmic axis), mean degree 6, averages over 3 graphs. Left: Erdős-Rényi (ER), Watts-Strogatz with p = 1 (WS), Barabási-Albert (BA) and the clustered Barabási-Albert variant (HK), with the formula ln N / ln 6 (dashed). Right: Watts-Strogatz for p = 0, 0.01, 0.1 and 1 with the lattice formula N/(2k) (dashed).





mean increase of L per doubling of N (N >= 400):
        ER: 0.39
    WS p=1: 0.41
  WS p=0.1: 0.77
        BA: 0.24
        HK: 0.24
  ln 2 / ln 6 = 0.39 (ER formula)
L - ln N / ln 6 for ER: [0.17 0.18 0.18 0.18 0.17 0.18 0.19]


Four observations:

Erdős-Rényi. \(L\) grows linearly in \(\ln N\) with the slope \(1/\ln\langle k \rangle\) predicted by the formula. The formula underestimates \(L\) by a nearly constant amount of about 0.2: it is a leading-order result.
Watts-Strogatz, \(p = 1\). The same logarithmic growth, with practically the same values as Erdős-Rényi: the rewired graph is close to a random graph.
Watts-Strogatz, small \(p\). The lattice has \(L \approx N/(2k)\). For \(p > 0\) the curves leave the lattice line: the shortcuts act as soon as \(N\) is large enough for a typical ring to contain some of them. The logarithmic law is a statement about large \(N\) at fixed \(p\). For \(p = 0.01\) the curve still grows much faster than a logarithm up to \(N = 6400\), and for \(p = 0.1\) it approaches the logarithmic slope only slowly. Do not read “\(L \sim \log N\)” in the Watts-Strogatz row as valid at every size.
Barabási-Albert. At the same mean degree the paths of the scale-free graphs grow more slowly with \(N\) than those of the random graph, in line with the statement that for power-law degree distributions \(L\) grows no faster than \(\ln N / \ln \ln N\) (Newman 2003, sec. 3.1). The hubs act as shortcuts. The range of \(N\) available here is too narrow to distinguish \(\ln N/\ln\ln N\) from other slowly growing forms.

title: Scaling of Path Length and Clustering
text:
Clustering
?@fig-scaling-C shows \(C\) against \(N\) on logarithmic axes. A power law \(C \propto N^{-\delta}\) is a straight line of slope \(-\delta\).

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for name in ["ER", "WS p=0.1", "BA", "HK"]:
    ax.loglog(Ns, C[name], "o-", ms=4, label=name)
ax.loglog(Ns, 6 / (Ns - 1), "k--", lw=1, label=r"$\langle k \rangle / N$")
ax.set_xlabel("N")
ax.set_ylabel("C")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("fitted exponent delta in C ~ N^(-delta), N >= 400:")
for name in ["ER", "BA", "WS p=0.1", "HK"]:
    delta = -np.polyfit(np.log(Ns[2:]), np.log(C[name][2:]), 1)[0]
    print(f"  {name:>8}: delta = {delta:.2f}")
print("C(N = 6400): ", {name: round(float(C[name][-1]), 4) for name in ["ER", "BA", "WS p=0.1", "HK"]})







Figure 2: Average clustering coefficient C against N on logarithmic axes, mean degree 6. Erdős-Rényi follows /N (dashed, slope -1). Watts-Strogatz with p = 0.1 and the clustered Barabási-Albert variant (HK) stay at a finite value. The plain Barabási-Albert graph decreases, but more slowly than Erdős-Rényi.





fitted exponent delta in C ~ N^(-delta), N >= 400:
        ER: delta = 1.00
        BA: delta = 0.72
  WS p=0.1: delta = -0.00
        HK: delta = 0.04
C(N = 6400):  {'ER': 0.001, 'BA': 0.0088, 'WS p=0.1': 0.4393, 'HK': 0.2745}


The Erdős-Rényi clustering follows \(\langle k \rangle / N\) and goes to zero like \(1/N\) (fitted exponent close to 1). The Watts-Strogatz graph keeps a finite clustering for any \(N\): the rewiring probability fixes the fraction of triangles destroyed, not the size of the graph. The plain Barabási-Albert graph has a clustering that decreases with \(N\), with a fitted exponent between that of the random graph and zero; this is a numerical estimate in the range of sizes shown, not a theoretical exponent. The clustered variant of Triadic Closure stays close to a constant (fitted exponent 0.04, value about 0.27 at \(N = 6400\)), which is the property that the plain model lacks.






NoteExercise



Use the formula \(L \approx \ln N / \ln\langle k \rangle\) to estimate how many nodes an Erdős-Rényi graph with \(\langle k \rangle = 6\) needs to have \(L = 6\), and compare it with the size you would expect from the measured offset of about 0.2. Then predict from ?@fig-scaling-L the value of \(L\) for a Barabási-Albert graph with \(m = 3\) and \(N = 10^6\), and say how reliable that extrapolation is.








TipSolution





From \(\ln N = 6 \ln 6\) we get \(N = 6^6 \approx 4.7 \times 10^4\). Including the offset, \(L = 6\) is reached when \(\ln N / \ln 6 + 0.2 = 6\), which gives \(N = 6^{5.8} \approx 3.3 \times 10^4\), about 30% fewer nodes, so the leading-order formula is accurate only to within a factor of order one. For Barabási-Albert, extend the measured growth of about 0.25 per doubling of \(N\) from \(N = 6400\) (\(L \approx 4.1\)): \(\log_2(10^6 / 6400) \approx 7.3\) doublings give \(L \approx 6\). This is an extrapolation of a fit over one decade and a half in \(N\), and the true functional form is slower than linear in \(\ln N\), so treat it as an upper estimate of the order of magnitude, not as a prediction.









NoteExercise



Why is the clustering coefficient of the Watts-Strogatz graph independent of \(N\) while that of the Erdős-Rényi graph is not? Answer in terms of the number of triangles per node.








TipSolution





In the ring lattice each node has exactly \(3k(k-2)/8\) triangles around it (9 for \(k = 6\)), a number that depends only on \(k\). Rewiring a fraction \(p\) of the edges destroys a fraction of these triangles that depends only on \(p\), so \(C\) does not depend on \(N\). In the Erdős-Rényi graph a node of degree \(\langle k \rangle\) has about \(\langle k \rangle^2/2\) pairs of neighbours, and each pair is connected with probability \(p = \langle k \rangle / N\), so the expected number of triangles per node is about \(\langle k \rangle^3/(2N)\), which goes to zero as \(N\) grows.

title: Network Concepts
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Newman (2003), Sections 1 to 3.
Recommended: Newman (2018); Menczer et al. (2020).
A network (or graph) \(G = (V, E)\) is a set of \(N = |V|\) nodes and a set of \(E = |E|\) edges that join pairs of nodes (Newman 2003). In Module 1 you modelled an epidemic with ODEs that assume every individual meets every other one. A network drops that assumption: interactions happen only along edges.

title: Network Concepts
Network Concepts
text:
Adjacency matrix and degree
For an undirected, unweighted graph, the adjacency matrix has \(A_{ij} = 1\) if nodes \(i\) and \(j\) share an edge and \(A_{ij} = 0\) otherwise. The degree of node \(i\) is
\[
k_i = \sum_{j} A_{ij}, \qquad \langle k \rangle = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i k_i = \frac{2E}{N}.
\]
The degree distribution \(p_k\) is the fraction of nodes with degree \(k\). Its second moment \(\langle k^2 \rangle = \sum_k k^2 p_k\) appears in every result of this module: percolation, cascades and epidemic thresholds all depend on how broad \(p_k\) is (Newman 2003). Many real networks have right-skewed degree distributions, sometimes close to a power law \(p_k \sim k^{-\gamma}\) with \(2 < \gamma < 3\) (Newman 2003, sec. 3.3).

title: Network Concepts
text:
Paths and the small-world effect
A path is a sequence of edges that joins two nodes. The distance \(d_{ij}\) is the length of the shortest path. The average path length \(\ell\) averages \(d_{ij}\) over all pairs, and the diameter is the largest \(d_{ij}\). In many real networks \(\ell\) is small and grows slowly (about logarithmically) with \(N\). This is the small-world effect (Newman 2003, sec. 3.1; Watts and Strogatz 1998).

title: Network Concepts
text:
Clustering
The local clustering coefficient of node \(i\) is
\[
C_i = \frac{\text{number of edges among the neighbours of } i}{k_i (k_i - 1)/2}.
\]
It measures how often two neighbours of \(i\) are also neighbours of each other. Social networks tend to have much higher clustering than a random graph with the same \(N\) and \(E\) (Watts and Strogatz 1998; Newman 2003, sec. 3.2).

title: Network Concepts
text:
Centrality
Centrality measures rank nodes by importance. Each one encodes a different idea of “important” (Newman 2018):

Degree centrality: \(k_i / (N-1)\). Many direct contacts.
Closeness centrality: \((N-1) / \sum_{j} d_{ij}\). Short distances to everyone else (Sabidussi 1966).
Betweenness centrality: \(b_v = \sum_{s \neq v \neq t} \sigma_{st}(v) / \sigma_{st}\), where \(\sigma_{st}\) counts shortest paths from \(s\) to \(t\) and \(\sigma_{st}(v)\) counts those that pass through \(v\) (Freeman 1977). You will use betweenness as the “load” of a node in the cascade lab.
PageRank: stationary distribution of a random walk with random restarts, used for directed graphs (Page et al. 1999).

title: Network Concepts
text:
Communities
A community is a group of nodes with many edges inside the group and few edges to the rest of the network (Girvan and Newman 2002). A common quality score is the modularity
\[
Q = \frac{1}{2E}\sum_{ij}\left(A_{ij} - \frac{k_i k_j}{2E}\right)\delta(c_i, c_j),
\]
which compares the edges inside communities with the number expected in a random graph with the same degrees (Newman 2018). Here \(c_i\) is the community of node \(i\).

title: Network Concepts
text:
Worked example: the karate club
Figure 1 shows Zachary’s karate club, a social network of 34 club members (Zachary 1977). Node size is proportional to betweenness and colours show the communities found by greedy modularity maximization.








Figure 1: Zachary’s karate club. Node size is proportional to betweenness centrality; colours are communities found by greedy modularity maximization.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: Graphs from Edge Lists
section: Creating a Graph from an Edge List
text:
Creating a Graph from an Edge List
In practice, you often have data in the form of an edge list, which is a list of pairs of nodes that are connected by edges. You can create a graph directly from an edge list using the from_edgelist() method. For example:

# Define the edge list (actors that have worked together in movies)
edge_list = [
    ("Antonio Banderas", "Brad Pitt"),  # Interview with the Vampire (1994)
    ("Antonio Banderas", "Javier Bardem"),  # Automata (2014)
    ("Antonio Banderas", "Penelope Cruz"),  # Dolor y Gloria (2019)
    ("Antonio Banderas", "Tom Holland"),  # Uncharted (2022)
    ("Brad Pitt", "Javier Bardem"),  # F1 (2025)
    ("Javier Bardem", "Timothée Chalamet"),  # Dune (2021)
    ("Timothée Chalamet", "Zendaya"),  # Dune (2021)
    ("Tom Holland", "Zendaya"),  # Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021)
]

# Create a graph from the edge list
G_actors = nx.from_edgelist(edge_list)
# Draw the graph
pos = nx.spring_layout(G_actors, k=0.15, iterations=20)
# k is the optimal distance between nodes (default 1/sqrt(N))
# iterations is the number of force-directed update steps (default 50)

nx.draw(
    G_actors,
    pos=pos,
    with_labels=True,
    node_color='lightgreen',
    edge_color='gray',
    node_size=2000,
    font_size=12
    )
plt.show()
