title: Triadic Closure
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Holme and Kim (2002) for the original model (preferential attachment with triadic closure), and Newman (2003), Section 3.2, for the definitions of the clustering coefficient. For the maximum-likelihood fit of the tail exponent used below, see Eq. (3.7) of Clauset et al. (2009).
The three models of Comparing Graph Models each reproduce one feature of real networks and miss another. The summary is
One more ingredient closes the gap: triadic closure, the social rule “a friend of my friend becomes my friend”. The model that adds it to preferential attachment is due to Holme and Kim (Holme and Kim 2002).

title: Triadic Closure
text:
The model
The network grows as in the Barabási-Albert model: at each step a new node arrives with \(m\) edges.

The first edge attaches by preferential attachment, to node \(i\) with probability \(\Pi_i = k_i / \sum_j k_j\). Call its target \(w\).
For each of the other \(m-1\) edges, with probability \(p_t\) perform a triad formation step: connect the new node to a random neighbour of \(w\), which closes a triangle \(\text{new} - w - \text{neighbour}\). Otherwise attach by preferential attachment.

The triad probability is often written \(p\); we write \(p_t\) here to keep \(p\) for the edge probability of the random graph. At \(p_t = 0\) the model is the Barabási-Albert model, and for \(m = 1\) there is no second edge, so no triangle can ever be created. NetworkX implements the model as nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(n, m, p). Its documentation points out one detail: if every neighbour of \(w\) is already linked to the new node, the step falls back to preferential attachment.

title: Triadic Closure
text:
Clustering is tunable
Figure 1 varies \(p_t\) at fixed size.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import shortest_path

SEED = 7


def avg_path_length(G, n_src=300, seed=0):
    """Average distance in the largest component, from at most n_src random sources."""
    H = G.subgraph(max(nx.connected_components(G), key=len))
    nodes = list(H)
    A = nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(H, nodelist=nodes, format="csr")
    # SciPy's csgraph routines require int32 CSR index buffers in this environment.
    A.indices = A.indices.astype(np.int32)
    A.indptr = A.indptr.astype(np.int32)
    n = len(nodes)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    src = np.arange(n, dtype=np.int32) if n <= n_src else rng.choice(n, n_src, replace=False).astype(np.int32)
    return shortest_path(A, unweighted=True, indices=src).sum() / (len(src) * (n - 1))


pts = np.linspace(0, 1, 6)
C_pt, L_pt = [], []
for pt in pts:
    graphs = [nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(2000, 3, pt, seed=SEED + r) for r in range(4)]
    C_pt.append(np.mean([nx.average_clustering(G) for G in graphs]))
    L_pt.append(np.mean([avg_path_length(G) for G in graphs]))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.plot(pts, C_pt, "o-", label="C")
ax.set_xlabel(r"triad probability $p_t$")
ax.set_ylabel("C")
ax2 = ax.twinx()
ax2.plot(pts, L_pt, "s--", color="C1", label="L")
ax2.set_ylabel("L")
ax2.set_ylim(0, 6)
fig.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.12, 0.88))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print("p_t:", np.round(pts, 2))
print("C  :", np.round(C_pt, 3))
print("L  :", np.round(L_pt, 2))







Figure 1: Average clustering coefficient and average path length of the Holme-Kim graph (N = 2000, m = 3) as a function of the triad probability p_t, averaged over 4 graphs. The value at p_t = 0 is the Barabási-Albert graph. Clustering grows roughly linearly with p_t while the path length changes by less than 20%.





p_t: [0.  0.2 0.4 0.6 0.8 1. ]
C  : [0.019 0.121 0.231 0.339 0.457 0.594]
L  : [3.74 3.74 3.72 3.79 3.95 4.42]


The maximum clustering for \(m = 3\) is about 0.6, not 1. Only the edges after the first can close triangles, so at birth a new node with \(m\) edges has about \(m - 1\) closed pairs among its \(m(m-1)/2\) neighbour pairs, a local clustering of about \(2/m\) (0.67 for \(m = 3\)). This sets a ceiling well below 1. In other words the clustering is “finite”: it does not decay with \(N\), as the clustering figure in Scaling of Path Length and Clustering shows.

title: Triadic Closure
section: The degree distribution is still scale-free
text:
The degree distribution is still scale-free
The additional step changes who is connected to the new node but not the rich-get-richer mechanism, so the tail should stay a power law with exponent close to 3. Figure 2 compares the complementary cumulative distribution \(P(K \ge k)\) of the Barabási-Albert and the Holme-Kim graphs. For \(p(k) \sim k^{-\gamma}\) this distribution decays like \(k^{-(\gamma - 1)}\), so a slope of \(-2\) corresponds to \(\gamma = 3\). The exponent is estimated with the maximum-likelihood formula for discrete data, \(\hat\gamma \simeq 1 + n \big[\sum_{i} \ln \big(k_i / (k_{\min} - \tfrac12)\big)\big]^{-1}\), applied to the \(n\) nodes with \(k_i \ge k_{\min}\) (Clauset et al. 2009, Eq. 3.7).

def gamma_mle(deg, kmin):
    x = deg[deg >= kmin]
    return 1 + len(x) / np.sum(np.log(x / (kmin - 0.5)))


graphs = {
    "BA": nx.barabasi_albert_graph(50_000, 3, seed=1),
    "HK, p_t = 0.5": nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(50_000, 3, 0.5, seed=1),
    "HK, p_t = 1": nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(50_000, 3, 1.0, seed=1),
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for name, G in graphs.items():
    deg = np.array([d for _, d in G.degree()])
    ks = np.arange(3, deg.max() + 1)
    ccdf = np.array([(deg >= k).mean() for k in ks])
    ax.loglog(ks, ccdf, ".", ms=3, label=name)
    print(f"{name:>14}: k_max = {deg.max():5d}, gamma_hat(k_min = 10) = {gamma_mle(deg, 10):.2f}, "
          f"gamma_hat(k_min = 20) = {gamma_mle(deg, 20):.2f}, C = {nx.average_clustering(G):.3f}")
deg_ba = np.array([d for _, d in graphs["BA"].degree()])
ks = np.array([10, 1000])
ax.loglog(ks, (deg_ba >= 10).mean() * (ks / 10.0) ** -2, "k--", lw=1, label=r"slope $-2$")
ax.set_xlabel("k")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$P(K \geq k)$")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

            BA: k_max =   506, gamma_hat(k_min = 10) = 2.86, gamma_hat(k_min = 20) = 2.91, C = 0.001
 HK, p_t = 0.5: k_max =  1622, gamma_hat(k_min = 10) = 2.81, gamma_hat(k_min = 20) = 2.81, C = 0.268
   HK, p_t = 1: k_max =  2371, gamma_hat(k_min = 10) = 2.85, gamma_hat(k_min = 20) = 2.83, C = 0.590








Figure 2: Complementary cumulative degree distribution P(K >= k) of a Barabási-Albert graph and of Holme-Kim graphs with p_t = 0.5 and 1 (N = 50000, m = 3), on logarithmic axes. The dashed line has slope -2, which corresponds to p(k) ~ k^-3.





The estimates are between 2.8 and 2.9 for all three graphs. They are below 3 because the formula is an approximation and because the finite sample and the discrete lower cutoff \(k \ge m\) bias the estimate. The plain Barabási-Albert graph gives the same value, so the triad step does not change the exponent in a detectable way. For the Barabási-Albert model, Barabasi and Albert (1999) report a simulated exponent of \(2.9 \pm 0.1\) against the analytical value 3, which is consistent with these estimates.

title: Triadic Closure
text:
The completed comparison
Table 1 puts numbers in the summary table. All model graphs have \(N = 5000\) and mean degree 6. The two real networks are the ones used in Practice: Real Networks and Practice: Flights and Other Networks; they are small and, in the flights case, not connected, so \(L\) is computed on the largest component.



Table 1: Measured properties of the model graphs (N = 5000, mean degree 6, one graph each) and of two real networks. C_random = /N is the clustering of a random graph with the same N and mean degree. kmax/ measures how far the degree distribution extends beyond its mean.


import gzip

N = 5000
models = {
    "Erdős-Rényi": nx.fast_gnp_random_graph(N, 6 / (N - 1), seed=1),
    "Watts-Strogatz (p = 0.1)": nx.watts_strogatz_graph(N, 6, 0.1, seed=1),
    "Barabási-Albert (m = 3)": nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N, 3, seed=1),
    "Holme-Kim (m = 3, p_t = 0.5)": nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(N, 3, 0.5, seed=1),
}
enron = nx.Graph(nx.read_edgelist("data/ia-enron-only/ia-enron-only.edges"))
flights = nx.Graph(nx.read_graphml("data/openflights/openflights_usa.graphml.gz"))
rows = {**models, "Enron e-mail (data)": enron, "US flights (data)": flights}

print(f"{'network':<30}{'N':>6}{'<k>':>7}{'L':>6}{'C':>8}{'C/C_random':>12}{'kmax/<k>':>10}")
for name, G in rows.items():
    G.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(G))
    k = np.array([d for _, d in G.degree()], dtype=float)
    C = nx.average_clustering(G)
    print(f"{name:<30}{len(G):>6}{k.mean():>7.1f}{avg_path_length(G):>6.2f}{C:>8.3f}{C / (k.mean() / len(G)):>12.1f}{k.max() / k.mean():>10.1f}")

network                            N    <k>     L       C  C/C_random  kmax/<k>
Erdős-Rényi                     5000    6.0  4.98   0.001         0.8       2.7
Watts-Strogatz (p = 0.1)        5000    6.0  7.90   0.445       370.6       1.5
Barabási-Albert (m = 3)         5000    6.0  4.10   0.009         7.2      27.2
Holme-Kim (m = 3, p_t = 0.5)    5000    6.0  4.11   0.271       225.9      63.9
Enron e-mail (data)              143    8.7  2.97   0.434         7.1       4.8
US flights (data)                546   10.2  3.22   0.493        26.4      15.0




Only the Holme-Kim row has all three properties of the real rows at once: short paths, an absolute clustering of the same order as the real values (0.27 against 0.43 and 0.49) and a degree distribution that extends far beyond its mean. The ratio \(C/C_{\text{random}}\) alone is misleading, because \(C_{\text{random}}\) depends on \(N\): the plain Barabási-Albert graph has a ratio of 7, like the Enron network, but its clustering of 0.009 is not high in absolute terms. Two reservations apply. First, the conclusion is that these are only three features: degree assortativity, community structure and edge dynamics are not reproduced. The real networks of this table have negative degree correlations (flights) or none (Enron), a feature that none of the four models is built to produce. Second, a clustering far above \(C_{\text{random}}\) is partly a consequence of the degree heterogeneity; the next page quantifies how much with a null model that keeps the degrees.






NoteExercise



Generate Holme-Kim graphs with \(N = 2000\) and \(m = 1, 2, 3\) for \(p_t = 1\) and compute their clustering coefficient. Explain the value for \(m = 1\). Is the clustering larger for \(m = 2\) or for \(m = 3\), and why?








TipSolution





for m in (1, 2, 3):
    C = np.mean([nx.average_clustering(nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(2000, m, 1.0, seed=s)) for s in range(4)])
    print(m, round(C, 3))
For \(m = 1\) each new node has a single edge, so the graph is a tree and has no triangle at all: the clustering is zero. The measured values are 0, about 0.75 for \(m = 2\) and about 0.59 for \(m = 3\), so the clustering decreases with \(m\). For \(p_t = 1\) every edge after the first closes a triangle with the first target \(w\), so a new node of degree \(m\) is joined to \(w\) and to \(m-1\) neighbours of \(w\). Its \(m(m-1)/2\) neighbour pairs contain at least the \(m-1\) pairs \((w, x)\), so its local clustering is at least \(2/m\): 1 for \(m = 2\) and 2/3 for \(m = 3\). Larger \(m\) means more neighbour pairs that triadic closure does not close.









NoteExercise



The Barabási-Albert graph and the Holme-Kim graph with \(p_t = 1\) have almost the same exponent. Compute \(\langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle\) for both graphs of Figure 2 and use the heterogeneous mean-field threshold \(\lambda_c = \langle k \rangle/\langle k^2 \rangle\) of Epidemic Threshold to compare the predictions for SIS spreading. What does the prediction ignore?








TipSolution





for name, G in graphs.items():
    k = np.array([d for _, d in G.degree()], dtype=float)
    print(name, round(k.mean() / (k**2).mean(), 4))
With \(N = 50000\) the prediction is \(\langle k \rangle/\langle k^2 \rangle \approx 0.048\) for the Barabási-Albert graph, 0.030 for \(p_t = 0.5\) and 0.020 for \(p_t = 1\). The Holme-Kim graphs have a larger \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) (their largest hubs are bigger, see the \(k_{\max}\) printed above), hence a smaller predicted threshold. The mean-field formula uses only \(p(k)\). It assumes that the network is uncorrelated and locally tree-like, so it ignores the triangles that triadic closure adds: edges inside a triangle transmit the infection to nodes that may already be infected. Pastor-Satorras et al. (2015) discuss the effect of short loops on epidemic thresholds.

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Murray (2002), Chapter 11 (Reaction Diffusion, Chemotaxis, and Nonlocal Mechanisms).
Recommended: Britton (2003), Chapter 5 (Biological Motion) and Chapter 7 (Pattern Formation), in particular Sections 7.1 and 7.2 (pp. 205 to 210).
Original idea: Turing (1952), Summary and Section 1: morphogens that react and diffuse can turn a homogeneous state into a pattern. Kondo and Miura (Kondo and Miura 2010) give a modern, non-mathematical account.
In Module 3 you derived the diffusion equation \(\partial_t c = D\,\partial_{xx} c\) as the continuum limit of a random walk (From random walks to diffusion). A reaction-diffusion equation adds local production and decay to that transport term (Murray 2002, chap. 11).

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
text:
The General Form
For \(m\) species with concentrations \(w = (w_1, \dots, w_m)\) on a domain \(\Omega\),
\[
\partial_t w = D\,\Delta w + R(w), \qquad D = \operatorname{diag}(D_1, \dots, D_m).
\tag{1}\]

\(\Delta\) is the Laplacian, \(\partial_{xx}\) in 1D and \(\partial_{xx} + \partial_{yy}\) in 2D.
\(D_i > 0\) is the diffusion coefficient of species \(i\).
\(R(w)\) collects the reaction kinetics. With \(D = 0\) you recover an ODE system at every point, as in Module 1.

The model is incomplete without an initial condition \(w(x, 0)\) and boundary conditions on \(\partial\Omega\). You will meet Neumann (zero flux), Dirichlet (fixed value), and periodic conditions on the page Laplacian Eigenmodes.

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
section: The Scaling Used in This Module
text:
The Scaling Used in This Module
For two species \(u\) and \(v\) we use the nondimensional form of Murray (2003, sec. 2.3):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_t u &= \Delta u + \gamma f(u, v), \\
\partial_t v &= d\,\Delta v + \gamma g(u, v).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
Here \(d = D_v / D_u\) is the ratio of diffusion coefficients and \(\gamma\) measures the strength of the reactions relative to diffusion. In Murray’s scaling \(\gamma\) is proportional to the square of the domain length, so increasing \(\gamma\) at fixed domain is equivalent to enlarging the domain (Murray 2003, sec. 2.3). The Gierer-Meinhardt code in amlab.pdes_1d and amlab.pdes_2d uses exactly these symbols.

Where \(\gamma\) Comes From
Start from dimensional variables with a length scale \(\ell\) (for instance the domain length), a typical reaction rate \(r\) and diffusion coefficients \(D_u\), \(D_v\). The substitution \(\bar x = \ell x\), \(\bar t = (\ell^2/D_u)\,t\) turns the dimensional system into Equation 2 with
\[
d = \frac{D_v}{D_u}, \qquad \gamma = \frac{r\,\ell^2}{D_u}.
\tag{3}\]
So \(\gamma\) grows with the square of the length, which is the sense in which “increasing \(\gamma\) is equivalent to enlarging the domain”. Britton (2003, sec. 7.2) makes the same rescaling on a standard domain, \(x = \gamma_B X\), \(t = \gamma_B^2 T\), and obtains \(u_t = \gamma_B^2 f(u) + D\nabla^2 u\) with \(D = \operatorname{diag}(D_1, D_2)\) not normalised. His \(\gamma_B\) is a length scale and his \(\alpha = \gamma_B^2\) plays the role of the \(\gamma\) used here. The notation dictionary on the page about Turing’s original analysis compares these symbols with Turing’s own.
The single-equation case explains why two species are needed. For \(\partial_t u = \gamma f(u) + \Delta u\) the mode with wavenumber \(k\) grows like \(e^{\sigma t}\) with \(\sigma = \gamma f'(u_*) - k^2\). Diffusion only subtracts \(k^2\), so a state that is stable for the flat mode is stable for all modes. Britton (2003, sec. 7.2 and 7.4) describes this as the stabilising effect of diffusion in a single equation, and notes that Turing instability needs at least two.

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
text:
Examples

Fisher-KPP equation. One species, logistic growth plus diffusion: \(\partial_t u = D\,\partial_{xx} u + r u(1-u)\). It was proposed for the spread of an advantageous gene (Fisher 1937). It has travelling fronts with minimal speed \(c = 2\sqrt{rD}\) (Murray 2002, chap. 13).
Gierer-Meinhardt model. An activator \(u\) and an inhibitor \(v\) with \(f = a - bu + u^2/v\) and \(g = u^2 - v\) (Gierer and Meinhardt 1972). It forms stationary patterns and is the main example of this module.
Gray-Scott model. An autocatalytic reaction with feed and removal (Gray and Scott 1984). Its 2D simulations produce spots, stripes and self-replicating spots (Pearson 1993).
Chemical experiments. Stationary Turing patterns were first observed experimentally in the CIMA reaction (Castets et al. 1990).

title: Reaction-Diffusion Equations
text:
A First Simulation
Figure 1 shows a Fisher-KPP front with \(D = r = 1\). The dashed lines move at the predicted speed \(c = 2\).








Figure 1: Fisher-KPP front with \(D = r = 1\), explicit Euler with \(dx = 0.5\), \(dt = 0.05\). Dashed lines mark positions moving at speed \(c = 2\sqrt{rD} = 2\) from the front at \(t = 10\).





For an initial condition with compact support the front speed tends to the minimal speed \(c = 2\sqrt{rD}\) as \(t \to \infty\) (Murray 2002, chap. 13).






NoteExercise



Set \(D = 0\) in Equation 1. What happens to a spatial profile \(u(x, 0)\) under Fisher-KPP kinetics, and why can no front move?








TipSolution





Each point solves the logistic ODE \(\dot u = r u (1-u)\) independently. Points with \(u(x,0) > 0\) grow to \(1\) and points with \(u(x,0) = 0\) stay at \(0\). Without diffusion no point can influence its neighbours, so the region with \(u = 0\) never becomes invaded.

title: Animal Coat Patterns
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Murray (1988).
Recommended: Kondo and Miura (2010), the part on Turing patterns in vertebrate skin, and Britton (2003), Appendix C, Example C.10 (eigenvalues on a cylinder).
The classical biological application of Turing’s mechanism is Murray’s model of mammalian coat markings (Murray 1981; 1988; 2003, sec. 3.1). This page lists its main claims and uses your 1D tools to reproduce the central one: domain size controls the pattern.

title: Animal Coat Patterns
text:
The Model in Brief

A reaction-diffusion system sets up a spatial prepattern of a morphogen on the embryo’s skin during a short window of development (Murray 1981).
Pigment cells later read the prepattern: where the morphogen exceeds a threshold, they produce melanin (Murray 1981).
Only the scale and geometry of the domain were varied in Murray’s simulations. Very small domains stay uniform, and increasingly complex patterns, from stripes to spots, appear as the domain grows. The size and shape of the embryo when the mechanism operates therefore decide the marking (Murray 1988; 2003, sec. 3.1).

title: Animal Coat Patterns
text:
The Tail Prediction
A tail is close to a tapering cylinder. Its surface is periodic around the circumference and has zero flux at the two ends. The Laplacian eigenproblem on such a surface is solved by separation of variables, with eigenfunctions \(\cos(n\pi z/h)\,e^{im\phi}\) and eigenvalues
\[
k_{m,n}^2 = \frac{m^2}{r^2} + \frac{n^2\pi^2}{h^2}, \qquad m, n = 0, 1, 2, \dots,
\tag{1}\]
where \(r\) is the radius and \(h\) the length of the cylinder (Britton 2003, Appendix C, Example C.10). Modes with \(m = 0\) do not depend on the angle, so they are rings around the tail. Modes with \(m \ge 1\) vary around the circumference, and the combinations with \(n \ge 1\) give spots.
A mode can grow only if \(k_{m,n}^2\) lies in the unstable band. Because \(k_{m,n}^2 \ge m^2/r^2\), no mode with \(m \ge 1\) is unstable when \(1/r\) exceeds the upper edge \(k_2\) of the band, that is when \(r < 1/k_2\). For Case A the band is \(0.349 < k < 0.523\), so the critical radius is \(1/k_2 \approx 1.91\). A thinner cylinder carries only ring-shaped bands. Figure 1 shows this directly.








Figure 1: Circumferential mode numbers \(m\) that have at least one unstable axial partner \(n\), as a function of the cylinder radius \(r\), for Gierer-Meinhardt Case A on a cylinder of length \(h = 40\) with zero flux at the ends. For \(r\) below about \(1.91\) only \(m = 0\) is unstable (rings around the tail). The dashed line marks \(r = 1/k_2\).





The model therefore predicts that a spotted animal can have a striped tail, but a striped animal cannot have a spotted tail. The tail is striped near the tip, where \(r\) is small, and the full pattern is possible only where the radius is large enough (Murray 1988; 2003, sec. 3.1). The argument is linear: it says which modes can start to grow at a given radius, not which pattern the nonlinear terms finally select.

title: Animal Coat Patterns
text:
Domain Size in 1D
The same effect appears in 1D. Figure 2 shows the leading unstable Neumann mode for Case A (\(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), \(d = 30\), \(\gamma = 1\)) as the domain length grows.








Figure 2: Leading unstable Neumann mode \(n\) versus domain length \(L\) for Gierer-Meinhardt Case A, using the exact Neumann spectrum \(k_n = n\pi/L\). \(n = 0\) means no unstable mode, so the flat state persists. The dashed line is \(L\,k_{\max}/\pi\) for the continuous fastest-growing wavenumber.





Below \(L \approx 6\) and for \(9 < L < 12\) nothing grows. As \(L\) increases the leading mode jumps by one at a time, and the pattern wavelength stays close to \(2\pi/k_{\max} \approx 14.6\). In linear theory, a larger domain therefore holds more peaks at the same spacing rather than wider peaks.

title: Animal Coat Patterns
text:
Evidence and Limitations

Kondo and Miura (2010) credit Kondo and Asai (Kondo and Asai 1995) with the first observation of the dynamic properties of a Turing pattern in nature, in the stripes of the angelfish Pomacanthus imperator. They report that this dynamic behaviour is shared by many fish species, including the zebrafish, where the stripes rearrange slowly after laser ablation of pigment cells and keep their spacing, as a simulation predicts. See Evidence for Reaction-Diffusion in Real Systems.
Kondo and Miura (2010) stress that a simulation that reproduces a real pattern is not proof that the mechanism operates. One has to identify a dynamic property that the simulation predicts and test it, and to identify the interacting components.
Linear theory predicts the onset wavelength only. The final pattern also depends on nonlinear terms, domain growth, curvature, and timing (Murray 2003, sec. 2.6 and 3.1).







NoteExercise



Optional extension. Run the 1D solver with \(L = 10\), Neumann boundaries, \(dx = 1\) and \(dt = 0.01\) for Case A. You will see a pattern, although Figure 2 predicts none. Repeat with \(dx = 0.25\) and \(dt = 0.001\). Explain the difference with the effective domain length of the copy boundary condition on Boundary Conditions.








TipSolution





Copying \(u_0 = u_1\) and \(u_{N-1} = u_{N-2}\) places the zero-flux boundaries halfway between the first two and the last two grid points. The effective length is \((N-2)\,dx\). With \(dx = 1\) that is \(8\), and mode \(1\) has \(k = \pi/8 \approx 0.39\), inside the unstable band. With \(dx = 0.25\) it is \(9.5\), \(\pi/9.5 \approx 0.33\) lies below the band, and the flat state persists. This is a discretization effect that disappears under grid refinement, which is why you run the convergence check.

title: Animal Coat Patterns
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



Case A on a Neumann interval of length \(L = 10\) satisfies all four Turing conditions. Will a pattern form? Explain in one or two sentences.








TipSolution





No. The Turing conditions do not depend on the domain, but the admissible wavenumbers \(n\pi/10\) for \(n = 1, 2\) are \(0.31\) and \(0.63\), both outside the unstable band \(0.349 < k < 0.523\). No mode grows, so the flat state persists.

title: Turing’s Original Analysis
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Turing (1952), Sections 6 to 10 (pp. 46 to 65): reactions and diffusion in a ring of cells, the six types of behaviour, and the numerical example. Sections 1 to 5 are background on the chemistry.
Recommended: Britton (2003), Section 7.2 (pp. 206 to 210), for the same linear analysis in modern notation, and Kondo and Miura (2010), the section “The Original Turing Model”.
The pages of this module use the notation of the textbook literature. Turing’s paper, written before computers could be used for such questions, is organised differently: a ring of cells instead of a continuum, and a classification of the possible forms of instability. Reading it explains where the conditions of Turing Conditions come from and which claims are Turing’s own.

title: Turing’s Original Analysis
text:
What the Source Says

The paper proposes that reacting and diffusing chemicals, called morphogens, can account for the main phenomena of morphogenesis. A homogeneous system can develop a pattern through an instability of the homogeneous equilibrium that is triggered by random disturbances (Turing 1952, Summary).
The model is deliberately simple. Mechanical effects are set aside, and tissue is either a set of point-like cells or a continuum. The analysis is linear and applies only while the state is close to homogeneous. Turing calls this a serious assumption, justified because the early pattern should resemble the later one (Turing 1952, sec. 2 and 11).
Two morphogens \(X\) and \(Y\) on a ring of \(N\) identical cells are studied first. Cell-to-cell diffusion constants are \(\mu\) and \(\nu\), and the reaction rates are \(f(X, Y)\) and \(g(X, Y)\) (Turing 1952, sec. 6).
Linearization at the equilibrium gives four “marginal reaction rates” \(a, b, c, d\). The ring is then decoupled by Fourier components, and each component \(s\) obeys a pair of linear equations with its own pair of exponents (Turing 1952, sec. 6 and 7).
After a long time the component with the largest real part of the exponent dominates. If that exponent is real the pattern is stationary, and if it is complex the waves travel (Turing 1952, sec. 8).
The number of lobes on the ring is obtained by dividing the circumference by a “chemical wave-length”. This is generally not an integer, and the observed number is one of the two nearest integers, usually the nearest (Turing 1952, sec. 8 and 11).

Two cautions follow from the table. First, Turing’s \(d\) is the entry \(g_v\) of the Jacobian, not a diffusion ratio. Second, Britton’s \(\gamma_B\) is a length scale and his reaction scale is \(\alpha = \gamma_B^2\), so Britton’s \(\alpha\) plays the role of the \(\gamma\) used here. Both Britton’s rescaling and the one in these notes make \(\gamma\) proportional to the square of the domain length.
For the continuum, Turing’s equation (9.1) is \((p - a + \mu' U)(p - d + \nu' U) = bc\). Expanding the determinant \(\det(J - U\,\mathrm{diag}(\mu', \nu') - pI)\) with \(J = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}\) gives exactly this quadratic, so it is the dispersion relation of the Dispersion Relation page written in his symbols, with \(k^2 = U\).

title: Turing’s Original Analysis
text:
The Six Cases
Turing finds six essentially different forms of the onset of instability (Turing 1952, sec. 8 and 11). The table lists them with the labels that Kondo and Miura (2010) use in their Figure 2A.

Case (d) is the one that matters for this module. Turing states that it requires \(bc < 0\) (Turing 1952, Equation 9.4a). In the notation of these notes, \(bc = f_v g_u\), which is the sign requirement for the cross terms derived on the Turing Conditions page. For two morphogens only (a) to (d) are possible, and cases (e) and (f) need three or more (Turing 1952, sec. 11). This agrees with Britton, who shows that for two equations the coefficient \(a_1(\lambda) = (D_1 + D_2)\lambda - \alpha(f_u^* + g_v^*)\) is positive as soon as \(\operatorname{tr} J < 0\), so that a Hopf (oscillatory) instability with \(k \ne 0\) is impossible (Britton 2003, sec. 7.4.1).






WarningA discrepancy between sources



The caption of Figure 2A in Kondo and Miura (2010) describes the six states as those toward which “the two-factor RD system” can converge, and case V (travelling waves) is among them. By Turing’s analysis and by Britton’s trace argument, a system of two reaction-diffusion equations cannot produce cases (e) and (f). The review’s figure is best read as a list of what reaction-diffusion systems in general can do, with the oscillatory finite-wavelength cases requiring a third component.

title: Turing’s Original Analysis
text:
Turing’s Dappling Remark
Turing links the simplest case (a) to “dappled” colour patterns and shows a two-dimensional example of a patchy pattern from this type of instability. He also notes that if dappling arose in this way, the pattern would have to be laid down very early in development, since later the distances would exceed what diffusion can cover (Turing 1952, sec. 11 and Figure 2). His main biological examples of case (d) are the tentacles of Hydra and whorled leaves, which he discusses as approximations to a ring (Turing 1952, sec. 11). Compare this with the later work on mammalian coats on Animal Coat Patterns.

title: Turing’s Original Analysis
text:
The Numerical Example, Recomputed
In Section 10 Turing gives a specific system on a ring of \(N = 20\) cells. In his special units (time unit \(1000\) s) the cell-to-cell diffusion constants are \(\mu = 1/2\) for \(X\) and \(\nu = 1/4\) for \(Y\). The kinetics are
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(X, Y) &= \tfrac{1}{16} - \tfrac{1}{32}\left(50XY + 7X^2 - 55(1+\gamma_T)\right), \\
g(X, Y) &= \tfrac{1}{32}\left(50XY + 7X^2 - 55(1+\gamma_T)\right) - \tfrac{1}{16}Y,
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
where \(\gamma_T\) is the catalyst parameter, which is slowly increased in the paper to drive the system through the instability (Turing 1952, sec. 10). At \(\gamma_T = 0\) the equilibrium is \(X = Y = 1\). The code differentiates these functions numerically and scans the Fourier modes of the ring.








Figure 1: Growth rate of the Fourier components of Turing’s 20-cell example at \(\gamma_T = 0\). Dots are the ring modes \(s = 0, \dots, 10\), with eigenvalues \(4\sin^2(\pi s/N)\) of the cell-to-cell Laplacian. The solid curve is the same system with the continuum value \((2\pi s/N)^2\). The dashed line marks zero growth.






import numpy as np

a, b, c, d = jac.ravel()
print("marginal rates a, b, c, d =", np.round([a, b, c, d], 4))
print("tr J = %.3f, det J = %.4f" % (np.trace(jac), np.linalg.det(jac)))
for s in (2, 3, 4, 5):
    print("s =", s, " largest Re p = %.4f" % top_rate(4 * np.sin(np.pi * s / n_cells) ** 2))
lam = np.linspace(0.5, 1.5, 100001)
rates = np.array([top_rate(x) for x in lam[::100]])
lam_best = lam[::100][np.argmax(rates)]
print("best lambda = %.3f, growth there = %.2e" % (lam_best, rates.max()))
print("matching s on the ring = %.3f" % (n_cells / np.pi * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(lam_best) / 2)))

marginal rates a, b, c, d = [-2.     -1.5625  2.      1.5   ]
tr J = -0.500, det J = 0.1250
s = 2  largest Re p = -0.0663
s = 3  largest Re p = -0.0035
s = 4  largest Re p = -0.0120
s = 5  largest Re p = -0.0646
best lambda = 1.000, growth there = -6.94e-12
matching s on the ring = 3.333


The marginal rates are \(a = -2\), \(b = -1.5625\), \(c = 2\), \(d = 1.5\) as printed in the paper, with \(\operatorname{tr} J = -0.5 < 0\) and \(\det J = 0.125 > 0\). The growth rate has its maximum, equal to zero, at \(\lambda = 1\), that is \(s = 3.333\) lobes on the ring. This is the system exactly at the onset of instability (\(I = 0\)), as in the paper. The ring offers only integer lobe numbers, and the table gives, for \(s = 3\) and \(s = 4\), the rates \(-0.0035\) and \(-0.0120\). Their difference, \(0.0085\), matches Turing’s \(0.0084\) and implies, as he notes, that the three-lobed component gains a factor \(e\) over the four-lobed one in about \(118\) time units, roughly \(33\) hours. Turing’s printed values for the other modes differ slightly from the recomputed ones (for \(s = 2\) he gives \(-0.0648\) and the code gives \(-0.0663\)). The difference is small enough to be rounding, but I have not been able to trace it.
Two lessons from the example are worth carrying over to the laboratory.

Which species is the activator. The entry \(g_v = 1.5 > 0\) means that \(Y\) activates itself, while \(f_u = -2 < 0\). Since \(Y\) has the smaller diffusion constant (\(\nu < \mu\)), this is the situation described on the Turing Conditions page with the roles of the two species exchanged: the self-activating species diffuses more slowly. In the notation of these notes \(u = Y\), \(v = X\), \(d = \mu/\nu = 2\).
Discretisation shifts the preferred mode. The curve built from \((2\pi s/N)^2\) peaks at \(\lambda = 1\), that is at \(s = N/(2\pi) \approx 3.18\) lobes, while the cell-to-cell Laplacian gives \(3.33\). The explicit Euler solvers of the laboratory use the same kind of operator on a periodic grid, so the mode that they favour can differ from the continuum prediction when the wavelength spans only a few grid points.







NoteExercise




Convert Turing’s example to the notation of these notes with \(u = Y\) and \(v = X\). Compute \(f_u, f_v, g_u, g_v\), check the four Turing conditions at \(d = 2\), and find \(d_c\). (b) Show that the eigenvalues of the periodic three-point Laplacian on \(N\) grid points with spacing \(dx\) are \(-(4/dx^2)\sin^2(\pi s/N)\), \(s = 0, \dots, N-1\), and verify this numerically with np.roll.









TipSolution






Swapping the roles of the species gives \(f_u = 1.5\), \(f_v = 2\), \(g_u = -1.5625\), \(g_v = -2\). Then \(\operatorname{tr} J = -0.5\), \(\det J = 1.5 \cdot (-2) - 2 \cdot (-1.5625) = 0.125\), and \(d f_u + g_v = 3 - 2 = 1 > 0\). The fourth condition reads \(1^2 > 4 \cdot 2 \cdot 0.125 = 1\), which holds with equality. So \(d = 2\) is exactly the critical ratio, in agreement with \(I = 0\).

from amlab.turing import critical_diffusion_ratio, turing_conditions

jac = (1.5, 2.0, -1.5625, -2.0)
print(critical_diffusion_ratio(*jac), turing_conditions(*jac, 2.0), turing_conditions(*jac, 2.5))
The first value is \(2\), the second is False because of the strict inequality, and the third is True.

The vectors \(e^{2\pi i s j/N}\) are eigenvectors of the shift matrices, and \(e^{i\theta} - 2 + e^{-i\theta} = -4\sin^2(\theta/2)\) with \(\theta = 2\pi s/N\).

import numpy as np

n, dx = 20, 1.0
lap = -2 * np.eye(n) + np.roll(np.eye(n), 1, axis=0) + np.roll(np.eye(n), -1, axis=0)
numeric = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(lap / dx**2))
exact = np.sort(-4 / dx**2 * np.sin(np.pi * np.arange(n) / n) ** 2)
print(np.abs(numeric - exact).max())

The feed rate \(f\) and kill rate \(k\) decide what the Gray-Scott solver produces. Pearson (1993) mapped this \((f, k)\) plane with forward Euler on a periodic \(256 \times 256\) grid of physical size \(2.5 \times 2.5\), time step \(1\), and diffusion coefficients \(d_1 = 2 \times 10^{-5}\), \(d_2 = 10^{-5}\). title: Gray-Scott Parameters
text:
Connection Back to Turing Analysis
The steady-state, Jacobian, and mode-matrix pipeline from Turing Numerics still applies. Only the spectrum changes: with periodic boundaries the wavenumbers are \(2\pi n/L\).
The trivial state \((u, v) = (1, 0)\) has Jacobian \(\operatorname{diag}(-f, -(f+k))\), so it is linearly stable for every mode. The patterns in Figure 1 therefore start from the finite-amplitude square, not from a Turing instability of \((1, 0)\) (Pearson 1993). Most of Pearson’s patterns occur where no nontrivial uniform state exists at all.
The nontrivial homogeneous equilibria satisfy \(u_* v_* = f + k\). Substituting into \(u_* v_*^2 = f(1 - u_*)\) gives
\[
u_* = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 \pm \sqrt{1 - \frac{4(f+k)^2}{f}}\right), \qquad v_* = \frac{f+k}{u_*},
\tag{1}\]
which exist when \(4(f+k)^2 \le f\). The Jacobian at any homogeneous equilibrium is
\[
J_{\mathrm{GS}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
-v_*^2 - f & -2u_*v_* \\
v_*^2 & 2u_*v_* - (f+k)
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{2}\]

Implement both helpers. Keep only equilibria with \(u_* > 0\).

TipSolution





def gray_scott_equilibria(f=0.040, k=0.060):
    equilibria = [(1.0, 0.0)]
    discriminant = 1 - 4 * (f + k) ** 2 / f
    if discriminant >= 0:
        root = np.sqrt(discriminant)
        for sign in (+1, -1):
            u_star = 0.5 * (1 + sign * root)
            if u_star > 0:
                equilibria.append((u_star, (f + k) / u_star))
    return equilibria


def gray_scott_jacobian(u_star, v_star, f=0.040, k=0.060):
    return np.array(
        [
            [-v_star**2 - f, -2 * u_star * v_star],
            [v_star**2, 2 * u_star * v_star - (f + k)],
        ]
    )









NoteExercise



For Type A (\(f = 0.040\), \(k = 0.060\)), do nontrivial equilibria exist? What about Type C?








TipSolution





Type A: \(4(f+k)^2/f = 4 \cdot 0.01 / 0.04 = 1\), so the discriminant is \(0\) and the two nontrivial equilibria merge at \(u_* = 0.5\), \(v_* = 0.2\), a saddle-node point. In floating point the discriminant comes out as about \(-2 \times 10^{-16}\), so the code above returns only \((1, 0)\). Type C: \(4 \cdot 0.127^2 / 0.062 \approx 1.04 > 1\), so only \((1, 0)\) exists. In both cases the pattern cannot come from a Turing instability of a nontrivial uniform state that is stable without diffusion.



Once both helpers work, reuse find_unstable_modes_2d from Unstable Modes in 2D. Swap in gray_scott_jacobian, use \(D = \operatorname{diag}(d_1, d_2)\) with no \(\gamma\), and replace \(\pi/L\) by \(2\pi/L\) for the periodic spectrum.






NoteExercise



Type D (\(f = 0.078\), \(k = 0.061\)) has nontrivial equilibria. List them, compute \(\operatorname{tr} J\) and \(\det J\) at each one, and scan the periodic modes on \(L = 250\) with \(d_1 = 0.1\), \(d_2 = 0.05\). Is any of them Turing unstable?

    jac = gray_scott_jacobian(u_star, v_star, f, k)
    diffusion = np.diag([d1, d2])
    unstable_modes = []
    # TODO: loop over (n, m), including (0, 0), with k2 = (2 pi / L)**2 (n**2 + m**2)
    # TODO: store ((n, m), growth_rate) when the growth rate is positive
    return unstable_modes








TipSolution





There are three equilibria. \((1, 0)\) is stable, with \(\det J > 0\) and \(\operatorname{tr} J < 0\), and no mode grows. The upper state \(u_* \approx 0.548\), \(v_* \approx 0.254\) has \(\det J < 0\): it is a saddle, unstable already without diffusion, so the flat mode \((0, 0)\) grows too. The lower state \(u_* \approx 0.452\), \(v_* \approx 0.307\) is stable without diffusion and no mode grows for \(d_1/d_2 = 2\). So none of them shows a Turing instability, in line with Pearson (1993).
def find_unstable_modes_gs(u_star, v_star, f, k, d1=0.1, d2=0.05, length=250.0, num_modes=60):
    jac = gray_scott_jacobian(u_star, v_star, f, k)
    diffusion = np.diag([d1, d2])
    unstable_modes = []
    for n in range(num_modes):
        for m in range(num_modes):
            k2 = (2 * np.pi / length) ** 2 * (n**2 + m**2)
            growth_rate = np.max(np.linalg.eigvals(jac - k2 * diffusion).real)
            if growth_rate > 0:
                unstable_modes.append(((n, m), growth_rate))
    unstable_modes.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    return unstable_modes


f, k = 0.078, 0.061
for u_star, v_star in gray_scott_equilibria(f, k):
    jac = gray_scott_jacobian(u_star, v_star, f, k)
    modes = find_unstable_modes_gs(u_star, v_star, f, k)
    print(f"({u_star:.3f}, {v_star:.3f})  tr = {np.trace(jac):.4f}  det = {np.linalg.det(jac):.5f}  unstable modes: {len(modes)}")

title: Turing Conditions
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Turing (1952), Sections 6 to 9, read together with the guide on Turing’s Original Analysis.
Recommended: Britton (2003), Chapter 7, Sections 7.2 to 7.4.1 (pp. 206 to 217), for the derivation with spatial modes, and Murray (2003), Chapter 2, Sections 2.1 to 2.6.
Turing (1952) showed that diffusion can destabilize a uniform state that is stable without diffusion. This is called diffusion-driven or Turing instability. This page derives the four conditions for it in the notation of Murray (2003, sec. 2.3).

title: Turing Conditions
text:
The Question
Take the linearized system from Laplacian Eigenmodes. Each mode with wavenumber \(k\) grows like \(e^{\sigma t}\), where \(\sigma\) solves
\[
\det\left(\gamma J - k^2 D - \sigma I\right) = 0, \qquad D = \operatorname{diag}(1, d).
\]
You want the uniform state to be:

stable to the flat mode \(k = 0\) (stable without diffusion), and
unstable to at least one mode with \(k \neq 0\).

title: Turing Conditions
section: Trace and Determinant of the Mode Matrix
text:
Trace and Determinant of the Mode Matrix
For \(A(k^2) = \gamma J - k^2 D\),
\[
\operatorname{tr} A = \gamma (f_u + g_v) - (1 + d)k^2,
\]
\[
h(k^2) \equiv \det A = d\,k^4 - \gamma\,(d f_u + g_v)\,k^2 + \gamma^2 (f_u g_v - f_v g_u).
\tag{1}\]
Stability at \(k = 0\) requires \(\operatorname{tr} J < 0\) and \(\det J > 0\). Then \(\operatorname{tr} A < 0\) for every \(k\), so the only way to get \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma > 0\) is \(h(k^2) < 0\) for some \(k^2 > 0\), which gives one real positive \(\sigma\).
\(h\) is a quadratic in \(k^2\) with positive constant term. It becomes negative only if its minimum lies at \(k^2 > 0\) and is negative. The minimum is at
\[
k_m^2 = \frac{\gamma\,(d f_u + g_v)}{2d}, \qquad
h_{\min} = \gamma^2\left[\det J - \frac{(d f_u + g_v)^2}{4d}\right].
\tag{2}\]

title: Turing Conditions
text:
The Four Conditions
Collecting the requirements gives the Turing conditions (Murray 2003, sec. 2.3):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&f_u + g_v < 0, \\
&f_u g_v - f_v g_u > 0, \\
&d f_u + g_v > 0, \\
&(d f_u + g_v)^2 - 4 d\,(f_u g_v - f_v g_u) > 0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]
All derivatives are evaluated at the steady state. The conditions do not contain \(\gamma\) or the domain size. They are necessary and sufficient for the linearized problem to have a band of growing wavenumbers \(k > 0\) while the flat mode is stable. They are not necessary for patterns in general: the Gray-Scott patterns of Gray-Scott Parameters grow from finite-amplitude perturbations. On a finite domain you also need an admissible wavenumber inside the unstable band (see Dispersion Relation and Domain Size and Mode Selection).

title: Turing Conditions
text:
Britton’s Notation
Britton (2003, sec. 7.4.1) derives the same conditions with diffusion coefficients \(D_1\), \(D_2\) and the scale \(\alpha\) (his version of \(\gamma\)), and with the spatial eigenvalue \(\lambda = k^2\). His mode matrix is \(\alpha J - \lambda D\), and he writes its characteristic polynomial as \(\sigma^2 + a_1(\lambda)\sigma + a_2(\lambda) = 0\) with
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_1(\lambda) &= (D_1 + D_2)\lambda - \alpha (f_u + g_v), \\
a_2(\lambda) &= D_1 D_2 \lambda^2 - \alpha (D_2 f_u + D_1 g_v)\lambda + \alpha^2 \det J.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\]
So \(-a_1\) and \(a_2\) are the trace and determinant of the mode matrix. With \(D_1 = 1\), \(D_2 = d\) and \(\alpha = \gamma\) they are \(-\operatorname{tr} A\) and \(h(k^2)\) of Equation 1. Both roots have negative real part if and only if \(a_1 > 0\) and \(a_2 > 0\). Requiring this at \(\lambda = 0\) gives \(\operatorname{tr} J < 0\) and \(\det J > 0\), which also makes \(a_1(\lambda) > 0\) for every \(\lambda\). Hence a Hopf (oscillatory) instability with \(k \ne 0\) cannot occur in a system of two equations, and the only way to lose stability is \(a_2 < 0\). The remaining two inequalities of Equation 3 are his conditions \(D_2 f_u + D_1 g_v > 0\) and \((D_2 f_u + D_1 g_v)^2 > 4 D_1 D_2 \det J\), which are Equation 3 with \(D_1 = 1\), \(D_2 = d\). The critical wavenumber on an infinite domain is \(\lambda_c = \tfrac{\alpha}{2}\left(f_u/D_1 + g_v/D_2\right)\), which equals \(k_m^2\) in Equation 2. Turing’s own symbols \(a, b, c, d, \mu, \nu\) are compared with both on Turing’s Original Analysis.

title: Turing Conditions
text:
What the Signs Tell You

The first and third conditions force \(d \neq 1\). If both species diffuse equally, no Turing instability exists.
They also force \(f_u\) and \(g_v\) to have opposite signs: the trace condition excludes two positive entries, and two negative entries would make \(d f_u + g_v\) negative. Call the species with \(f_u > 0\) the activator. Then \(g_v < 0\) and \(d > -g_v / f_u > 1\): the inhibitor must diffuse faster than the activator.
The mirror case is equally possible. If \(f_u < 0\) then \(g_v > 0\), the species \(v\) is the activator, and \(d < -g_v/f_u < 1\): the activator again diffuses more slowly. Turing’s own numerical example is of this type, with his self-activating morphogen \(Y\) diffusing more slowly than \(X\) (Turing’s Original Analysis).
With \(f_u g_v < 0\), the second condition needs \(f_v g_u < 0\). Either the activator promotes the inhibitor and the inhibitor suppresses the activator (\(g_u > 0\), \(f_v < 0\)), or the opposite cross signs hold (Murray 2003, sec. 2.3).

The usual summary is short-range activation with long-range inhibition (Britton 2003, chap. 7 summary and Section 7.1; Kondo and Miura 2010). In this model the longer range of the inhibitor comes from its faster diffusion. Kondo and Miura (2010) point out that the range can also be produced by other forms of signalling, so \(d > 1\) is the diffusive realisation of the requirement and not the requirement itself.

title: Turing Conditions
text:
The Critical Diffusion Ratio
At the onset \(h_{\min} = 0\), so the critical ratio \(d_c\) solves
\[
f_u^2\,d_c^2 + 2\,(2 f_v g_u - f_u g_v)\,d_c + g_v^2 = 0,
\tag{5}\]
taking the root with \(d_c f_u + g_v > 0\) (Murray 2003, sec. 2.3). For \(d > d_c\) a band of wavenumbers is unstable.

title: Turing Conditions
text:
Worked Example: Gierer-Meinhardt
From Linearization, \(f_u = b(1-a)/(1+a)\), \(f_v = -b^2/(1+a)^2\), \(g_u = 2(1+a)/b\), \(g_v = -1\), and \(\det J = b\). So \(f_u > 0\) needs \(a < 1\), and \(u\) is the activator. With \(a = 0.4\) and \(b = 1\):

from amlab.turing import critical_diffusion_ratio, gierer_meinhardt_jacobian, turing_conditions

fu, fv, gu, gv = gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a=0.40, b=1.00)
print(f"f_u = {fu:.4f}, f_v = {fv:.4f}, g_u = {gu:.4f}, g_v = {gv:.4f}")
print(f"d_c = {critical_diffusion_ratio(fu, fv, gu, gv):.2f}")
for d in (20, 30):
    print(f"d = {d}: Turing conditions hold? {bool(turing_conditions(fu, fv, gu, gv, d))}")

f_u = 0.4286, f_v = -0.5102, g_u = 2.8000, g_v = -1.0000
d_c = 26.24
d = 20: Turing conditions hold? False
d = 30: Turing conditions hold? True


So \(d = 20\) gives no Turing instability and \(d = 30\) does. You will test this prediction in the laboratory.






NoteExercise



For Gierer-Meinhardt with \(b = 1\), show that the fourth condition reads \(d f_u - 1 > 2\sqrt{d}\), and solve it for \(\sqrt{d}\).








TipSolution





With \(g_v = -1\) and \(\det J = b = 1\), the third and fourth conditions together say \(d f_u - 1 > 2\sqrt{d}\). This is a quadratic inequality in \(s = \sqrt d\): \(f_u s^2 - 2s - 1 > 0\). For \(f_u > 0\) it holds for \(s > \left(1 + \sqrt{1 + f_u}\right)/f_u\). With \(a = 0.4\), \(f_u = 3/7\) and \(s > 5.122\), so \(d > 26.24\).

title: Laplacian in 1D
text: The first implementation step is the spatial derivative. In one dimension the Laplacian is the second derivative, and you approximate it with a centered finite difference on a grid with spacing \(dx\) (LeVeque 2007, chap. 1).

title: Laplacian in 1D
text:
The Centered Difference
\[
\Delta u = \frac{d^2 u}{dx^2} \approx \frac{u(x+dx) - 2u(x) + u(x-dx)}{dx^2}.
\tag{1}\]






TipWhere does this formula come from?



Expand \(u\) around \(x\) with Taylor’s theorem:
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x+dx) &= u(x) + u'(x)\,dx + \tfrac{1}{2} u''(x)\,dx^2 + \tfrac{1}{6} u'''(x)\,dx^3 + \mathcal{O}(dx^4), \\
u(x-dx) &= u(x) - u'(x)\,dx + \tfrac{1}{2} u''(x)\,dx^2 - \tfrac{1}{6} u'''(x)\,dx^3 + \mathcal{O}(dx^4).
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding the two lines cancels the odd terms:
\[
\frac{u(x+dx) - 2u(x) + u(x-dx)}{dx^2} = u''(x) + \mathcal{O}(dx^2).
\]
The error is second order in \(dx\): halving \(dx\) divides it by about four. You will test this on Time-Step Stability.

title: Laplacian in 1D
text:
Vectorize with np.roll
On the grid \(x_i = i\,dx\), the formula uses the neighbours \(u_{i-1}\) and \(u_{i+1}\). np.roll(values, 1) shifts the array one place to the right, so position \(i\) holds \(u_{i-1}\). Rolling wraps the ends around, which is exactly a periodic boundary. For other boundaries you overwrite the edge values after each step (Boundary Conditions).






NoteExercise



Write a helper that computes this second derivative for a 1D field.
import numpy as np

def laplacian_1d(values, dx):
    # TODO: use the left and right neighbors of each grid point
    lap =
    return lap / dx**2








TipSolution





def laplacian_1d(values, dx):
    lap = -2 * values
    lap += np.roll(values, shift=1)
    lap += np.roll(values, shift=-1)
    return lap / dx**2

title: Laplacian in 1D
text:
Validate on a Known Function
Test the helper on \(u(x) = \cos(2\pi m x / L)\), a periodic function with \(u'' = -(2\pi m/L)^2 u\).

import numpy as np


def laplacian_1d(values, dx):
    lap = -2 * values
    lap += np.roll(values, shift=1)
    lap += np.roll(values, shift=-1)
    return lap / dx**2


length, m = 40.0, 3
for num_points in (40, 80, 160):
    dx = length / num_points
    x = np.arange(num_points) * dx
    u = np.cos(2 * np.pi * m * x / length)
    exact = -((2 * np.pi * m / length) ** 2) * u
    error = np.max(np.abs(laplacian_1d(u, dx) - exact))
    print(f"dx = {dx:.3f}   max error = {error:.2e}")

dx = 1.000   max error = 4.08e-03
dx = 0.500   max error = 1.03e-03
dx = 0.250   max error = 2.57e-04


Each halving of \(dx\) divides the error by four, as the Taylor argument predicts.






NoteExercise



The course package applies the stencil to both species at once with np.roll(uv, 1, axis=1), where uv has shape (2, N). Why is axis=1 needed?








TipSolution





Axis 0 indexes the species \(u\) and \(v\), axis 1 indexes space. Without axis=1, NumPy flattens the array, so the last point of \(u\) would become the left neighbour of the first point of \(v\).

title: Time-Step Stability
text: Explicit Euler is simple, but it is only conditionally stable for diffusion. If \(dt\) is too large for the grid, the simulation produces a pattern that is not in the PDE and then overflows. This page derives the bound, shows the artefact, and gives a convergence check you should run before trusting any reaction-diffusion figure (LeVeque 2007, chap. 9).

title: Time-Step Stability
text:
The Stability Bound in 1D
Apply explicit Euler and the 3-point Laplacian to pure diffusion \(u_t = D\,u_{xx}\):
\[
u_j^{n+1} = u_j^n + r\left(u_{j+1}^n - 2u_j^n + u_{j-1}^n\right), \qquad r = \frac{D\,dt}{dx^2}.
\]
Insert a Fourier mode \(u_j^n = G^n e^{i k j\,dx}\) (von Neumann analysis). The amplification factor per step is
\[
G(k) = 1 - 4r\sin^2\left(\frac{k\,dx}{2}\right).
\tag{1}\]
The scheme is stable when \(|G| \le 1\) for every \(k\). The worst case is the grid-scale sawtooth \(k = \pi/dx\), where \(G = 1 - 4r\). Requiring \(1 - 4r \ge -1\) gives
\[
dt \le \frac{dx^2}{2D} \quad \text{(1D)}.
\tag{2}\]

title: Time-Step Stability
text:
The Bound in 2D
With the 5-point stencil, the same argument gives \(G = 1 - 4r\left[\sin^2(k_x dx/2) + \sin^2(k_y dx/2)\right]\). The worst mode is the checkerboard, with \(G = 1 - 8r\), so
\[
dt \le \frac{dx^2}{4D} \quad \text{(2D, 5-point stencil)}.
\tag{3}\]
For a system, use the largest diffusion coefficient. In the Gierer-Meinhardt scaling that is \(d\). The reaction terms add a further, usually weaker, restriction (LeVeque 2007, chap. 9).

from amlab.turing import euler_dt_max

settings = [
    ("GM 1D, d = 30, dx = 1", 1.0, 30.0, 1, 0.01),
    ("GM 1D, d = 30, dx = 0.5", 0.5, 30.0, 1, 0.001),
    ("GM 2D, d = 30, dx = 1", 1.0, 30.0, 2, 0.005),
    ("Gray-Scott 2D, D1 = 0.1, dx = 1", 1.0, 0.1, 2, 2.0),
]
for label, dx, diff, ndim, dt in settings:
    bound = euler_dt_max(dx, diff, ndim)
    print(f"{label:34s} bound = {bound:.5f}   dt used = {dt:<6} ok: {dt <= bound}")

GM 1D, d = 30, dx = 1              bound = 0.01667   dt used = 0.01   ok: True
GM 1D, d = 30, dx = 0.5            bound = 0.00417   dt used = 0.001  ok: True
GM 2D, d = 30, dx = 1              bound = 0.00833   dt used = 0.005  ok: True
Gray-Scott 2D, D1 = 0.1, dx = 1    bound = 2.50000   dt used = 2.0    ok: True

title: Time-Step Stability
text:
A Numerical Artefact
Figure 1 runs Case A (\(d = 30\), \(dx = 1\)), where the bound is \(1/60 \approx 0.0167\), with \(dt = 0.016\) and \(dt = 0.018\).








Figure 1: Left: maximum deviation from the steady state for two time steps. Right: profile of \(v\) for \(dt = 0.018\) after 25 steps, showing the grid-scale sawtooth that the PDE does not contain.





With \(dt = 0.016\) the noise decays within a few time units and the deviation then stays small. The Turing mode grows only at rate \(\sigma \approx 0.02\), so it becomes visible on longer runs. With \(dt = 0.018\) the deviation grows by a fixed factor per step, close to \(|1 - 4r| = 1.16\), and the profile alternates up and down between neighbouring points. That sawtooth is the signature of a violated stability bound. Do not interpret it as a pattern.

title: Time-Step Stability
text:
A Convergence Check
A stable run can still be inaccurate. To check, refine the grid and compare. The Laplacian error is \(\mathcal{O}(dx^2)\) and the Euler error is \(\mathcal{O}(dt)\).
Refining is subtle: if you halve \(dx\) and only halve \(dt\), the ratio \(dt/dx^2\) doubles and you can cross the bound. Starting from \(dx = 1\), \(dt = 0.01\), halving both gives \(dt = 0.005 > 0.25/60\), which is unstable. Divide \(dt\) by four whenever you halve \(dx\).
The check below uses periodic boundaries and a smooth initial perturbation, so the coarse grid points are a subset of the fine ones. It compares successive refinements \(e_1 = \max|w_h - w_{h/2}|\) and \(e_2 = \max|w_{h/2} - w_{h/4}|\) at \(t = 50\). The observed order is \(p = \log_2(e_1/e_2)\).

import numpy as np

from amlab.turing import simulate_gm_1d


def smooth_start(x, length=40.0):
    mode3 = np.cos(6 * np.pi * x / length)
    return 0.01 * np.array([mode3 + 0.5 * np.cos(10 * np.pi * x / length), mode3])


def run(dx, dt):
    return simulate_gm_1d(d=30.0, dx=dx, dt=dt, t_end=50.0, bc="periodic", initial=smooth_start)[1]


space = [run(1.0, 0.01), run(0.5, 0.0025), run(0.25, 0.000625)]
e1 = np.max(np.abs(space[0] - space[1][:, ::2]))
e2 = np.max(np.abs(space[1] - space[2][:, ::2]))
print(f"space and time (dx halved, dt / 4): e1 = {e1:.2e}, e2 = {e2:.2e}, p = {np.log2(e1 / e2):.2f}")

time = [run(1.0, 0.01), run(1.0, 0.005), run(1.0, 0.0025)]
e1 = np.max(np.abs(time[0] - time[1]))
e2 = np.max(np.abs(time[1] - time[2]))
print(f"time only (dx = 1, dt halved):     e1 = {e1:.2e}, e2 = {e2:.2e}, p = {np.log2(e1 / e2):.2f}")

space and time (dx halved, dt / 4): e1 = 1.53e-03, e2 = 3.91e-04, p = 1.97
time only (dx = 1, dt halved):     e1 = 2.23e-06, e2 = 1.11e-06, p = 1.00


The first line gives \(p \approx 2\), the expected second order. The second gives \(p \approx 1\), the order of explicit Euler. The time error at \(dt = 0.01\) is much smaller than the space error at \(dx = 1\), so for this problem \(dx\) controls the accuracy. In your own work, report both checks.






NoteExercise



You run Gierer-Meinhardt in 2D with \(d = 30\) and \(dx = 1\). What is the largest stable \(dt\)? Would \(dt = 0.01\), which is safe in 1D, work?








TipSolution





The 2D bound is \(dx^2/(4d) = 1/120 \approx 0.0083\). So \(dt = 0.01\) is unstable in 2D, even though it is stable in 1D. The 2D solver page uses \(dt = 0.005\) and \(dt = 0.008\).

title: Animation in 1D
text:
Explore






NoteExercise



Predict first, then run the animation to check.

Run Case A (\(d = 30\)) and Case B (\(d = 20\)). Which one keeps its peaks?
In Case A, count the half-wavelengths at \(t = 100\) and at \(t = 500\). Does the count match the leading mode \(n = 5\) from Unstable Modes in 1D, or does mode \(6\) win for some seeds?
Change the seed. Do the peak positions move? Does the spacing change?









TipSolution





Case A keeps its peaks and Case B returns to the flat state, with \(\max v - \min v\) at rounding level by \(t = 500\). With \(dx = 1\), \(dt = 0.01\) and seeds \(0\) to \(9\), every Case A run shows five half-wavelengths at \(t = 500\), the leading mode \(n = 5\). At \(t = 100\) the amplitude is still small (about \(0.04\)) and a few seeds still show six, because modes \(5\) and \(6\) grow at almost the same rate. Changing the seed moves the peaks, and for this domain the final profile is one of two mirror images, but the spacing stays the same.
import numpy as np
from amlab.turing import simulate_gm_1d


def count_half_waves(v):
    slope = np.sign(np.diff(v[1:-1]))
    slope = slope[slope != 0]
    return 1 + np.sum(slope[1:] != slope[:-1])


for seed in range(10):
    counts = [
        count_half_waves(simulate_gm_1d(d=30.0, t_end=t, bc="neumann", seed=seed)[1][1])
        for t in (100, 500)
    ]
    print(seed, counts)

Plot a Snapshot

title: Domain Size and Mode Selection
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Britton (2003), Chapter 7, Sections 7.2 and 7.3 (pp. 206 to 214): spatial modes, temporal eigenvalues, the dispersion relation, and the domain size as bifurcation parameter.
Recommended: Turing (1952), Sections 8 and 9: the number of lobes on a ring is obtained by dividing the circumference by the “chemical wave-length”.
Technical background: Britton (2003), Appendix C, Sections C.3 to C.5 (eigenvalues of the Laplacian and separation of variables).
The Dispersion Relation page fixes \(\gamma\) and asks which Neumann modes fall into the unstable band. Britton turns the question around: the Turing conditions say that a band of unstable wavenumbers exists, but a finite domain only offers the discrete wavenumbers \(k_n\). Whether a given mode is unstable then depends on the size of the domain. Britton (2003, sec. 7.1) stresses that this is the relevant bifurcation parameter in development, because the embryo grows while the chemistry stays the same.

title: Domain Size and Mode Selection
text:
What the Source Says

With the scaled equation \(u_t = \gamma^2 f(u) + D\nabla^2 u\) on a standard domain, increasing the scale factor \(\gamma\) is “equivalent to increasing domain size” (Britton 2003, sec. 7.2). (Britton’s \(\gamma^2\) is the \(\gamma\) of these notes, see Reaction-Diffusion Equations.)
Define \(\rho(\lambda) = \max_i \operatorname{Re}\sigma_i(\lambda)\), where \(\lambda = k^2\) is a spatial eigenvalue. This function is what Britton calls the dispersion relation (Britton 2003, sec. 7.3). The steady state needs \(\rho(0) < 0\).
On an infinite domain every \(\lambda \ge 0\) is allowed, so instability occurs as soon as some \(\lambda\) has \(\rho(\lambda) > 0\). On a finite domain the potential instability is realised only if the interval of unstable \(\lambda\) contains an eigenvalue \(\lambda_n\) (his Figure 7.3).
The \(n\)th mode loses stability at a parameter value where \(a_2(\lambda_n) = 0\), with \(a_2\) the determinant of the mode matrix. Britton calls this the mode-\(n\) Turing bifurcation (Britton 2003, Equations 7.4.31 and 7.4.32).
Close to such a bifurcation the linear theory predicts growth of a multiple of the mode \(F_n(x)\), and, under conditions he does not derive, the nonlinear solution tends to a steady state close to that multiple (Britton 2003, Example 7.1 and p. 214). If several modes are unstable, the one with the largest growth rate dominates while the linear approximation holds (Britton 2003, sec. 7.2).

title: Domain Size and Mode Selection
section: The Bifurcation Values in Closed Form
text:
The Bifurcation Values in Closed Form
Use the notation of the Turing Conditions page, with \(s = d f_u + g_v\) and \(\Delta = s^2 - 4d \det J\). The mode matrix of a mode with \(k^2 = \lambda\) has determinant
\[
h(\lambda) = d\lambda^2 - \gamma s \lambda + \gamma^2 \det J.
\]
On the standard interval \((0, \pi)\) with Neumann conditions, \(\lambda_n = n^2\). Mode \(n\) is unstable when \(h(n^2) < 0\). Read as a quadratic inequality in \(\gamma\),
\[
\det J\,\gamma^2 - s\,n^2\gamma + d\,n^4 < 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n^2\,\gamma_- < \gamma < n^2\,\gamma_+, \qquad
\gamma_\pm = \frac{s \pm \sqrt{\Delta}}{2\det J}.
\tag{1}\]
On a physical interval of length \(L\) with the original scaling, \(\gamma = 1\) and the substitution \(x = L\xi/\pi\) gives the standard interval with the effective value \(\gamma_{\mathrm{eff}} = (L/\pi)^2\). So mode \(n\) is unstable for
\[
\pi n \sqrt{\gamma_-} < L < \pi n \sqrt{\gamma_+}.
\tag{2}\]
Two consequences follow without further computation.

Each mode is unstable on an interval of \(\gamma\) (or of \(L\)), not only above a threshold. The intervals have the constant ratio \(\gamma_+/\gamma_-\) and slide to larger \(L\) in proportion to \(n\).
Modes \(n\) and \(n+1\) are unstable together for some \(L\) exactly when \(\left((n+1)/n\right)^2 < \gamma_+/\gamma_-\). Otherwise there is a window of \(L\) in which neither is unstable, and the uniform state is stable even though the Turing conditions hold. As \(d \downarrow d_c\) the ratio \(\gamma_+/\gamma_-\) tends to \(1\) and the intervals shrink to points.









Figure 1: Mode selection for Gierer-Meinhardt with \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), \(d = 30\), \(\gamma = 1\). The shaded band is the unstable interval \(k_1 < k < k_2\). Each curve is the Neumann wavenumber \(k_n = n\pi/L\) of mode \(n\), drawn thick where it lies inside the band. Mode \(n\) can only be unstable for the lengths \(L\) at which its curve crosses the band.





For Case A the constants are \(\gamma_- \approx 3.66\) and \(\gamma_+ \approx 8.20\), so \(\gamma_+/\gamma_- \approx 2.24\). Since \(2.24 < 4\) and \(2.24 < 9/4\), modes \(1\) and \(2\) never grow together and neither do modes \(2\) and \(3\), while \(2.24 > 16/9\) lets modes \(3\) and \(4\) overlap. This reproduces the lengths found on the Dispersion Relation page: mode \(1\) for \(6.01 < L < 8.99\), mode \(2\) for \(12.02 < L < 17.99\), mode \(3\) for \(18.03 < L < 26.98\).

title: Domain Size and Mode Selection
text:
Prediction Against Simulation
The linear theory predicts the first unstable mode. To see how much of it survives in the nonlinear model, integrate the 1D Gierer-Meinhardt system from the uniform state plus 1% noise for several lengths. The code uses zero-flux boundaries placed exactly at the ends of the domain (a ghost value equal to the edge value, so the length is \(N\,dx\)) and counts the sign changes of \(u - \bar u\). A pattern with \(n\) half-wavelengths, \(\cos(n\pi x/L)\), has \(n\) sign changes.

import numpy as np

from amlab.turing import dispersion_relation, gierer_meinhardt_jacobian, unstable_modes_1d

a, b, d = 0.40, 1.00, 30.0
u_star = (a + 1) / b
jac = gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a, b)


def simulate(length, dx=1.0, t_end=400.0, seed=0):
    n_pts = int(round(length / dx))
    dt = 0.4 * dx**2 / (2 * d)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    uv = np.array([[u_star], [u_star**2]]) * (1 + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal((2, n_pts)))
    diff = np.array([[1.0], [d]])
    for _ in range(int(round(t_end / dt))):
        padded = np.concatenate([uv[:, :1], uv, uv[:, -1:]], axis=1)
        lap = (padded[:, 2:] - 2 * uv + padded[:, :-2]) / dx**2
        u, v = uv
        uv = uv + dt * (diff * lap + np.array([a - b * u + u**2 / v, u**2 - v]))
    return uv


def grid_mode(length, dx=1.0):
    """Leading unstable mode for the discrete operator with exact zero flux."""
    n_pts = int(round(length / dx))
    n = np.arange(n_pts)
    k2 = 4 / dx**2 * np.sin(n * np.pi / (2 * n_pts)) ** 2
    rates = dispersion_relation(k2, *jac, d)
    return int(n[np.argmax(rates)]) if rates.max() > 0 else 0


print(" L   continuum  grid(dx=1)  simulated")
for length in (4, 8, 10, 15, 22, 30, 40):
    modes = unstable_modes_1d(d=d, length=length, num_modes=60)
    lead = modes[0][0] if modes else 0
    uv = simulate(length)
    amplitude = np.ptp(uv[0])
    signs = np.sign(uv[0] - uv[0].mean())
    seen = int(np.sum(signs[1:] != signs[:-1])) if amplitude > 1e-3 else 0
    print(f"{length:3d}  {lead:9d}  {grid_mode(length):10d}  {seen:9d}")

 L   continuum  grid(dx=1)  simulated
  4          0           0          0
  8          1           1          1
 10          0           0          0
 15          2           2          2
 22          3           3          3
 30          4           4          4
 40          5           6          6


The rows for \(L = 4\) and \(L = 10\) show \(0\) in all three columns: nothing grows and the flat state persists, in line with the gaps of Figure 1. The three columns also agree in every other row except \(L = 40\). There two modes have almost the same growth rate (about \(0.0214\) for \(n = 5\) and \(0.0206\) for \(n = 6\)), and the answer depends on the grid. On the grid with \(dx = 1\) the discrete operator has \(\lambda_n = (4/dx^2)\sin^2(n\pi/2N)\) instead of \((n\pi/L)^2\), which shifts the preferred mode from \(5\) to \(6\), and the simulation follows the discrete prediction. With \(dx = 0.5\) and four different noise seeds the simulation gave \(5, 6, 5, 5\) half-wavelengths. When two modes are this close, the noise and the discretisation decide, and linear theory is only informative to within one mode. This is the same caveat as for the 2D case on Unstable Modes in 2D.






NoteExercise



Show that the intervals of modes \(n\) and \(n+1\) overlap exactly when \(\left((n+1)/n\right)^2 < \gamma_+/\gamma_-\), and find the smallest \(d\) for which modes \(1\) and \(2\) can be unstable together for Gierer-Meinhardt with \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\).








TipSolution





The intervals \((n^2\gamma_-, n^2\gamma_+)\) and \(((n+1)^2\gamma_-, (n+1)^2\gamma_+)\) overlap when the lower end of the second is below the upper end of the first, \((n+1)^2\gamma_- < n^2\gamma_+\). Dividing by \(n^2\gamma_-\) gives the condition.
For \(n = 1\) we need \(\gamma_+/\gamma_- > 4\), that is \((s + \sqrt\Delta)/(s - \sqrt\Delta) > 4\), which is equivalent to \(\sqrt\Delta > 3s/5\). Squaring, \(s^2 - 4d\det J > 9s^2/25\), so \(16 s^2/25 > 4 d \det J\). With \(b = 1\) (\(\det J = 1\)) and \(s = d f_u - 1\), \(f_u = 3/7\), solve \(4(3d/7 - 1)^2 = 25 d\).
import numpy as np
from amlab.turing import gierer_meinhardt_jacobian

fu, fv, gu, gv = gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(0.4, 1.0)
det = fu * gv - fv * gu
d = np.linspace(27, 200, 200000)
s = d * fu + gv
ratio = (s + np.sqrt(s**2 - 4 * d * det)) / (s - np.sqrt(s**2 - 4 * d * det))
print(d[np.argmax(ratio > 4)])
Writing \(t = \sqrt d\), the condition is \(\tfrac{3}{7}t^2 - \tfrac{5}{2}t - 1 = 0\) at the threshold, so \(t = (5/2 + \sqrt{25/4 + 12/7})/(6/7) \approx 6.209\) and \(d \approx 38.55\), which the code confirms. Modes \(1\) and \(2\) can therefore coexist only for \(d > 38.55\).

def gierer_meinhardt_pde_2d(t, uv, gamma=1, a=0.40, b=1.00, d=30, dx=1.0):
    u, v = uv
    lu = laplacian_2d(u, dx)
    lv = laplacian_2d(v, dx)

    g = u**2 - v
    du_dt = lu + gamma * f
    dv_dt = d * lv + gamma * g
    return np.array([du_dt, dv_dt])

Once the right-hand side is available, the full update is explicit Euler applied to the whole array,

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Britton (2003), Appendix C, Sections C.3 to C.5 (spectrum of the Laplacian, separation of variables, systems with linear kinetics).
Recommended: Britton (2003), Chapter 7, Section 7.2 (pp. 207 to 210), where the spatial modes are introduced for the Turing problem.
The linearized system \(\partial_t \eta = D\,\Delta\eta + \gamma J\eta\) couples every point to its neighbours. You decouple it by expanding \(\eta\) in eigenfunctions of the Laplacian, which depend on the domain and the boundary conditions (Murray 2003, sec. 2.3; Britton 2003, chap. 7).

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text:
The Eigenvalue Problem
Look for functions \(\phi\) and numbers \(k^2 \ge 0\) with
\[
\Delta \phi + k^2 \phi = 0 \quad \text{in } \Omega,
\tag{1}\]
plus the boundary condition of the model. The eigenvalue of \(\Delta\) is \(\lambda = -k^2\), and \(k\) is the wavenumber. The wavelength of the mode is \(2\pi / k\).

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text:
On an Interval \((0, L)\)









Boundary condition
Condition
Eigenfunctions
Wavenumbers




Neumann (zero flux)
\(\phi'(0) = \phi'(L) = 0\)
\(\cos(n\pi x / L)\)
\(k_n = n\pi/L\), \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\)


Dirichlet (fixed value)
\(\phi(0) = \phi(L) = 0\)
\(\sin(n\pi x / L)\)
\(k_n = n\pi/L\), \(n = 1, 2, \dots\)


Periodic
\(\phi(0) = \phi(L)\), \(\phi'(0) = \phi'(L)\)
\(\cos(2n\pi x/L)\), \(\sin(2n\pi x/L)\)
\(k_n = 2n\pi/L\), \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\)



Mode \(n\) with Neumann conditions fits \(n\) half-wavelengths into the interval. Mode \(0\) is the flat perturbation. For periodic conditions each \(n \ge 1\) has two independent eigenfunctions with the same \(k_n\).








Figure 1: First four Neumann eigenfunctions \(\cos(n\pi x/L)\) on \((0, L)\).

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text:
On a Rectangle \((0, L_x) \times (0, L_y)\)
Separation of variables gives products of the 1D eigenfunctions. With Neumann conditions on all four edges,
\[
\phi_{n,m}(x, y) = \cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L_x}\right)\cos\left(\frac{m\pi y}{L_y}\right), \qquad
k_{n,m}^2 = \left(\frac{n\pi}{L_x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{m\pi}{L_y}\right)^2.
\tag{2}\]
For Dirichlet conditions replace cosines by sines and start at \(n, m \ge 1\). For periodic conditions replace \(\pi/L\) by \(2\pi/L\). Different pairs \((n, m)\) can share almost the same \(k^2\). That is why 2D domains can select stripes, spots, or mixtures (Murray 2003, sec. 2.5).

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
text:
Mode Decomposition
Expand the perturbation as
\[
\eta(x, t) = \sum_n c_n(t)\,\phi_n(x), \qquad c_n(t) \in \mathbb{R}^2.
\]
Because \(\Delta \phi_n = -k_n^2 \phi_n\), the modes separate and each coefficient solves a \(2 \times 2\) linear ODE:
\[
\dot c_n = A_n c_n, \qquad A_n = \gamma J - k_n^2 D.
\tag{3}\]
So \(c_n(t) \propto e^{\sigma t}\), where \(\sigma\) is an eigenvalue of \(A_n\). Britton calls the \(\sigma\) the temporal eigenvalues, to distinguish them from the spatial eigenvalues \(\lambda_n = k_n^2\) of the Laplacian. He also records that the \(\lambda_n\) are all positive for Dirichlet conditions and all positive except \(\lambda_0 = 0\) for Neumann conditions (Britton 2003, sec. 7.2). The uniform state is linearly stable when every admissible mode has \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma < 0\). The next page turns this into the Turing conditions and the dispersion relation.

title: Laplacian Eigenmodes
section: Other Domains and When the Method Applies
text:
Other Domains and When the Method Applies
The same separation of variables works on other domains. Britton (2003, Appendix C, Sections C.3 and C.6) gives the following cases.

Unbounded domain. If the domain is the whole line or space and the function is only required to stay bounded, every \(k \ge 0\) is an eigenvalue, with eigenfunctions \(e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}\). The sum over modes becomes a Fourier integral. Turing instability is then a statement about a continuum of wavenumbers, so the unstable band alone decides the outcome on an infinite domain (Britton 2003, sec. 7.3 and C.3).
Mixed conditions on a rectangle. With Dirichlet conditions on \(x = 0, a\) and Neumann conditions on \(y = 0, b\), the eigenfunctions are \(\sin(m\pi x/a)\cos(n\pi y/b)\) with \(m \ge 1\), \(n \ge 0\) and \(k^2 = m^2\pi^2/a^2 + n^2\pi^2/b^2\) (Britton 2003, Example C.9).
Surface of a cylinder. Periodic in the angle and zero-flux along the axis, the eigenvalues are \(m^2/r^2 + n^2\pi^2/h^2\) for a cylinder of radius \(r\) and length \(h\) (Britton 2003, Example C.10). This is the geometry used for the tail argument on Animal Coat Patterns.

Note a difference in indexing. Britton starts the Dirichlet modes of Example C.2 at \(n = 0\) and writes \(k_n = (n+1)\pi/L\), so that the list of wavenumbers is the same as the table above with \(n \ge 1\). His periodic example uses the interval \((0, 2\pi)\), where \(k_n = n\).
The cylinder formula can be checked on a grid. The code builds the finite-difference Laplacian with periodic wrapping in the angle and zero flux in \(z\), and compares its lowest eigenvalues with \(m^2/r^2 + n^2\pi^2/h^2\). Eigenvalues with \(m \ne 0\) appear twice, as the cosine and sine modes.

import numpy as np

r, h, n_phi, n_z = 2.0, 10.0, 32, 20
dphi, dz = 2 * np.pi / n_phi, h / n_z
shift = np.roll(np.eye(n_phi), 1, axis=0) + np.roll(np.eye(n_phi), -1, axis=0)
lap_phi = (shift - 2 * np.eye(n_phi)) / (r * dphi) ** 2
lap_z = -2 * np.eye(n_z) + np.eye(n_z, k=1) + np.eye(n_z, k=-1)
lap_z[0, 0] = lap_z[-1, -1] = -1
lap_z /= dz**2
lap = np.kron(lap_phi, np.eye(n_z)) + np.kron(np.eye(n_phi), lap_z)

numeric = np.sort(-np.linalg.eigvalsh(lap))[:9]
exact = np.sort([(m / r) ** 2 + (n * np.pi / h) ** 2 for m in range(-4, 5) for n in range(5)])[:9]
print(np.round(numeric, 4) + 0.0)
print(np.round(exact, 4))

[0.     0.0985 0.2492 0.2492 0.3477 0.3477 0.3915 0.6407 0.6407]
[0.     0.0987 0.25   0.25   0.3487 0.3487 0.3948 0.6448 0.6448]


The two lists agree to within about 1%, and the remaining difference shrinks as the grid is refined.
Separation of variables does not apply to every problem. Britton (2003, sec. C.4) lists three requirements: the linear operator must be separable, the initial and boundary conditions must be imposed on lines of constant time and constant space coordinate, and the boundary operator must be Neumann, Dirichlet, periodic or of Robin type (\(\alpha u + \beta\,\partial u/\partial n = 0\) with \(\alpha, \beta \ge 0\)). He notes that a problem on a growing domain cannot be solved directly by separation of variables. This is why the argument on Domain Size and Mode Selection compares fixed domains of different lengths and does not follow a single growing one.






NoteExercise



On \((0, 40)\) with Neumann conditions, which mode \(n\) has wavenumber closest to \(k = 0.4\)? How many half-wavelengths does it fit into the domain?








TipSolution





\(k_n = n\pi/40\), so \(n = 40k/\pi \approx 5.09\). The closest mode is \(n = 5\), with five half-wavelengths, which is two and a half full wavelengths.

title: Unstable Modes in 2D
text: In 1D you scanned the Neumann modes \(n\). On a rectangle the modes are pairs \((n, m)\) (Murray 2003, sec. 2.5). This page extends the scan and compares it with the 2D simulation.

title: Unstable Modes in 2D
text:
Modes on a Rectangle
With Neumann boundaries on \([0, L_x] \times [0, L_y]\) (see Laplacian Eigenmodes),
\[
k_{n,m}^2 = \left(\frac{n\pi}{L_x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{m\pi}{L_y}\right)^2, \qquad
A_{n,m} = \gamma J - k_{n,m}^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d).
\tag{1}\]
Mode \((n, 0)\) varies only in \(x\) and \((0, m)\) only in \(y\); both are stripes. Modes with \(n, m \ge 1\) are checkerboards of spots. For periodic boundaries replace \(\pi/L\) by \(2\pi/L\).

title: Unstable Modes in 2D
text:
Extend the Mode Scan

def find_unstable_modes_2d(a=0.40, b=1.00, d=30.0, gamma=1.0, length_x=20.0, length_y=50.0, num_modes=12):
    jac = np.array(gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a, b)).reshape(2, 2)
    diffusion = np.diag([1.0, d])
    unstable_modes = []

    for n in range(num_modes):
        for m in range(num_modes):
            if n == 0 and m == 0:
                continue
            k2 = (n * np.pi / length_x) ** 2 + (m * np.pi / length_y) ** 2
            a_nm = gamma * jac - k2 * diffusion
            growth_rate = np.max(np.linalg.eigvals(a_nm).real)
            if growth_rate > 0:
                unstable_modes.append(((n, m), growth_rate))

    unstable_modes.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    return unstable_modes
