title: Critical Coupling
text: This page summarizes Kuramoto’s self-consistency argument for the limit \(N \to \infty\), following Strogatz (2000, sec. 4). Work in the rotating frame, so \(g\) is symmetric about \(0\).

title: Critical Coupling
text:
Steady states with constant \(r\)
Look for steady solutions in which \(r\) and \(\psi\) are constant. In the rotating frame, with \(g\) symmetric, you can choose the origin of phases so that \(\psi = 0\) (Strogatz 2000). Then the mean-field equation reads
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i - K r \sin\theta_i.
\tag{1}\]
Each oscillator is a nonuniform oscillator (Flows on the Circle) with \(a = Kr\). The population splits in two groups:

Locked oscillators, \(|\omega_i| \le Kr\), sit at a stable fixed point with \(\sin\theta_i = \omega_i/(Kr)\) and \(|\theta_i| \le \pi/2\).
Drifting oscillators, \(|\omega_i| > Kr\), circulate around the circle. Their stationary distribution is symmetric under \(\theta \to \theta + \pi\) together with \(\omega \to -\omega\), so they add nothing to \(r\) (Strogatz 2000).

title: Critical Coupling
text:
Self-consistency
Only the locked oscillators contribute to \(r\). Using \(\omega = Kr\sin\theta\) to change variables,
\[
r = K r \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^2\theta \; g(Kr\sin\theta)\, d\theta.
\tag{2}\]
\(r = 0\) always solves Equation 2: this is the incoherent state. A partially locked state with \(r > 0\) must satisfy
\[
1 = K \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^2\theta \; g(Kr\sin\theta)\, d\theta.
\tag{3}\]
Letting \(r \to 0^+\) and using \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = \pi/2\) gives the threshold where this branch starts:
\[
K_c = \frac{2}{\pi g(0)}.
\tag{4}\]
This is Kuramoto’s formula for the critical coupling (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000).

title: Critical Coupling
text:
Two cases you will use
Lorentzian frequencies. For \(g(\omega) = \gamma / [\pi(\gamma^2 + \omega^2)]\), Equation 4 gives \(K_c = 2\gamma\) and Equation 3 can be solved exactly:
\[
r = \sqrt{1 - \frac{K_c}{K}}, \qquad K \ge K_c.
\tag{5}\]
Normal frequencies. For a normal density with standard deviation \(\sigma\), \(K_c = 2\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma/\pi = \sqrt{8/\pi}\,\sigma \approx 1.596\,\sigma\). There is no closed form for \(r(K)\), so you solve Equation 3 numerically.

title: Critical Coupling
text:
Square-root onset
For any smooth \(g\) with \(g''(0) < 0\), expanding Equation 3 for small \(r\) gives
\[
r \approx \sqrt{\frac{16}{\pi K_c^3}}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{-g''(0)}}, \qquad \mu = \frac{K - K_c}{K_c},
\tag{6}\]
so \(r\) grows like \(\sqrt{K - K_c}\) just above threshold (Strogatz 2000). The transition from incoherence to partial locking is continuous. The same square-root law appears at a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation.








Figure 1: Order parameter in the limit \(N \to \infty\). Solid: exact Lorentzian result Equation 5 with \(\gamma = 1\) (\(K_c = 2\)). Dashed: near-onset approximation Equation 6 for a normal density with \(\sigma = 1\) (\(K_c \approx 1.60\)), valid only close to \(K_c\).

title: Critical Coupling
text:
Measure the transition
The simulation below integrates the mean-field equations \(\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + K r \sin(\psi - \theta_i)\) for \(N\) oscillators, with \(r\) and \(\psi\) recomputed at every step. Blue dots are locked (\(|\omega_i| \le Kr\)), red ones drift. The bottom panel compares your measurements with the \(N \to \infty\) theory of this page.


Set \(K = 1\), below \(K_c \approx 1.60\). Is \(r\) exactly zero? Compare \(N = 50\) with \(N = 1000\), and relate the size of the fluctuations to \(N^{-1/2}\).
Raise \(K\) just past \(K_c\). A cluster forms. Watch the percentage of locked oscillators grow as you increase \(K\).
Press Sweep K automatically. It follows the protocol of the lab: 20 values of \(K\) from 0 to 5, each run to \(t = 100\) with \(r\) averaged over \(90 \le t \le 100\), starting from the final phases of the previous \(K\). Compare the dots with the curve. Where do they disagree most? Think about finite \(N\) and about how slowly \(r\) settles near \(K_c\).
Switch to the Lorentzian density. Check \(K_c = 2\) and the exact law \(r = \sqrt{1 - K_c/K}\) from Equation 5.



Build this in Python. In the lab you write the code behind this figure: Kuramoto Lab: Bifurcation Diagram. You integrate \(N\) oscillators with solve_ivp, average \(r(t)\) over \(90 \le t \le 100\) for 20 values of \(K\), and draw the measured points over the theoretical curve.

title: Critical Coupling
section: What the argument does not show
text:
What the argument does not show
Kuramoto’s argument finds the steady states. It does not prove which of them are stable, nor that the population approaches them. These questions were settled only by much later work, which Strogatz (2000) reviews. Finite \(N\) adds fluctuations of order \(N^{-1/2}\) on top of these curves (Finite-Size Effects).






NoteExercise



Check that Equation 6 agrees with the Lorentzian result Equation 5 near \(K_c\).








TipSolution





For \(\gamma = 1\), \(g(0) = 1/\pi\), \(K_c = 2\) and \(g''(0) = -2/\pi\). Then Equation 6 gives \(r \approx \sqrt{16/(8\pi)}\,\sqrt{\mu\pi/2} = \sqrt{\mu}\). The exact result is \(r = \sqrt{(K - K_c)/K} = \sqrt{\mu K_c/K}\), which tends to \(\sqrt{\mu}\) as \(K \to K_c\).









NoteExercise



Your frequencies are normal with \(\sigma = 0.5\). What is \(K_c\)? What happens to \(K_c\) if you double the spread of frequencies?








TipSolution





\(K_c = \sqrt{8/\pi}\times 0.5 \approx 0.80\). Since \(g(0) \propto 1/\sigma\), \(K_c\) is proportional to \(\sigma\). Doubling the spread doubles \(K_c\): a more diverse population needs stronger coupling to synchronize.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text: The formulas in Critical Coupling hold in the limit \(N \to \infty\). Your simulations use finite \(N\). This page covers the last two steps of the workflow: interpretation and limitations.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Two finite-\(N\) effects

Noise floor. For incoherent phases, \(\mathbb{E}[r^2] = 1/N\) (The Order Parameter). Below \(K_c\) you measure \(r_\infty\) of order \(N^{-1/2}\), not zero.
Sampling of frequencies. With \(N\) random draws, the empirical frequency distribution differs from \(g\). The transition point of one sample moves around \(K_c\), and the sharp corner of the \(N \to \infty\) curve is rounded off.

Simulations and physical arguments suggest that the fluctuations of \(r(t)\) are of order \(N^{-1/2}\), except very close to \(K_c\) where they may be amplified. As of 2000 there were no rigorous convergence results for finite \(N\) (Strogatz 2000, sec. 5.1). Both effects shrink as \(N\) grows. Figure 1 shows them with a normal frequency density, \(\sigma = 1\), so \(K_c \approx 1.60\).








Figure 1: Time-averaged order parameter against \(K\) for three population sizes (normal frequencies, \(\sigma = 1\), one random sample each, RK4 with \(\Delta t = 0.1\) up to \(t = 80\), average over \(40 \le t \le 80\)). Error bars show the standard deviation of \(r(t)\) in that window. Dotted lines mark \(K_c\) and the noise floors \(N^{-1/2}\).

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Interpretation

Below \(K_c\), each curve sits near its own floor \(N^{-1/2}\): about \(0.14\), \(0.07\) and \(0.03\).
Near \(K_c\) the fluctuations of \(r(t)\) are largest. The transition is sharpest for the largest \(N\).
The \(N = 50\) sample rises before \(K_c\). Its 50 frequencies have a sample standard deviation of about \(0.88\), smaller than \(\sigma = 1\), so this particular population is easier to synchronize. A different seed would move its curve.
Well above \(K_c\), the three curves agree. Most oscillators are locked and sampling details matter little.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Limitations

One sample of frequencies per \(N\) is not enough to separate the two finite-size effects. Average over several seeds if you need error bars on \(r_\infty\) itself, not just on \(r(t)\).
Close to \(K_c\), \(r(t)\) settles slowly. A fixed time window can stop too early.
The mean-field model has all-to-all coupling. Real oscillators often interact through a network, which changes the threshold. Module 5 returns to this with the swing equation for power grids.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Averaging over samples
This part is optional.






NoteExercise



Repeat Figure 1 with 10 seeds for each \(N\) and plot the mean of \(r_\infty\) over seeds. Then plot \(r_\infty\sqrt{N}\) against \(K\). Below \(K_c\) the curves for different \(N\) should collapse onto a single curve. Where does the collapse fail?








TipSolution





At \(K = 0\) all three curves start at \(r_\infty\sqrt{N} \approx 0.89\), the mean of \(\sqrt{N}\,r\) for independent uniform phases (\(\sqrt{\pi}/2\)). Up to \(K \approx 1\) they stay together and rise slowly, to about \(1.6\): coupling below threshold enhances the fluctuations but keeps them of order \(N^{-1/2}\). Close to \(K_c\) the curves separate: \(r_\infty\) no longer scales like \(N^{-1/2}\), and the largest population departs first. The run takes about 15 seconds.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from amlab.synchronization.kuramoto_sweep import critical_coupling, order_parameter_sweep

sigma = 1.0
kc = critical_coupling(1 / (np.sqrt(2 * np.pi) * sigma))
k_values = np.linspace(0, 4, 17)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))
for n in [50, 200, 1000]:
    r_seeds = []
    for seed in range(10):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        omega = rng.normal(0, sigma, n)
        theta0 = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n)
        r_mean, _ = order_parameter_sweep(k_values, omega, theta0, t_end=80, dt=0.1, t_average=40)
        r_seeds.append(r_mean)
    r_avg = np.mean(r_seeds, axis=0)
    axs[0].plot(k_values, r_avg, "o-", label=f"N = {n}")
    axs[1].plot(k_values, r_avg * np.sqrt(n), "o-", label=f"N = {n}")
for ax in axs:
    ax.axvline(kc, color="black", linestyle=":")
    ax.set_xlabel("Coupling strength K")
    ax.legend()
axs[0].set_ylabel(r"mean of $r_\infty$ over seeds")
axs[1].set_ylabel(r"$r_\infty \sqrt{N}$")
axs[1].set_xlim(0, kc)
axs[1].set_ylim(0, 5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Kuramoto Lab: Finite-Size Effects
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



You run a simulation with \(N = 400\) and \(K = 1.0\) (normal frequencies, \(\sigma = 1\)) and find \(r_\infty \approx 0.05\). A classmate says this shows weak partial synchronization. Is that right?








TipSolution





No. \(K = 1.0\) is below \(K_c \approx 1.60\), so the \(N \to \infty\) prediction is \(r_\infty = 0\). The measured value is consistent with the incoherent noise floor \(N^{-1/2} = 0.05\). To claim partial synchrony you would need \(r_\infty\) well above \(N^{-1/2}\) and a value that does not decrease as you increase \(N\).

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
The London Millennium Footbridge opened on 10 June 2000. On the opening day it moved sideways, unexpectedly, when crowds crossed it (Dallard et al. 2001). The engineers found that the lateral force from pedestrians depended on the motion of the deck. They concluded that the same effect could occur on any bridge with a lateral frequency below about 1.3 Hz carrying enough pedestrians. The bridge was retrofitted with viscous and tuned mass dampers (Dallard et al. 2001).
Strogatz et al. (2005) explained the onset with a Kuramoto-type model. Bridge wobbling and crowd synchrony are two sides of one instability, and both appear when the crowd exceeds a critical size.

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Modelling assumptions

The bridge is a single lateral vibration mode, a damped harmonic oscillator.
Each pedestrian is a phase oscillator whose sideways force is periodic in the stepping phase.
Pedestrians do not interact with each other. They interact only through the bridge.

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Bridge
Let \(X(t)\) be the lateral displacement of the relevant mode. With \(N\) pedestrians,
\[
M\ddot X + B\dot X + KX = G\sum_{i=1}^N \sin\Theta_i,
\qquad
\Omega_0 = \sqrt{K/M}.
\tag{1}\]
\(M\), \(B\) and \(K\) are the modal mass, damping and stiffness, and \(G\) is the maximum lateral force of one pedestrian (Strogatz et al. 2005). Here \(K\) is a stiffness, not the Kuramoto coupling.

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Pedestrians
Pedestrian \(i\) has natural stepping frequency \(\Omega_i\), drawn from a density \(P(\Omega)\). The bridge perturbs the gait according to
\[
\dot\Theta_i = \Omega_i + C A \sin(\Psi - \Theta_i + \alpha),
\qquad i = 1, \dots, N,
\tag{2}\]
where \(C\) measures the sensitivity to vibrations and \(\alpha\) is a phase lag. The amplitude \(A\) and phase \(\Psi\) of the bridge are defined by
\[
X = A\sin\Psi, \qquad \dot X = A\,\Omega_0\cos\Psi.
\tag{3}\]
Strogatz et al. (2005) call Equation 2 hypothetical but testable. It has the same form as the firefly equation in Phase Locking, with a stimulus whose strength \(CA\) grows with the wobble.

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Feedback loop
Compare Equation 2 with the mean-field Kuramoto equation in The Order Parameter. The bridge plays the role of the mean field. Crowd coherence is measured with the usual order parameter
\[
R e^{i\Phi} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N e^{i\Theta_j}.
\tag{4}\]
A small wobble nudges some pedestrians into step. Their forces add coherently and drive the bridge harder, which entrains more pedestrians. For small crowds, \(R\) fluctuates at the level \(N^{-1/2}\) and the bridge barely moves (Strogatz et al. 2005).

title: The Millennium Bridge
text:
Critical crowd size
For \(\alpha = \pi/2\) and \(P(\Omega)\) symmetric about \(\Omega_0\), Strogatz et al. (2005) obtain
\[
N_c = \frac{4\zeta}{\pi}\,\frac{K}{G\,C\,P(\Omega_0)},
\qquad \zeta = \frac{B}{\sqrt{4MK}},
\tag{5}\]
where \(\zeta\) is the damping ratio. Since \(4\zeta K = 2B\sqrt{K/M} = 2B\Omega_0\), the same result reads
\[
N_c = \frac{2B\,\Omega_0}{\pi\,G\,C\,P(\Omega_0)}.
\tag{6}\]
Compare with \(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0))\) in Critical Coupling. More damping raises the threshold. A narrower spread of gait frequencies (larger \(P(\Omega_0)\)) lowers it. Strogatz et al. (2005) estimated \(C \approx 16\ \text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\) from crowd tests on the bridge. Eckhardt et al. (2007) analyse the model in more detail.






NoteExercise



Check that Equation 6 is dimensionless. Use \([G] = \text{N}\), \([B] = \text{kg/s}\), \([C] = \text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}\) and \([P] = \text{s}\) (a density over angular frequency).








TipSolution





The numerator \(B\Omega_0\) has units \(\text{kg}\,\text{s}^{-2}\). The denominator \(GCP\) has units \((\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2})(\text{m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1})(\text{s}) = \text{kg}\,\text{s}^{-2}\). The ratio is dimensionless, as a number of pedestrians should be.









NoteExercise



Take \(P(\Omega)\) normal with mean \(\Omega_0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). Write \(N_c\) in terms of \(\sigma\). How does \(N_c\) change if the damping is doubled?








TipSolution





\(P(\Omega_0) = 1/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma)\), so \(N_c = 2\sqrt{2\pi}\,B\,\Omega_0\,\sigma/(\pi G C)\). \(N_c\) is proportional to \(B\), so doubling the damping doubles the critical crowd size. This is the reasoning behind adding dampers.



You will simulate this model in the graded Kuramoto Assignment.

title: Vicsek Lab: Vectorized Update
text:
TipOptional extension



This page is optional. Loops are slow in Python: the double loop of Update Rule costs \(O(N^2)\) interpreted operations per step. You can compute all neighbor averages at once with a distance matrix. The amlab code uses this version.

title: Vicsek Lab: Vectorized Update
text:
Vectorized version






NoteExercise



Rewrite vicsek_equations() without loops. Build the matrix of pairwise distances, turn it into a boolean neighbor matrix, and compute all average directions with matrix products.

TipHint





If neighbors is the boolean \(N \times N\) matrix with entry True when \(|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j| \le r\), then neighbors @ np.sin(theta) sums \(\sin\theta_j\) over the neighbors of every particle at once. The diagonal is True, so each particle counts itself.









TipSolution





import numpy as np
import scipy.spatial


def vicsek_equations(
    xy: np.ndarray,
    theta: np.ndarray,
    noise: float = 0.1,
    box_size: float = 25,
    dt: float = 1,
    radius_interaction: float = 1,
    v0: float = 0.03,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Update the state of the particles based on the Vicsek model.

    Parameters
    ----------
    xy : np.ndarray
        Position of the particles.
    theta : np.ndarray
        Angle of the particles.
    noise : float, optional
        Noise parameter, eta, default is 0.1.
    box_size : float, optional
        Dimension of the space, L, default is 25.
    dt : float, optional
        Time step, default is 1 [Vicsek1995]
    radius_interaction : float, optional
        Interaction radius, default is 1 [Vicsek1995]
    v0 : float, optional
        Speed of the particles, default is 0.03 [Vicsek1995]

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Updated position of the particles.
    np.ndarray
        Updated angle of the particles.
    """
    # Compute distance matrix and neighbor matrix
    d_matrix = scipy.spatial.distance.pdist(xy.T)
    d_matrix = scipy.spatial.distance.squareform(d_matrix)
    neighbors = d_matrix <= radius_interaction
    # Vectorized computation of average direction of neighbors (including itself)
    num_boids = xy.shape[1]
    sin_theta = np.sin(theta)
    cos_theta = np.cos(theta)
    # neighbors is (N, N), sin_theta/cos_theta is (N,)
    # Matrix-vector product: (N, N) @ (N,) -> (N,)
    sum_sin = neighbors @ sin_theta  # (N,)
    sum_cos = neighbors @ cos_theta  # (N,)
    count = neighbors.sum(axis=1)  # (N,)
    mean_sin = sum_sin / count
    mean_cos = sum_cos / count
    theta_avg = np.arctan2(mean_sin, mean_cos)
    # Add noise: uniform in [-noise/2, noise/2]
    noise_arr = noise * (np.random.uniform(size=num_boids) - 0.5)
    theta_new = theta_avg + noise_arr
    theta_new = np.mod(theta_new, 2 * np.pi)

    # Update position
    v = v0 * np.array([np.cos(theta_new), np.sin(theta_new)])
    xy_new = xy + dt * v
    # Periodic boundary conditions
    xy_new = np.mod(xy_new, box_size)

    return xy_new, theta_new

title: Vicsek Lab: Vectorized Update
text:
Limitations of this implementation
The distance in these functions is the plain Euclidean distance. With periodic boundaries, two particles near opposite edges are close to each other, but the code does not see them as neighbors. For small \(r\) compared with \(L\) the effect is limited to particles near the edges.

title: Vicsek Lab: Vectorized Update
text:
Minimum-image distance






NoteExercise



Fix the limitation. Replace the displacement \(\Delta\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{x}_i\) by dx - box_size * np.round(dx / box_size) in each coordinate before computing the norm. Compare the time-averaged order parameter with and without this correction for \(N = 100\), \(L = 5\).

    # TODO: displacements between all pairs, shape (2, N, N)

    # TODO: apply the minimum-image correction and compute the distances

    # TODO: same steps as the vectorized version from here on

TipHint





Broadcasting gives all displacements at once: xy[:, :, None] - xy[:, None, :] has shape (2, N, N). np.round(dx / box_size) is \(\pm 1\) exactly when the direct displacement is longer than half the box, so the correction picks the nearest periodic copy.









TipSolution





With \(L = 5\) and \(r = 1\), a large fraction of the box lies within \(r\) of an edge, so the correction matters. Averaged over the last 1000 of 3000 steps, it raises \(v_a\) from about \(0.76\) to \(0.82\) at \(\eta = 2\) and from about \(0.27\) to \(0.33\) at \(\eta = 4\). Without the correction, particles near the edges have fewer neighbours and align less.
import numpy as np
from amlab.collective_motion.vicsek import initialize_particles, vicsek_equations


def vicsek_equations_periodic(xy, theta, noise=0.1, box_size=25, dt=1, radius_interaction=1, v0=0.03):
    # Displacements between all pairs, shape (2, N, N)
    dx = xy[:, :, None] - xy[:, None, :]
    # Minimum-image convention: use the nearest periodic copy
    dx = dx - box_size * np.round(dx / box_size)
    dist = np.sqrt((dx**2).sum(axis=0))
    neighbors = dist <= radius_interaction
    # Average direction of neighbors, including the particle itself
    theta_avg = np.arctan2(neighbors @ np.sin(theta), neighbors @ np.cos(theta))
    theta_new = theta_avg + noise * (np.random.uniform(size=theta.size) - 0.5)
    theta_new = np.mod(theta_new, 2 * np.pi)
    v = v0 * np.array([np.cos(theta_new), np.sin(theta_new)])
    xy_new = np.mod(xy + dt * v, box_size)
    return xy_new, theta_new


def mean_order(update, noise, steps=3000, avg_steps=1000, seed=0):
    np.random.seed(seed)
    xy, theta = initialize_particles(100, box_size=5)
    phi = []
    for step in range(steps):
        xy, theta = update(xy, theta, noise=noise, box_size=5)
        if step >= steps - avg_steps:
            phi.append(np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta))))
    return np.mean(phi)


for noise in [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]:
    print(noise, round(mean_order(vicsek_equations, noise), 3), round(mean_order(vicsek_equations_periodic, noise), 3))


for noise in [2.0, 4.0]:
    print(noise, mean_order(vicsek_equations, noise), mean_order(vicsek_equations_periodic, noise))

title: Kuramoto Lab: Locating the Threshold
text:
This page is the interpretation step. You compare the transition in your Bifurcation Diagram with the critical coupling \(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0))\) from Critical Coupling.
In your animation script from Animation, set the coupling strength just below and just above the critical value to see the difference in the dynamics. Below \(K_c\) the oscillators remain incoherent. Above \(K_c\) they start to synchronize and form a cluster on the unit circle, as in Figure 1.








Figure 1: Comparison between the theoretical critical coupling \(K_c\) and the empirical transition point observed in simulations. Individual oscillators are blue dots and the order parameter is the red vector.











NoteExercise



Find \(K_c\) from \(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0))\) for your normal frequencies with \(\sigma = 1\). Estimate the empirical transition point from your points: the value of \(K\) where \(r\) starts to rise clearly above zero. Alternatively, fit the near-onset scaling \(r \approx \sqrt{16/(\pi K_c^3)}\,\sqrt{\mu/(-g''(0))}\) of Bifurcation Diagram to the points just above the transition. Do the two estimates agree?








TipSolution





For a normal density \(g(0) = 1/\sqrt{2\pi}\), so \(K_c = 2\sqrt{2\pi}/\pi = \sqrt{8/\pi} \approx 1.60\). With \(N = 1000\) and 20 values of \(K\) between 0 and 5, \(r_\infty\) stays below about \(0.1\) up to \(K \approx 1.3\) and jumps to about \(0.6\) between \(K \approx 1.6\) and \(K \approx 1.8\). The grid spacing is about \(0.26\), so the empirical threshold agrees with \(K_c\) within one grid step. The exact \(K\) of the jump moves with the seed, because each sample of frequencies differs from \(g\) (Finite-Size Effects).









NoteExercise



The empirical points in the normal case lie close to zero for \(K < K_c\) but not exactly at zero. Give two reasons.








TipSolution





First, a finite population has \(r\) of order \(N^{-1/2}\) even when incoherent (about \(0.045\) for the \(N = 500\) figures of Bifurcation Diagram, \(0.03\) for \(N = 1000\)). Second, the time window may be too short for \(r(t)\) to settle near \(K_c\), where the approach to the steady state is slow. Finite-Size Effects studies the first effect.

title: The Couzin Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Couzin et al. (2002), up to and including the section on hysteresis.
Recommended: Vicsek et al. (1995), for the model that Couzin et al. extend.
The Vicsek model is deliberately minimal: alignment, noise and self-propulsion. It has alignment only, so its groups spread out and have no boundary. Couzin et al. point out that models of this kind cannot form a self-bounded group when the error is greater than zero, because the particles neither avoid collisions nor are attracted to each other (Couzin et al. 2002). For animal groups such as fish schools and bird flocks two extra mechanisms are needed: collision avoidance (repulsion at short range) and group cohesion (attraction at longer range). Couzin et al. (2002) added both through a simple behavioural rule with three interaction zones. The model was built for three dimensions. The course uses a two-dimensional version.

title: The Couzin Model
The Couzin Model
text:
Rules
Repulsion has priority. Individuals try to keep a minimum distance from others at all times, a behaviour often observed in animals. You can read the zone of repulsion as personal space, or as collision avoidance. If \(n_r > 0\) neighbours are in the zor, the desired direction is
\[
\mathbf{d}_i(t+\tau) = -\sum_{j \in R_i(t)} \mathbf{r}_{ij}(t).
\tag{1}\]
Otherwise, orientation and attraction. If \(n_r = 0\), the individual responds to the neighbours in the zoo and in the zoa:
\[
\mathbf{d}_o(t+\tau) = \sum_{j \in O_i(t)} \frac{\mathbf{v}_j(t)}{|\mathbf{v}_j(t)|},
\qquad
\mathbf{d}_a(t+\tau) = \sum_{j \in A_i(t)} \mathbf{r}_{ij}(t).
\tag{2}\]
If only the zoo has neighbours, \(\mathbf{d}_i = \mathbf{d}_o\). If only the zoa has neighbours, \(\mathbf{d}_i = \mathbf{d}_a\). If both do, \(\mathbf{d}_i = \tfrac12(\mathbf{d}_o + \mathbf{d}_a)\). If the result is the zero vector, or no neighbour is detected, the individual keeps its direction, \(\mathbf{d}_i = \mathbf{v}_i\). We write the case of both zones as one rule, \(\mathbf{d}_i \propto \sum_{j \in O_i} \mathbf{v}_j/|\mathbf{v}_j| + \sum_{j \in A_i} \mathbf{r}_{ij}\). This is the same direction as \(\tfrac12(\mathbf{d}_o + \mathbf{d}_a)\): the factor \(\tfrac12\) only changes the length, and \(\mathbf{d}_i\) is normalised to a unit vector before it is used.
Noise. Decisions in animals are affected by sensory and movement errors. To model this, the desired direction is rotated by a random angle from a wrapped Gaussian with standard deviation \(\sigma\).
Limited turning. After every individual has computed \(\mathbf{d}_i\), all of them turn toward it with turning rate \(\theta\). If the angle between \(\mathbf{v}_i(t)\) and \(\mathbf{d}_i(t+\tau)\) is less than the maximum turning angle \(\theta\tau\), then \(\mathbf{v}_i(t+\tau) = \mathbf{d}_i(t+\tau)\). Otherwise the individual rotates by \(\theta\tau\) toward the desired direction. They move at constant speed \(s\).

title: The Couzin Model
text:
Collective states
Couzin et al. (2002) measure two quantities, the group polarization and the group angular momentum:
\[
p_{\text{group}} = \frac{1}{N}\left|\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{v}_i\right|,
\qquad
m_{\text{group}} = \frac{1}{N}\left|\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{r}_{ic} \times \mathbf{v}_i\right|,
\tag{3}\]
where \(\mathbf{r}_{ic}\) is the unit vector from the group centroid \(\mathbf{c}_{\text{group}} = N^{-1}\sum_i \mathbf{c}_i\) to individual \(i\). Both lie in \([0, 1]\). (The paper prints \(\mathbf{r}_{ic} = \mathbf{c}_i - \mathbf{c}_{\text{group}}\) without the normalisation, but then \(m_{\text{group}}\) would carry units of length and could exceed \(1\). The unit vector is what the stated range requires, and what the course code uses.) Varying the widths \(\Delta r_o = r_o - r_r\) and \(\Delta r_a = r_a - r_o\), they found four states:



State
\(p_{\text{group}}\)
\(m_{\text{group}}\)




Swarm
low
low


Torus (milling)
low
high


Dynamic parallel group
high
low


Highly parallel group
very high
low



We name three states: the polarized flock, the swarm and the mill (torus). The paper splits the polarized flock in two. In the dynamic parallel group the individuals are polarized and move as a coherent group, but they can move through the group and its density and shape fluctuate. In the highly parallel group the arrangement is almost static and rectilinear (Couzin et al. 2002). They appear as \(r_r\), \(r_o\), \(r_a\), the noise, the density and the field of view are varied: a different balance of short-range avoidance, mid-range alignment and long-range cohesion produces a different macroscopic organisation. The paper also finds that the torus is confined to a small range of widths when the field of perception is \(\alpha = 360^\circ\) and occupies more of parameter space as \(\alpha\) decreases, while fragmentation becomes common over the whole parameter space when \(\alpha\) is near \(230^\circ\).
The next figure shows three of these states in the course version of the model: \(N = 50\) individuals in the plane, \(r_r = 1\), \(\Delta r_a = 12\), \(\alpha = 270^\circ\), noise \(\sigma = 0.05\) rad, turning rate \(40^\circ\)/s, speed \(3\), \(\tau = 0.1\) s, starting at random in a \(25 \times 25\) square and run for \(2000\) steps.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from amlab.collective_motion.couzin import couzin_equations, initialize_particles_couzin


def group_measures(xy, theta):
    """Group polarization p and angular momentum m of the Couzin paper (two dimensions)."""
    p = abs(np.exp(1j * theta).mean())
    rel = xy - xy.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)               # position relative to the centroid
    rel = rel / np.linalg.norm(rel, axis=0)                 # unit vector r_ic
    m = abs(np.mean(rel[0] * np.sin(theta) - rel[1] * np.cos(theta)))   # z-component of r_ic x v_i
    return p, m


def run_couzin(delta_ro, delta_ra, steps=2000, seed=1, N=50):
    np.random.seed(seed)                                    # the amlab functions use NumPy's global generator
    xy, theta = initialize_particles_couzin(N, box_size=25.0)
    for _ in range(steps):
        xy, theta = couzin_equations(xy, theta, radius_alignment=1 + delta_ro,
                                     radius_attraction=1 + delta_ro + delta_ra)
    return xy, theta









Figure 1: Three collective states of the two-dimensional Couzin model with \(N = 50\) and \(\Delta r_a = 12\), shown relative to the group centroid after 2000 steps. Arrows are the headings, coloured by angle. Left: swarm (\(\Delta r_o = 0\)), cohesive but with low polarization. Centre: torus (\(\Delta r_o = 3\)), with low polarization and high angular momentum, so the individuals circle around an empty core. Right: parallel group (\(\Delta r_o = 12\)), with polarization close to one. The titles give \(p_{\mathrm{group}}\) and \(m_{\mathrm{group}}\) of Equation 3.





A scan of \(\Delta r_o\) at \(\Delta r_a = 12\) with three random seeds (3000 steps, average over the last 500) gives the following picture for this version of the model.

For \(\Delta r_o = 0\) to \(6\), \(p_{\text{group}}\) stays between \(0.09\) and \(0.23\). The angular momentum is high (\(0.58\) to \(0.77\)) for \(\Delta r_o\) from \(2\) to \(6\) in two of the three seeds, which is the torus. The third seed stays at \(m_{\text{group}} \approx 0.2\) and does not form a mill.
For \(\Delta r_o \ge 8\), \(p_{\text{group}} \ge 0.99\) in all seeds, with \(m_{\text{group}} \le 0.05\) except for one seed at \(\Delta r_o = 8\) (\(m_{\text{group}} = 0.83\)), which we did not investigate. These are highly parallel groups. In this scan we did not find a clean dynamic parallel group; looking for one by changing \(\Delta r_a\) and the field of view is a task for Practice: Collective Motion.
The transitions are much farther out than in the paper, whose Figure 4 has them at \(r_o \approx 1.5\) and \(2.5\) (that is, \(\Delta r_o \approx 0.5\) and \(1.5\)) for \(N = 100\) in three dimensions with \(r_a = 14\). Here the dimension, \(N\) and the starting region differ, and we did not look for the cause. Do not compare the thresholds, only the sequence of states.


Collective memory
The paper also finds collective memory: for the same parameters, the group state depends on the path taken through parameter space (Couzin et al. 2002). This is hysteresis, as in the spruce budworm model of Module 1 (Hysteresis). In the paper, \(r_a = 14\) is held fixed and \(r_o\) is increased and then decreased, with \(2000\) steps at each value. On the way up the group goes from swarm to torus (from \(r_o \approx 1.5\)) and to a polarized group (beyond \(r_o \approx 2.5\)). On the way down the polarization does not decrease, the angular momentum stays low and the torus is never entered, until the group falls back to a swarm below \(r_o \approx 1.5\) (Couzin et al. 2002).
The same effect appears in the course version. With \(\Delta r_a = 12\) we ran \(2000\) steps at \(\Delta r_o = 12\) (parallel group) or at \(\Delta r_o = 3\) (torus) and then \(2500\) steps at \(\Delta r_o = 7\), for seeds \(0\) to \(2\). Starting from the parallel group, all three runs stayed parallel (\(p_{\text{group}} \ge 0.998\), \(m_{\text{group}} \le 0.03\)). Starting from the torus, none became parallel (\(p_{\text{group}}\) between \(0.21\) and \(0.29\), \(m_{\text{group}}\) between \(0.20\) and \(0.72\)). Same parameters, different states. You can repeat this in the explorer below.

NoteExercise



Set \(\Delta r_o = 0\) in the Couzin model. Which rules remain, and which collective state do you expect?








TipSolution





With no zone of orientation there is no alignment, only repulsion and attraction. Individuals stay together but do not align, so you expect a swarm: low \(p_{\text{group}}\) and low \(m_{\text{group}}\). This matches the swarm region of Couzin et al. (2002).

title: The Couzin Model
text:
Bridge to crowds
The Couzin model is a natural bridge to crowd models. Like Vicsek, it is rule-based, usually has constant speed and uses local interactions. Like the crowd models, it has explicit repulsion (personal space) and avoidance. The next step is to replace the “desired direction” rules by forces and accelerations, and to add obstacles, exits and goals. That is the social force model of Helbing and Molnár (1995), applied to a crowd at a door in Faster Is Slower. Going from Vicsek to Couzin adds realism (cohesion and avoidance) while keeping a simple agent rule. The same Couzin rules, with a predator added, are used in The Confusion Effect.

title: Synchronization in Nature
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2024), Chapter 4, especially Section 4.5.
Recommended: Strogatz (2003).
Synchronization is the adjustment of the rhythms of self-sustained oscillators due to a weak interaction between them (Pikovsky et al. 2001). Two ingredients matter. Each unit oscillates on its own, with its own natural frequency. The units interact, and the interaction changes their timing, not their existence. This module models both ingredients with phase variables.

title: Synchronization in Nature
text:
Three classical examples

Fireflies
Males of some Southeast Asian firefly species, such as Pteroptyx malaccae, gather in trees and flash in unison. Buck (1988) reviews the field and laboratory evidence. A single firefly can also entrain to a periodic flashing light, which is the experiment behind the model in Phase Locking (Ermentrout and Rinzel 1984; Ermentrout 1991).


Metronomes on a moving base
Place two or more metronomes on a light board that rests on two cans. The board moves slightly with each swing, and this motion couples the pendulums. Pantaleone (2002) shows that the metronomes usually end up swinging in phase, with antiphase motion only under special conditions. He also shows that the system is a mechanical realization of the Kuramoto model.


Cardiac pacemaker cells
The sinoatrial node sets the heartbeat. Michaels et al. (1987) simulated two-dimensional arrays of electrically coupled sinus node cells with different intrinsic periods. The activation maps looked like a wave spreading from a single leading pacemaker, yet the pattern came from the mutual entrainment of all the spontaneously beating cells.

title: Synchronization in Nature
text:
Modelling choices
The examples share a structure, and the models in this module keep only that structure.








Example
Oscillator
Coupling




Fireflies
Flash cycle of one insect
Light from the other insects


Metronomes
Pendulum with escapement
Motion of the common base


Pacemaker cells
Membrane potential cycle
Electrical current between cells


Millennium Bridge
Gait of one pedestrian
Lateral motion of the deck (Strogatz et al. 2005)



Winfree (1967) proposed describing each unit by a phase alone and studying large populations of such phase oscillators. Kuramoto (1975) simplified Winfree’s model into the solvable form that now carries his name (Strogatz 2000). A different route treats the interaction as short pulses, as in the integrate-and-fire model of Mirollo and Strogatz (1990).






NoteExercise



Pick the metronome example. Name the state variable of one oscillator, the physical quantity that carries the coupling, and one parameter that you expect to control whether synchronization happens.








TipSolution





The state of one metronome is the angle of its pendulum, which you can reduce to a phase on the circle. The coupling is carried by the horizontal displacement of the base. A natural control parameter is the mass of the base relative to the pendulums: a heavier base moves less and couples the metronomes more weakly. The spread of natural frequencies (the tempo settings) matters too. Pantaleone (2002) analyses both.

title: Synchronization in Nature
text:
Where this module goes

Flows on the Circle introduces the phase variable for one oscillator.
Phase Locking couples one oscillator to a periodic stimulus.
The Kuramoto Model couples many oscillators to each other.

title: Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door
text:
TipOptional extension



This page extends the social force model. There, pedestrians avoid each other politely. Here the crowd is in a hurry, bodies touch, and a narrow door becomes a bottleneck. We ask two questions: does pushing harder get you out sooner, and can a column in front of the door help?
When many people squeeze through a narrow opening, a few of them lean on each other and form an arch across the door. The arch blocks the exit until it breaks. Two counterintuitive claims come from this picture:
Both claims have been tested, and the evidence is more mixed than the pictures suggest.
The model on this page lets you explore why the answer can depend so much on the system.
crumbs: Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door

title: Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door
text:
The model
We use the physics-based version of the social force model of Helbing et al. (2000). Pedestrians are discs of radius \(r_i \in [0.25, 0.35]\) m and mass \(m = 80\) kg. The motion of pedestrian \(i\) is
\[
m\,\frac{d\mathbf{v}_i}{dt} = m\,\frac{v^0 \mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{v}_i}{\tau}
+ \sum_{j}\Big[A\,e^{(r_{ij}-d_{ij})/B} + k\,g(r_{ij}-d_{ij})\Big]\mathbf{n}_{ij}
+ \sum_{j}\kappa\,g(r_{ij}-d_{ij})\,(\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ji}\cdot\mathbf{t}_{ij})\,\mathbf{t}_{ij}
+ \text{(walls and column)}.
\tag{1}\]
Compare it with the social force model:

The first term is the wish to move: the pedestrian wants to walk with speed \(v^0\) toward the exit and relaxes to it in a time \(\tau = 0.5\) s. Here \(v^0\) is the dial that says how much in a hurry the crowd is.
The second term is the social repulsion \(A e^{(r_{ij}-d_{ij})/B}\) with \(A = 2000\) N and \(B = 0.08\) m, plus a body force \(k\,g(r_{ij}-d_{ij})\) that acts only when two discs overlap (\(g(x) = x\) for \(x > 0\), else 0). Here \(r_{ij} = r_i + r_j\), \(d_{ij}\) is the distance between the centres and \(\mathbf{n}_{ij}\) points from \(j\) to \(i\). The stiffness is \(k = 1.2 \times 10^5\) kg/s\(^2\).
The third term is sliding friction between bodies in contact, with \(\kappa = 2.4 \times 10^5\) kg/(m s). It acts along the tangent \(\mathbf{t}_{ij}\) and is what makes a crowd jam like a granular material.

Walls and the column act on a pedestrian in the same way as a fixed disc or line would.
The setup. A room of \(12 \times 12\) m with one door of width 1 m in the bottom wall, and 150 pedestrians placed at random without overlap. Whoever crosses the door line has escaped. We measure:

the evacuation time: when the last person crosses the door line;
the flow: people per second through the door, measured between the 10th and the 90th percentile of the exits;
the pressure on the people within 2 m of the door: the sum of the contact (body) forces on a person divided by the perimeter \(2\pi r\), in N/m (Helbing et al. 2000);
the pause: the time since the last person crossed. We call a pause longer than 2 s an arch.







NoteTwo numerical choices




Time step. The contact stiffness is large, so the time step is small: \(\Delta t = 0.002\) s. We checked that \(\Delta t = 0.001\) s gives the same statistics at twice the cost.
The door jambs. The exponential social force acts along wall faces. At the free ends of the wall, the two door jambs, only the contact force acts. Without this change, the two jambs together can repel a slow pedestrian more strongly than it pushes, and it stalls in the middle of the doorway. This is a modification of the published model that we found necessary at low desired speeds.

title: Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door
text:
The code
crowd_exit.py has the whole model in one class, CrowdSim, and the parameters in a dataclass, CrowdParams. The most important idea is that only near pairs of pedestrians interact, so we find them with a KD-tree, the same one used in the Couzin code:
pairs = cKDTree(pos).query_pairs(2 * p.r_max + self.CUTOFF, output_type="ndarray")
i, j = pairs[:, 0], pairs[:, 1]
dxy = pos[i] - pos[j]                        # from j to i
d = np.hypot(dxy[:, 0], dxy[:, 1])
n_vec = dxy / d[:, None]
f, body = self._contact(d, r[i] + r[j], n_vec, vel[j] - vel[i])
F[:, 0] += np.bincount(i, f[:, 0], n) - np.bincount(j, f[:, 0], n)   # Newton's third law
F[:, 1] += np.bincount(i, f[:, 1], n) - np.bincount(j, f[:, 1], n)
A short experiment of your own:
from amlab.collective_motion.crowd_exit import CrowdParams, run_evacuation, sweep

r = run_evacuation(CrowdParams(v0=4.0), seed=0)
print(r["evac_time"], r["flow"], r["door_pressure"])

# faster is slower: 5 random rooms per speed (about 10 s per evacuation)
res = sweep("v0", [1.5, 2.5, 4.0, 6.0], n_seeds=5)
print(res["values"], res["evac_time"], res["flow"])

# the column: its distance from the door at a fixed speed
base = CrowdParams(v0=4.0, obstacle=True)
res = sweep("obs_gap", [0.8, 1.2, 2.0], base=base, n_seeds=5)
Runs that do not finish within t_max (300 s by default) are reported with complete < 1.

title: Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door
text:
Experiment 1: faster is slower
run_experiments.py crowd produces the figures below. It takes about 20 minutes (less on a fast computer), because every point is an average over 5 evacuations. Run it with --seeds 3 for a faster draft.






Figure 1: Evacuation time, flow and pressure against the desired speed.



The curves have two regimes:

Slow crowds (below about 2 m/s) are limited by how fast people walk. A faster wish to move means faster evacuation.
Fast crowds (above about 3 m/s) are limited by the door. The evacuation takes longer again, from about 137 s at 2.5 m/s to about 162 s at 8 m/s: the flow drops by about a quarter. The pressure at the door grows by a factor of more than 200 over the whole range. That is the faster-is-slower effect (Helbing et al. 2000).

The position of the minimum depends on the size of the room, the width of the door and the contact parameters. Do not read the number 2.5 m/s as a property of real crowds: read the model as a mechanism, not as a prediction.

text:
Experiment 2: a column in front of the door
We fix the crowd at \(v^0 = 4\) m/s and compare the room without a column with a column of radius 0.5 m at several distances from the door (measured from the door line to the nearest point of the column).






Figure 2: Flow and pressure with a column at different distances from the door.

Too close (0.5 m or less): the column makes things worse. The space between the column and the door is narrower than a body, and the column itself becomes the bottleneck.
At 0.8 m the flow is about 20% higher than without a column, and the evacuation is shorter (123 s against 139 s). This is a distance close to the width of the door, as in the silo experiments (Zuriguel et al. 2011).
At 1.2 m the flow is lower than without a column, and at 2 m it is the same within the noise.
The pressure near the door does not change much, except for the blocked cases. So in this model the benefit does not show up as a lower pressure within 2 m of the door. To test the idea that the column shields the door, measure the contact forces only on the people closest to it (door_pressure(radius=1.0)).

With only 5 rooms per point, differences smaller than about 0.1 people/s are not significant. Increase --seeds before you trust a small difference.
So the effect of the column depends strongly on its position, as in the silo and sheep experiments (Zuriguel et al. 2011, 2016). A common explanation is that the column takes the load of the people behind it, so that fewer arches form at the door, and that the people who go around it reach the door from the sides instead of head-on (Zuriguel et al. 2011). The model reproduces the dependence on position. Whether it reproduces the mechanism is for you to find out.






WarningThe experiments with people did not find this



In the drills with people, the flow rate did not change measurably. The obstacle only made the sideways rushes weaker (Garcimartı́n et al. 2018). Our model is closer to the silo and the sheep than to those drills. Possible reasons, which the model can help to test but does not settle: people in a drill may push less than our discs do, and they avoid each other actively. Always ask whether the conditions of a simulation match those of the experiment before you compare them.








NoteExercise 1: how hard is the push?



At \(v^0 = 6\) m/s, what is the force with which a pedestrian pushes when it is at rest, according to the first term of Equation 1? Compare it with the weight of a person of 80 kg.








TipSolution





At rest (\(\mathbf{v} = 0\)) the wish-to-move term is \(m v^0/\tau = 80 \times 6/0.5 = 960\) N. The weight is \(80 \times 9.8 \approx 784\) N. So at 6 m/s every person pushes with a force larger than their own weight, and a crowd of such people transmits a large force through the bodies to the front rows. This is why the pressure grows so fast with the desired speed in Figure 1.









NoteExercise 2: why a minimum?



Explain in two sentences why the evacuation time has a minimum as a function of the desired speed, using the words walking and door.








TipSolution





At low speed the people need a long time to arrive and to move through the door one after the other, so the evacuation is limited by how fast they walk. At high speed they arrive quickly, but the pushing forms arches that block the door, so the evacuation is limited by how often the arches break. The best speed is where the two limits balance.









NoteExercise 3: a column that is too close



The door is 1 m wide and a person is 0.5 to 0.7 m wide. Why does a column placed 0.2 m from the door make things worse?








TipSolution





At 0.2 m the space between the column and the door line is narrower than a body (0.5 to 0.7 m), so nobody can pass between them, and the people who get around the column still have to turn toward the door. The column itself becomes the bottleneck. The sheep experiment found the same: an obstacle too close to the door made the flow worse (Zuriguel et al. 2016).




Build this in Python. Option D of Practice: Collective Motion asks you to write the evacuation model with contact forces, find the speed with the shortest evacuation time and test a column.

title: Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door
section: What this model does not do
text:
What this model does not do

The pedestrians are discs with no vision and no strategy. Real people are not circular, can turn their shoulders, and avoid pushing when they can.
The room is a square with a single door, and the people start at random positions. Real evacuations have corridors, stairs and smoke.
The results come from a few random rooms for every point. The error bars in Figure 1 are the standard deviation over 5 runs. Differences smaller than that are not significant.
The contact stiffness and the time step are chosen for speed. A much smaller time step gives the same statistics, but the very large pressures are only qualitative.
The idea for this page came from a short video simulation. The effects it shows (arches, the column) are real and published, but the exact thresholds in the video (the gap between the tips of the obstacle, the angle of its faces) are not in the papers cited here, and we have not tested them.

title: Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door
text:
Going further

Obstacle shape. Replace the circle by a wedge or a short wall, with the tip toward the crowd. Does a slanted face lead the people to the sides better?
A few pushers. Give only 10% of the people a high desired speed. How many are needed to slow everybody down?
Arch statistics. Collect the times between consecutive exits from many runs (run_evacuation returns them as gaps) and plot their distribution on a logarithmic scale. What share of the total time is spent in pauses longer than 2 s, and how does it change with the desired speed?
Granular flow. Models of grains in a silo use the same kind of contact forces (stiffness and friction), with gravity in place of the wish to move. This is the system of the first experiments on obstacles (Zuriguel et al. 2011).

title: The Order Parameter
text:
To visualize the Kuramoto model, picture each phase \(\theta_j\) as a point \(e^{i\theta_j}\) running around the unit circle in the complex plane (Strogatz 2000).
Figure 1: Oscillators (blue dots) on the unit circle. The order parameter (red) points towards the centroid of the phases.

title: The Order Parameter
text:
Definition
The complex order parameter is the centroid of these points:
\[
r e^{i\psi} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N e^{i\theta_j}.
\tag{1}\]

\(r \in [0, 1]\) is the coherence. \(r = 1\) when all phases coincide. \(r \approx 0\) when the phases are spread around the circle.
\(\psi\) is the mean phase, the phase of the collective rhythm.

In Figure 1 the initial phases cover only part of the circle, so the red vector has a clear length and direction. To see the vector move as the phases evolve, run the script amlab/odes_coupled/kuramoto.py. You build the same animation yourself in Animation.

title: The Order Parameter
text:
Mean-field form
Multiply Equation 1 by \(e^{-i\theta_i}\) and take the imaginary part:
\[
r\sin(\psi - \theta_i) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i).
\]
The Kuramoto model therefore becomes
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + K r \sin(\psi - \theta_i),\quad i = 1, \dots, N.
\tag{2}\]
This rewriting is exact for every \(N\) (Strogatz 2000). Each oscillator no longer sees the others one by one. It sees only the mean field: it is pulled toward the mean phase \(\psi\) with effective strength \(Kr\). Computing \(r\) and \(\psi\) costs \(O(N)\) operations per step, while the double sum in the pairwise form costs \(O(N^2)\).

title: The Order Parameter
text:
Feedback between coherence and coupling
Equation 2 shows why synchronization can appear spontaneously (Strogatz 2000):

Oscillators are pulled toward \(\psi\) with strength \(Kr\).
If more of them cluster, \(r\) grows.
A larger \(r\) increases the pull \(Kr\), which recruits more oscillators.

The loop is opposed by the spread of natural frequencies. Oscillators whose \(|\omega_i|\) exceeds \(Kr\) cannot follow the mean field and keep drifting. The balance sets a threshold coupling \(K_c\), derived in Critical Coupling.






NoteExercise



Suppose the \(N\) phases are independent and uniform on \([0, 2\pi)\). Show that \(\mathbb{E}[r^2] = 1/N\). What does this imply for the value of \(r\) you measure in an incoherent simulation?








TipSolution





\[
r^2 = \left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_j e^{i\theta_j}\right|^2 = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{j,k} e^{i(\theta_j - \theta_k)}.
\]
The \(N\) terms with \(j = k\) equal \(1\). For \(j \ne k\) the phases are independent, so \(\mathbb{E}[e^{i(\theta_j-\theta_k)}] = \mathbb{E}[e^{i\theta_j}]\,\mathbb{E}[e^{-i\theta_k}] = 0\). Hence \(\mathbb{E}[r^2] = N/N^2 = 1/N\). An incoherent population with \(N = 100\) shows \(r\) of order \(0.1\), not \(0\). You will see this floor in Finite-Size Effects.









NoteExercise



Compute \(r\) for three oscillators at phases \(0\), \(2\pi/3\) and \(4\pi/3\), and for three oscillators at \(0\), \(0\) and \(\pi\).








TipSolution





The first three points are the cube roots of unity, which sum to zero, so \(r = 0\). For the second set, \(e^{0} + e^{0} + e^{i\pi} = 1\), so \(r = 1/3\) and \(\psi = 0\).

Order Parameter






NoteExercise



Complete the function that computes the order parameter. It returns \(r\), \(\psi\) and the two coordinates \(r\cos\psi\) and \(r\sin\psi\) of the red dot.
def kuramoto_order_parameter(theta: np.ndarray) -> tuple:
    # TODO: compute r * exp(i * phi)
    order_param =  # replace this line
    r = np.abs(order_param)
    phi = np.angle(order_param)
    rcosphi = np.real(order_param)
    rsinphi = np.imag(order_param)
    return r, phi, rcosphi, rsinphi








TipSolution





axis=0 averages over oscillators, so the same function also works on the 2D array sol.y and returns \(r(t)\).
def kuramoto_order_parameter(theta: np.ndarray) -> tuple:
    order_param = np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta), axis=0)
    r = np.abs(order_param)
    phi = np.angle(order_param)
    rcosphi = np.real(order_param)
    rsinphi = np.imag(order_param)
    return r, phi, rcosphi, rsinphi

Write the Animation Update Function
The core loop is expanded to include updates for the order parameter plot and noise diagnostic plot. The pipeline is as follows:

update xy_tail.
update the particle artists.

update the noise diagnostic dict_noise and its plot.

As you can see, steps 1-3 remain the same as in Animation Loop. Use this checklist:

plt_particles.set_data(...) and plt_current.set_data(...)
append vicsek_order_parameter(theta) to the window list
set line data for the order parameter plot
compute a recent average
update dict_noise[noise_eta] and redraw the noise curve







NoteExercise



Complete update_animation(), following the comments for each step. Keep the function inside run_simulation so it can access the state variables with nonlocal.
def update_animation(frame: int):
    nonlocal xy, xy_tail, theta, noise_eta, v0, radius_interaction, box_size, dict_noise, ls_order_param

    # TODO: advance the Vicsek equations

    # TODO: update the tail tensor
    # TODO: update the particle artists with set_data

    # TODO: update the order parameter history and plot

    # TODO: compute a recent average and update dict_noise

    # TODO: update the noise diagnostic plot with set_data


    return (plt_particles, plt_current, line_order_param, line_noise)








TipHint





Keep only the last ORDER_WINDOW values with ls_order_param[-ORDER_WINDOW:]. For the recent average, take the mean of the last third of that window. line_noise.set_data(*zip(*dict_noise.items())) turns the dictionary into x and y lists.









TipSolution





def update_animation(frame: int):
    nonlocal \
        xy, \
        xy_tail, \
        theta, \
        noise_eta, \
        v0, \
        radius_interaction, \
        box_size, \
        dict_noise, \
        ls_order_param
    xy, theta = vicsek_equations(
        xy,
        theta,
        v0=v0,
        dt=dt,
        radius_interaction=radius_interaction,
        box_size=box_size,
        noise=noise_eta,
    )

    # Update tails
    xy_tail = np.roll(xy_tail, shift=-1, axis=2)
    xy_tail[:, :, -1] = xy
    plt_particles.set_data(xy_tail[0].flatten(), xy_tail[1].flatten())
    plt_current.set_data(xy[0], xy[1])

    # Update order parameter
    ls_order_param.append(vicsek_order_parameter(theta))
    ls_order_param = ls_order_param[-ORDER_WINDOW:]
    x_vals = np.arange(len(ls_order_param))
    line_order_param.set_data(x_vals, ls_order_param)

    # Average the last ORDER_WINDOW//3 values to get the order parameter (similar to Couzin)
    order_param = np.mean(ls_order_param[-ORDER_WINDOW // 3 :])
    dict_noise[noise_eta] = order_param
    dict_noise = dict(sorted(dict_noise.items()))
    if dict_noise:
        line_noise.set_data(*zip(*dict_noise.items()))
    else:
        line_noise.set_data([], [])
    return (plt_particles, plt_current, line_order_param, line_noise)

title: Flows on the Circle
text:
A periodic rhythm can be described by a single angle, the phase \(\theta\). The phase lives on the circle: \(\theta\) and \(\theta + 2\pi\) are the same state. A one-dimensional flow on the circle is
\[
\dot\theta = f(\theta), \qquad f(\theta + 2\pi) = f(\theta).
\tag{1}\]
Unlike a flow on the line, a flow on the circle can return to its starting point. This is the simplest model of an oscillator (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.1).

title: Flows on the Circle
text:
Uniform oscillator
The simplest choice is a constant speed, \(\dot\theta = \omega\). The solution is \(\theta(t) = \omega t + \theta_0\) and the period is \(T = 2\pi/\omega\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.2).

title: Flows on the Circle
text:
Nonuniform oscillator
A phase that speeds up and slows down along the cycle obeys
\[
\dot\theta = \omega - a \sin\theta, \qquad \omega > 0,\; a \ge 0.
\tag{2}\]
This equation appears in the firefly model, in overdamped pendulums and in Josephson junctions (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.3 to 4.6). Its behaviour depends on the ratio \(a/\omega\).

For \(a < \omega\) there are no fixed points. The phase circulates, slowest near \(\theta = \pi/2\).
At \(a = \omega\) a half-stable fixed point appears at \(\theta = \pi/2\). This is a saddle-node bifurcation on the circle (see Saddle-Node Bifurcation).
For \(a > \omega\) there are two fixed points with \(\sin\theta^* = \omega/a\). One is stable and one is unstable. The oscillation stops.

For \(a < \omega\) the period is
\[
T = \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{d\theta}{\omega - a\sin\theta} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\omega^2 - a^2}}.
\tag{3}\]
As \(a \to \omega^-\) the period diverges like \(T \approx \dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,\pi}{\sqrt{\omega}}\,(\omega - a)^{-1/2}\). The trajectory spends almost all its time in the bottleneck left behind by the fixed points that are about to appear (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.3).








Figure 1: Nonuniform oscillator with \(\omega = 1\). Left: the vector field \(f(\theta)\) for three values of \(a\). Right: the period from Equation 3 and the square-root scaling near \(a = \omega\).











NoteExercise



Take \(a > \omega\). Find the two fixed points of Equation 2 in \([0, 2\pi)\) and decide which one is stable.








TipSolution





The fixed points satisfy \(\sin\theta^* = \omega/a < 1\), so \(\theta_1^* = \arcsin(\omega/a) \in (0, \pi/2)\) and \(\theta_2^* = \pi - \theta_1^*\). The derivative of the vector field is \(f'(\theta) = -a\cos\theta\). At \(\theta_1^*\) the cosine is positive, so \(f' < 0\) and the point is stable. At \(\theta_2^*\) the cosine is negative and the point is unstable.









NoteExercise



Check Equation 3 numerically for \(\omega = 1\) and \(a = 0.8\). Integrate the ODE with solve_ivp and measure the time it takes \(\theta\) to grow by \(2\pi\).








TipSolution





The formula gives \(T = 2\pi/\sqrt{1 - 0.64} = 2\pi/0.6 \approx 10.47\).
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

def rhs(t, theta, omega, a):
    return omega - a * np.sin(theta)

def one_turn(t, theta, omega, a):
    return theta[0] - 2 * np.pi

one_turn.terminal = True
sol = solve_ivp(rhs, (0, 100), [0.0], args=(1.0, 0.8), events=one_turn, rtol=1e-10)
print(sol.t_events[0][0])  # about 10.472

title: Phase Locking
text: A single firefly can lock its flashing to a periodic light. The model below, from Strogatz (2024, sec. 4.5), is based on Ermentrout and Rinzel (1984). It is the smallest model of synchronization: one oscillator driven by one rhythm.

title: Phase Locking
text:
The model
Let \(\Theta(t)\) be the phase of the stimulus and \(\theta(t)\) the phase of the firefly. A flash happens when a phase passes through \(0\). The stimulus runs at constant frequency \(\Omega\). The firefly has natural frequency \(\omega\) and is pulled toward the stimulus with strength \(A > 0\):
\[
\dot\Theta = \Omega, \qquad \dot\theta = \omega + A\sin(\Theta - \theta).
\tag{1}\]
If the stimulus is ahead (\(0 < \Theta - \theta < \pi\)), the firefly speeds up. If it is behind, the firefly slows down.

title: Phase Locking
text:
Phase difference
The quantity you care about is the phase difference \(\phi = \Theta - \theta\). It obeys
\[
\dot\phi = \Omega - \omega - A\sin\phi.
\tag{2}\]
With the dimensionless time \(\tau = At\) and detuning \(\mu = (\Omega - \omega)/A\), this becomes
\[
\phi' = \mu - \sin\phi,
\tag{3}\]
which is the nonuniform oscillator from Flows on the Circle.

title: Phase Locking
text:
Locking range

If \(|\mu| \le 1\), Equation 3 has a stable fixed point \(\phi^* = \arcsin\mu\). The firefly runs at the stimulus frequency \(\Omega\) with a constant phase lag. This is phase locking, or entrainment.
If \(|\mu| > 1\), there are no fixed points and \(\phi\) keeps increasing. The firefly drifts relative to the stimulus. This is phase drift.

In the original variables the firefly entrains when
\[
\omega - A \le \Omega \le \omega + A.
\tag{4}\]
Outside this range, the time for \(\phi\) to grow by \(2\pi\) is
\[
T_{\text{drift}} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{(\omega - \Omega)^2 - A^2}}.
\tag{5}\]
Both predictions can be tested with a flashing light, because \(\omega\) and the width of the locking range are measurable (Strogatz 2024, sec. 4.5). Real fireflies differ between species. Some can even shift their own natural frequency, which needs an extra adaptation variable (Ermentrout 1991).








Figure 1: Phase difference \(\phi = \Theta - \theta\) for a firefly with \(\omega = 1\) and \(A = 0.2\). Inside the locking range (\(\Omega = 1.15\)) the difference settles to \(\arcsin\mu\). Outside it (\(\Omega = 1.3\)) the difference keeps growing, one turn every \(T_{\text{drift}}\).





Predicted drift period for Omega = 1.3: 28.10








NoteExercise



Use Figure 1 and the printed value. Measure the drift period in the plot for \(\Omega = 1.3\) and compare it with Equation 5.








TipSolution





With \(\omega = 1\), \(\Omega = 1.3\) and \(A = 0.2\), Equation 5 gives \(T_{\text{drift}} = 2\pi/\sqrt{0.09 - 0.04} = 2\pi/\sqrt{0.05} \approx 28.1\). In the plot \(\phi\) climbs by about \(2\pi \approx 6.28\) every 28 time units, with slow stretches where \(\phi\) is near \(\pi/2\), the bottleneck.









NoteExercise



A firefly has a natural period of \(0.9\) s and entrains to stimulus periods between \(0.78\) s and \(1.06\) s. Estimate \(A\).








TipSolution





Convert periods to angular frequencies with \(\Omega = 2\pi/T\). The extremes of the locking range are \(\Omega_{\max} = 2\pi/0.78 \approx 8.06\) and \(\Omega_{\min} = 2\pi/1.06 \approx 5.93\) rad/s. By Equation 4, \(\Omega_{\max} - \Omega_{\min} = 2A\), so \(A \approx 1.06\) rad/s. The midpoint, \(6.99\) rad/s, is close to \(\omega = 2\pi/0.9 \approx 6.98\) rad/s, which is a consistency check. (These numbers are illustrative, chosen for the exercise.)

title: Phase Locking
text:
Explore locking and drift
The figure integrates Equation 1 with \(\omega = 1\), starting from \(\phi(0) = 0\), with the same Runge-Kutta scheme as Figure 1. The left panel shows both phases on the circle; each flashes as it passes the top. The middle panel is the flow Equation 2 on the circle, with its fixed points (filled: stable, hollow: unstable).


With \(\Omega = 1.15\) and \(A = 0.2\), where does \(\phi\) settle? Compare it with \(\arcsin\mu\) for \(\mu = 0.75\). Who flashes first, the light or the firefly?
Raise \(\Omega\) slowly. At which value does locking break? Watch the two fixed points in the flow panel just before it happens, and compare with Equation 4.
Set \(\Omega = 1.3\). Check the measured drift period against Equation 5. Where on the circle does \(\phi\) move slowly, and why?
Keep \(\Omega = 1.3\) and increase the coupling \(A\). What is the smallest \(A\) that entrains the firefly?
Now set \(\Omega = 0.85\), below \(\omega\). The firefly still locks. What is the sign of the phase lag, and what does it mean for the order of the flashes?



Build this in Python. In the lab you write the code behind this figure: Kuramoto Lab: Pairwise vs Mean Field. With \(N = 2\) oscillators, your pairwise right-hand side reduces to \(\phi' = \Delta\omega - K\sin\phi\) for \(\phi = \theta_2 - \theta_1\), the same equation as here with \(A = K\).

title: Phase Locking
text:
From one oscillator to many
Here the stimulus is fixed and does not respond to the firefly. In a swarm every firefly is both a stimulus and a responder. The Kuramoto model treats that case.

title: The Social Force Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Helbing and Molnár (1995).
Recommended: Helbing et al. (2000), for the extension to escape panic used in Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door.
Helbing and Molnár (1995) model pedestrians as if they were subject to “social forces”. These forces are not physical. They measure the motivation of a pedestrian to change velocity in response to a goal, to other people and to walls. Unlike the Vicsek and Couzin models, this is a continuous-time model with acceleration, so speeds can change.
It is the natural next step after The Couzin Model. There, a desired direction is computed from rules for the zones of repulsion, orientation and attraction. Here, the desired direction is replaced by a desired velocity, and forces and accelerations take the place of the rules. Obstacles, exits and goals then enter naturally, as terms of the force.

title: The Social Force Model
text:
Equation of motion
Pedestrian \(\alpha\) wants to walk in the direction \(\mathbf{e}_\alpha\) of its next target at desired speed \(v^0_\alpha\). Deviations from the desired velocity relax on a time scale \(\tau_\alpha\):
\[
\mathbf{F}^0_\alpha = \frac{1}{\tau_\alpha}\left(v^0_\alpha \mathbf{e}_\alpha - \mathbf{v}_\alpha\right).
\tag{1}\]
The total social force adds repulsion from other pedestrians \(\beta\), repulsion from borders \(B\) and optional attractions \(i\) (Helbing and Molnár 1995):
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{w}_\alpha}{dt} = \mathbf{F}^0_\alpha + \sum_\beta \mathbf{F}_{\alpha\beta} + \sum_B \mathbf{F}_{\alpha B} + \sum_i \mathbf{F}_{\alpha i} + \text{fluctuations},
\tag{2}\]
where \(\mathbf{w}_\alpha\) is the preferred velocity. The actual velocity equals \(\mathbf{w}_\alpha\), capped at a maximum speed \(v^{\max}_\alpha\).

title: The Social Force Model
text:
Repulsion
The repulsion from pedestrian \(\beta\) is the gradient of a potential, \(\mathbf{f}_{\alpha\beta} = -\nabla_{\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta}} V_{\alpha\beta}[b(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta})]\), with \(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta} = \mathbf{r}_\alpha - \mathbf{r}_\beta\). The equipotential lines are ellipses stretched in the walking direction of \(\beta\), because \(\beta\) needs room for its next step:
\[
2b = \sqrt{\left(|\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta}| + |\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta} - v_\beta \Delta t\, \mathbf{e}_\beta|\right)^2 - (v_\beta \Delta t)^2}.
\tag{3}\]
Forces from behind count less. A situation outside the angle of sight \(2\varphi\) is weighted by a factor \(c\) with \(0 < c < 1\).
In their simulations Helbing and Molnár (1995) used \(V_{\alpha\beta}(b) = V^0 e^{-b/\sigma}\) and \(U_{\alpha B}(d) = U^0 e^{-d/R}\) with \(V^0 = 2.1\ \text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}\), \(\sigma = 0.3\) m, \(U^0 = 10\ \text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}\), \(R = 0.2\) m, \(\Delta t = 2\) s, \(\tau_\alpha = 0.5\) s, \(2\varphi = 200^\circ\) and \(c = 0.5\). Desired speeds were normal with mean \(1.34\) m/s and standard deviation \(0.26\) m/s.








Figure 1: Magnitude of the repulsive social force from a standing pedestrian (\(v_\beta = 0\), so \(b = |\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\beta}|\)) and from a wall, with the parameters of Helbing and Molnár (1995).

title: The Social Force Model
text:
Collective effects
With only these local rules, simulations reproduced two effects seen in real crowds (Helbing and Molnár 1995):

Lane formation in counterflowing crowds: people walking in the same direction form lanes.
Oscillations at bottlenecks: at a narrow door, the passing direction switches back and forth between the two groups.







NoteExercise



A pedestrian walks at \(1.0\) m/s and wants \(1.34\) m/s. What acceleration does Equation 1 give with \(\tau = 0.5\) s? How long does it take to close most of the gap?








TipSolution





The acceleration is \((1.34 - 1.0)/0.5 = 0.68\ \text{m s}^{-2}\). Without other forces, the gap decays like \(e^{-t/\tau}\), so after about \(3\tau = 1.5\) s only \(5\%\) of it is left.









NoteExercise



Name one difference between the social force model and the Vicsek model, in the rules and in the question each model answers.








TipSolution





In the rules: Vicsek particles have fixed speed and only turn; social force pedestrians accelerate and decelerate, and each has its own goal. In the question: Vicsek asks when a group with no goal starts moving together. The social force model asks how people with goals share space, which is why Helbing and Molnár (1995) propose it as a tool for planning pedestrian areas.

text:
Full Script
At this point you have built every piece.






NoteExercise



Assemble run_simulation() in vicsek_animation_full.py: parameters, state, figure, the three plots, the sliders, update_animation, the animation object and the callbacks. Run it and move the noise slider slowly from 0 to 5. The red curve should drop from \(r \approx 1\) towards \(r \approx 0\).








TipSolution





def run_simulation(dt: float = 1.0) -> None:
    # Parameters
    num_boids = 100
    noise_eta = 0.5
    box_size = 10.0
    radius_interaction = 1.0
    v0 = 0.03
    ORDER_WINDOW = 3000
    TAIL_LEN = 20

    # Initialize state
    xy, theta = initialize_particles(num_boids, box_size)

    # Order parameter history and noise diagnostic
    ls_order_param = []
    dict_noise = {}

    # Create figure and axes
    fig, ax_plane, ax_order, ax_sliders, ax_noise = make_figure()

    # Initialize plots
    xy_tail, plt_particles, plt_current = init_particles_plot(ax_plane, xy, box_size, tail_len=TAIL_LEN)
    line_order_param = init_order_plot(ax_order, order_window=ORDER_WINDOW)
    line_noise = init_noise_plot(ax_noise)

    # Create sliders
    ax_num_boids, ax_radius_interaction, ax_noise_eta, ax_v0, ax_box_size = make_slider_axes(ax_sliders)
    slider_num_boids, slider_radius_interaction, slider_noise_eta, slider_v0, slider_box_size = make_sliders(
        ax_num_boids=ax_num_boids,
        ax_radius_interaction=ax_radius_interaction,
        ax_noise_eta=ax_noise_eta,
        ax_v0=ax_v0,
        ax_box_size=ax_box_size,
        num_boids=num_boids,
        radius_interaction=radius_interaction,
        noise_eta=noise_eta,
        v0=v0,
        box_size=box_size,
    )

    def update_animation(frame: int):
        nonlocal xy, xy_tail, theta, dict_noise, ls_order_param
        xy, theta = vicsek_equations(
            xy,
            theta,
            v0=v0,
            dt=dt,
            radius_interaction=radius_interaction,
            box_size=box_size,
            noise=noise_eta,
        )
        xy_tail = np.roll(xy_tail, shift=-1, axis=2)
        xy_tail[:, :, -1] = xy
        plt_particles.set_data(xy_tail[0].flatten(), xy_tail[1].flatten())
        plt_current.set_data(xy[0], xy[1])

        ls_order_param.append(vicsek_order_parameter(theta))
        ls_order_param = ls_order_param[-ORDER_WINDOW:]
        line_order_param.set_data(np.arange(len(ls_order_param)), ls_order_param)

        dict_noise[noise_eta] = np.mean(ls_order_param[-ORDER_WINDOW // 3 :])
        dict_noise = dict(sorted(dict_noise.items()))
        line_noise.set_data(*zip(*dict_noise.items()))
        return (plt_particles, plt_current, line_order_param, line_noise)

    # Create the animation object
    ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update_animation, interval=0, blit=True)

    # Slider callbacks
    def update_sliders(_):
        nonlocal radius_interaction, noise_eta, v0, box_size
        ani.event_source.stop()
        noise_eta = slider_noise_eta.val
        v0 = slider_v0.val
        box_size = slider_box_size.val
        radius_interaction = slider_radius_interaction.val
        ax_plane.set_xlim(0, box_size)
        ax_plane.set_ylim(0, box_size)
        ani.event_source.start()

    def update_num_boids(_):
        nonlocal xy, theta, num_boids, xy_tail
        ani.event_source.stop()
        num_boids = int(slider_num_boids.val)
        xy, theta = initialize_particles(num_boids, box_size=box_size)
        xy_tail = np.repeat(xy[:, :, np.newaxis], TAIL_LEN, axis=2)
        plt_particles.set_data(xy_tail[0].flatten(), xy_tail[1].flatten())
        plt_current.set_data(xy[0], xy[1])
        ani.event_source.start()

    for slider in (slider_radius_interaction, slider_noise_eta, slider_v0, slider_box_size):
        slider.on_changed(update_sliders)
    slider_num_boids.on_changed(update_num_boids)

    plt.show()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_simulation()
The full script with all functions defined is in amlab/collective_motion/vicsek_animation.py. You can run it and experiment with the sliders to see how the Vicsek model behaves under different conditions.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Initialization
text: In this lab you implement the Kuramoto model, animate it, and measure the transition to synchrony. You follow the course workflow: prediction, implementation, validation, experiment, interpretation and limitations. The theory is in The Kuramoto Model, The Order Parameter and Critical Coupling.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Initialization
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



Before writing code, answer these questions on paper. You will check them later.

Take \(N = 100\) oscillators with normal frequencies, \(\sigma = 1\). What is \(K_c\)?
What value of \(r\) do you expect at \(t = 0\) for uniform random phases? (The Order Parameter has an exercise on this.)
For \(K = 10\) and for \(K = 0.1\), sketch what the phases on the circle will look like at \(t = 10\).









TipSolution





\(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0)) = \sqrt{8/\pi} \approx 1.60\). At \(t = 0\), \(r\) is of order \(1/\sqrt{N} = 0.1\). For \(K = 10 \gg K_c\) most phases gather in a tight cluster. For \(K = 0.1 \ll K_c\) they stay spread around the circle.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Initialization
text:
Initialize Oscillators
The phases \(\theta_i\) are sampled uniformly on \([0, 2\pi)\) and the natural frequencies \(\omega_i\) from a normal distribution with standard deviation \(\sigma\) (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000).






NoteExercise



Write a function that initializes the oscillators. The outputs theta and omega are 1D arrays of length num_oscillators.

    # Assign a random initial phase to each oscillator

    return theta, omega








TipHint





A NumPy random generator rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) has methods for sampling:

Uniform distribution: rng.uniform(low=0.0, high=2 * np.pi, size=num_oscillators)
Normal distribution: rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=sigma, size=num_oscillators)

A fixed seed makes your runs reproducible.









TipSolution





Remember to import NumPy first.
import numpy as np


def initialize_oscillators(num_oscillators: int, sigma: float = 1.0, seed: int = None):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # Assign a random initial phase to each oscillator
    theta = rng.uniform(low=0.0, high=2 * np.pi, size=num_oscillators)

    # Assign a random natural frequency to each oscillator
    omega = rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=sigma, size=num_oscillators)
    return theta, omega

text:
Plot the Oscillators
To visualize the oscillators, plot their phases on the unit circle. The x-coordinate is \(\cos(\theta_i)\) and the y-coordinate is \(\sin(\theta_i)\). This way, each oscillator corresponds to a point on the circle. Figure 1 shows an example.








Figure 1: Sample visualization of oscillators on the unit circle. Each blue dot represents an oscillator with phase \(\theta_i\).

Apply NumPy’s cos and sin functions to the whole theta array: x = np.cos(theta) and y = np.sin(theta). Then use plt.subplots() to create the axes and ax.scatter(x, y) to draw the points.









TipSolution





Set up the figure and axes with subplots, then plot the points with scatter.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

theta, omega = initialize_oscillators(100, seed=1)
x = np.cos(theta)
y = np.sin(theta)

# First, we prepare the figure and axes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
# fig is the Figure, a "canvas" where everything is drawn
# ax is the Axes, a "subplot" where we can plot data
# A single figure can have multiple axes (e.g. for subplots)
ax.set_title("Kuramoto Model")  # Title of the plot
ax.set_xlabel("Cos(theta)")  # Name of x-axis
ax.set_ylabel("Sin(theta)")  # Name of y-axis
ax.set_xlim(-1.1, 1.1)  # Limits for x-axis
ax.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.1)  # Limits for y-axis
ax.set_aspect("equal")  # Make the circle look circular
ax.grid(True)  # Show grid lines
# Draw unit circle (optional, but it helps to visualize the boundary)
circle = plt.Circle((0, 0), 1, color="lightgray", fill=False)
ax.add_artist(circle)

# Now we are ready to plot the oscillators as blue dots
ax.scatter(x, y, s=50, color="blue", alpha=0.5)
# s is the size of the dots
# alpha is the transparency (0 is fully transparent, 1 is fully opaque)
# we want the oscillators to be somewhat transparent so we can see overlaps

# Finally, we show the plot and close it to free up memory
plt.show()
plt.close()
