title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
section: From an Interval to a Rectangle
text:
From an Interval to a Rectangle
The 1D solver already gives the full workflow. In 2D, the ideas stay the same but the geometry becomes richer.



Data shape

A field on \([0, L_x] \times [0, L_y]\) becomes a matrix.



Diffusion stencil

The second derivative becomes the 5-point Laplacian.



Visible payoff

Mode pairs generate spots, stripes, fronts, and labyrinths.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Rectangular Grid and 5-Point Stencil
\[
\Delta u(x,y) \approx \frac{u(x+dx,y) + u(x-dx,y) + u(x,y+dx) + u(x,y-dx) - 4u(x,y)}{dx^2}
\]
lap = -4 * field
lap += np.roll(field, 1, axis=0)
lap += np.roll(field, -1, axis=0)
lap += np.roll(field, 1, axis=1)
lap += np.roll(field, -1, axis=1)
lap = lap / dx**2
This is still the same vectorized idea from the 1D case, now applied along two axes.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Boundary Conditions in 2D



Neumann

Copy the nearest interior row or column.



Dirichlet

Pin the edge to a prescribed value.



Periodic

Keep the np.roll() wrapping and do not overwrite the edges.


For zero flux on a rectangle,
uv[:, 0, :] = uv[:, 1, :]
uv[:, -1, :] = uv[:, -2, :]
uv[:, :, 0] = uv[:, :, 1]
uv[:, :, -1] = uv[:, :, -2]

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Gierer-Meinhardt in 2D Uses Mode Pairs
With Neumann boundaries on \([0, L_x] \times [0, L_y]\),
\[
\lambda_{n_x,n_y} = -\left(\frac{n_x\pi}{L_x}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{n_y\pi}{L_y}\right)^2.
\]
The temporal matrix is still
\[
A_{n_x,n_y} = J + \lambda_{n_x,n_y} D.
\]
So the 1D workflow survives intact. The only change is that one mode number becomes a pair.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
section: Domain Geometry Changes the Leading Pattern
text:
Domain Geometry Changes the Leading Pattern
Take \(L_x = 20\), \(L_y = 50\), \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), \(\gamma = 1\).

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Gray-Scott Reuses the Same Solver
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = d_1 \Delta u - u v^2 + f(1-u),
\qquad
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = d_2 \Delta v + u v^2 - (f+k)v
\]
The numerical recipe is nearly unchanged.

Same rectangular grid
Same 5-point stencil
Same explicit Euler update
Different reaction term
Periodic boundaries instead of Neumann

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Periodic Boundaries Change the Spectrum
For periodic boundaries on a rectangle,
\[
\lambda_{m,n} = -\left(\frac{2\pi m}{L_x}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{2\pi n}{L_y}\right)^2.
\]
That is the main conceptual bridge from Gierer-Meinhardt to Gray-Scott.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 2D
text:
The Core 2D Update Loop
for _ in range(num_steps):
    lap_u = np.roll(u, 1, axis=0) + np.roll(u, -1, axis=0)
    lap_u += np.roll(u, 1, axis=1) + np.roll(u, -1, axis=1) - 4 * u
    lap_v = np.roll(v, 1, axis=0) + np.roll(v, -1, axis=0)
    lap_v += np.roll(v, 1, axis=1) + np.roll(v, -1, axis=1) - 4 * v
    u += dt * (d1 * lap_u - u * v**2 + f * (1 - u))
    v += dt * (d2 * lap_v + u * v**2 - (f + k) * v)
With periodic boundaries, this loop is complete. With Neumann or Dirichlet data, the edge values must be overwritten after each Euler step.

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
When Many Oscillators Talk
The main question in this session is no longer what one trajectory does, but when a whole population of oscillators starts moving coherently.

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
Ingredients of the Kuramoto Model



State

Each oscillator carries a phase \(\theta_i(t)\) on the unit circle.



Heterogeneity

Each oscillator has a natural frequency \(\omega_i\) drawn from a distribution.



Coupling

All-to-all sinusoidal interaction tries to align phases when \(K > 0\).


\[
\dot \theta_i = \omega_i + \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{K}{N} \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i)
\]

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
The Macroscopic Observable
\[
r e^{i \Psi} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N e^{i \theta_j}
\]



Order parameter \(r\)

\(r \approx 0\) means incoherence. \(r \approx 1\) means strong phase alignment.



Mean phase \(\Psi\)

The average direction tells you where the synchronized pack is located on the circle.

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
Mean-Field Interpretation
\[
\dot \theta_i = \omega_i + K r \sin(\Psi - \theta_i)
\]



Positive feedback

If a small amount of coherence appears, the effective coupling \(K r\) grows and recruits more oscillators.



Critical onset

Synchronization appears when the coupling becomes strong enough relative to the spread of natural frequencies.

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
From Theory to Bifurcation Diagram



What we plot

Draw the long-time average of \(r\) against the coupling strength \(K\).



Common mistake

Do not compare empirical data from one frequency distribution against the exact theory for another. The deck now makes that warning explicit instead of hiding it in a later slide.

title: Coupled ODEs
text:
What the Full Simulation Shows



Visual cues to look for


points clustering on the unit circle,
growth of the order parameter,
sensitivity to \(K\), \(N\), and the frequency distribution,
mismatch between finite-\(N\) simulations and asymptotic theory.


Python stack


solve_ivp() for time integration,
matplotlib.animation for the circle dynamics,
matplotlib.widgets.Slider for parameter control.

The main numerical integrator for initial value problems in the course.



numpy

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Three Models, One Solver Pattern



SIR epidemic model

\[
\dot S = -\beta S I, \quad
\dot I = \beta S I - \gamma I, \quad
\dot R = \gamma I
\]
Track growth, peak prevalence, and the role of \(R_0 = \beta / \gamma\).



Saturating rate law

\[
v(S) = \frac{V_{\max} S}{K_m + S}
\]
Use this to discuss why many rates stop growing linearly at large substrate levels.



Spruce budworm

\[
\dot x = r x \left(1 - \frac{x}{k}\right) - \frac{x^2}{1 + x^2}
\]
This is the cleanest example of threshold behavior and bistability in the session.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Bistability Is a Modeling Signal



Spruce budworm takeaways


The balance between logistic growth and saturating predation creates multiple equilibria.
Small perturbations can push the system toward a low-population or high-population regime.
The same ODE solver works, but the interpretation now matters as much as the integration.

Use the full module page when you want the phase-line analysis and parameter exploration.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Geometry Enters the Picture
The solver workflow is still the same, but now the state has two components and the right picture is a trajectory in the phase plane, not just a time series.
\[
\dot x = f(x, y; \theta), \qquad \dot y = g(x, y; \theta)
\]

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Session Arc



CDIMA reaction

Use one worked chemical system to build the language of nullclines and fixed points.



Van der Pol

See how nonlinear damping creates a stable limit cycle.



FitzHugh-Nagumo

Compare oscillation with excitability in a fast-slow system.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Phase-Plane Workflow



Integrate

Use solve_ivp() exactly as before, but now the state vector is (x, y).



Plot

Show trajectories directly in the phase plane.



Analyze

Find the curves where \(\dot x = 0\) and \(\dot y = 0\).



Classify

Use the Jacobian to distinguish stable points, saddles, and oscillatory behavior.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Nullclines, Fixed Points, Stability



Nullclines

Solve
\[
f(x, y; \theta) = 0, \qquad g(x, y; \theta) = 0
\]
to find where the vector field changes direction.



Fixed point

Intersections of the nullclines are the equilibrium candidates.



Linear test

Evaluate the Jacobian near the equilibrium and inspect its eigenvalues.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
CDIMA Is the Template
\[
\dot x = a - x - \frac{4xy}{1 + x^2}, \qquad
\dot y = b x \left(1 - \frac{y}{1 + x^2}\right)
\]



Why it matters

This model has all the ingredients you need for the rest of the session: nullclines, fixed points, stability, and trajectory comparison.



Classroom target

Start here before you move to Van der Pol or FitzHugh-Nagumo. It is the cleanest worked example in the module.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations in 2D
text:
Two Signatures to Compare



Van der Pol oscillator

\[
\dot x = \mu (y - f(x)), \qquad
\dot y = -\frac{x}{\mu}, \qquad
f(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - x
\]
Look for a self-sustained stable limit cycle.



FitzHugh-Nagumo

\[
\epsilon \dot v = f(v) - w + I_{\mathrm{app}}, \qquad
\dot w = v - \gamma w
\]
Look for excitable transients and timescale separation.

title: Collective Motion
text:
Local Rules, Global Order
Collective motion is the first session where the main model is not a continuous-time ODE. The dynamics come from a repeated update rule applied to many agents at once.

title: Collective Motion
text:
Session Arc



Base rule

Start with Vicsek alignment, noise, constant speed, and periodic boundaries.



Observable

Measure the transition with the order parameter instead of relying on animation alone.



Extensions

Then ask what changes when you add repulsion, predators, or richer decision rules.

title: Collective Motion
section: Why This Is Not an ODE Session
text:
Why This Is Not an ODE Session



Previous sessions

State changes came from derivatives and continuous-time rate laws.



This session

Each time step updates headings and positions directly from neighbor information, so a simulation loop is more natural than solve_ivp().

title: Collective Motion
text:
Vicsek Update Rule
\[
\theta_i(t + \Delta t) = \langle \theta_j(t) \rangle_{j \in \mathcal N_i} + \frac{\eta}{2} \xi_i
\]
\[
\mathbf x_i(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf x_i(t) + v_0 \Delta t (\cos \theta_i, \sin \theta_i)
\]

At each step, every boid aligns with neighbors inside a radius \(r\), adds noise, moves at constant speed, and wraps back into the box with periodic boundary conditions.

title: Collective Motion
text:
What Moves the Transition



Noise \(\eta\)

Higher noise breaks alignment and pushes the system toward disorder.



Density

More local contacts make alignment easier.



Interaction radius \(r\)

This sets who can influence whom at each step.



Speed \(v_0\)

This controls how quickly local alignment propagates through the box.

title: Collective Motion
section: The Order Parameter Is the Summary Statistic
text:
The Order Parameter Is the Summary Statistic





Order parameter versus noise






Average velocity versus density




Use the average normalized velocity to quantify how ordered the flock is. The interesting part is the transition, not just the animation.

title: Collective Motion
section: The Session Extends in Two Directions
text:
The Session Extends in Two Directions



Couzin model

Add a repulsion zone so agents avoid collisions instead of only aligning.



Predator extension

Add an escape rule, then decide whether the predator is passive, autonomous, or includes eating-spawning dynamics.

title: Collective Motion
text:
Minimal Simulation Loop
for step in range(num_steps):
    theta = update_angles(xy, theta, radius=r, noise=eta)
    xy = xy + speed * dt * np.vstack((np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)))
    xy = xy % box_size
    order[step] = compute_order_parameter(theta)
This is the discrete-time analogue of the solver loop from the ODE sessions.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
From State Vectors to Fields
The key change in the PDE session is spatial structure. The state is no longer a short vector of variables. It is a field sampled on a grid.



Mathematical object

u(x, t)
The unknown is now a field over space, not a short ODE state vector.



Coupling mechanism

Diffusion enters through the Laplacian, which links each location to its neighbors.



Lecture goal

Turn the theory they already saw into concrete calculations for Gierer-Meinhardt and the later Gray-Scott transition.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Flow for This Session



Boundary conditions

Implement Neumann, Dirichlet, and periodic conditions on Cartesian grids.



Laplacian

Write the centered finite-difference stencil with vectorized shifts.



Explicit Euler

Advance the full field with a direct time-stepping loop.



Turing application

Compute the equilibrium, the Jacobian, the mode matrix, and the unstable-mode list.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Boundary Conditions on Cartesian Grids
The same implementation logic works in 1D and on rectangles.



Neumann

Zero flux means copy the nearest interior value.
u[0] = u[1], u[-1] = u[-2]



Dirichlet

Fix the value at the boundary after every Euler step.
u[0] = u_left, u[-1] = u_right



Periodic

Wrap one edge onto the other. With np.roll(), the stencil already does it.


On a rectangle, the zero-flux pattern is
uv[:, 0, :] = uv[:, 1, :]
uv[:, -1, :] = uv[:, -2, :]
uv[:, :, 0] = uv[:, :, 1]
uv[:, :, -1] = uv[:, :, -2]

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Vectorized Laplacian



1D stencil

\[
\Delta u(x) \approx \frac{u(x+\Delta x) - 2u(x) + u(x-\Delta x)}{\Delta x^2}
\]
lap_u = np.roll(u, 1) - 2 * u + np.roll(u, -1)
lap_u = lap_u / dx**2



2D preview

\[
\Delta u \approx u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j}
\]
The same np.roll() idea extends later to rectangular grids.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Explicit Euler Closes the Solver
Once the right-hand side is available, the PDE update is just
\[
U^{n+1} = U^n + \Delta t\,G(U^n).
\]
du_dt, dv_dt = gierer_meinhardt_pde(0, uv, dx=dx)
uv[0] = uv[0] + dt * du_dt
uv[1] = uv[1] + dt * dv_dt
uv[:, 0] = uv[:, 1]
uv[:, -1] = uv[:, -2]
The order matters. First apply Euler, then reimpose the boundary data.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Gierer-Meinhardt Is the Working Example
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \Delta u + \gamma \left(a - b u + \frac{u^2}{v}\right),
\qquad
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = d\,\Delta v + \gamma (u^2 - v)
\]
This is the model we use to turn the Turing theory into concrete calculations.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Compute the Homogeneous Equilibrium
Set the reaction terms to zero:
\[
f(u, v) = a - bu + \frac{u^2}{v} = 0,
\qquad
g(u, v) = u^2 - v = 0.
\]
From \(g(u_*, v_*) = 0\),
\[
v_* = u_*^2.
\]
Substitute into \(f = 0\):
\[
a - bu_* + 1 = 0
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
u_* = \frac{a+1}{b},
\qquad
v_* = \left(\frac{a+1}{b}\right)^2.
\]
For \(a = 0.4\) and \(b = 1\),
\[
u_* = 1.4,
\qquad
v_* = 1.96.
\]

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
section: Compute the Jacobian at the Equilibrium
text:
Compute the Jacobian at the Equilibrium
At a general point \((u, v)\),
\[
J(u, v) =
\begin{pmatrix}
-b + 2u/v & -u^2/v^2 \\
2u & -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
At \((u_*, v_*)\) this becomes
\[
J_* =
\begin{pmatrix}
2b/(a+1) - b & -\left(b/(a+1)\right)^2 \\
2(a+1)/b & -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For \(a = 0.4\) and \(b = 1\),
\[
J_* =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.4286 & -0.5102 \\
2.8 & -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
section: Turing Conditions Define the Parameter Window
text:
Turing Conditions Define the Parameter Window
\[
f_u + g_v < 0,
\qquad
f_u g_v - f_v g_u > 0,
\qquad
g_v + d f_u > 2\sqrt{d(f_u g_v - f_v g_u)}
\]



Interpretation

The homogeneous equilibrium is stable without spatial variation, but some spatial mode can grow.



Worked comparison

At \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), the point \(d = 30\) is inside the Turing window, while \(d = 20\) is outside.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
section: Spatial Modes on a Finite Interval
text:
Spatial Modes on a Finite Interval
For Neumann boundary conditions on \([0, L]\),
\[
\phi_n(x) = \cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right),
\qquad
\lambda_n = -\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}\right)^2,
\qquad
n = 0, 1, 2, \dots
\]
This is the step the professor emphasized. The spatial part is solved by hand, and those \(\lambda_n\) are what enter the temporal calculation.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
From \(\lambda_n\) to \(A_n\) and \(\sigma_n\)
For each mode \(n\),
\[
A_n = J + \lambda_n D,
\qquad
D = \operatorname{diag}(1, d).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
A_n = J - k_n^2 D,
\qquad
k_n = \frac{n\pi}{L}.
\]
The temporal eigenvalues of mode \(n\) are the roots of
\[
\det\left(A_n - \sigma^{(n)} I\right) = 0.
\]
Positive \(\sigma^{(n)}\) means that spatial mode is unstable.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
section: Code Turns the Theory into a Mode List
text:
Code Turns the Theory into a Mode List
unstable_modes = []
for n in range(1, num_modes):
    lambda_n = -(n * np.pi / length) ** 2
    A_n = J + lambda_n * D
    growth_rate = np.max(np.linalg.eigvals(A_n).real)
    if growth_rate > 0:
        unstable_modes.append((n, growth_rate))

unstable_modes.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
This list does two things.

It tells you which modes are unstable.
Its first entry predicts the dominant early wavelength.

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Worked Example with \(L = 40\)
Take \(\gamma = 1\), \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\).



Case A

\(d = 30\)

Turing conditions satisfied
Unstable 1D modes: \(n = 5, 6\)
Growth rates: \(\sigma^{(5)} \approx 0.0214\), \(\sigma^{(6)} \approx 0.0206\)
Dominant mode: \(n = 5\)




Case B

\(d = 20\)

Third Turing condition fails
No unstable 1D modes
Perturbations decay back to the homogeneous state

title: Partial Differential Equations in 1D
text:
Same Checklist for Gray-Scott
The pipeline does not change.

Compute the homogeneous equilibrium.
Compute the Jacobian.
Compute the Laplacian eigenvalues.
Build \(A_n = J + \lambda_n D\).
Compute the temporal eigenvalues \(\sigma_n\).

The conceptual change is the boundary condition.

Gierer-Meinhardt usually uses Neumann boundaries.
Gray-Scott usually uses periodic boundaries.

At the usual Gray-Scott base state \((u, v) = (1, 0)\), the linearized system is damped, so the classical Turing calculation becomes interesting only at a nontrivial homogeneous equilibrium when one exists.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
One Repository, Many Contributors
This session turns version control into a team workflow. The goal is not only to push code, but to make changes traceable, reviewable, and easy to merge.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Set Up the Shared Repository



Host the repo

Create the repository, fill in the basics, and decide who owns the remote.



Add collaborators

Invite teammates first. Review only works if the right people can see and comment on the code.



Clone locally

Work in VS Code or the terminal from a local clone, not by editing files in the browser.



First shared commit

Create a simple README or starter file once, then push it so everyone starts from the same baseline.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Branch-Based Workflow
git clone <repo-url>
git checkout -b feature/short-task-name
git add .
git commit -m "Implement the first draft"
git push -u origin feature/short-task-name

Do not work directly on main. Each branch should map to one small task so the review is focused and conflicts stay manageable.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Pull Request Anatomy



Base and compare

The base branch should be main. The compare branch should be the feature branch you just pushed.



Title and description

The title states the change. The description explains the intent, what changed, and what needs review.



Assignee and reviewer

Assign the person doing the work and the person who will review it.



Work in progress

Use [WIP] in the title when the branch is not ready for review yet.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Review and Merge



Files changed

Review only the diff against main, not the whole repository.



Line comments

Comment directly on the lines that need clarification or revision.



Review outcome

Choose comment, approve, or request changes based on the actual state of the branch.



Merge only when ready

Once comments are resolved and the team agrees, merge and stop working on that branch.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Issues Keep the Team Organized



Issue

Describe one task or bug clearly and assign it to one person.



Branch

Create a dedicated branch to address that issue only.



Pull request

Open a PR from that branch and mention the issue number in the description.



Merge and close

After the PR is merged, the issue becomes the record of why the change happened.

title: GitHub Teamwork
text:
Team Working Agreement



Do


keep PRs small,
write descriptive branch names,
review before merging,
update main locally after a merge.




Avoid


committing directly to main,
asking for review on unfinished work,
mixing unrelated tasks in one branch,
ignoring review comments.

title: Flocking Without Noise: The Cucker–Smale Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Cucker and Smale (2007), Section I and the statement of Theorem 2 in Section III.
Recommended: Vicsek et al. (1995), for the model that Cucker and Smale take as their starting point.
This page is optional. The Vicsek model and the Couzin model are studied by simulation. Cucker and Smale (2007) propose a flocking model for which one can prove that the birds end up with a common velocity. The price is a different structure: every bird listens to every other bird, with a weight that decays with distance, and the birds have inertia.

title: Flocking Without Noise: The Cucker–Smale Model
text:
The model
Take \(k\) birds with positions \(\mathbf{x}_i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and velocities \(\mathbf{v}_i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d\). Each bird accelerates toward the velocities of the others, weighted by how close they are (Cucker and Smale 2007):
\[
\dot{\mathbf{x}}_i = \mathbf{v}_i, \qquad
\dot{\mathbf{v}}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{k} a_{ij}\,(\mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i),
\tag{1}\]
\[
a_{ij} = \frac{K}{\left(\sigma^2 + \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\|^2\right)^{\beta}},
\qquad K, \sigma > 0,\ \beta \ge 0.
\tag{2}\]
The exponent \(\beta\) controls how fast the influence decays with distance. Three differences with the Vicsek model are worth noting.









Vicsek
Cucker–Smale




Speed
constant, only the heading changes
free, the birds have inertia


Interaction graph
\(a_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\) (within radius \(r\)), changes in time
all pairs, weights \(a_{ij} > 0\) that decay with distance


Noise
yes, with strength \(\eta\)
none


Time
discrete
continuous (a discrete version is also given in the paper)


Result
simulation, order–disorder transition
theorem: flocking for every initial condition if \(\beta < 1/2\)



The paper makes the contrast explicit: the Vicsek weights correspond to the step function \(\eta(y) = 1\) for \(y \le r^2\) and \(0\) otherwise, whereas Equation 2 decreases continuously. In the Vicsek case, convergence depends on the connectivity of the whole sequence of interaction graphs. In the Cucker–Smale case the graph is always complete, so one can work directly with the initial state (Cucker and Smale 2007).

title: Flocking Without Noise: The Cucker–Smale Model
text:
Flocking and the two spreads
Measure the spread of the flock in velocity and in position by
\[
\Lambda(t) = \frac12 \sum_{i \ne j} \|\mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{v}_j\|^2,
\qquad
\Gamma(t) = \frac12 \sum_{i \ne j} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\|^2 .
\tag{3}\]
The flock has reached a common velocity when \(\Lambda(t) \to 0\), and it stays together when \(\Gamma(t)\) remains bounded. Theorem 2 of Cucker and Smale (2007) gives sufficient conditions on the initial values \(\Gamma_0\) and \(\Lambda_0\):

if \(\beta < 1/2\), the flock converges for every initial condition;
if \(\beta = 1/2\), it converges when \(\Lambda_0\) is small enough compared with \(K\);
if \(\beta > 1/2\), it converges when an explicit inequality linking \(\Gamma_0\), \(\Lambda_0\), \(K\), \(\sigma\) and \(\beta\) holds. Roughly, the flock must start compact enough for its members to feel each other.

These conditions are sufficient, not necessary. The key step of the proof is an energy inequality. Let \(\phi_t\) be the Fiedler number (the second smallest eigenvalue) of the weighted graph Laplacian \(L_{\mathbf{x}} = D - A\) of the weights \(a_{ij}(t)\), and \(\Phi_t = \min_{0 \le \tau \le t} \phi_\tau\). Then
\[
\Lambda(t) \le \Lambda_0\, e^{-2 t \Phi_t}.
\tag{4}\]
Because all the weights are positive, \(\phi_t > 0\), and the velocities contract. The difficulty is that \(\phi_t\) shrinks when the flock spreads out, and the spread \(\Gamma\) in turn grows with the velocity differences. The proof closes this loop, which is possible for every initial condition when \(\beta < 1/2\) (Cucker and Smale 2007).

title: Flocking Without Noise: The Cucker–Smale Model
text:
Numerical experiment
The code below integrates Equation 1 with \(k = 20\) birds in the plane, \(K = 0.5\), \(\sigma = 1\), and initial velocities uniform in \([-0.5, 0.5]^2\). It compares two exponents (\(\beta = 0.25 < 1/2\) and \(\beta = 2 > 1/2\)) and two initial regions for the positions, a compact square of side \(3\) and a wide square of side \(30\).

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp


def cucker_smale_rhs(t, state, k, K, sigma, beta):
    x = state[:2 * k].reshape(k, 2)
    v = state[2 * k:].reshape(k, 2)
    d2 = ((x[:, None, :] - x[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)
    a = K / (sigma**2 + d2) ** beta                   # weights a_ij
    dv = a @ v - a.sum(axis=1)[:, None] * v           # sum_j a_ij (v_j - v_i)
    return np.concatenate([v.ravel(), dv.ravel()])


def simulate(beta, spread, k=20, K=0.5, sigma=1.0, T=60.0, seed=1, vmax=0.5):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    x0 = rng.uniform(0, spread, (k, 2))
    v0 = rng.uniform(-vmax, vmax, (k, 2))
    t_eval = np.linspace(0, T, 601)
    sol = solve_ivp(cucker_smale_rhs, (0, T), np.concatenate([x0.ravel(), v0.ravel()]),
                    t_eval=t_eval, args=(k, K, sigma, beta), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-11)
    x = sol.y[:2 * k].T.reshape(-1, k, 2)
    v = sol.y[2 * k:].T.reshape(-1, k, 2)
    return sol.t, x, v


def spreads(x, v):
    """Gamma and Lambda of the spreads equation, for every saved time."""
    gamma = 0.5 * ((x[:, :, None, :] - x[:, None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=(1, 2, 3))
    lam = 0.5 * ((v[:, :, None, :] - v[:, None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=(1, 2, 3))
    return gamma, lam









Figure 1: Cucker–Smale flocks with \(k = 20\) birds. Left: velocity spread \(\Lambda(t)\) on a logarithmic scale; the black line is the bound of Equation 4 for the first case, computed from the Fiedler number of the weight matrix. Right: position spread \(\Gamma(t)^{1/2}\). With \(\beta = 0.25\) both starting regions flock. With \(\beta = 2\) the compact start flocks, while the wide start does not within the simulated time.





What the experiment shows, for this seed:

With \(\beta = 0.25\), \(\Lambda\) falls below \(10^{-12}\) at \(t \approx 2.4\) from the compact start and at \(t \approx 6.9\) from the wide start, and \(\Gamma^{1/2}\) stays at its initial value. Both flock, as Theorem 2(i) predicts.
With \(\beta = 2\) and the compact start, the flock also forms, more slowly (\(\Lambda < 10^{-12}\) at \(t \approx 23.8\)).
With \(\beta = 2\) and the wide start, the weights \(a_{ij}\) are tiny at the initial distances. After \(t = 60\) the velocity spread has only dropped from \(66\) to \(29\), and \(\Gamma^{1/2}\) has grown from \(240\) to \(393\): the flock is spreading out instead of aligning. No theorem guarantees flocking here, and the simulation shows none within the time simulated.
The black curve in Figure 1 is the bound Equation 4. The measured \(\Lambda(t)\) stays below it at every saved time where \(\Lambda > 10^{-12}\) (below that value the integrator tolerance dominates). The measured decay is slightly faster than the bound.







NoteExercise



Show that the mean velocity \(\bar{\mathbf{v}} = \frac1k \sum_i \mathbf{v}_i\) is constant along solutions of Equation 1. What does this say about the direction in which a Cucker–Smale flock ends up moving? Compare with the Vicsek model.








TipSolution





Since \(a_{ij} = a_{ji}\),
\[
\sum_i \dot{\mathbf{v}}_i = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}(\mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\mathbf{v}_j - \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\mathbf{v}_i = 0,
\]
because exchanging the names \(i\) and \(j\) turns the first sum into the second. If the velocities converge to a common limit \(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\), then \(\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \bar{\mathbf{v}}(0)\). The final direction is fixed by the initial data. In the experiment above, the velocity of every bird at \(t = 60\) agrees with \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}(0)\) to about \(10^{-11}\) in the three flocking runs.
In the Vicsek model there is no conserved momentum, because the speed is fixed and only the heading is averaged and perturbed. The direction of the flock is selected spontaneously, by symmetry breaking (The Vicsek Model).









NoteExercise



For \(\beta = 2\), repeat the experiment with starting squares of side \(3\), \(4\), \(5\), \(8\) and \(12\), using the same seed. How does the time needed for \(\Lambda\) to fall below \(10^{-12}\) depend on the side? Explain it with Equation 2.








TipSolution





for side in [3, 4, 5, 8, 12]:
    t, x, v = simulate(2.0, float(side))
    gamma, lam = spreads(x, v)
    below = np.where(lam < 1e-12)[0]
    print(side, t[below[0]] if len(below) else None, lam[-1])
For this seed the time is \(23.8\) for side \(3\) and \(54.5\) for side \(4\). For side \(5\) it is not reached within \(t = 60\) (\(\Lambda(60) \approx 3 \times 10^{-5}\), still decaying), and for sides \(8\) and \(12\) the final values are \(\Lambda(60) \approx 1.1\) and \(6.0\). The weights scale like \((\sigma^2 + d^2)^{-\beta}\), so for \(\beta = 2\) a modest increase of the typical distance \(d\) reduces the coupling by a large factor, and the contraction rate \(\phi_t\) of Equation 4 drops with it. This is the mechanism behind the condition on \(\Gamma_0\) for \(\beta > 1/2\).

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Vicsek et al. (1995).
Recommended: Couzin et al. (2002); Helbing and Molnár (1995).
Further reading: Grégoire and Chaté (2004) and Chaté et al. (2008) on the order of the transition; Flocking Without Noise (optional) for a flocking model with a convergence theorem.
Many systems show coherent motion without a leader: birds, fish, bacteria, pedestrians, robots. The modelling question is how local rules can generate global order. The strategy is to propose the simplest agent-based rule that can flock. The result is the Vicsek model (Vicsek et al. 1995): \(N\) self-propelled particles that move at constant speed and copy the average heading of their neighbours, with some noise. There is no leader and no global signal, yet the whole group can move in one direction.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
From Kuramoto to flocking
The Kuramoto model synchronizes phases in time. The Vicsek model aligns headings in space. Recall the Kuramoto equations,
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \frac{K}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i),
\qquad
r e^{i\psi} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N e^{i\theta_j}.
\tag{1}\]
(Other papers write \(R\) for the order parameter. These notes write \(r\) as in Strogatz (2000), and on this page \(r\) is the interaction radius.) The Vicsek model keeps the idea of an angle that is pulled toward the mean angle of the others, but changes four things.









Kuramoto
Vicsek




Unit
phase \(\theta_i\) of an oscillator that stays in place
heading \(\theta_i\) of a particle that moves, with position \(\mathbf{x}_i\)


Time
continuous
discrete steps


What opposes order
spread of the natural frequencies \(\omega_i\)
random noise added to each heading


Who interacts
all pairs, with weight \(K/N\)
neighbours within a radius \(r\)


Order parameter
\(r = \left\lvert\frac1N\sum_j e^{i\theta_j}\right\rvert\)
\(v_a\), the same formula applied to the headings



The key difference is the last-but-one row. Neighbours are local in space, and because the particles move, the set of neighbours changes in time: the interaction network is dynamic.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
State variables and parameters
Consider \(N\) particles in a two-dimensional box of side \(L\) with periodic boundary conditions.

Position: \(\mathbf{x}_i(t) \in [0, L)^2\).
Heading angle: \(\theta_i(t) \in (-\pi, \pi]\).
Constant speed \(v_0\), so that \(\mathbf{v}_i(t) = v_0(\cos\theta_i(t), \sin\theta_i(t))\). (Other papers call the speed \(v\). Here it is \(v_0\), to keep it apart from the velocity vectors \(\mathbf{v}_i\).)

The parameters, in the notation of Vicsek et al. (1995), are the interaction radius \(r\), the noise amplitude \(\eta\) and the density \(\rho = N/L^2\).

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Rules
The neighbours of particle \(i\) at time \(t\) (Equation 2) are all particles within distance \(r\), including \(i\) itself:
\[
\mathcal{N}_i(t) = \{\, j : \lVert \mathbf{x}_j(t) - \mathbf{x}_i(t) \rVert \le r \,\}.
\tag{2}\]
Distances are measured on the periodic box, that is, to the nearest periodic copy of \(\mathbf{x}_j\). The local average direction (Equation 3) is the argument of the sum of the unit vectors,
\[
\theta_i^{\text{avg}}(t) = \operatorname{Arg}\Big(\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i(t)} e^{i\theta_j(t)}\Big)
= \operatorname{atan2}\Big(\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i(t)} \sin\theta_j(t),\ \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i(t)} \cos\theta_j(t)\Big),
\tag{3}\]
and the noise \(\xi_i(t)\) is drawn independently for every particle and every step, uniformly from \([-\eta/2, \eta/2]\). At every time step \(\Delta t\) all particles update at the same time:
\[
\theta_i(t + \Delta t) = \theta_i^{\text{avg}}(t) + \xi_i(t),
\tag{4}\]
\[
\mathbf{x}_i(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf{x}_i(t) + v_0 \Delta t \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_i(t + \Delta t) \\ \sin\theta_i(t + \Delta t) \end{bmatrix} \pmod{L}.
\tag{5}\]
In one sentence: align with the neighbours, add noise, move forward. The noise amplitude \(\eta\) runs from \(0\) (no noise) to \(2\pi\) (a random heading every step). We take \(\Delta t = 1\). Vicsek et al. (1995) used \(r = 1\), \(\Delta t = 1\) and \(v_0 = 0.03\), and measured all distances in units of \(r\). The two control parameters are the noise \(\eta\) and the density \(\rho = N/L^2\).

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Noise as temperature
Noise competes with alignment. For large \(\eta\) the headings are randomized and the motion is disordered. For small \(\eta\) alignment wins and the motion is coherent. Vicsek et al. (1995) describe the noise as a temperature-like variable: the alignment rule plays the role of the ferromagnetic interaction in a spin model, and the particles are the “spins”. Two limits of the speed are instructive (Vicsek et al. 1995):

For \(v_0 \to 0\) the particles do not move, and the model becomes an analogue of the XY model of a ferromagnet.
For \(v_0 \to \infty\) the particles are completely mixed between two updates, which corresponds to the mean-field behaviour of a ferromagnet.

The authors used \(v_0 = 0.03\), so that particles always interact with their actual neighbours and move enough to change the configuration after a few updates. In their simulations the results did not depend on \(v_0\) in the range \(0.003 < v_0 < 0.3\).
The analogy has a limit. The particles are self-driven, with constant speed, so the net momentum is not conserved in a collision. The model is a non-equilibrium system, which is what makes the transition “novel” (Vicsek et al. 1995).

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Order parameter
Collective motion is measured by the normalized average velocity
\[
v_a = \frac{1}{N v_0}\left|\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{v}_i\right| = \left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N e^{i\theta_i}\right|,
\tag{6}\]
which is the Kuramoto order parameter applied to headings. \(v_a \approx 1\) when all particles move the same way and \(v_a \approx 0\) when headings are random.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
What do simulations show?
Vary the density, the noise and the speed, and look at the particles. The chunk below defines a vectorized update with periodic distances and a function that returns the state after a number of steps from a random start. Nothing in it is specific to the figures that follow.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def vicsek_step(xy, theta, eta, L, r=1.0, v0=0.03, rng=np.random):
    """One synchronous Vicsek update with periodic (minimum-image) distances."""
    dx = xy[:, :, None] - xy[:, None, :]            # displacements, shape (2, N, N)
    dx -= L * np.round(dx / L)                      # nearest periodic copy
    nbr = (dx**2).sum(axis=0) <= r**2               # N_i(t), includes i itself
    theta_avg = np.arctan2(nbr @ np.sin(theta), nbr @ np.cos(theta))
    theta_new = theta_avg + eta * (rng.uniform(size=theta.size) - 0.5)
    xy_new = (xy + v0 * np.array([np.cos(theta_new), np.sin(theta_new)])) % L
    return xy_new, theta_new


def order_parameter(theta):
    return abs(np.exp(1j * theta).mean())


def run(N, L, eta, steps, seed):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    xy = rng.uniform(0, L, (2, N))
    theta = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, N)
    for _ in range(steps):
        xy, theta = vicsek_step(xy, theta, eta, L, rng=rng)
    return xy, theta









Figure 1: Four snapshots of the Vicsek model with \(N = 300\) particles, \(v_0 = 0.03\), \(r = 1\). Arrows show the headings, coloured by angle. (a) Random initial state. (b) Low density and low noise after 200 steps: local groups with different headings. (c) High noise after 2000 steps: no collective direction. (d) High density and low noise after 2000 steps: one global flock. The title of each panel gives \(v_a\).





Reading Figure 1:

Low density or high noise: disordered motion, panel (c). With \(N = 300\) the value of \(v_a\) is of the order of \(1/\sqrt{N} \approx 0.06\).
Moderate settings: clusters and moving groups, panel (b). In the runs behind this figure the groups are a transient. For the seed shown, \(v_a\) grows from \(0.41\) at \(t = 200\) to \(0.96\) at \(t = 1500\) and is \(1.00\) from \(t = 3000\) on, because the groups wrap around the periodic box and merge. A second seed gives the same sequence (\(0.17\), \(0.98\), \(1.00\) at the same times).
High density and low noise: global flocking, panel (d).


Spontaneous symmetry breaking
The rules are invariant under a rotation of all headings by the same angle, so the model has no preferred direction. In the ordered phase, however, the flock does move in one direction, and which one is decided by the random initial condition and the noise. Figure 2 repeats the same experiment \(300\) times (\(N = 100\), \(L = 5\), \(\eta = 0.5\), \(300\) steps) and records the direction \(\psi = \arg\big(\sum_j e^{i\theta_j}\big)\) of the flock.








Figure 2: Spontaneous symmetry breaking in the Vicsek model: 300 independent runs with \(N = 100\), \(L = 5\), \(\eta = 0.5\) after 300 steps. Left: histogram of the direction \(\psi\) of the flock, which is spread over the whole circle. Right: histogram of the order parameter \(v_a\), which is close to one in every run.





Every run is ordered (\(v_a\) between about \(0.98\) and \(0.99\)), but the directions are uniformly spread: the modulus of the average of \(e^{i\psi}\) over the \(300\) runs is \(0.04\), which is what you expect from \(300\) independent random angles (\(1/\sqrt{300} \approx 0.06\)). Order in each run, no order across runs.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Central numerical experiment
Fix the density \(\rho\) (that is, \(N\) and \(L\)) and vary the noise. The expected result is \(\langle v_a \rangle \approx 1\) for small \(\eta\), a transition region around a critical noise \(\eta_c\), and \(\langle v_a \rangle \approx 0\) for large \(\eta\), where \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) is a time average after the transient. This is the plot of Figure 2(a) of Vicsek et al. (1995), discussed next. Finite-size effects are an essential part of the discussion.

Kinetic phase transition
Vicsek et al. (1995) found that \(v_a\) falls from near \(1\) to near \(0\) as the noise increases, and rises as the density increases. Near the transition they reported the scaling laws
\[
v_a \sim \big(\eta_c(\rho) - \eta\big)^{\beta}, \qquad v_a \sim \big(\rho - \rho_c(\eta)\big)^{\delta},
\]
with \(\beta = 0.45 \pm 0.07\) and \(\delta = 0.35 \pm 0.06\). They interpreted it as a continuous transition. Later simulations of much larger systems by Grégoire and Chaté (2004) and Chaté et al. (2008) found that the onset of collective motion is discontinuous. Near the threshold, the ordered phase organizes into dense travelling bands. Small simulations like the ones in this course cannot distinguish the two scenarios.






NoteA note on the figures of the original paper



Two details of Vicsek et al. (1995) do not match each other, and it is worth knowing them when you reproduce the figures.

The density. The text writes \(\rho = N/L\), and Figure 3 and the quoted critical noise \(\eta_c(\infty) = 2.9 \pm 0.05\) refer to \(\rho = 0.4\). The system sizes in the caption of Figure 2 (\(N = 40\), \(L = 3.1\); \(N = 100\), \(L = 5\); \(N = 400\), \(L = 10\); \(N = 4000\), \(L = 31.6\); \(N = 10000\), \(L = 50\)) all correspond to \(N/L^2 \approx 4\). A check with \(N = 400\), \(L = 10\) (\(\rho = 4\)), averaged over the last 1000 of 3000 steps, gives \(v_a = 0.79\), \(0.54\) and \(0.19\) at \(\eta = 2\), \(3\) and \(4\): the curve crosses the middle of its range near \(\eta = 3\), as in Figure 2(a) and in the quoted \(\eta_c\). We therefore read the density as \(\rho = 4\) in Figures 2(a) and 3(a), and the printed \(0.4\) as a misprint. The paper itself does not settle this.
Figure 1(c). The caption describes the motion for \(L = 7\), \(\eta = 2.0\) and \(N = 300\) as random with some correlation. In our runs the same parameters give \(v_a \approx 0.8\) at all times from \(t = 50\) to \(t = 5000\), comparable to the \(v_a \approx 0.8\) of Figure 2(a) at \(\eta = 2\). Panel (c) of Figure 1 uses \(\eta = 5\) to show the disordered phase.









Figure 3: Order parameter against noise at density \(\rho = 4\) for \(N = 40\) and \(N = 100\), one realization each, generated with amlab.collective_motion.vicsek. Compare with Figure 2(a) of Vicsek et al. (1995).









NoteExercise



In Figure 3, \(v_a\) stays around \(0.1\) to \(0.2\) at the largest noise, instead of going to zero. Why? Use what you know from the Kuramoto model.








TipSolution





At high noise the headings are close to independent and uniform. Then \(v_a\) is the modulus of the mean of \(N\) random unit vectors, so \(\mathbb{E}[v_a^2] = 1/N\) (The Order Parameter). The root-mean-square value is \(1/\sqrt{N}\), that is \(0.16\) for \(N = 40\) and \(0.10\) for \(N = 100\). The mean of \(v_a\) is \(\sqrt{\pi/(4N)}\), that is \(0.14\) and \(0.09\). This is the size of the values in the figure.









NoteExercise



Compare the Vicsek model with the mean-field Kuramoto model. Name one analogue of the coupling strength \(K\) and one analogue of the frequency spread \(\sigma\).








TipSolution





Alignment plays the role of coupling. Its effective strength grows with the number of neighbours inside radius \(r\), so the density \(\rho\) (or \(r\) itself) acts like \(K\). The noise \(\eta\) plays the role of the disorder that opposes alignment, like \(\sigma\). One important difference: in the Vicsek model the neighbours change as particles move, so the interaction network is itself dynamic.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Implementation checklist
To reproduce the plot of \(\langle v_a \rangle\) against \(\eta\), follow these steps (Vicsek: the Update Rule onwards implements them one by one):

Initialize random positions in the box and random headings.
At each time step, for all particles at the same time:

find the neighbours within radius \(r\), using periodic distances;
compute the average direction with \(\operatorname{atan2}\) of the sums of sines and cosines;
add the uniform noise on \([-\eta/2, \eta/2]\);
update the positions with the new headings.

Discard the transient (burn-in), then time-average \(v_a(t)\).







WarningCommon pitfalls




Noise convention. \(\eta\) is the full width of the interval. The noise lies in \([-\eta/2, \eta/2]\), not in \([-\eta, \eta]\).
Periodic distances. With periodic boundaries, two particles on opposite edges of the box are close. The distance must be to the nearest periodic copy, as in vicsek_step above. The basic loop of Update Rule uses plain Euclidean distances, and Vectorized Update shows the correction and its effect on \(v_a\).
Averaging angles. The plain mean of \(0.1\) and \(2\pi - 0.1\) is \(\pi\). Average the unit vectors and recover the angle with \(\operatorname{atan2}\).
Transient. The ordering takes hundreds to thousands of steps, as the groups of panel (b) above show. Measure \(v_a\) only after it has stopped drifting.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Modelling choices
Every term of the model encodes a modelling choice. Asking how to change each one leads to the other models of this module.



Assumption
What it represents
Natural variation




Constant speed \(v_0\)
self-propulsion, no stopping
free speed with inertia, as in the social force model (The Social Force Model) and in Flocking Without Noise


Metric interaction radius \(r\)
who influences whom
weights that decay with distance (Cucker–Smale), or several zones (Couzin)


Alignment by averaging
imitation of the neighbours
add repulsion and attraction (The Couzin Model)


Uniform noise \(\eta\) on the heading
imperfect sensing or decision
Gaussian noise, as in the Couzin model


Periodic box
no walls, no goals
walls, obstacles and exits (Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door)



Vicsek et al. (1995) list some of these variations themselves: velocities that do not have a fixed modulus, further kinds of particle interaction, lattice versions, hard-core repulsion, and semi-periodic or open boundaries.






NoteExercise



Choose one assumption of the table and change it in vicsek_step. Predict first, then check by simulation, what happens to \(v_a\) at a fixed noise.








TipSolution





One possible choice is to let the speed depend on the number of neighbours, for example \(v = v_0 / |\mathcal{N}_i|\) (crowded particles slow down). The alignment is unchanged, so the order–disorder transition remains, but the ordered phase becomes less mobile in dense groups, and the mixing that carries information between groups slows down. This is a prediction to test, not a result: run vicsek_step with the modified speed for \(\eta = 1\) and compare the time to order and the final \(v_a\) with the original model.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Take-home messages

A minimal local rule can generate global coherent motion.
Flocking can be measured with a simple order parameter, \(v_a\).
The model has an order–disorder transition as the noise or the density varies.
Collective motion is a modelling playground: assumptions lead to mechanisms, and mechanisms to patterns.

title: The Vicsek Model
text:
Explore the model
The figure runs the update rules Equation 4 and Equation 5 in your browser with the parameters of the lab: \(r = 1\), \(v_0 = 0.03\), \(\Delta t = 1\), and by default \(N = 100\), \(L = 10\), \(\eta = 0.5\). Colour encodes the heading.


Watch \(v_a\) grow from its random initial value. Do the particles align all at once, or in local groups first?
Raise the noise to \(\eta = 5\). Which value does \(v_a\) fluctuate around? Compare with the dashed line \(1/\sqrt{N}\) and with the first exercise above.
Fix \(\eta = 2\) and \(N = 100\). Compare \(L = 25\) (\(\rho = 0.16\)) with \(L = 5\) (\(\rho = 4\)). Which density orders the flock, and why?
Set \(N = 100\) and \(L = 5\) (\(\rho = 4\)), then press Sweep η from 0 to 5. Compare your points with Figure 3.



Build this in Python. In the lab you write the code behind this figure: the update rule and animation in Vicsek Lab: Animation, and the curve of \(v_a\) against \(\eta\) in Vicsek Lab: Order Parameter.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
TipOptional extension



This page is optional. It combines the Vicsek model with the repulsion rule of the Couzin model.
In the Couzin model, avoidance takes absolute priority: if an individual senses another within its zone of repulsion, it turns away and ignores alignment and attraction (Couzin et al. 2002). You can implement a similar rule in the Vicsek model to simulate predator avoidance (Vicsek et al. 1995). The predator can be a fixed point, a random walker, or even the mouse cursor. In all cases, if a boid senses the predator within a certain radius, it will turn directly away from it.
Below is a guide on how to implement this in your Vicsek animation. You can choose to implement one or more types of predators (static, random walk, mouse-following) and compare their effects on the collective behavior of the particles.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Static Predator
The simplest case is a predator fixed at a given position. To implement this:

Set the predator’s position (e.g., xy_pred = np.array([L/2, L/2]) for the center).
In your Vicsek update function, check for boids within the predator radius and set their direction directly away from the predator (as in the Couzin rule).
In your animation, draw the predator as a red circle.

Where to add: - Set xy_pred before the animation loop in your main script. - Pass xy_pred to your Vicsek update at each frame. - Draw the predator in the plotting section (after initializing the axes).






TipWhere to include the code






Set xy_pred before the animation loop: In run_simulation, set xy_pred = np.array([box_size/2, box_size/2]) (or wherever you want the static predator) before entering the animation.
Pass xy_pred to the Vicsek update: In the update_animation function, pass xy_pred as an argument to vicsek_equations.
Draw the predator: After initializing the axes in run_simulation, add the predator circle with circle_predator = plt.Circle(xy_pred, radius_predator, color="red", fill=False) and ax_plane.add_artist(circle_predator).
Update the predator’s position in the plot (if needed): For a static predator, this is only needed once. For moving predators, update circle_predator.set_center(xy_pred) in each animation frame.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Random Walk Predator
To make the predator more dynamic, let it perform a random walk:

At each animation frame, update xy_pred by adding a small random displacement (e.g., xy_pred += np.random.normal(0, step_size, 2)).
Apply periodic boundary conditions to keep the predator in the box.
The avoidance rule for boids remains unchanged.

Where to add: - In your animation update function, before updating the boids, update xy_pred with a random walk step. - Pass the new xy_pred to the Vicsek update. - Update the predator’s position in the plot.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Mouse-Following Predator
For an interactive experience, let the predator follow the mouse:

Use a mouse event callback to update xy_pred to the mouse position whenever the mouse moves over the plot.
The avoidance rule for boids is the same: those within the predator radius turn directly away.

Where to add:

Register a mouse motion callback (e.g., with fig.canvas.mpl_connect('motion_notify_event', on_mouse_move)).
In the callback, update xy_pred to the mouse coordinates if the mouse is over the main plot.
The animation update function will use the current xy_pred as usual.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Integration
In all cases, the predator logic is integrated as follows:

The predator’s position (xy_pred) is set or updated before each Vicsek update.
The Vicsek update function receives xy_pred and applies the Couzin avoidance rule.
The predator is drawn as a red circle in the main plot.
For the mouse-following version, the mouse callback is registered during figure setup.

This modular approach allows you to experiment with different predator behaviors by simply changing how xy_pred is updated, while keeping the avoidance rule and animation structure consistent.

title: Vicsek Lab: Predator Avoidance
text:
Practice
Option B of Practice: Collective Motion asks you to implement this model in a script named vicsek_predator.py. A reference version is in amlab/collective_motion/vicsek_predator.py.

title: Kuramoto Lab: The ODE
text: This page covers the implementation and validation steps. You write the right-hand side of the Kuramoto model and check it in two regimes where you know the answer.

title: Kuramoto Lab: The ODE
text:
Implementation: define the ODE
Choose between the pairwise form of the Kuramoto model and the mean-field form. They are mathematically identical (The Order Parameter). The mean field approximation is often more efficient for large populations, as it avoids computing pairwise interactions.

TipSolution





The function below uses the mean-field form, which is cheaper than computing pairwise interactions. It computes the order parameter at each call and uses it to calculate the derivatives.
def kuramoto_ode(t, theta, omega, coupling_strength=1.0):
    # Wrapping is optional: sin and exp are 2 pi-periodic
    theta = np.mod(theta, 2 * np.pi)
    order_param = np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta))
    r = np.abs(order_param)
    phi = np.angle(order_param)
    dtheta_dt = omega + coupling_strength * r * np.sin(phi - theta)
    return dtheta_dt

title: The Kuramoto Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2000), Sections 1 to 4.
Recommended: Strogatz et al. (2005).
The Kuramoto model describes a large population of coupled oscillators with different natural frequencies. Each oscillator \(i\) has a phase \(\theta_i\) and a natural frequency \(\omega_i\) (Kuramoto 1975, 2003; Strogatz 2000). It is the standard example of how collective synchronization emerges from simple interactions among oscillators that are not identical. Physicists, biologists and engineers use it to study circadian rhythms, synchronized neurons and the stability of power grids (Strogatz 2000).

title: The Kuramoto Model
text:
From limit cycles to phases
For any system of weakly coupled, nearly identical limit-cycle oscillators, the long-term dynamics reduce to phase equations of the form
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \sum_{j=1}^N \Gamma_{ij} \left( \theta_j - \theta_i \right),\quad i = 1, \dots, N,
\tag{1}\]
where \(\Gamma_{ij}\) is the coupling function that describes how oscillator \(j\) influences oscillator \(i\) through their phase difference (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000). This reduction keeps the timing of each oscillator and discards its amplitude. Winfree (1967) first proposed studying populations in this way.

title: The Kuramoto Model
text:
Kuramoto’s choice
Kuramoto took the simplest case: equally weighted, all-to-all, purely sinusoidal coupling,
\[
\Gamma_{ij}(\theta) = \frac{K}{N} \sin \theta.
\tag{2}\]
Substituting into Equation 1 gives the Kuramoto model:
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \frac{K}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i), \quad i = 1, \dots, N.
\tag{3}\]

\(K \ge 0\) is the coupling strength.
The factor \(1/N\) keeps the total input to each oscillator finite as \(N\) grows.
The natural frequencies \(\omega_i\) are drawn from a density \(g(\omega)\) that is unimodal and symmetric about its mean \(\Omega\) (Strogatz 2000).

Two oscillators with \(\theta_j\) slightly ahead of \(\theta_i\) give \(\sin(\theta_j - \theta_i) > 0\), so \(i\) speeds up toward \(j\). The coupling always pulls phases together. What competes against it is the spread of natural frequencies.

title: The Kuramoto Model
text:
Rotating frame
Move to a frame that rotates at the mean frequency, \(\theta_i \to \theta_i + \Omega t\). The coupling depends only on phase differences, so Equation 3 keeps its form and the new frequencies have mean zero. From now on you can assume \(g(\omega) = g(-\omega)\) (Strogatz 2000).

title: The Kuramoto Model
section: Frequency densities used in this module
text:
Frequency densities used in this module








Density
\(g(\omega)\)
\(g(0)\)




Normal, standard deviation \(\sigma\)
\(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\, e^{-\omega^2/(2\sigma^2)}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\)


Lorentzian (Cauchy), scale \(\gamma\)
\(\dfrac{\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2 + \omega^2)}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{\pi\gamma}\)



The Lorentzian case gives closed-form results (Critical Coupling). The normal case is the default in the lab. The initial phases are drawn uniformly on \([0, 2\pi)\) unless stated otherwise.






NoteExercise



Show that Equation 3 with \(N = 2\) reduces to the firefly equation of Phase Locking for the phase difference \(\phi = \theta_2 - \theta_1\). What is the locking condition?








TipSolution





With \(N = 2\), \(\dot\theta_1 = \omega_1 + \tfrac{K}{2}\sin(\theta_2 - \theta_1)\) and \(\dot\theta_2 = \omega_2 + \tfrac{K}{2}\sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\). Subtracting,
\[
\dot\phi = (\omega_2 - \omega_1) - K\sin\phi.
\]
This is the phase-difference equation of Phase Locking with detuning \(\omega_2 - \omega_1\) and strength \(K\). The two oscillators lock when \(|\omega_2 - \omega_1| \le K\).

title: The Confusion Effect: Predator and Prey
text:
TipOptional extension



This page extends the Couzin model. It adds a hunting predator to the school you already know and asks one question: does blending in really protect you?
In open water prey have no shelter. A fish cannot hide, but it can be one of hundreds of look-alikes. A predator that has to track one individual while other bodies keep crossing its line of sight loses the target again and again. This is the confusion effect (Landeau and Terborgh 1986; Krause and Ruxton 2002). The same logic explains why the animal that looks different (marked, limping, the wrong size) is the one that gets taken: the oddity effect (Landeau and Terborgh 1986).
The Couzin model has no predator. Predator Avoidance adds one, but as a point that scares particles away. Here the predator is a hunter with a limited ability to track, and the school is the same Couzin school as before.

title: The Confusion Effect: Predator and Prey
text:
Three effects, one hunt








Effect
What the predator experiences
How the model implements it




Confusion
Look-alikes cross the line of sight and tracking resets
A new prey inside the line of sight breaks the lock. Three broken locks waste the pass


Confused strike
A strike at one fish among many often misses
The strike succeeds with probability \(P = 1/(1 + c\,\bar n)\)


Oddity
A visually different fish keeps the lock
An odd prey is targeted first, its lock cannot be broken, and it is captured with certainty



The ideas come from the literature on predator confusion: from experiments with live predators (Ioannou et al. 2012), and from simulations in which confusion alone is enough for swarming to evolve (Olson et al. 2013). The lock and strike rules below are teaching simplifications in the same spirit. They are not a fit to any data set.

title: The Confusion Effect: Predator and Prey
section: From the Couzin model to a hunt
text:
From the Couzin model to a hunt
The school. Prey follow exactly the rules of the Couzin model: repulsion first, then orientation and attraction, a blind sector behind, limited turning, Gaussian noise. The only dial we turn is cohesion, the width of the zone of attraction, \(\Delta r_a = r_a - r_o\). We add one reflex: a prey within 4 body lengths of the predator turns directly away from it (at \(120^\circ\)/s, and \(1.15\times\) faster).
The predator. It moves faster than the prey (\(5\) against \(3\) body lengths per second), has a \(140^\circ\) frontal field of view, a range of \(22\) body lengths and a limited turning rate. It is always in one of four states:

Search. Turn toward the nearest prey. As soon as prey are inside the field of view, pick a target: an odd prey if one is visible, otherwise the most isolated visible prey.
Lock. Chase the target. At every step, count the prey that lie within \(\pm 8^\circ\) of the target’s bearing and up to 8 body lengths behind it. These are the look-alikes in the line of sight. If a new one has entered the window, the lock breaks.
Lost. Continue straight for 0.3 s, then look for a target again. After three broken locks the pass is wasted.
Recover. After a capture, a miss or a wasted pass: go straight for 3 s, then search again.

If the predator gets within 0.9 body lengths of its target, it strikes. Let \(\bar n\) be the mean number of look-alikes in the line of sight during the approach:
\[
P(\text{capture}) = \frac{1}{1 + c\,\bar n}.
\tag{1}\]
With \(c = 1\) one look-alike halves the chance of a capture, two reduce it to one third. With \(c = 0\) the strike never misses, and only the broken locks protect the school. An odd prey skips both rules: no lock breaks and \(P = 1\).

Explore the hunt

While it is locked, a dashed line and a white ring mark the target. A white ring that expands from the target is a broken lock. A green arrow with a white outline is an odd prey.


Press Dispersed (\(\Delta r_a = 0\)) and watch about 20 attacks. Then press Bait ball (\(\Delta r_a = 10\)) and do the same. Which one has the higher capture probability, and why do the locks break more often in the second case?
In the bait ball, set the confusion \(c\) to 0 and wait for 20 attacks. What still protects the school?

text:
How the code extends couzin.py
The new module couzin_predator.py reuses initialize_particles_couzin and checks itself against couzin_equations. Only one thing changes in the school: the loop over individuals becomes array operations, so that a full hunt runs in a second.
dx = x[None, :] - x[:, None]        # dx[i, j] = x_j - x_i
dy = y[None, :] - y[:, None]
d = np.hypot(dx, dy)
visible = (d <= radius_attraction) & (np.abs(wrap_pi(bearing - theta[:, None])) <= half_fov)
rep = visible & (d < radius_repulsion)                         # zone of repulsion
ori = visible & (d >= radius_repulsion) & (d < radius_alignment)   # zone of orientation
att = visible & (d >= radius_alignment) & (d < radius_attraction)  # zone of attraction
With the noise switched off the two versions must agree:
from amlab.collective_motion.couzin_predator import check_against_original
print(check_against_original())   # about 1e-13: they are the same model
The predator is one class, ConfusionSim, with the four states above. The heart of the lock state is a few lines:
# Look-alikes in the line of sight. A *new* one crossing it resets the lock.
cross = (np.abs(wrap_pi(bearing - bearing[t])) < np.deg2rad(p.lock_tol_deg)) \
        & (dist < dist[t] + p.clutter_depth)
cross[t] = False
new = cross & ~self._prev_cross
if new.any():
    self.breaks += 1            # lock broken
To run your own experiment:

res = sweep("d_attract", [0, 4, 8, 12], base=HuntParams(), n_seeds=8, steps=3000)
print(res["values"], res["capture_prob"])
sweep runs n_seeds independent hunts for every value and returns the captures per attack, pooled over the runs. ConfusionSim has stats, events and school_metrics() if you want to measure anything else.

title: The Confusion Effect: Predator and Prey
section: Experiment: how much does blending in help?
text:
Experiment: how much does blending in help?
run_experiments.py confusion reproduces the figure below in about two minutes. Each point pools 8 hunts of 300 s (\(\approx\) 250 to 550 attacks). The shaded band is a 95% interval for the proportion.






Figure 1: Capture probability per attack against cohesion, number of odd prey and school size.



What the figure shows:

Cohesion. The capture probability falls from about 0.39 for a school with no attraction to about 0.06 for a tight ball: a factor of 6 to 7. The curve is not monotonic for small \(\Delta r_a\). There the school breaks into subgroups and its density depends on the run.
Oddity. One odd prey in a tight school raises the capture probability from 0.07 to 0.25, three of them to 0.38, although all other prey are unchanged.
School size. A school of 10 is much more vulnerable than one of 40 or more, but beyond a few dozen the gain saturates. Diminishing returns with group size are a familiar pattern in the literature on group living (Krause and Ruxton 2002).







NoteExercise 1: confusion without a confused strike



Set \(c = 0\) in the bait ball (\(\Delta r_a = 10\)). Is the school still safer than a dispersed one?








TipSolution





Yes. With \(c = 0\) every strike that reaches its target is a capture, so the strike no longer helps the school. But a tight school still breaks the lock often, and after three broken locks the pass is wasted. Run sweep("d_attract", [0, 10], base=HuntParams(confusion=0.0)) and compare. The two rules are separate mechanisms, and you can switch one of them off at a time.









NoteExercise 2: risk per fish



The capture probability is per attack. Suppose a predator attacks a school once a minute, whatever its size. For a school of \(N\) prey, what is the risk for one fish per minute, if the predator picks its target uniformly at random and the capture probability is \(P(N)\)?








TipSolution





The risk per fish is \(P(N)/N\). Both factors fall as the school grows: the predator is more confused and the attack is shared by more fish. So the individual benefit of joining a group is larger than the fall of \(P\) alone suggests. Note that our predator does not pick uniformly: it prefers the most isolated fish, so the fish at the edge carries more of the risk than \(P/N\). You can measure this by recording which index is captured and its distance to the centroid.









NoteExercise 3: the odd prey



Predict, then test: with \(n_\text{odd}\) odd prey in a bait ball, what fraction of the attacks should target an odd prey, if the predator always chooses an odd prey when it sees one? Why does the capture probability not reach 1?








TipSolution





The predator targets an odd prey only when one is visible, which means inside its \(22\)-body-length range and its \(140^\circ\) field of view. If it does not see one, it falls back on the most isolated prey, and the confusion rules apply. So the share of “odd attacks” is the share of attacks in which an odd prey is visible, and it grows with \(n_\text{odd}\). Odd attacks succeed with certainty, the others with the low probability of the bait ball. The result is a mixture, which is why the curve in Figure 1 rises but stays below 1.




Build this in Python. Option C of Practice: Collective Motion asks you to add a predator to your own Couzin code and measure the capture probability against cohesion.

title: The Confusion Effect: Predator and Prey
section: What this model does not do
text:
What this model does not do

It is a teaching model. The lock window, the strike rule and the parameters are chosen so that the mechanisms are visible. They are not fitted to data, and the numbers in Figure 1 should not be read as predictions for real fish.
There is one predator and no learning. Real predators learn to target the edge or to herd the school. A prey can also respond in ways we do not model (the fountain or flash expansion).
Confusion in real animals comes from limits of vision and attention. We replace them by a geometric rule: a look-alike in a window around the target.
Isolation is not the only cue. In the model the predator prefers isolated and odd prey, which is why the school’s edge is the dangerous place.
The idea for this page came from a short video simulation. The mechanisms of the video (a lock that resets, three tries) are one way to implement the confusion effect. They are not a published model, so we cite the research papers above instead.

title: The Confusion Effect: Predator and Prey
text:
Going further

From agents to equations. Count the captures per unit time against the prey density, by changing \(N\) and the box. The curve is a functional response, and you can compare it to the Holling types in the predator-prey equations. How does confusion change its shape? This is also the question that Olson et al. (2013) ask for their model.
Evolution of cohesion. Let every prey have its own \(\Delta r_a\), replace the captured prey by a mutated copy of a survivor, and see whether cohesion evolves upward. This is close to the experiment of Ioannou et al. (2012).
A smarter predator. Make it aim at the edge, or at the centroid. Does the capture probability change?

title: Vicsek Lab: Validation
text:
Before animating the Vicsek model, validate your implementation in limits where you know the answer (Vicsek et al. 1995). Here you use static plots to see how the interaction radius \(r\) affects alignment. With \(r = 0\) each particle only sees itself, so the headings perform independent random walks. With \(r = L\) every particle sees every other (up to the edges, see the limitation in Vectorized Update), so the model becomes a mean-field alignment.
You will run the Vicsek model for a few time steps and visualize the headings of all particles for different values of \(r\). This will help you see the transition from random motion to local and global alignment as the interaction radius increases.






NoteExercise



Run the code below with three interaction radii: \(r = 0\), \(r = L / 10\), and \(r = L\), where \(L\) is the box size. What do you observe? How does the interaction radius affect the alignment of the particles?
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Initialize parameters
num_particles = 100
box_size = 10 # L
interaction_radius = 1.0 # r
noise_strength = 0.1 # eta
v0 = 0.03 # speed of particles

# Initialize particle positions and headings
xy, theta = initialize_particles(num_particles, box_size)

# Update positions and headings for a few time steps
for t in range(10):
    xy, theta = vicsek_equations(
    xy=xy,
    theta=theta,
    noise=noise_strength,
    box_size=box_size,
    radius_interaction=interaction_radius,
    v0=v0,
    )

# Plot the headings of the particles
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))
plt.quiver(
    xy[0],
    xy[1],
    np.cos(theta),
    np.sin(theta),
    angles='xy',
    scale_units='xy',
    scale=2,  # bigger scale means smaller arrows
)
# Limit the plot to the box size
plt.xlim(0, box_size)
plt.ylim(0, box_size)
plt.title('Particle headings after 10 time steps')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.grid()
plt.show()








TipSolution





Radius \(r = 0\). For \(r = 0\), there is no interaction between particles, so they will move in random directions based on their initial headings and noise. The plot will show a random distribution of arrows with no clear alignment.





Particle headings for \(r = 0\)




Radius \(r = L / 10\). For \(r = L / 10\), particles will interact with others within a radius of one-tenth of the box size. This means that each particle will have a limited chance to align with nearby particles, leading to small local clusters of aligned particles. The plot will show groups of arrows pointing in similar directions, indicating partial alignment.





Particle headings for \(r = L / 10\)




Radius \(r = L\). For \(r = L\), particles will interact with all other particles in the box. This means that each particle will tend to align with the average direction of all particles, leading to global alignment. The plot will show arrows mostly pointing in the same direction, indicating strong alignment.





Particle headings for \(r = L\)

        pass

For \(r = L\) (and \(L = 10\)) almost every pair is within the radius, so after a few steps all headings are close to the common mean and \(v_a\) is close to \(1\), reduced slightly by the noise. For \(r = 0\) the headings do not interact and \(v_a\) stays of order \(1/\sqrt{N} = 0.1\) at all times. If your code gives something else, check the neighbor search and the angle average.

title: Vicsek Lab: Update Rule
text:
All boids have the same speed module \(v_0\), but their headings change based on neighbors. Every time step \(\Delta t\), each boid averages the headings of neighbors within radius \(r\) and adds noise \(\eta\). Then it moves in the new heading direction. This happens simultaneously to all boids. Follow the equations in Vicsek et al. (1995) to implement the update step. A summary follows.
The positions of the \(i\)th particle is updated as:
\[
\mathbf{x}_i(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf{x}_i(t) + v_0 \Delta t \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta_i(t + \Delta t)) \\ \sin(\theta_i(t + \Delta t)) \end{bmatrix}.
\tag{1}\]
where \(v_0\) is the speed. Vicsek et al. (1995) used \(v_0 = 0.03\).
It is important to remember that particles stay within the box. You apply periodic boundary conditions, meaning that a particle that goes out of the box on one side reappears on the opposite side. You can implement this with the modulo operator, if you assume that the positions are in the range \([0, L]\):
\[
\mathbf{x}_i(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf{x}_i(t + \Delta t) \mod L,
\tag{2}\]
To use Equation 1 you first need the new heading \(\theta_i(t + \Delta t)\):
\[
\theta_i(t + \Delta t) = \theta_i^{\text{avg}}(t) + \xi_i(t),
\qquad
\theta_i^{\text{avg}}(t) = \operatorname{atan2}\Big(\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i}\sin\theta_j(t),\ \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i}\cos\theta_j(t)\Big),
\tag{3}\]
where \(\mathcal{N}_i\) is the set of neighbors within radius \(r\) of particle \(i\), including \(i\) itself, and \(\xi_i(t)\) is a random variable uniformly distributed in \([-\eta/2, \eta/2]\), drawn independently for every particle and every step, as in The Vicsek Model. In code, noise / 2 * np.random.uniform(-1, 1) is such a variable. Vicsek et al. (1995) used \(r = 1\) and noise values \(\eta\) between \(0\) and \(5\) in their Figure 2.


Outline the steps for one time step before you code:

For each particle \(i\), find its neighbors within radius \(r\).
Compute the average heading of these neighbors.
Add noise to the average heading to get the new heading \(\theta_i(t + \Delta t)\).
Update the position of each particle based on its new heading.
Apply periodic boundary conditions to ensure particles stay within the box.

For the first step you compare every particle with every other particle. You can use nested loops or a distance matrix. Start with the loop version. Once you know the neighbors, average their headings as unit vectors, then add noise following Equation 3.






WarningDo not average angles directly



The plain mean of \(0.1\) and \(2\pi - 0.1\) is \(\pi\), the opposite direction. Average \(\cos\theta_j\) and \(\sin\theta_j\) separately and recover the angle with np.arctan2.








WarningPeriodic distances



The loops below measure the plain Euclidean distance. With periodic boundaries, two particles near opposite edges of the box are close to each other, but this code does not see them as neighbors. The effect is small when \(r \ll L\) and clearly visible in the small boxes of this lab. The correction, the minimum-image distance, is in Vectorized Update.

def vicsek_equations(xy, theta, dt=1.0, noise=0.1, box_size=10, radius_interaction=1, v0=0.03):
    xy_new = xy.copy()
    theta_new = theta.copy()
    num_boids = len(theta)
    for i in range(num_boids):
        ls_theta_neighbors = []
        for j in range(num_boids):
            dist = np.linalg.norm(xy[:, i] - xy[:, j])
            if dist <= radius_interaction:
                ls_theta_neighbors.append(theta[j])
        ls_theta_neighbors = np.array(ls_theta_neighbors)
        theta_new[i] = np.arctan2(
            np.mean(np.sin(ls_theta_neighbors)), np.mean(np.cos(ls_theta_neighbors))
        )
        theta_new[i] += noise / 2 * np.random.uniform(-1, 1)

        v = v0 * np.array([np.cos(theta_new[i]), np.sin(theta_new[i])])
        xy_new[:, i] = xy_new[:, i] + dt * v

    xy_new = np.mod(xy_new, box_size)
    return xy_new, theta_new
