title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
This is a graded assignment. It is worth 10% of your final grade.
Your goal is to review the theory of synchronization of weakly coupled oscillators, study the Kuramoto model numerically, and then simulate the Millennium Bridge crowd-bridge synchrony model (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000; Pikovsky et al. 2001; Strogatz et al. 2005; Eckhardt et al. 2007). The Kuramoto lab pages (Kuramoto Model onwards) give you the building blocks. The theory is in Critical Coupling and The Millennium Bridge.

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
Kuramoto Model
Start from the basic Kuramoto model with all-to-all symmetric coupling:
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \frac{K}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j-\theta_i),
\qquad i=1,\dots,N.
\tag{1}\]
Here \(\theta_i \in [0,2\pi)\) is the phase of oscillator \(i\), \(K>0\) is the coupling constant, and the natural frequencies \(\omega_i\) are sampled from a unimodal symmetric distribution \(g(\omega)\).

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
Numerical Integration
Write a Python script that integrates the Kuramoto equations numerically. Start with the following values:

\(N=100\) oscillators.
\(g(\omega)\) equal to the standard normal distribution.
\(K=7\).

For the initial condition, write a function that assigns phases either randomly over the whole circle, the disperse case, or over a small arc, the concentrated case. For the numerical integration, you may write your own scheme, for instance explicit Euler, or use scipy.integrate. In either case, produce the following outputs:

A graph of \(r(t)\), the order parameter, versus time. In the subcritical case \(K<K_c\), the asymptotic value \(r_\infty\) should be approximately zero up to fluctuations, while for \(K>K_c\) you should observe \(r_\infty \in (0,1)\) for large \(t\). The amplitude of the fluctuations should decrease as \(N\) grows, typically like \(\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})\).
An animation of the oscillators moving on the unit circle. You may also plot the centroid \(re^{i\psi}\).

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
Critical Coupling
Review Critical Coupling and Sections 3 and 4 of Strogatz (2000) until you are comfortable with the derivation of the critical coupling \(K_c\). For more detail, see Pikovsky et al. (2001). Then compare the theoretical prediction with the value obtained numerically.

Sample 20 values of \(K\) between \(K_{\min}\) and \(K_{\max}\) such that \(K_{\min}<K_c<K_{\max}\). A reasonable choice is \(K_{\min}=K_c/3\) and \(K_{\max}=3K_c\).
For each sampled value of \(K\), estimate \(r_\infty\) by making sure that \(r(t)\) has reached its saturation regime, then average over a tail window to reduce fluctuations. A reasonable choice is to average over the last 300 time steps. Keep both the mean and standard deviation.
Plot \(r_\infty(K)\) with error bars and identify the approximate value of \(K_c\), comparing it with the theoretical prediction.
Validate your results with different choices of \(g(\omega)\), for instance normal distributions with different variance, and check whether the theoretical prediction for \(K_c\) remains consistent.
Plot the smooth theoretical curve defined implicitly by the self-consistency equation (4.5) of Strogatz (2000) together with your numerical points:

\[
1 = K\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^2\theta\, g\big(Kr\sin\theta\big)\,d\theta.
\tag{2}\]

If you are not able to solve the implicit equation numerically for a general distribution \(g(\omega)\), include at least the Cauchy case, where the formula is explicit:

\[
g(\omega) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+\omega^2)},
\qquad
r_\infty(K) = \sqrt{1-\frac{K_c}{K}}.
\tag{3}\]
Check that your numerical points approach the theoretical curve more closely as \(N\) becomes large.

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
Millennium Bridge Crowd Synchrony
Read The Millennium Bridge first. The model couples one lateral bridge mode to \(N\) pedestrian phase oscillators (Strogatz et al. 2005):
\[
M\ddot X + B\dot X + KX = G\sum_{i=1}^N \sin\Theta_i,
\qquad
\dot\Theta_i = \Omega_i + C\,A\sin\big(\Psi-\Theta_i+\alpha\big),
\tag{4}\]
with \(\Omega_0 = \sqrt{K/M}\) and the bridge amplitude and phase given by
\[
A = \sqrt{X^2 + \big(\dot X/\Omega_0\big)^2},
\qquad
\Psi = \operatorname{atan2}\big(X,\ \dot X/\Omega_0\big).
\tag{5}\]
Here \(K\) is the bridge stiffness, not the Kuramoto coupling. Crowd synchrony is measured with \(R e^{i\Phi} = N^{-1}\sum_j e^{i\Theta_j}\).
For \(\alpha = \pi/2\) and a frequency density \(P(\Omega)\) symmetric about \(\Omega_0\), the critical crowd size is
\[
N_c = \frac{2B\,\Omega_0}{\pi\,G\,C\,P(\Omega_0)}.
\tag{6}\]
If \(P\) is normal with mean \(\Omega_0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), then \(P(\Omega_0) = 1/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma)\).

title: Kuramoto Assignment (Graded)
text:
Required Numerical Experiment
Implement a numerical solver for the coupled bridge-pedestrian system. You may use scipy.integrate.solve_ivp, which is recommended here, or another standard ODE solver such as RK4. Use random initial phases \(\Theta_i(0) \sim \mathrm{Unif}[0,2\pi)\) and small initial bridge motion, for instance \(X(0) \approx 0\) and \(\dot X(0) \approx 0\).
Perform the following controlled crowd-ramp experiment:

Start with \(N=N_0\) pedestrians. Every \(\Delta T\) seconds, increase the crowd size by \(\Delta N\), adding new pedestrians with fresh initial phases and natural frequencies, until reaching \(N_{\max}\).
Compute the theoretical value of \(N_c\) using your chosen parameters and frequency distribution.
Define the first time at which the crowd reaches the theoretical threshold,

\[
t_c = \inf\{t : N(t) \ge N_c\}.
\tag{7}\]

Produce three stacked plots, and in each one draw a vertical dashed line at \(t=t_c\) labeled “\(N=N_c\)”:

\(N(t)\) versus \(t\), the crowd-size staircase.
\(A(t)\) versus \(t\), the bridge wobble amplitude.
\(R(t)\) versus \(t\), the degree of synchronization.

Briefly describe what happens before and after \(t_c\), and comment on whether the observed onset of wobbling and synchrony is close to the theoretical prediction.

Reference code is available in amlab/odes_coupled/bridge.py. It uses a different, nondimensional formulation of the bridge-pedestrian coupling, so its parameters do not map one to one onto the equations above. Use it for ideas, but do not copy it.

text: In this lab you implement the Vicsek model (Vicsek et al. 1995), validate it, and animate it. The rules are in The Vicsek Model.

title: Vicsek Lab: Initialization
text:
Why not solve_ivp?
In Module 1 you used ODE solvers like scipy.integrate.solve_ivp() for continuous-time systems. The Vicsek model is a discrete-time, agent-based model. At each step all particles update their heading and position from their neighbours and some noise. There is no differential equation to integrate, so you implement it with a loop over time steps.

title: Vicsek Lab: Initialization
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



Before you code, write down your expectations.

With noise \(\eta = 0\) and a large interaction radius, what is the order parameter after many steps?
With \(\eta = 2\pi\), what is it for \(N = 100\)?
At fixed noise, does increasing the density help or hurt alignment?









TipSolution





With no noise and every particle seeing every other, all headings converge to one direction and \(v_a \to 1\). With \(\eta = 2\pi\) every heading is random at every step, so \(v_a\) is of order \(1/\sqrt{N} = 0.1\). Higher density means more neighbours inside the radius, which averages out the noise and helps alignment (Vicsek et al. 1995).

Draw Particles
To show the movement of the particles, draw them to look like “tadpoles”: a big head with a smaller tail. Translating this to code, you will - create xy_tail with shape (2, N, TAIL_LEN), and - create the two Line2D artists with ax_plane.plot(...).
def init_particles_plot(ax_plane: Axes, xy: np.ndarray, box_size: float, tail_len: int):
    # build a tail tensor by repeating xy across a third axis
    xy_tail = np.repeat(xy[:, :, np.newaxis], tail_len, axis=2)

    (plt_particles,) = ax_plane.plot(
        xy_tail[0].flatten(), xy_tail[1].flatten(),
        linestyle="", marker=".", markersize=2, color="grey"
    )

    # current positions (bigger black circles)

        xy[0], xy[1],
        linestyle="", marker="o", markersize=3, color="black"
    )

    # set plot limits
    ax_plane.set_xlim(0, box_size)
    ax_plane.set_ylim(0, box_size)
    ax_plane.set_aspect("equal")

    return xy_tail, plt_particles, plt_current

title: Vicsek Lab: Order Parameter
text:
The order parameter \(v_a\) of The Vicsek Model is defined as the magnitude of the average velocity vector normalized by the speed:
\[
v_a(t) = \frac{1}{N v_0} \left|\sum_{i=1}^N v_0 \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta_i(t)) \\ \sin(\theta_i(t)) \end{bmatrix}\right| = \frac{1}{N} \left|\sum_{i=1}^N \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta_i(t)) \\ \sin(\theta_i(t)) \end{bmatrix}\right|.
\tag{1}\]
The figures below are produced by amlab, whose axis labels write the order parameter as \(\varphi\). It is the same quantity \(v_a\).
You can compute this at each time step to see how the system evolves. In the disordered phase, \(v_a \approx 0\) because the headings are random and cancel out. In the ordered phase, \(v_a \approx 1\) because all particles align in the same direction.






NoteExercise

    return phi








TipSolution





The speed \(v_0\) cancels, so np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * theta))) gives the same value.
def vicsek_order_parameter(theta: np.ndarray, v0: float = 0.03) -> float:
    """
    Compute the normalized order parameter (mean velocity divided by v0), as in Vicsek et al. (1995).
    """
    vx = v0 * np.cos(theta)
    vy = v0 * np.sin(theta)
    avg_vx = np.mean(vx)
    avg_vy = np.mean(vy)
    return float(np.sqrt(avg_vx**2 + avg_vy**2) / v0)

text:
Experiment: reproduce Figure 2
Try to reproduce Figure 2 of the original paper (Vicsek et al. 1995), which shows the order parameter \(v_a\) as a function of noise \(\eta\) and of the density \(\rho = N / L^2\). Run simulations for different values of \(N\), \(L\), and \(\eta\), compute the order parameter at each time step, and then average it over time to get a single value for each combination of parameters.
For reference, here are the parameters used in the original paper for Figure 2(a):

Number of particles \(N\): from 40 up to 10000. Start with the two smallest values, 40 and 100, and try larger ones only if you have time.
Density \(\rho\): constant at 4.0
Box size L: computed from density and number of particles, so \(L = \sqrt{N / \rho}\).

title: Vicsek Lab: Order Parameter
text:
Interpretation

Both figures show the two routes to order in Vicsek et al. (1995): less noise, or more density.
The curves for \(N = 40\) and \(N = 100\) are close. With systems this small you cannot tell whether the transition is continuous or discontinuous; that question needed much larger simulations (Grégoire and Chaté 2004; Chaté et al. 2008).

title: Kuramoto Lab: Bifurcation Diagram
text: This page is the experiment step. You scan the coupling \(K\), measure the steady-state coherence \(r_\infty\) and compare it with theory. As \(K\) increases, the system moves from incoherence (\(r \approx 0\)) to partial synchrony (\(r > 0\)) (Kuramoto 2003; Strogatz 2000).

title: Kuramoto Lab: Bifurcation Diagram
text:
Theory to compare with
For any symmetric unimodal frequency density \(g(\omega)\), the critical coupling is (Critical Coupling)
\[
K_c = \frac{2}{\pi g(0)}.
\tag{1}\]
For a Cauchy (Lorentzian) distribution with scale parameter \(\gamma\),
\[
g(\omega)=\frac{1}{\pi} \frac{\gamma}{\omega^2+\gamma^2},
\tag{2}\]
so \(g(0)=1/(\pi\gamma)\) and the critical coupling simplifies to
\[
K_c = 2\gamma.
\tag{3}\]
In this case the order parameter has a closed form:
\[
r_\infty(K)=
\begin{cases}
0, & K \le K_c, \\
\sqrt{1-\frac{K_c}{K}}, & K > K_c.
\end{cases}
\tag{4}\]
Warning: Equation 4 holds only for the Cauchy distribution.








Figure 1: Kuramoto diagram: theoretical curve from Equation 4 and empirical points (drawn from a normal distribution). Why is there a mismatch?





For any other smooth symmetric density with \(g''(0) < 0\), the theoretical order parameter near onset is (Strogatz 2000)
\[
r \approx \sqrt{\frac{16}{\pi K_c^3}} \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{-g''(0)}}
\tag{5}\]
where \(\mu\) measures the distance from the critical point (a dimensionless reduced coupling) and \(g''(0)\) is the second derivative of the frequency distribution at \(0\).
\[
\mu = \frac{K - K_c}{K_c}
\tag{6}\]
This formula comes from expanding the self-consistency equation for small \(r\). It captures the square-root growth of \(r\) just above \(K_c\) and fails far from it.
For a normal distribution with standard deviation \(\sigma\):
\[
g(\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} \exp\left(-\frac{\omega^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
\tag{7}\]
\[
g''(\omega) = \left( \frac{\omega^2}{\sigma^4} - \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \right) g(\omega)
\tag{8}\]

Your plot should look like Figure 1.









NoteExercise



Do your two curves match? Figure 1 shows a mismatch. Explain why, and fix it.








TipSolution





The mismatch occurs because the closed-form theoretical curve Equation 4 is derived for a Cauchy frequency distribution, while the empirical data in Figure 1 is generated from a normal distribution.
To fix this you have two consistent options:

Keep the normal distribution and use a matching theoretical prediction (typically only an approximation near onset, such as Equation 5).
Keep the closed-form curve Equation 4 and generate the empirical data using a Cauchy distribution.









Figure 2: Kuramoto diagram: empirical points (normal frequencies) and a matching theoretical prediction (see Equation 5 for the near-onset scaling).





Alternatively, fix the mismatch by changing the empirical distribution to a Cauchy distribution, which matches the closed-form curve Equation 4.








Figure 3: Kuramoto diagram: theoretical curve Equation 4 and empirical points (Cauchy frequencies).

title: Module 2: Synchronization and Collective Behaviour
text:
This module studies how order appears in large groups of interacting units. You start with one oscillator on the circle and one oscillator driven by a rhythm, move to the Kuramoto model of many coupled oscillators and the Millennium Bridge, and end with models of flocks, schools and crowds. The main tools are phase equations, order parameters and agent-based simulation (Strogatz 2024; Strogatz 2000; Vicsek et al. 1995; Couzin et al. 2002).

Session Structure
Session 10: Synchronization: from one oscillator to many
Synchronization in Nature Flows on the Circle Phase Locking
Session 11: The Kuramoto model
The Kuramoto Model The Order Parameter Critical Coupling The Millennium Bridge
Session 12: Laboratory: Kuramoto and the Millennium Bridge
Initialization The ODE Pairwise vs Mean Field (optional) Animation Bifurcation Diagram Locating the Threshold Full Simulation (optional) Finite-Size Effects Kuramoto Assignment (graded)
Session 13: Modelling collective behaviour: Vicsek and Couzin
The Vicsek Model The Couzin Model The Social Force Model Flocking Without Noise: Cucker–Smale (optional)
Session 14: Laboratory: collective motion
Initialization Update Rule Vectorized Update (optional) Order Parameter Validation Animation Animation Loop Interactive Animation (optional) Sliders (optional) Callbacks and Full Script (optional) Predator Avoidance (optional) The Confusion Effect (optional) Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door (optional) Practice: Collective Motion


Learning Goals
By the end of this module you should be able to:

Describe an oscillator by its phase and analyse flows on the circle, including the saddle-node bifurcation of the nonuniform oscillator.
Derive the locking range of an oscillator driven by a periodic stimulus.
Write the Kuramoto model, rewrite it in mean-field form, and state the critical coupling \(K_c = 2/(\pi g(0))\).
Simulate the Kuramoto model, measure \(r_\infty(K)\), and separate real synchronization from finite-size fluctuations.
Explain the Millennium Bridge instability as a feedback loop between crowd synchrony and bridge motion, and compute the critical crowd size.
Implement the Vicsek model, with periodic distances and a correct average of angles, and explain the roles of noise and density in the transition to collective motion.
Explain why the Vicsek model breaks rotational symmetry spontaneously, and why it is a non-equilibrium analogue of a ferromagnet.
Describe the zones of the Couzin model and the collective states they produce (swarm, torus, parallel groups), and explain collective memory as hysteresis.
Compare the rules and the questions of the Vicsek, Couzin and social force models.
(Optional) State the flocking result of the Cucker–Smale model and compare its assumptions with those of the Vicsek model.
Add a predator to a collective-motion model, measure how cohesion changes the capture probability, and explain why pushing harder at a narrow door can make an evacuation slower.








References

Couzin, Iain D, Jens Krause, Richard James, Graeme D Ruxton, and Nigel R Franks. 2002. “Collective Memory and Spatial Sorting in Animal Groups.” Journal of Theoretical Biology 218 (1): 1–11. https://doi.org/10.1006/jtbi.2002.3065.


Strogatz, Steven H. 2024. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos: With Applications to Physics, Biology, Chemistry, and Engineering. Chapman; Hall/CRC.


Strogatz, Steven H. 2000. “From Kuramoto to Crawford: Exploring the Onset of Synchronization in Populations of Coupled Oscillators.” Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena 143 (1–4): 1–20. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4.


Vicsek, Tamás, András Czirók, Eshel Ben-Jacob, Inon Cohen, and Ofer Shochet. 1995. “Novel Type of Phase Transition in a System of Self-Driven Particles.” Physical Review Letters 75 (6): 1226–29. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.75.1226.

title: Practice: Collective Motion
text: This is an ungraded practice page. Choose one option and work on it after the lab. It uses the code you wrote in the Vicsek animation lab and the models of Vicsek and Couzin.

title: Practice: Collective Motion
text:
Option A: Couzin model
Theory: The Couzin Model.

Implement the Couzin rules and motion in two dimensions.
Animate the individuals moving. Reuse the structure of Animation.
Implement the group polarization \(p_{\text{group}}\) and the angular momentum \(m_{\text{group}}\) defined in Couzin et al. (2002). Compare \(p_{\text{group}}\) with the Vicsek order parameter.
Explore the widths \(\Delta r_o\) and \(\Delta r_a\) and find the four collective behaviours described by Couzin et al. (2002): swarm, torus, dynamic parallel group and highly parallel group.







TipOptional extension




Add sliders to change parameters in real time.
Test collective memory: slowly increase \(\Delta r_o\) and then decrease it again, and check whether the group state follows the same path both ways.
Implement the model in 3D, as in the original paper.

title: Practice: Collective Motion
section: Option B: Vicsek model with predator avoidance
text:
Option B: Vicsek model with predator avoidance
Guide: Predator Avoidance.
The predator can be a fixed point, a random walker, or your mouse cursor. Particles inside the predator radius turn directly away from it, as in the Couzin repulsion rule.

Implement the full Vicsek animation from Animation.
Add the predator avoidance rule and draw the predator.
Explore the parameter space. How does the predator affect the order parameter? Is there a regime where the group splits and later merges again? Can you find a regime where the particles escape the predator?

title: Practice: Collective Motion
text:
Option C: Confusion effect
Theory: The Confusion Effect.

Start from your Couzin code (Option A) and add one predator that swims toward the nearest prey, faster than the prey.
Make the predator lock on the most isolated prey in its field of view. Break the lock whenever another prey enters a narrow window around the line of sight, and give up the pass after three broken locks.
When the predator reaches its target, capture it with probability \(1/(1 + c\,\bar n)\), where \(\bar n\) is the mean number of look-alikes in the window during the approach.
Measure the captures per attack for several widths of the zone of attraction \(\Delta r_a\). Is a tight school safer?







TipOptional extension




Add an odd prey that cannot lose its lock, and see how the capture probability changes.
Measure the captures per unit time against the density of prey, and compare the curve with the Holling functional responses.



A reference version is in amlab/collective_motion/couzin_predator.py, with an animation in couzin_predator_animation.py.

title: Practice: Collective Motion
text:
Option D: Faster is slower
Theory: Faster Is Slower: Crowds at a Door and The Social Force Model.

Implement pedestrians as discs with the wish-to-move term, the repulsion and the body force of the model. Add walls with one door.
Measure the evacuation time and the flow through the door for several desired speeds. Find the speed with the shortest evacuation.
Add a column in front of the door and move it. Does the flow change?







TipOptional extension




Add sliding friction between bodies, and compare the pressure at the door with and without it.
Give only 10% of the people a high desired speed. How many are needed to slow everybody down?



A reference version is in amlab/collective_motion/crowd_exit.py, with an animation in crowd_exit_animation.py.

title: Practice: Collective Motion
text:
Option E: Cucker–Smale flocking
Theory: Flocking Without Noise: The Cucker–Smale Model.

Integrate the model with scipy.integrate.solve_ivp for \(k = 20\) birds in the plane and reproduce the velocity spread \(\Lambda(t)\) of the figure on that page.
Measure the flocking time, the first time at which \(\Lambda < 10^{-6}\), as a function of \(\beta\) and of the size of the starting square.
Compute the Fiedler number of the weight matrix at every saved time and compare \(\Lambda(t)\) with the bound \(\Lambda_0 e^{-2t\Phi_t}\).







TipOptional extension




Replace the weights \(a_{ij}\) by the Vicsek weights (\(a_{ij} = 1\) if \(\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\| \le r\) and \(0\) otherwise). Does the flock still reach a common velocity from your initial conditions? How does it depend on \(r\)?
Add noise to the velocity equation and look at how \(\Lambda\) behaves for small and large noise.

title: Practice: Collective Motion
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



In the Vicsek model you double both \(N\) and \(L^2\), keeping the density and the noise fixed. Which features of the order parameter curve \(v_a(\eta)\) should stay the same, and which should change?








TipSolution





The density \(\rho = N/L^2\) is unchanged, so in the ordered phase \(v_a\) should be about the same. At high noise, \(v_a\) is set by the finite-size floor of order \(1/\sqrt{N}\), which decreases by a factor \(\sqrt{2}\). The transition region should become sharper. This is the pattern in Figure 2(a) of Vicsek et al. (1995).

title: Vicsek Lab: Animation Loop
text:
Write the Animation Update Function
This is the core loop:

advance the Vicsek dynamics by one step (vicsek_equations).
update xy_tail.
update the particle artists.

Use this checklist:

call vicsek_equations(...)
update xy_tail with np.roll(...)
plt_particles.set_data(...) and plt_current.set_data(...)







NoteExercise



Complete update_animation(), following the comments for each step.
def update_animation(frame: int):
    nonlocal xy, xy_tail, theta, noise_eta, v0, radius_interaction, box_size

    # TODO: advance the Vicsek equations

    # TODO: update the tail tensor
    # TODO: update the particle artists with set_data

    return (plt_particles, plt_current)


Tip: blitting requires you to return artists If you set blit=True, your update function must return an iterable of the artists that changed, as shown above. If you forget to return them, the animation will run but the plot will not update (it will look frozen).
Move the function update_animation inside run_simulation so it can access the state variables with nonlocal.






TipHint





Use the tail trick. Store the last TAIL_LEN positions:

shift the tensor with np.roll(...),
write the newest positions into the last slice.

This avoids creating new arrays each frame.









TipSolution





def update_animation(frame: int):
    nonlocal \
        xy, \
        xy_tail, \
        theta, \
        noise_eta, \
        v0, \
        radius_interaction, \
        box_size
    xy, theta = vicsek_equations(
        xy,
        theta,
        v0=v0,
        dt=dt,
        radius_interaction=radius_interaction,
        box_size=box_size,
        noise=noise_eta,
    )

    # Update tails
    xy_tail = np.roll(xy_tail, shift=-1, axis=2)
    xy_tail[:, :, -1] = xy
    plt_particles.set_data(xy_tail[0].flatten(), xy_tail[1].flatten())
    plt_current.set_data(xy[0], xy[1])

    return (plt_particles, plt_current)

ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update_animation, interval=0, blit=True)

Assemble run_simulation(): parameters, initial state, figure, particle artists, the update function and the animation object. Run the script and check that the particles move and align.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Pairwise vs Mean Field
text:
TipOptional extension



This page is optional. You can compare the pairwise form of the ODE with the mean-field form. Implement both versions and see how they differ in computational cost and in the resulting dynamics. The mean-field form is much faster for large populations and gives the same trajectories.

title: Kuramoto Lab: Pairwise vs Mean Field
text:
Pairwise form
You can write the right-hand side in two ways (The Kuramoto Model and The Order Parameter):
\[
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \frac{K}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i)
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + K r \sin(\psi - \theta_i).
\]
The pairwise form is straightforward but expensive for large \(N\). The mean-field form is cheaper and shows how each oscillator responds to the whole population.






NoteExercise



Write kuramoto_ode_pairwise(), which follows the pairwise form of the model in The Kuramoto Model directly. Rename your first function kuramoto_ode_meanfield(). Check that both return the same derivatives for the same input.
def kuramoto_ode_pairwise(t, theta, omega, coupling_strength=1.0):
    # TODO: build the matrix of phase differences theta_j - theta_i

    # TODO: sum sin(theta_j - theta_i) over j and scale by K / N
    return dtheta_dt








TipHint





Broadcasting builds the full matrix of differences in one line: theta[None, :] - theta[:, None] has entry \(\theta_j - \theta_i\) in row \(i\), column \(j\).
Once both functions exist, switching between them is as simple as changing the ODE function in the solve_ivp() call inside the update_function() of Animation:
sol = solve_ivp(
    kuramoto_ode_pairwise, # Change this to the other ODE function
    (0, dt),
    theta,
    args=(omega, coupling_strength),
    )
This is why modularity matters. By keeping your code organized and modular, you can swap out one component (like the ODE function) without rewriting the animation code. A modular structure also saves work in the Kuramoto Assignment, where you implement a different model of coupled oscillators, the Millennium Bridge.









TipSolution





def kuramoto_ode_pairwise(t, theta, omega, coupling_strength=1.0):
    # Row i, column j holds theta_j - theta_i
    diff = theta[None, :] - theta[:, None]
    dtheta_dt = omega + coupling_strength / len(theta) * np.sin(diff).sum(axis=1)
    return dtheta_dt


theta, omega = initialize_oscillators(100, seed=1)
print(np.allclose(
    kuramoto_ode_pairwise(0, theta, omega, 2.0),
    kuramoto_ode_meanfield(0, theta, omega, 2.0),
))  # True

title: Kuramoto Lab: Pairwise vs Mean Field
text:
Computational cost






NoteExercise



Time both ODE functions with %timeit (or time.perf_counter()) for \(N = 100\), \(1000\) and \(5000\). How does the cost grow with \(N\) in each case?








TipSolution





The pairwise version builds an \(N \times N\) matrix of phase differences, so one evaluation costs \(O(N^2)\) time and memory. The mean-field version computes one complex mean, which costs \(O(N)\). Going from \(N = 1000\) to \(N = 5000\) should multiply the pairwise time by roughly 25 and the mean-field time by roughly 5. Both give the same trajectories up to round-off.

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Pearson (1993).
Recommended: Murray (2003), Section 2.5 (scale and geometry effects).
This laboratory lifts the 1D workflow to a rectangle. The main change is the Laplacian. The Euler loop, the boundary logic, and the validation steps stay the same. If your 1D code was modular, you mostly change the array shape.

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
Rectangular Domains
You work on \([0, L_x] \times [0, L_y]\). After discretization each field becomes a matrix.

The row index stores the \(x\) position, the column index the \(y\) position.
The full state has shape (2, num_x, num_y), one matrix for \(u\) and one for \(v\).

num_x = int(length_x / dx)
num_y = int(length_y / dx)
uv = np.ones((2, num_x, num_y))
You still update the whole matrix at once. Shift it up, down, left, and right, and combine the shifted copies.

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
The 5-Point Stencil
\[
\Delta u = \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}
\approx \frac{u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j}}{dx^2}.
\tag{1}\]
Applying the 1D centered difference in each direction gives this stencil, with error \(\mathcal{O}(dx^2)\) (LeVeque 2007, chap. 3).






NoteExercise



Implement the stencil with np.roll(). Each call shifts the whole matrix by one grid cell along one direction.
import numpy as np

def laplacian_2d(field, dx):
    # TODO: combine the four nearest neighbours and the centre point with np.roll
    lap =
    return lap / dx**2








TipSolution





def laplacian_2d(field, dx):
    lap = -4 * field
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=1, axis=0)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=-1, axis=0)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=1, axis=1)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=-1, axis=1)
    return lap / dx**2

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
Boundary Conditions on a Rectangle
The same three options as in Boundary Conditions, now on four edges.

Periodic: leave the array unchanged; np.roll already wraps each side onto the opposite one.
Neumann: copy the nearest interior row or column onto each edge.
Dirichlet: overwrite each edge with prescribed values.

def apply_boundary_conditions(uv, bc="neumann", dirichlet_values=(1.4, 1.96)):
    if bc == "periodic":
        return uv
    if bc == "neumann":
        uv[:, 0, :] = uv[:, 1, :]
        uv[:, -1, :] = uv[:, -2, :]
        uv[:, :, 0] = uv[:, :, 1]
        uv[:, :, -1] = uv[:, :, -2]
        return uv
    if bc == "dirichlet":
        for species, value in enumerate(dirichlet_values):
            uv[species, 0, :] = value
            uv[species, -1, :] = value
            uv[species, :, 0] = value
            uv[species, :, -1] = value
        return uv
    raise ValueError("bc must be 'periodic', 'neumann', or 'dirichlet'")

title: Laplacian in 2D
text:
Validate the Stencil
Test on \(u = \cos(2\pi x/L_x)\cos(4\pi y/L_y)\) with periodic wrapping, where \(\Delta u = -\left[(2\pi/L_x)^2 + (4\pi/L_y)^2\right] u\).

import numpy as np


def laplacian_2d(field, dx):
    lap = -4 * field
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=1, axis=0)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=-1, axis=0)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=1, axis=1)
    lap += np.roll(field, shift=-1, axis=1)
    return lap / dx**2


length_x, length_y = 20.0, 50.0
for dx in (1.0, 0.5, 0.25):
    x = np.arange(int(length_x / dx)) * dx
    y = np.arange(int(length_y / dx)) * dx
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(x, y, indexing="ij")
    u = np.cos(2 * np.pi * xx / length_x) * np.cos(4 * np.pi * yy / length_y)
    exact = -((2 * np.pi / length_x) ** 2 + (4 * np.pi / length_y) ** 2) * u
    print(f"dx = {dx:.2f}   max error = {np.max(np.abs(laplacian_2d(u, dx) - exact)):.2e}")

dx = 1.00   max error = 1.14e-03
dx = 0.50   max error = 2.86e-04
dx = 0.25   max error = 7.15e-05


The error again drops by four for each halving of \(dx\).






ImportantStability in 2D



The 5-point stencil halves the stable time step: \(dt \le dx^2/(4D)\) instead of \(dx^2/(2D)\). With \(d = 30\) and \(dx = 1\) that is \(dt \le 0.0083\), so the 1D choice \(dt = 0.01\) fails in 2D (Time-Step Stability).








TipOptional extension



A 9-point stencil that also uses the diagonal neighbours gives a more isotropic Laplacian. amlab.pdes_2d.gray_scott.laplacian_9pt implements one. Compare the two stencils on the test function above.

title: Gray-Scott Model
text:
The Gray-Scott model combines diffusion with an autocatalytic reaction and produces spots, stripes, worms, and labyrinths depending on the parameters (Gray and Scott 1984; Pearson 1993).
This page follows the 2D Gierer-Meinhardt solver, and the jump is small.
The PDE system is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} &= d_1 \Delta u - u v^2 + f(1-u), \\
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} &= d_2 \Delta v + u v^2 - (f+k) v,
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
where \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) are the diffusion coefficients, \(f\) is the feed rate, and \(k\) is the kill rate.
Figure 1: Gray-Scott model. Example snapshot of \(v(x, y)\) for \(d_1=0.1\), \(d_2=0.05\), \(f=0.040\), and \(k=0.060\).

title: Gray-Scott Model
text:
Start from the Homogeneous State
Gray-Scott is usually initialized near the steady state \((u, v) = (1, 0)\), then a small patch is perturbed.






NoteExercise



Set \(u = 0.5\), \(v = 0.25\) on a central square and add 10% noise there.
import numpy as np

n = 250
dt = 2.0
uv = np.ones((2, n, n), dtype=np.float32)
uv[1] = 0.0

c = n // 2
r = 12

uv[0, c - r : c + r, c - r : c + r] = 0.5
uv[1, c - r : c + r, c - r : c + r] = 0.25

noise = 0.1 * np.random.randn(2, 2 * r, 2 * r)
uv[:, c - r : c + r, c - r : c + r] *= 1 + noise

text:
Reuse the 2D Laplacian






NoteExercise



We will start with the 5-point stencil. If you implemented the previous page cleanly, you can reuse that helper almost unchanged.
import numpy as np

def laplacian(field):
    # TODO: write the 5-point stencil with np.roll
    return lap

    lap += np.roll(field, shift=-1, axis=0)

title: Gray-Scott Model
text:
Implement the Gray-Scott PDE






NoteExercise



Write the Gray-Scott right-hand side from Equation 1.
import numpy as np

def gray_scott_pde(t, uv, d1=0.1, d2=0.05, f=0.040, k=0.060):
    u, v = uv
    lu = laplacian(u)
    lv = laplacian(v)

    # TODO: compute the autocatalytic term uv^2
    uv2 =

    # TODO: write du_dt and dv_dt
    du_dt =
    dv_dt =
    return np.array([du_dt, dv_dt])








TipSolution





def gray_scott_pde(t, uv, d1=0.1, d2=0.05, f=0.040, k=0.060):
    u, v = uv
    lu = laplacian(u)
    lv = laplacian(v)
    uv2 = u * v * v

    du_dt = d1 * lu - uv2 + f * (1 - u)
    dv_dt = d2 * lv + uv2 - (f + k) * v
    return np.array([du_dt, dv_dt])









Tip



Reference code is available in amlab/pdes_2d/gray_scott.py.

title: Unstable Modes in 1D
text: The Turing test on Turing Numerics says that some spatial mode should grow. It does not tell you which one. On a finite interval only discrete wavenumbers exist, so you scan them one by one (Murray 2003, sec. 2.5).

title: Unstable Modes in 1D
text:
Scan the Neumann Modes
For Neumann conditions on \((0, L)\) the admissible wavenumbers are \(k_n = n\pi/L\). Each mode has the matrix
\[
A_n = \gamma J - k_n^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d).
\]






NoteExercise



Compute the largest real part of the eigenvalues of each \(A_n\), keep the positive ones, and sort them from fastest to slowest.

def find_unstable_modes_1d(a=0.40, b=1.00, d=30.0, gamma=1.0, length=40.0, num_modes=20):
    jac = np.array(gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a, b)).reshape(2, 2)
    diffusion = np.diag([1.0, d])
    unstable_modes = []

    for n in range(num_modes):
        k2 = (n * np.pi / length) ** 2
        a_n = gamma * jac - k2 * diffusion
        growth_rate = np.max(np.linalg.eigvals(a_n).real)
        if growth_rate > 0:
            unstable_modes.append((n, growth_rate))

    unstable_modes.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    return unstable_modes



The first entry of the list is the dominant linear mode. It predicts the earliest visible wavelength in the simulation.

The band in \(k^2\) scales with \(\gamma\), so \(k\) scales with \(\sqrt{\gamma}\). With \(\gamma = 2\) the band is \(0.494 < k < 0.739\), and the unstable Neumann modes are \(n = 7, 8, 9\), with \(n = 8\) fastest. Since \(\gamma J - k^2 D = \gamma\,(J - (k^2/\gamma) D)\), the whole dispersion curve is rescaled: \(\sigma_\gamma(k^2) = \gamma\,\sigma_1(k^2/\gamma)\). This matches the statement that increasing \(\gamma\) acts like enlarging the domain.

title: Turing Space
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Britton (2003), Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1 (pp. 214 to 217): the curve of potential marginal Turing instability in the plane of the diffusion coefficients.
Recommended: Murray (2003), Chapter 2, Section 2.5.
The Turing space is the set of parameters for which the four Turing conditions hold (Murray 2003, sec. 2.5). For Gierer-Meinhardt you can draw it in the \((a, d)\) plane at fixed \(b\).
Britton draws the same set in the plane of the two diffusion coefficients. Its boundary is the curve \((D_2 f_u + D_1 g_v)^2 = 4 D_1 D_2 \det J\), taken where \(D_2 f_u + D_1 g_v > 0\). It is the envelope of the curves \(a_2(\lambda) = 0\) over all \(\lambda\) and separates the region of potential Turing instability from the region without it (Britton 2003, Equations 7.4.28 and 7.4.29). With \(D_1 = 1\) and \(D_2 = d\) this is the critical ratio \(d_c\) of the Turing Conditions page. The diagram below fixes the kinetics through \(a\) and \(b\) and varies \(d\) instead.

title: Turing Space
text:
The Region in Closed Form
From Linearization, the Gierer-Meinhardt Jacobian at the steady state has \(f_u = b(1-a)/(1+a)\), \(g_v = -1\), and \(\det J = b\). The four conditions reduce to:

\(\det J = b > 0\), always true.
\(\operatorname{tr} J < 0\), that is \(f_u < 1\).
\(f_u > 0\), that is \(a < 1\) (needed for \(d f_u + g_v > 0\)).
\(d f_u - 1 > 2\sqrt{b d}\), which gives

\[
\sqrt{d} > \frac{\sqrt{b} + \sqrt{b + f_u}}{f_u}, \qquad f_u = \frac{b(1-a)}{1+a}.
\tag{1}\]
For \(b = 1\) the trace condition holds for every \(a > 0\), and the Turing space is the region above the curve Equation 1 with \(0 < a < 1\).








Figure 1: Turing space of Gierer-Meinhardt for \(b = 1\) (shaded), computed with amlab.pdes_1d.is_turing_instability. The dashed line is the boundary from Equation 1. The markers are the two test cases of the laboratory.

title: Turing Space
text:
Reading the Diagram

The curve diverges as \(a \to 1\), because \(f_u \to 0\) and activation disappears.
For \(a = 0.4\) the boundary sits at \(d_c \approx 26.24\). Case A lies inside, Case B outside.
The diagram depends only on \(a\), \(b\) and \(d\). It does not depend on \(\gamma\) or on the domain. Whether a pattern appears on a given domain also needs an admissible mode in the unstable band (Dispersion Relation).

The same diagram appears in the interactive simulator at bam-applied-math-lab.streamlit.app, where you can click on a point of the \((a, d)\) plane and watch the resulting 1D simulation.






NoteExercise



Increase \(b\) from \(1\) to \(2\) at \(a = 0.4\). Does the critical ratio \(d_c\) increase or decrease? Compute it with Equation 1, and check whether the trace condition still holds.








TipSolution





With \(b = 2\), \(f_u = 2 \cdot 0.6 / 1.4 = 6/7 \approx 0.857 < 1\), so the trace condition holds. Then \(\sqrt{d_c} = (\sqrt 2 + \sqrt{2.857})/0.857 \approx (1.414 + 1.690)/0.857 \approx 3.62\), so \(d_c \approx 13.1\). The critical ratio decreases.

\partial_t v = d\,\Delta v + \gamma \left(u^2 - v\right).
\tag{1}\]

def gierer_meinhardt_pde(t, uv, gamma=1, a=0.40, b=1.00, d=30, dx=1.0):
    u, v = uv
    lu = laplacian_1d(u, dx)
    lv = laplacian_1d(v, dx)

    f = a - b * u + (u**2) / v
    g = u**2 - v
    du_dt = lu + gamma * f
    dv_dt = d * lv + gamma * g
    return np.array([du_dt, dv_dt])

title: Turing Numerics
text:
This is the prediction step of the laboratory. You turn the theory of Turing Conditions and Dispersion Relation into three small functions: equilibrium, Jacobian, and Turing test (Turing 1952; Murray 2003, sec. 2.3). The fourth, the mode scan, follows on Unstable Modes in 1D. You will reuse all four in 2D and in the assignment.
The workflow is always the same:

title: Turing Numerics
text:
Compute the Equilibrium
The steady state from Linearization is one line of code each.
def gierer_meinhardt_equilibrium(a=0.40, b=1.00):
    u_star = (a + 1) / b
    v_star = u_star**2
    return u_star, v_star

title: Turing Numerics
section: Write the Jacobian at the Fixed Point
text:
Write the Jacobian at the Fixed Point






NoteExercise



Use the general Jacobian from Linearization and evaluate it at \((u_*, v_*)\).
def gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a=0.40, b=1.00):
    u_star, v_star = gierer_meinhardt_equilibrium(a, b)
    # TODO: return fu, fv, gu, gv








TipSolution





def gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a=0.40, b=1.00):
    u_star, v_star = gierer_meinhardt_equilibrium(a, b)
    fu = -b + 2 * u_star / v_star
    fv = -(u_star**2) / (v_star**2)
    gu = 2 * u_star
    gv = -1.0
    return fu, fv, gu, gv
Simplified, this is \(f_u = b(1-a)/(1+a)\), \(f_v = -b^2/(1+a)^2\), \(g_u = 2(1+a)/b\), \(g_v = -1\). You can also write the entries directly in \(a\) and \(b\):
def gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a=0.40, b=1.00):
    fu = 2 * b / (a + 1) - b
    fv = -((b / (a + 1)) ** 2)
    gu = 2 * (a + 1) / b
    gv = -1.0
    return fu, fv, gu, gv

def is_turing_instability(a, b, d):
    fu, fv, gu, gv = gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a, b)
    det = fu * gv - fv * gu
    cond1 = (fu + gv) < 0
    cond2 = det > 0
    cond3 = (d * fu + gv) > 0
    cond4 = (d * fu + gv) ** 2 > 4 * d * det
    return cond1 & cond2 & cond3 & cond4
The course package writes the last two conditions as the single inequality \(d f_u + g_v > 2\sqrt{d \det J}\), which is equivalent.



If your implementation is vectorized, it works with scalars and with arrays. Validate it carefully: you reuse it in 2D and in the assignment.

title: Evidence for Reaction-Diffusion in Real Systems
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Kondo and Miura (2010), the whole review (Science 329, pp. 1616 to 1620).
Recommended: Turing (1952), the last part of Section 11 on biological examples, and Murray (1988) for the coat-pattern application discussed on Animal Coat Patterns.
The linear theory of this module says what a reaction-diffusion system can do. It does not say that a real tissue does it. This page collects what Kondo and Miura (2010) report as evidence, separates simulation matches from experimental tests, and lists the caveats that the authors themselves give. Everything stated about a biological system below is a statement of that review. The chemical experiments with the CIMA reaction cited on Reaction-Diffusion Equations are not discussed in the review and are not covered here.

title: Evidence for Reaction-Diffusion in Real Systems
text:
What the Source Says

The Turing mechanism differs from a classic morphogen gradient in that the reaction lets the system make its own pattern without a pre-existing prepattern. Kondo and Miura note that the gradient model can be seen as the special case in which the reaction is removed and the source enters as a boundary condition (Kondo and Miura 2010, 1616 to 1617).
Turing patterns arise autonomously and regenerate after experimental disturbance, which makes them attractive for developmental processes that show self-regulation (Kondo and Miura 2010, 1617).
Gierer and Meinhardt showed that the essential requirement is “short-range positive feedback with long-range negative feedback”. The interacting elements need not be molecules, and the signal need not travel by diffusion: relayed cell-to-cell signals, chemotaxis, mechanochemical interactions and neural interactions can play the same role (Kondo and Miura 2010, 1617).
A simulation that reproduces a pattern is not proof. In the authors’ words, the presence of water does not imply the presence of waves. To show that a wave exists one has to identify a dynamic property that the simulation predicts and test it (Kondo and Miura 2010, 1617).
Experiments are easiest on the skin, where the pattern is two-dimensional and can be perturbed. In many other tissues perturbations may be lethal, which is one reason why demonstrations are hard (Kondo and Miura 2010, 1617 and 1620).

title: Evidence for Reaction-Diffusion in Real Systems
text:
Examples Reported in the Review









System
Proposed activation and inhibition
Evidence described in the review
Status stated in the review




Stripes on the skin of fish (Pomacanthus imperator, zebrafish)
Interactions between pigment cells: mutual inhibition of black and yellow cells acts as a positive feedback loop
Dynamic behaviour of the pattern. After laser ablation of pigment cells in two black stripes of zebrafish, the lower stripe shifts and settles with the spacing preserved, which a Turing simulation predicts
The network differs from Turing’s original one but fits the activation and inhibition description. Molecular identification is under way


Hair follicle spacing in mouse
Wnt as short-range activator, Dkk as long-range inhibitor
A simulation predicted a ringed Wnt expression pattern that does not occur naturally, and ectopic production of Wnt was reported to confirm it. Changing the amount of the factors changes the pattern as simulated
Described as a critically important result because the same two factors act in other patterning processes


Feather buds in chick
not specified in the review
The periodic pattern regenerates when the skin is recombined from dissociated cells
Listed among well-studied examples


Travelling wave of hair formation in a mouse mutant
FGF and BMP
A wave moves across the skin over the life of the animals, which corresponds to the oscillatory travelling case
Identified in the review with the travelling-wave case of Turing’s classification


Left-right asymmetry
Nodal enhances itself and Lefty, and Lefty inhibits Nodal
Lefty spreads further than Nodal, as long-range inhibition requires
Fulfils the basic requirements according to the review


Limb precartilage condensation
Transforming growth factor beta as candidate activator
Dissociated limb cells in culture form nearly periodic patterns, and adding the factor changes them as predicted by the model
No inhibitor identified


Lung branching, Hydra regeneration
Wnt and Dkk are involved
Same molecules as in the skin examples
Involvement of the same molecules does not by itself prove the same mechanism



The review also lists seashell, feather and fish-skin patterns that have been simulated with modified reaction-diffusion systems, and observes that a close resemblance “points strongly” to the mechanism. Combined with the warning above, this resemblance is to be read as motivation for a test, not as the test. The caption of the review’s Figure 4 adds that the involvement of the mechanism in some of the listed phenomena has not been fully accepted by experimental researchers.

title: Evidence for Reaction-Diffusion in Real Systems
text:
Regeneration in the Model
The one dynamic property that the review stresses most for the skin is robustness: the pattern re-forms with its characteristic spacing after a disturbance. The same property is easy to check in the laboratory model. The code evolves the 1D Gierer-Meinhardt system of Case A on \((0, 40)\) to a pattern, then resets the fields to the uniform state with 1% noise on the interval \((14, 26)\), which contains one peak, and lets the system evolve again. The procedure is an analogy to the ablation experiment, not a model of fish skin: in the model the chemical concentrations are reset, whereas in the experiment the pigment cells are removed.


peak positions before: [6, 20, 33]
peak positions after:  [6, 20, 33]








Figure 1: Regeneration in the 1D Gierer-Meinhardt model, Case A (\(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), \(d = 30\), \(\gamma = 1\), \(L = 40\), \(dx = 1\)). Top, the pattern of \(u\) at \(t = 400\). Middle, the same field right after the interval \((14, 26)\), shaded, is reset to the uniform state plus noise. Bottom, the field after another \(400\) time units. Dots mark the peaks of the two regular patterns.





In this run the peaks sit at the same grid positions before and after the reset. With the noise of two other seeds the result was the same, and for a reset of the interval \((0, 12)\) one peak moved by one grid point in two of the three seeds. The pattern is not a memory of the removed region. It is pinned by the parts that were left intact and by the boundary conditions, and the new peak fits into the gap with the same spacing, as in the zebrafish experiment.






NoteExercise



A group simulates a two-species reaction-diffusion model on a fish-shaped domain and obtains a stripe pattern that looks like the one on the animal. Using only the criteria of Kondo and Miura (2010), list three observations that would make the claim stronger, and one statement that the simulation cannot support. Then explain why the condition \(d > 1\) of the Turing Conditions page is not by itself a prediction about molecular diffusion in tissue.








TipSolution





Stronger evidence comes from the dynamic properties that the model predicts and that can be measured: the response of the pattern to a perturbation such as ablation of part of it, the rearrangement of stripes as the animal grows, and the effect of changing one interaction, for instance by a mutation or an inhibitor, on the spacing. In each case the model must predict the outcome before the experiment, as the Wnt example does. The simulation alone cannot support the statement that the molecules in the model are the ones in the animal, because a similar pattern can come from different networks.
The inequality \(d > 1\) was derived for diffusing species with the Laplacian as the only transport term. The review stresses that the real requirement is short-range positive and long-range negative feedback, and that this range can be created by other forms of signalling, such as cell-to-cell relays. In the zebrafish example the circuit consists of two negative interactions between pigment cells that act as a positive loop, and it does not have the structure of the diffusing pair of the original model. The ratio \(d\) is the diffusive way of realising the longer range of inhibition.

title: Assignment: Pattern Formation
text:
ImportantGraded assignment



This assignment is graded and counts for 10% of the final grade. It is released in two stages: Parts 1 and 2 (Gierer-Meinhardt in 1D) with the 1D laboratory, and Parts 3 and 4 (Gierer-Meinhardt and Gray-Scott in 2D) with the 2D laboratory. Under the course AI policy, you may not use generative AI to solve graded assignments.
You will take an analytical and a numerical approach to two reaction-diffusion systems that show Turing instability for suitable parameters, Gierer-Meinhardt and Gray-Scott (Turing 1952; Gierer and Meinhardt 1972; Gray and Scott 1984; Pearson 1993).
The governing equations are
\[
u_t = D_1 \Delta u + \gamma f(u, v), \qquad
v_t = D_2 \Delta v + \gamma g(u, v),
\]
with
\[
\text{Gierer-Meinhardt: } f(u, v) = a - bu + \frac{u^2}{v}, \qquad g(u, v) = u^2 - v, \qquad a, b > 0,
\]
\[
\text{Gray-Scott: } f(u, v) = -uv^2 + F(1-u), \qquad g(u, v) = uv^2 - (F + k)v, \qquad F, k > 0.
\]
For Gierer-Meinhardt, consider the equations on a rectangle \(\Omega_2 = (0, L_1) \times (0, L_2)\) with Neumann zero-flux boundary conditions, and start by reducing the problem to one dimension, \(\Omega_1 = (0, L_1)\).
Use the session pages as a guide:
Turing Conditions Turing Numerics Unstable Modes in 1D Gierer-Meinhardt Solver in 1D Time-Step Stability Gierer-Meinhardt Solver in 2D Gray-Scott

title: Assignment: Pattern Formation
text:
Part 1: Gierer-Meinhardt in 1D, Analysis
The Turing conditions are
\[
f_u + g_v < 0, \qquad \det J = f_u g_v - f_v g_u > 0, \qquad D_1 g_v + D_2 f_u > 2 \sqrt{D_1 D_2 \det J} > 0.
\]
These conditions do not depend on \(\gamma\) or on the size of the region. They are necessary but not sufficient. On a finite region you must also check that unstable spatial modes exist, which depends on the Laplacian eigenvalues \(\lambda_n\).

Take \(\gamma = 1\), \(D_1 = 1\), and \(D_2 = d > 0\). Find the region of \((a, b, d)\) where the conditions hold (the Turing space). Plot its section at \(b = 1\) in the \((a, d)\) plane.
Solve the Sturm-Liouville problem on the interval with Neumann boundary conditions and identify the spectrum of the Laplacian. For each spatial mode, the temporal eigenvalues are those of

\[
A_n = \gamma J + \lambda_n D =
\begin{pmatrix}
\gamma f_u + \lambda_n D_1 & \gamma f_v \\
\gamma g_u & \gamma g_v + \lambda_n D_2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det(A_n - \sigma^{(n)} I) = 0.
\]
List the unstable modes and the leading mode. 3. On \((0, L)\) with \(L = 40\), decide which of these parameter sets gives Turing instability and find the leading mode: - Case A: \(\gamma = 1\), \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), \(d = 30\) - Case B: \(\gamma = 1\), \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), \(d = 20\)

title: Assignment: Pattern Formation
text:
Part 2: Gierer-Meinhardt in 1D, Simulation
Implement a 1D finite-difference scheme in space and explicit Euler in time.

Use \(N = 40\) spatial points, \(dx = 1\) (so \(L = N\,dx = 40\)), and \(dt = 0.01\).
Stability check. State the explicit Euler bound for your scheme and show that \(dt = 0.01\) satisfies it. Run one case with a time step above the bound and describe what goes wrong.
Start from the homogeneous steady state plus 1% noise. In one case the perturbation should decay; in the other the unstable mode should grow.
Integrate for \(5 \times 10^4\) steps of size \(dt = 0.01\), saving one frame every 500 steps. Join the 100 frames into an animation.
Convergence check. Repeat Case A with \(dx\) halved and \(dt\) divided by four. Report whether the number of peaks and their spacing change, and quantify the difference.
Compare the number of half-wavelengths with the leading mode from Part 1.
Run at least one experiment of your own (parameters, interval length, or numerical settings) and comment on what changed.

title: Assignment: Pattern Formation
text:
Part 3: Gierer-Meinhardt in 2D

Extend your scheme and your analysis to the rectangle \(\Omega_2 = (0, L_1) \times (0, L_2)\). State the explicit Euler bound in 2D and choose \(dt\) accordingly. Say what pattern you expect.
For \(L_1 = 20\) and \(L_2 = 50\), decide whether Cases A and B give Turing instability, count the unstable modes \((n, m)\), and find the leading mode.
Test your predictions against the simulation.

title: Assignment: Pattern Formation
text:
Part 4: Gray-Scott in 2D
Gray-Scott models the autocatalytic reaction
\[
U + 2V \rightarrow 3V, \qquad V \rightarrow P,
\]
where \(P\) is inert and \(V\) activates its own production. The PDE system is
\[
u_t = D_1 \Delta u - uv^2 + F(1-u), \qquad
v_t = D_2 \Delta v + uv^2 - (F + k)v.
\]
Focus on numerical observation and description of the patterns, following Pearson (1993). Use periodic boundary conditions on the square \([0, L] \times [0, L]\).

Take \(N = 250\) and \(dx = 1\), so \(L = 250\).
Start from \((u^*, v^*) = (1, 0)\). Set \((u, v) = (0.5, 0.5)\) on a central \(20 \times 20\) square and add 10% noise there. Later, place similar squares at other positions.
Use explicit Euler with \(dt = 2\). Check that the scheme is stable for this \(dx\) and \(dt\), and show that larger values break it.
Take \(D_1 = 0.1\), \(D_2 = 0.05\) and integrate for:

Type A: \(F = 0.040\), \(k = 0.060\)
Type B: \(F = 0.014\), \(k = 0.047\)
Type C: \(F = 0.062\), \(k = 0.065\)
Type D: \(F = 0.078\), \(k = 0.061\)
Type E: \(F = 0.082\), \(k = 0.059\)

Integrate up to \(t = 5 \times 10^4\), saving one image every \(\Delta t = 200\), and build an animation from the 250 frames.
Describe each solution type. You may compare with Munafo’s classification, which extends Pearson’s.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Britton (2003), Appendix C, Sections C.3 and C.4 (spectra of the Laplacian and the conditions under which separation of variables applies).
Recommended: Britton (2003), Chapter 7, Section 7.2, for why zero-flux conditions are the default in the Turing problem.
In the ODE sessions the solver handled all the bookkeeping. In a PDE the boundary conditions are part of the model, and they decide which spatial modes exist (Laplacian Eigenmodes). With explicit Euler you enforce them by hand after every update.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Three Common Choices
Britton chooses zero-flux conditions for the Turing analysis partly because they are natural in many biological settings and partly because they are passive: they are unlikely to cause pattern formation themselves (Britton 2003, sec. 7.2). Separation of variables also works for Robin conditions, \(\alpha u + \beta\,\partial u/\partial n = 0\) with \(\alpha, \beta \ge 0\), but not directly on a growing domain (Britton 2003, sec. C.4).








Condition
Meaning
Implementation after each Euler step




Periodic
The ends are identified, \(u(0) = u(L)\)
Nothing: np.roll already wraps


Neumann (zero flux)
No material crosses the boundary, \(u_x = 0\)
Copy the nearest interior value onto the edge


Dirichlet (fixed value)
The boundary is held at a prescribed value
Overwrite the edge with that value




Neumann boundary conditions
Zero flux means zero slope at the boundary. A simple implementation copies the nearest interior value:
\[
u_0 = u_1, \qquad u_{N-1} = u_{N-2}.
\tag{1}\]
This sets the difference \((u_1 - u_0)/dx\) to zero. As an approximation of \(u_x = 0\) at \(x_0\) it is only first order in \(dx\). As a centered difference it is second order at the midpoint \(x_0 + dx/2\), so in effect the zero-flux boundaries sit halfway between the first two and the last two grid points. The effective domain length is \((N-2)\,dx\), not \(N\,dx\). It is the scheme used in the course package and in the assignment. Ghost-point schemes that place the boundary exactly exist (LeVeque 2007, chap. 2).
On a fine grid the difference in length is small. On a coarse grid it can shift a mode into or out of the unstable band (see the optional extension on Animal Coat Patterns).


Periodic boundary conditions
The left and right endpoints are neighbours. The rolled Laplacian from Laplacian in 1D is already correct, so no extra step is needed.


Dirichlet boundary conditions
You prescribe fixed values, for example the steady state \((u_*, v_*)\), and write them into the edges.

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Implement a Boundary Helper






NoteExercise



Write one helper that applies any of the three conditions to a (2, N) array after each Euler step.
def apply_boundary_conditions_1d(uv, bc="neumann", dirichlet_values=(1.4, 1.96)):
    # TODO: periodic: return uv unchanged
    # TODO: neumann: copy index 1 onto 0 and index -2 onto -1, for both species
    # TODO: dirichlet: write dirichlet_values into both ends
    return uv








TipSolution





def apply_boundary_conditions_1d(uv, bc="neumann", dirichlet_values=(1.4, 1.96)):
    if bc == "periodic":
        return uv
    if bc == "neumann":
        uv[:, 0] = uv[:, 1]
        uv[:, -1] = uv[:, -2]
        return uv
    if bc == "dirichlet":
        for species, value in enumerate(dirichlet_values):
            uv[species, 0] = value
            uv[species, -1] = value
        return uv
    raise ValueError("bc must be 'periodic', 'neumann', or 'dirichlet'")

title: Boundary Conditions
text:
Why the Choice Matters
The boundary condition changes the admissible wavenumbers. On \((0, 40)\) the Neumann modes are \(k_n = n\pi/40\), while periodic modes are \(k_n = 2n\pi/40\), so the periodic spectrum is twice as sparse.

from amlab.turing import unstable_modes_1d

for bc in ("neumann", "periodic"):
    print(bc, unstable_modes_1d(a=0.40, b=1.00, d=30.0, length=40.0, bc=bc))

neumann [(5, 0.021415536663643042), (6, 0.020554871787465512)]
periodic [(3, 0.020554871787465512)]


With Neumann conditions modes \(5\) and \(6\) grow. With periodic conditions only mode \(3\) (wavenumber \(6\pi/40 \approx 0.47\)) is unstable, which equals the Neumann mode \(6\).






Warning



The periodic option of amlab.pdes_1d.find_unstable_spatial_modes uses the wavenumbers \((n+1)\pi/L\), which are the Neumann wavenumbers shifted by one index, not the periodic ones \(2n\pi/L\). Use amlab.turing.unstable_modes_1d(..., bc="periodic") when you need the periodic spectrum.








NoteExercise



Dirichlet conditions with \(u = u_*\), \(v = v_*\) at both ends allow only \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) modes with \(n \ge 1\). For Case A on \(L = 40\), which modes are unstable?








TipSolution





The Dirichlet wavenumbers are the same \(n\pi/L\) as the Neumann ones, without \(n = 0\). So modes \(5\) and \(6\) are unstable, but the eigenfunctions are sines, which vanish at the boundary instead of having zero slope there.

title: Dispersion Relation
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Britton (2003), Chapter 7, Section 7.3 (pp. 211 to 214): the dispersion relation, potential Turing instability and the mode-\(n\) bifurcation.
Recommended: Turing (1952), Section 9 (pp. 54 to 56): the instability \(I(U)\) as a function of the wavelength and the “chemical wave-length” of the fastest-growing wave.
The Turing conditions tell you whether some mode grows. The dispersion relation tells you which modes grow and how fast (Murray 2003, sec. 2.5 and 2.6).

title: Dispersion Relation
text:
Growth Rate Versus Wavenumber
For each wavenumber \(k\), the growth rates are the roots of
\[
\sigma^2 - \operatorname{tr}A(k^2)\,\sigma + h(k^2) = 0, \qquad A(k^2) = \gamma J - k^2\operatorname{diag}(1, d),
\tag{1}\]
with \(h(k^2) = \det A(k^2) = d\,k^4 - \gamma (d f_u + g_v) k^2 + \gamma^2 \det J\), as on the Turing Conditions page. The function \(k \mapsto \operatorname{Re}\sigma(k^2)\), taking the larger root, is the dispersion relation. Britton writes it as \(\rho(\lambda) = \max_i \operatorname{Re}\sigma_i(\lambda)\) with \(\lambda = k^2\), and recalls that the name comes from waves in fluids, where waves of different wavelength travel at different speeds (Britton 2003, sec. 7.3). Turing derived the same function for the continuum as his Equation (9.1), \((p - a + \mu' U)(p - d + \nu' U) = bc\) with \(U = k^2\), and called the real part of its largest root \(I(U)\) (Turing 1952, sec. 9).

title: Dispersion Relation
text:
The Unstable Band
\(\sigma > 0\) exactly when \(h(k^2) < 0\). The roots of \(h\) give the band
\[
k_1^2 < k^2 < k_2^2, \qquad
k_{1,2}^2 = \frac{\gamma}{2d}\left[(d f_u + g_v) \mp \sqrt{(d f_u + g_v)^2 - 4 d \det J}\right].
\tag{2}\]
The band has width proportional to \(\gamma\) in \(k^2\). At \(d = d_c\) it shrinks to the single value \(k_c^2 = \gamma (d_c f_u + g_v)/(2 d_c)\) (Murray 2003, sec. 2.3).

title: Dispersion Relation
text:
The Fastest-Growing Mode
The fastest-growing wavenumber \(k_{\max}\) maximizes \(\operatorname{Re}\sigma(k^2)\). Near onset it is close to \(k_m\), the minimizer of \(h\), but the two are not equal in general, because \(\sigma\) also depends on the trace. You find \(k_{\max}\) numerically. The corresponding wavelength \(2\pi/k_{\max}\) predicts the spacing of the first visible pattern. Nonlinear effects can change the spacing later (Murray 2003, sec. 2.6). Turing called \(2\pi/k_{\max}\) the chemical wavelength. On a ring it is generally not a divisor of the circumference, and the number of lobes that form is one of the two integers nearest to circumference divided by chemical wavelength, usually the nearest (Turing 1952, sec. 8 and 11). For the numbers below, \(L k_{\max}/\pi = 5.46\), and the fastest Neumann mode is \(n = 5\).
On a finite domain only discrete wavenumbers exist. With Neumann conditions on \((0, L)\), \(k_n = n\pi/L\). The mode that grows fastest is the admissible \(k_n\) with the largest \(\sigma\). If no \(k_n\) falls into the band, the uniform state stays stable even when the Turing conditions hold.








Figure 1: Dispersion relation of Gierer-Meinhardt with \(a = 0.4\), \(b = 1\), \(\gamma = 1\). Dots mark the Neumann modes \(k_n = n\pi/L\) for \(L = 40\).





For \(d = 20\) every mode decays. At \(d = d_c \approx 26.24\) the curve touches zero. For \(d = 30\) a band of modes grows.

import numpy as np

from amlab.turing import dispersion_relation, gierer_meinhardt_jacobian, unstable_band

jac = gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(0.40, 1.00)
d = 30
k1_sq, k2_sq = unstable_band(*jac, d)
k = np.linspace(np.sqrt(k1_sq), np.sqrt(k2_sq), 2001)
k_max = k[np.argmax(dispersion_relation(k**2, *jac, d))]

print(f"unstable band: {np.sqrt(k1_sq):.3f} < k < {np.sqrt(k2_sq):.3f}")
print(f"fastest-growing k = {k_max:.3f}, wavelength = {2 * np.pi / k_max:.1f}")
print(f"closest Neumann mode on L = 40: n = {k_max * 40 / np.pi:.2f}")

unstable band: 0.349 < k < 0.523
fastest-growing k = 0.429, wavelength = 14.6
closest Neumann mode on L = 40: n = 5.46


The fastest wavenumber \(k_{\max} \approx 0.43\) corresponds to a wavelength of about \(14.6\), which lies between the Neumann modes \(n = 5\) and \(n = 6\) on \(L = 40\). Both modes grow, at almost the same rate, and mode \(5\) is slightly faster. The laboratory checks which one the simulation selects.

title: Dispersion Relation
section: Domain Size as the Bifurcation Parameter
text:
Domain Size as the Bifurcation Parameter
Britton treats the size of the domain as the parameter that is varied. A mode \(n\) is unstable only for an interval of \(\gamma\) (equivalently, of \(L\)), and the uniform state can be stable for domains of intermediate size. The closed forms of these intervals, a figure of the mode curves \(k_n = n\pi/L\) crossing the band, and a comparison with simulations are on Domain Size and Mode Selection.






NoteExercise



Keep \(d = 30\) and \(\gamma = 1\) with Neumann conditions. Mode \(n\) is unstable when \(k_1 < n\pi/L < k_2\). For which domain lengths \(L < 20\) is no mode \(n \ge 1\) unstable?








TipSolution





The code above gives \(k_1 \approx 0.349\) and \(k_2 \approx 0.523\). Mode \(n\) is unstable for \(n\pi/k_2 < L < n\pi/k_1\):

\(n = 1\): \(6.01 < L < 8.99\),
\(n = 2\): \(12.02 < L < 17.99\),
\(n = 3\): \(18.03 < L < 26.98\).

No mode is unstable for \(L \le 6.01\), for \(8.99 \le L \le 12.02\), and in the narrow gap \(17.99 \le L \le 18.03\). Beyond that the intervals overlap. Small domains and some intermediate sizes stay uniform even though the Turing conditions hold (Murray 2003, sec. 2.5).

title: Gierer-Meinhardt Model in 1D
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Gierer and Meinhardt (1972).
Recommended: Murray (2003), Sections 2.3 to 2.6.
The Gierer-Meinhardt model is an activator-inhibitor system that produces spatial patterns when diffusion and reaction act together (Gierer and Meinhardt 1972). In this laboratory you build a 1D solver for it and compare the simulation with the Turing analysis of the previous page.
In the ODE sessions, solve_ivp() handled time integration for a short state vector. Here the state is a field sampled on a grid, so you write the update rule yourself: build the Laplacian, evaluate the reactions, advance with explicit Euler, and enforce the boundary conditions.

title: Gierer-Meinhardt Model in 1D
text:
The Model
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} &= \Delta u + \gamma \left(a - b u + \frac{u^2}{v}\right), \\
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} &= d\,\Delta v + \gamma \left(u^2 - v\right),
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
on \((0, L)\) with zero-flux (Neumann) boundary conditions.

\(u(x,t)\) is the activator. Through the term \(u^2 / v\), a local increase in \(u\) reinforces its own production.
\(v(x,t)\) is the inhibitor. Larger \(v\) reduces the ratio \(u^2 / v\) and suppresses activation.
\(a\) is a baseline source of \(u\) and \(b\) is its linear decay rate.
\(\gamma\) sets the reaction rate relative to diffusion.
\(d\) is the diffusion ratio. The activator diffuses with coefficient \(1\), so \(d > 1\) means the inhibitor spreads faster.

The homogeneous steady state is \(u_* = (a+1)/b\), \(v_* = u_*^2\) (see Linearization). This is the flat state you test for pattern formation.
In short, the activator builds local peaks, and the inhibitor spreads the suppressing signal over a wider region.

title: Gierer-Meinhardt Model in 1D
text:
What Turing Instability Means Here
Turing instability does not mean the model explodes. It means the flat state is stable to uniform perturbations but unstable to some spatially varying ones (Turing 1952).

If every point is nudged in the same way, the system returns to \((u_*, v_*)\).
If one region is nudged above its neighbours, that difference can grow into a pattern.







NoteDoes no Turing instability mean that the inhibitor dominates?





Not necessarily. It means the balance between activation, inhibition, and diffusion does not selectively amplify spatial modes. The inhibitor may be too strong, the activator too weak, the inhibitor may diffuse too slowly (small \(d\)), or the steady state may already be unstable for reasons unrelated to diffusion (for example \(\operatorname{tr} J > 0\)).



Diffusion does not only smooth the field. For suitable reaction parameters, a fast-diffusing inhibitor makes a subset of spatial perturbations grow instead of decay.

title: Gierer-Meinhardt Model in 1D
text:
What the Modes Mean
The instability does not amplify every spatial perturbation equally. On a finite domain with fixed boundary conditions, only certain spatial shapes are natural building blocks. These are the modes. For Neumann conditions on \([0, L]\) they are \(\cos(n\pi x/L)\), \(n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) (Laplacian Eigenmodes).

Mode \(0\) is flat, with no spatial variation.
Mode \(1\) has the longest non-constant wavelength the domain allows.
Mode \(2\) oscillates twice as fast in space, mode \(3\) three times as fast.
Higher modes have shorter wavelengths and finer structure.

A mode is unstable when a tiny perturbation with that shape grows in the linearized system. The leading mode has the largest growth rate, so it usually sets the early spacing of the pattern. Later, the nonlinear dynamics can merge peaks, saturate amplitudes, or shift the final profile. That is why the leading mode predicts the early pattern best, even if the long-time state looks different.
