title: Module 4: Space and Pattern Formation
text: This module adds space to the dynamics of Modules 1 to 3. You study reaction-diffusion equations, derive the conditions under which diffusion destabilizes a uniform state (Turing 1952; Britton 2003, chap. 7; Murray 2003), and build finite-difference solvers for the Gierer-Meinhardt and Gray-Scott models in one and two dimensions (Gierer and Meinhardt 1972; Pearson 1993). Every simulation is checked against the linear theory and against the stability and convergence limits of the numerical scheme. The module closes with the question of what reaction-diffusion models do and do not show about real tissue (Kondo and Miura 2010).

title: Module 4: Space and Pattern Formation
text:
Why Not scipy.integrate.solve_ivp?
In Modules 1 and 2, solve_ivp() handled the time integration because the state was a short ODE vector. Here the main numerical work is different. You discretize space first, update every grid point at every step, and enforce the boundary conditions yourself after each step. That is why this module uses explicit Euler loops.






TipScripts or notebooks?



Use notebooks to test stencils, plot snapshots, or inspect intermediate arrays. Use Python scripts for smooth animations. If your 1D solver still feels shaky, fix it before you start the 2D pages: the 2D code is much easier once the 1D stencil and Euler update are routine.








Note



Explicit Euler is simple and transparent, but it is only conditionally stable. If a simulation explodes immediately, reduce dt, increase dx, or test on a smaller grid first (Time-Step Stability).

title: Gray-Scott: Sliders
text: This page finishes the interactive simulator of Gray-Scott: Interaction. You add sliders for \(d_1\), \(d_2\), \(f\), and \(k\), and make the animation respect the pause flag. As before, the handlers use nonlocal, so they live inside one function that owns uv, pause, and the parameters. This page is an optional extension.

title: Gray-Scott: Sliders
text:
Add Sliders for the Parameters






NoteExercise



Read the slider values into the model parameters and pause the simulation.
from matplotlib.widgets import Slider

ax_d1 = ax_sliders.inset_axes([0.0, 0.8, 0.8, 0.1])
ax_d2 = ax_sliders.inset_axes([0.0, 0.6, 0.8, 0.1])
ax_f = ax_sliders.inset_axes([0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 0.1])
ax_k = ax_sliders.inset_axes([0.0, 0.2, 0.8, 0.1])

slider_d1 = Slider(ax_d1, "D1", 0.01, 0.2, valinit=d1, valstep=0.01)
slider_d2 = Slider(ax_d2, "D2", 0.01, 0.2, valinit=d2, valstep=0.01)
slider_f = Slider(ax_f, "F", 0.01, 0.09, valinit=f, valstep=0.001)
slider_k = Slider(ax_k, "k", 0.04, 0.07, valinit=k, valstep=0.001)

def update_sliders(_):
    # TODO: read the slider values into d1, d2, f, and k
    # TODO: pause the simulation so the new pattern is easier to inspect

slider_d1.on_changed(update_sliders)
slider_d2.on_changed(update_sliders)
slider_f.on_changed(update_sliders)
slider_k.on_changed(update_sliders)








TipSolution





def update_sliders(_):
    nonlocal d1, d2, f, k, pause
    d1 = slider_d1.val
    d2 = slider_d2.val
    f = slider_f.val
    k = slider_k.val
    pause = True

title: Gray-Scott: Sliders
text:
Put It Together
Inside your animation callback, respect the pause flag before advancing the PDE.
def update_frame(_):
    nonlocal uv
    if pause:
        return [im]

    for _ in range(anim_speed):
        uv = uv + gray_scott_pde(0, uv, d1=d1, d2=d2, f=f, k=k) * dt

    im.set_array(uv[1])
    return [im]
This setup is enough to create your own Gray-Scott experiments. Try drawing thin lines, large blobs, or repeated point sources and see which parameter sets erase the perturbation and which ones amplify it.






Tip



Reference code is available in amlab/pdes_2d/gray_scott.py. Run it with python -m amlab.pdes_2d.gray_scott.


Return to the assignment to complete Parts 3 and 4.

title: Gray-Scott: Sliders
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



You move the slider for \(d_1\) from \(0.1\) to \(0.2\) while keeping \(dx = 1\) and \(dt = 2\). What happens to the simulation, and why?








TipSolution





It blows up. The 2D explicit Euler bound is \(dt \le dx^2/(4 d_1)\), which drops from \(2.5\) to \(1.25\), so \(dt = 2\) is now unstable and a grid-scale checkerboard grows. Reduce \(dt\) below \(1.25\) when you increase \(d_1\) (Time-Step Stability).

title: Linearization
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Britton (2003), Chapter 7, Section 7.2 (pp. 207 to 208): the uniform steady state, the perturbation \(\hat u\) and its linearization with the Jacobian \(J^*\).
Recommended: Murray (2003), Chapter 2, Section 2.3, and Turing (1952), Section 6 (the marginal reaction rates \(a, b, c, d\), which are the entries of \(J\)).
A pattern starts as a small perturbation of a spatially uniform state. To decide whether that perturbation grows, you linearize the reaction-diffusion system around the uniform state (Murray 2003, sec. 2.3).

title: Linearization
text:
Homogeneous Steady States
Take the scaled two-species system
\[
\partial_t w = D\,\Delta w + \gamma R(w), \qquad w = \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix}, \quad D = \operatorname{diag}(1, d), \quad R = \begin{pmatrix} f \\ g \end{pmatrix}.
\]
A homogeneous steady state is a constant \(w_* = (u_*, v_*)\) with \(R(w_*) = 0\). Since \(\Delta w_* = 0\), it solves the PDE for every choice of Neumann or periodic boundary conditions. Britton chooses zero-flux conditions for this analysis partly because they are natural and partly because they are passive and unlikely to cause a pattern themselves. Dirichlet conditions with the value \(w_*\), or any other conditions compatible with the constant solution, would also do (Britton 2003, sec. 7.2).

title: Linearization
text:
The Linearized System
Write \(w = w_* + \eta\) with \(\eta\) small and keep only linear terms:
\[
\partial_t \eta = D\,\Delta \eta + \gamma J \eta,
\tag{1}\]
which is Britton’s linearized system with his \(\alpha\) replaced by \(\gamma\) (Britton 2003, Equation 7.2.3), and where
\[
J =
\begin{pmatrix}
f_u & f_v \\
g_u & g_v
\end{pmatrix}_{(u_*, v_*)}
\tag{2}\]
is the Jacobian of the kinetics at the steady state. Two limits are worth keeping in mind.

Without diffusion, \(\dot\eta = \gamma J\eta\). Stability is decided by \(\operatorname{tr} J\) and \(\det J\), as for the 2D systems of Module 1.
With diffusion, the Laplacian couples neighbouring points. The page Laplacian Eigenmodes shows how to decouple it.

title: Linearization
text:
The Gierer-Meinhardt Steady State
For the Gierer-Meinhardt kinetics (Gierer and Meinhardt 1972),
\[
f(u, v) = a - b u + \frac{u^2}{v}, \qquad g(u, v) = u^2 - v, \qquad a, b > 0.
\]
From \(g = 0\) you get \(v_* = u_*^2\). Substituting into \(f = 0\) gives \(a - b u_* + 1 = 0\), so
\[
u_* = \frac{a+1}{b}, \qquad v_* = \left(\frac{a+1}{b}\right)^2.
\tag{3}\]
At a general point the Jacobian is
\[
J(u, v) =
\begin{pmatrix}
-b + 2u/v & -u^2/v^2 \\
2u & -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
At \((u_*, v_*)\) this becomes
\[
f_u = \frac{b(1-a)}{1+a}, \qquad f_v = -\frac{b^2}{(1+a)^2}, \qquad g_u = \frac{2(1+a)}{b}, \qquad g_v = -1.
\tag{4}\]






NoteExercise



Compute \(\operatorname{tr} J\) and \(\det J\) at the Gierer-Meinhardt steady state. For which \(a\) is the steady state stable without diffusion when \(b = 1\)?








TipSolution





\(\det J = f_u g_v - f_v g_u = -\frac{b(1-a)}{1+a} + \frac{2b}{1+a} = b > 0\).
\(\operatorname{tr} J = \frac{b(1-a)}{1+a} - 1\). For \(b = 1\) this equals \(-\frac{2a}{1+a}\), which is negative for every \(a > 0\). So with \(b = 1\) the steady state is a stable node or focus of the kinetics for all \(a > 0\).

title: Linearization
text:
Checking the Algebra Numerically
The helper amlab.turing.gierer_meinhardt_jacobian implements Equation 4. A finite-difference Jacobian of the kinetics gives the same entries.

import numpy as np

from amlab.turing import gierer_meinhardt_jacobian, gierer_meinhardt_steady_state

a, b = 0.40, 1.00
u_s, v_s = gierer_meinhardt_steady_state(a, b)


def kinetics(u, v):
    return np.array([a - b * u + u**2 / v, u**2 - v])


h = 1e-6
jac_fd = np.column_stack(
    [
        (kinetics(u_s + h, v_s) - kinetics(u_s - h, v_s)) / (2 * h),
        (kinetics(u_s, v_s + h) - kinetics(u_s, v_s - h)) / (2 * h),
    ]
)
jac_exact = np.array(gierer_meinhardt_jacobian(a, b)).reshape(2, 2)
print("steady state:", (u_s, v_s))
print("max difference:", np.abs(jac_fd - jac_exact).max())
print("det J =", np.linalg.det(jac_exact))

steady state: (1.4, 1.9599999999999997)
max difference: 2.525508691064715e-10
det J = 1.0000000000000002

title: SIR Simulation
SIR Simulation
text:
Implement the SIR Dynamics
The update is synchronous: compute all changes from the old state, then apply them.






NoteExercise



Write step_sir(G, beta, mu), one synchronous step of the SIR update. It differs from step_sis in one place: an infected node that recovers moves to “R”, and “R” nodes never change.
def step_sir(G, beta, mu):
    # TODO: read current states from G.nodes[u]["state"]
    # TODO: build new_state dict with values in {"S","I","R"}
    # TODO: write new_state back via nx.set_node_attributes
    return G








TipSolution






def step_sir(G, beta, mu):
    current = {u: G.nodes[u]["state"] for u in G.nodes()}
    new_state = current.copy()

    for u in G.nodes():
        if current[u] == "S":
            m = sum(1 for v in G.neighbors(u) if current[v] == "I")
            if m > 0:
                p_infect = 1 - (1 - beta) ** m
                if np.random.random() < p_infect:
                    new_state[u] = "I"

        elif current[u] == "I":
            if np.random.random() < mu:
                new_state[u] = "R"

        else:
            # "R" stays "R"
            pass

    nx.set_node_attributes(G, new_state, "state")
    return G










NoteExercise



Wrap step_sir into a simulator. Compared to SIS, you track all three counts: \(S(t), I(t), R(t)\). Stop early when no node is infected, since nothing can change after that.
def run_sir(G, beta, mu, steps=100, initial_infected=5, seed=SEED):
    # TODO
    return S_counts, I_counts, R_counts








TipSolution






def run_sir(G, beta, mu, steps=100, initial_infected=5, seed=SEED):
    H = G.copy()

    # Make the whole run reproducible (step_sir uses np.random.random)
    np.random.seed(seed)

    initialize_state(H, initial_infected=initial_infected, seed=seed)

    def counts(H):
        S = sum(H.nodes[u]["state"] == "S" for u in H.nodes())
        I = sum(H.nodes[u]["state"] == "I" for u in H.nodes())
        R = sum(H.nodes[u]["state"] == "R" for u in H.nodes())
        return S, I, R

    S0, I0, R0 = counts(H)
    S_counts = [S0]
    I_counts = [I0]
    R_counts = [R0]

    for _ in range(steps):
        if I_counts[-1] == 0:
            break
        step_sir(H, beta=beta, mu=mu)
        S, I, R = counts(H)
        S_counts.append(S)
        I_counts.append(I)
        R_counts.append(R)

    return S_counts, I_counts, R_counts

title: SIR Simulation
text:
Run and Visualize
The “epidemic curve” in SIR typically shows a single peak in \(I(t)\) and then decay to zero.








Figure 1: SIR epidemic curve (fractions of S, I, R over time) on one network realization.

title: SIR Simulation
text:
Key Questions to Answer
Here are two precise, testable questions that are specific to SIR:

Can the network become fully infected? That is, does there exist a time \(t\) such that \(I(t)=N\)?
Can the network become fully “healed”? That is, does there exist a time \(t\) such that \(I(t)=0\)?

In SIR, the second question has a clean answer:

Yes. For a finite graph with \(\mu>0\), you eventually reach \(I(t)=0\) and then you are stuck forever (absorbing state).

The first question depends on \((\beta,\mu)\) and the network. It can happen transiently, but it is not an absorbing state.






NoteExercise



Answer these questions, using Figure 1 and your own runs:

In SIR, is “fully healed” the same as “everyone is susceptible again”? Why not?
What does “final epidemic size” mean here? (Hint: look at \(R(\infty)\).)
Can you have an epidemic with a large peak but small final size? Or vice versa?
Compare two graphs with the same \(N\) and similar average degree: which features (hubs, clustering, path length) do you expect to increase \(R(\infty)\)?









TipSolution






No. When \(I = 0\) every node is either S or R. The recovered nodes stay immune, so the network does not return to its initial state. In SIS, by contrast, \(I = 0\) means everyone is susceptible again.
The final epidemic size is \(R(\infty)/N\), the fraction of nodes that were ever infected, including the initial ones. You read it from the last value of the R curve once \(I = 0\).
A large peak with a small final size is impossible: every node that is infected at the peak ends in R, so \(R(\infty) \ge \max_t I(t)\). The reverse is possible. On a ring or a lattice with few shortcuts the infection travels as a slow front: only a few nodes are infected at any time, but the front can eventually reach most of the network.
Hubs and short paths increase \(R(\infty)\). The SIR threshold \(T_c = \langle k \rangle / (\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle)\) decreases when the degree distribution is broader (Newman 2002), and short paths let the outbreak reach distant parts of the network before it dies out. High clustering tends to decrease \(R(\infty)\), because many infection attempts hit neighbours that are already infected or recovered.

title: SIR Simulation
text:
What’s Next?
Compare SIS and SIR: how does permanent immunity change the long-run outcome? The next page asks when an epidemic can spread at all.

title: Degree and Clustering
text:
Degree
The degree \(k\) of a node is the number of edges connected to it. In an undirected graph, the degree of a node is simply the number of neighbors it has.

# Degree of a node
print("Degree of 'bread':", G_foods.degree("bread"))

Degree of 'bread': 3


The average degree of an undirected graph is given by:
\[\langle k \rangle = \frac{2E}{N}\]
where \(E\) is the number of edges and \(N\) is the number of nodes.

# Average degree of the graph
ls_degrees = [G_foods.degree(node) for node in G_foods.nodes()]
avg_degree = sum(ls_degrees) / len(ls_degrees)
print("Average degree:", avg_degree)

Average degree: 2.5714285714285716



Degrees in Directed Graphs
In a directed graph, you distinguish between in-degree (number of incoming edges) and out-degree (number of outgoing edges).

print("In-degree of 'antelope' (number of prey):", D_food_chain.in_degree("antelope"))
print("Out-degree of 'antelope' (number of predators):", D_food_chain.out_degree("antelope"))

In-degree of 'antelope' (number of prey): 1
Out-degree of 'antelope' (number of predators): 2

title: Degree and Clustering
text:
Clustering Coefficient
Many real networks have triangles: if A is connected to B and C, there is a higher-than-random chance that B is also connected to C (Watts and Strogatz 1998; Newman 2018). This tendency is captured by the clustering coefficient.
For an undirected graph, the local clustering coefficient of node \(i\) is:
\[
C_i = \frac{2T_i}{k_i(k_i - 1)}
\]
where \(k_i\) is the degree of node \(i\), and \(T_i\) is the number of triangles that include node \(i\). If \(k_i < 2\), define \(C_i = 0\).
In the food graph, \(C_{\text{bread}} = 1/3\): “bread” has three neighbors, and only one neighbor-pair is connected.
The average clustering coefficient is:
\[
C = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N C_i.
\]
In NetworkX:

nx.clustering(G) returns \(C_i\) for every node.
nx.average_clustering(G) returns the average \(C\).

You will use \(C\) later to compare random vs small-world vs scale-free synthetic networks.

# Local clustering coefficient for each node
clustering = nx.clustering(G_foods)
print("Local clustering:")
for node, c in clustering.items():
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

print("Average clustering:", nx.average_clustering(G_foods))

# Another common global measure is transitivity
# (ratio of triangles to connected triples)
print("Transitivity:", nx.transitivity(G_foods))

Local clustering:
  bread: 0.333
  cheese: 1.000
  chocolate: 0.167
  cured ham: 0.333
  cookies: 1.000
  milk: 1.000
  watermelon: 0.000
Average clustering: 0.5476190476190477
Transitivity: 0.375








NoteExercise



Compute the local clustering coefficient of “chocolate” by hand from the drawing of G_foods. Then check your answer with nx.clustering.








TipSolution





“chocolate” has four neighbours (bread, cookies, milk and watermelon), so there are \(4 \cdot 3 / 2 = 6\) neighbour pairs. Only cookies and milk are connected, so \(C_{\text{chocolate}} = 1/6 \approx 0.167\).

print(nx.clustering(G_foods, "chocolate"))

0.16666666666666666

title: Drawing Graphs
text:
Visualization
Printing the graph object gives you a summary of its structure, but it does not show the connections. To visualize the graph, you can use the draw() function from networkx, which uses Matplotlib to display the graph.

# Draw the graph
nx.draw(
    G,
    with_labels=True,  # show node labels (IDs)
    node_color='lightblue',  # color of the nodes (vertices)
    edge_color='gray',  # color of the edges (links)
    node_size=2000,  # size of the nodes (vertices)
    font_size=12  # size of the labels (IDs)
    )
plt.show()









Layouts
The draw() function has a pos parameter that lets you specify the layout of the graph. A layout is a way to position the nodes in the graph for visualization. networkx provides several built-in layouts, such as spring_layout, circular_layout and shell_layout.
Circular layout arranges the nodes in a circle. You can control the distance between the nodes using the scale parameter, higher values will make the nodes farther apart.

# Use the circular layout for visualization
pos = nx.circular_layout(G, scale=2)  # scale controls the distance between the nodes
nx.draw(
    G,
    pos=pos,  # specify the layout
    with_labels=True,
    node_color='lightblue',
    edge_color='gray',
    node_size=2000,
    font_size=12
    )
plt.show()








Spring layout uses a force-directed algorithm to position the nodes in a way that minimizes edge crossings and evenly distributes the nodes. You can control the distance between the nodes using the k parameter, which is a scaling factor for the optimal distance between nodes. Higher values will make the nodes farther apart. You can also control the number of iterations of the algorithm using the iterations parameter.

# Use the spring layout for visualization
pos = nx.spring_layout(G, k=0.5, iterations=20)
nx.draw(
    G,
    pos=pos,  # specify the layout
    with_labels=True,
    node_color='lightblue',
    edge_color='gray',
    node_size=2000,
    font_size=12
    )
plt.show()

nlist = [["Spain", "Portugal", "France", "Italy"], ["Netherlands", "Germany", "USA", "Canada"]]

title: Configuration Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Newman (2003), Section 4.2 (generalized random graphs and the configuration model), up to the clustering coefficient of Eq. (31).
Recommended: Molloy and Reed (1995) for the giant component criterion, Motter and Lai (2002) for an example of networks generated from a prescribed degree distribution.
The Erdős-Rényi model fixes only the mean degree. Real networks have a degree distribution of their own, and many of the quantities of this module depend on it: the giant component after failures, the epidemic threshold and the cascade size all contain \(\langle k^2 \rangle\). To study the effect of the degree distribution alone, we need a random graph in which the degrees are exactly those of a given network and everything else is random. This is the configuration model, and its sampling by degree-preserving randomisation is the standard null model of network science (Newman 2003, sec. 4.2).

title: Configuration Model
text:
Definition
Given a degree sequence \((k_1, \dots, k_N)\) with an even sum, give node \(i\) exactly \(k_i\) “stubs” (half-edges). Pair all the stubs uniformly at random. Every graph with this degree sequence appears with the same probability, as a multigraph, that is, a graph that may contain self-loops and parallel edges (Newman 2003, sec. 4.2). Two consequences are used throughout the module:

Follow a random edge to the node at its other end. That node has degree \(k\) with probability \(k p_k / \langle k \rangle\), and so \(\langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle\) neighbours on average, counting the edge we arrived by. Its excess degree (the number of other edges) has mean \(\kappa - 1\) with \(\kappa = \langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle\).
A branching process with mean offspring \(\kappa - 1\) grows if \(\kappa > 2\), which is the criterion of Molloy and Reed (Molloy and Reed 1995) used in Robustness and Percolation.

The function below implements the definition in three lines. NetworkX has the same model as nx.configuration_model(degree_sequence), which returns a MultiGraph.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import shortest_path

SEED = 7


def stub_matching(degrees, rng):
    """Edge list of the configuration model: shuffle the stubs and pair them."""
    stubs = np.repeat(np.arange(len(degrees)), degrees)
    rng.shuffle(stubs)
    return list(zip(stubs[::2], stubs[1::2]))


def avg_path_length(G, n_src=600, seed=0):
    """Average distance in the largest component, from at most n_src random sources."""
    H = G.subgraph(max(nx.connected_components(G), key=len))
    nodes = list(H)
    A = nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(H, nodelist=nodes, format="csr")
    # SciPy's csgraph routines require int32 CSR index buffers in this environment.
    A.indices = A.indices.astype(np.int32)
    A.indptr = A.indptr.astype(np.int32)
    n = len(nodes)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    src = np.arange(n, dtype=np.int32) if n <= n_src else rng.choice(n, n_src, replace=False).astype(np.int32)
    return shortest_path(A, unweighted=True, indices=src).sum() / (len(src) * (n - 1))


enron = nx.Graph(nx.read_edgelist("data/ia-enron-only/ia-enron-only.edges"))
flights = nx.Graph(nx.read_graphml("data/openflights/openflights_usa.graphml.gz"))
for G in (enron, flights):
    G.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(G))

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
sequences = {
    "Poisson, <k> = 6 (N = 5000)": np.random.default_rng(1).poisson(6, 5000),
    "Barabási-Albert, m = 3 (N = 5000)": np.array([d for _, d in nx.barabasi_albert_graph(5000, 3, seed=1).degree()]),
    "Enron e-mail (N = 143)": np.array([d for _, d in enron.degree()]),
    "US flights (N = 546)": np.array([d for _, d in flights.degree()]),
}
print(f"{'degree sequence':<36}{'E':>7}{'loops':>7}{'parallel':>10}{'lost (%)':>10}")
for name, degs in sequences.items():
    degs = degs.copy()
    if degs.sum() % 2:
        degs[0] += 1
    edges = stub_matching(degs, rng)
    M = nx.MultiGraph()
    M.add_nodes_from(range(len(degs)))
    M.add_edges_from(edges)
    assert [M.degree(i) for i in range(len(degs))] == list(degs)   # degrees are exact (a loop counts twice)
    loops = nx.number_of_selfloops(M)
    S = nx.Graph(M)
    S.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(S))
    parallel = M.number_of_edges() - loops - S.number_of_edges()   # edges merged into an existing one
    print(f"{name:<36}{len(edges):>7}{loops:>7}{parallel:>10}{100 * (loops + parallel) / len(edges):>10.1f}")

degree sequence                           E  loops  parallel  lost (%)
Poisson, <k> = 6 (N = 5000)           14973      1        11       0.1
Barabási-Albert, m = 3 (N = 5000)     14991      6        56       0.4
Enron e-mail (N = 143)                  623      1        44       7.2
US flights (N = 546)                   2781     20       446      16.8


The degrees are exact. Every degree sequence produces some self-loops and parallel edges, and their share grows with the heterogeneity of the sequence: two hubs \(i\) and \(j\) are expected to be joined by \(k_i k_j / 2E\) edges, which is larger than one when both degrees are large. Removing the loops and merging parallel edges (“erasing”) gives a simple graph, but it no longer has the original degrees. For a sparse and homogeneous sequence the loss is small; for the flights sequence it is a sizeable fraction of the edges.

title: Configuration Model
text:
Degree-preserving randomisation
To sample simple graphs with exactly the degrees of an observed network, start from the network and repeat a double-edge swap: pick two edges \((u,v)\) and \((x,y)\) and replace them by \((u,x)\) and \((v,y)\), unless one of these edges already exists. Each swap keeps every degree, so after many swaps the graph is a sample of the simple-graph version of the configuration model. In NetworkX the function is nx.double_edge_swap(G, nswap, max_tries). How many swaps are enough? Figure 1 follows the clustering of the two data networks as a function of the number of swaps in units of \(E\).

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
swaps_E = np.array([0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10])
for ax, (name, G) in zip(axes, [("Enron e-mail", enron), ("US flights", flights)]):
    E = G.number_of_edges()
    curves = []
    for r in range(3):
        H = G.copy()
        values, done = [], 0
        for s in swaps_E:
            todo = int(s * E) - done
            if todo > 0:
                nx.double_edge_swap(H, nswap=todo, max_tries=100 * E, seed=SEED + r + done)
                done += todo
            values.append(nx.average_clustering(H))
        assert sorted(d for _, d in H.degree()) == sorted(d for _, d in G.degree())
        curves.append(values)
    ax.semilogx(np.maximum(swaps_E, 0.03), np.mean(curves, axis=0), "o-")
    ax.set_xlabel("swaps / E")
    ax.set_ylabel("average clustering C")
    ax.set_title(name)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print("the assertion inside the loop checks that the degree sequence never changes")







Figure 1: Average clustering coefficient of the Enron and US flights networks during degree-preserving randomisation, against the number of double-edge swaps in units of the number of edges E. Lines are averages over 3 runs; the starting values (plotted at 0.03) are the clustering of the original networks. The Enron curve flattens after about E swaps. The flights curve drops in the first 0.1E swaps, then recovers slowly and is flat from about 2E swaps on.





the assertion inside the loop checks that the degree sequence never changes


The Enron clustering levels off after about \(E\) swaps. The flights clustering is not monotone: the first swaps remove the triangles, and then it recovers slowly as the hubs rearrange, to a plateau from about \(2E\) swaps on. We use \(10E\) swaps below. (The plot checks only one quantity; other properties may need more swaps.)

title: Configuration Model
section: How much of the clustering is explained by the degrees?
text:
How much of the clustering is explained by the degrees?
A standard question compares the clustering of a real network with that of a random graph. The answer depends on which random graph. The table compares each data network with two nulls: the Erdős-Rényi graph \(G(N, E)\), which keeps only the number of nodes and edges, and the degree-preserving randomisation, which also keeps every degree. It shows the average of the local clustering coefficients, the transitivity (three times the number of triangles divided by the number of connected triples (Newman 2003, Eq. (3)), nx.transitivity), the average path length and the degree assortativity coefficient \(r\) (the correlation between the degrees at the two ends of an edge).



Table 1: Real networks against two null models, averaged over 5 realisations of each null. C is the average local clustering, T the transitivity, L the average path length in the largest component and r the degree assortativity coefficient. Enron: 143 nodes and 623 edges; US flights: 546 nodes and 2781 edges.


def profile(G):
    return dict(C=nx.average_clustering(G), T=nx.transitivity(G), L=avg_path_length(G),
                r=nx.degree_assortativity_coefficient(G))


print(f"{'network / null':<28}{'C':>8}{'T':>8}{'L':>7}{'r':>8}")
for name, G in [("Enron", enron), ("US flights", flights)]:
    N, E = G.number_of_nodes(), G.number_of_edges()
    er = [profile(nx.gnm_random_graph(N, E, seed=SEED + s)) for s in range(5)]
    sw = []
    for s in range(5):
        H = G.copy()
        nx.double_edge_swap(H, nswap=10 * E, max_tries=100 * E, seed=SEED + s)
        sw.append(profile(H))
    for label, rows in [("real", [profile(G)]), ("G(N, E)", er), ("degree-preserving", sw)]:
        m = {key: np.mean([row[key] for row in rows]) for key in rows[0]}
        print(f"{name + ' ' + label:<28}{m['C']:>8.3f}{m['T']:>8.3f}{m['L']:>7.2f}{m['r']:>8.2f}")

network / null                     C       T      L       r
Enron real                     0.434   0.359   2.97   -0.02
Enron G(N, E)                  0.062   0.063   2.52   -0.02
Enron degree-preserving        0.107   0.114   2.55   -0.05
US flights real                0.493   0.313   3.20   -0.34
US flights G(N, E)             0.018   0.018   2.96   -0.01
US flights degree-preserving   0.428   0.229   2.67   -0.40




Two lessons follow.

The conclusion depends on the null. The Enron network has \(C = 0.43\) against \(0.06\) for \(G(N,E)\) and \(0.11\) for the degree-preserving null: the clustering is high even after the degrees are taken into account, which is consistent with a triadic-closure mechanism. The flights network has \(C = 0.49\) against \(0.02\) for \(G(N,E)\), but \(0.43\) for the degree-preserving null: most of the local clustering comes from the degree sequence. The airports of degree 2 or 3 have a mean local clustering of 0.79 in the data; when such a small node is attached to two large hubs, the hubs are very likely to be linked to each other, even in a random graph with the same degrees. The transitivity tells a more cautious story, with a smaller excess over the null.
Simple graphs with hubs are disassortative. The degree-preserving null of the flights network has \(r \approx -0.4\), close to the real value, because hubs cannot have many parallel edges and so are joined mostly to small nodes. The assortativity of the flights network is largely explained by the degree sequence as well.

title: Configuration Model
section: A formula for the clustering of the configuration model
text:
A formula for the clustering of the configuration model
For the configuration model, the transitivity is
\[
T = \frac{1}{N}\,\frac{\big(\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle\big)^2}{\langle k \rangle^3},
\tag{1}\]
the value \(\langle k \rangle / N\) of the Poisson random graph times a factor that grows with the width of the degree distribution (Newman 2003, Eq. (31)). It goes to zero as \(1/N\) for a fixed distribution, unless \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) grows with \(N\). The next chunk tests the formula on random power-law sequences (\(p_k \propto k^{-\gamma}\), minimum degree \(k_{\min}\), maximum degree \(\sqrt{3N}\)) and on the two data networks.

def power_law_sequence(N, gamma, kmin, kmax, rng):
    ks = np.arange(kmin, kmax + 1)
    p = ks ** (-gamma)
    s = rng.choice(ks, N, p=p / p.sum())
    if s.sum() % 2:
        s[0] += 1
    return s


def eq_cm(degs):
    k = np.asarray(degs, dtype=float)
    return ((k**2).mean() - k.mean()) ** 2 / (len(k) * k.mean() ** 3)


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
print(f"{'sequence':<26}{'N':>7}{'k_max':>7}{'formula':>9}{'measured':>10}")
for gamma, kmin in [(3.0, 3), (2.5, 2)]:
    for N in (2000, 8000, 32000):
        s = power_law_sequence(N, gamma, kmin, int(np.sqrt(3 * N)), rng)
        T = []
        for r in range(3):
            G = nx.Graph(nx.configuration_model(list(s), seed=SEED + r))
            G.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(G))
            T.append(nx.transitivity(G))
        print(f"{f'gamma = {gamma}, kmin = {kmin}':<26}{N:>7}{s.max():>7}{eq_cm(s):>9.4f}{np.mean(T):>10.4f}")
for name, G in [("Enron e-mail", enron), ("US flights", flights)]:
    degs = [d for _, d in G.degree()]
    H = G.copy()
    nx.double_edge_swap(H, nswap=10 * G.number_of_edges(), max_tries=10**7, seed=SEED)
    print(f"{name:<26}{len(G):>7}{max(degs):>7}{eq_cm(degs):>9.4f}{nx.transitivity(H):>10.4f}"
          f"   (sqrt(2E) = {np.sqrt(2 * G.number_of_edges()):.0f})")

sequence                        N  k_max  formula  measured
gamma = 3.0, kmin = 3        2000     63   0.0054    0.0049
gamma = 3.0, kmin = 3        8000    125   0.0020    0.0018
gamma = 3.0, kmin = 3       32000    219   0.0007    0.0007
gamma = 2.5, kmin = 2        2000     68   0.0098    0.0089
gamma = 2.5, kmin = 2        8000    148   0.0071    0.0059
gamma = 2.5, kmin = 2       32000    304   0.0031    0.0027
Enron e-mail                  143     42   0.1141    0.1167   (sqrt(2E) = 35)
US flights                    546    153   0.5141    0.2277   (sqrt(2E) = 75)


For the synthetic sequences the formula is accurate to within about 20%. For the Enron network it agrees closely with the degree-preserving null. For the flights network it overestimates by a factor of more than two. In that network the largest degree (153) is twice \(\sqrt{2E} \approx 75\): hubs of that size would need parallel edges, which a simple graph does not allow, so the simple null has fewer triangles around them than the multigraph formula assumes. The formula is a result for \(N \to \infty\) with bounded \(k_{\max}/\sqrt{N}\); use the numerical null whenever the largest degrees are comparable to \(\sqrt{2E}\).

title: Configuration Model
text:
Does clustering matter for spreading?
The heterogeneous mean-field threshold of Epidemic Threshold uses only \(p_k\). The configuration model lets us test the effect of everything else. Take a clustered scale-free graph from Triadic Closure (\(N = 3000\), \(m = 3\), \(p_t = 0.9\)), randomise it with \(10E\) double-edge swaps, and run the discrete-time SIR model of SIR on Networks on both. The swapped graph has the same degrees and almost no triangles; it also loses any degree correlations of the original, so the comparison measures the effect of all the structure beyond the degrees.

from amlab.networks_spreading import run_sir_fast

G_hk = nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(3000, 3, 0.9, seed=2)
G_sw = G_hk.copy()
nx.double_edge_swap(G_sw, nswap=10 * G_sw.number_of_edges(), max_tries=10**7, seed=2)
print(f"C: clustered = {nx.average_clustering(G_hk):.2f}, randomised = {nx.average_clustering(G_sw):.3f}")

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
betas = [0.02, 0.03, 0.04]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.8))
for G, label in [(G_hk, "clustered (Holme-Kim)"), (G_sw, "degree-preserving randomisation")]:
    means, errs = [], []
    for beta in betas:
        sizes = np.array([run_sir_fast(G, beta, 0.2, initial_infected=5, rng=rng) for _ in range(400)])
        means.append(sizes.mean())
        errs.append(sizes.std() / np.sqrt(len(sizes)))
    ax.errorbar(betas, means, yerr=errs, fmt="o-", capsize=3, label=label)
    print(label, np.round(means, 3))
ax.set_xlabel(r"infection probability $\beta$")
ax.set_ylabel("final epidemic size")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

C: clustered = 0.52, randomised = 0.013
clustered (Holme-Kim) [0.012 0.07  0.2  ]
degree-preserving randomisation [0.027 0.134 0.268]








Figure 2: Mean final epidemic size (fraction of nodes ever infected) of the discrete-time SIR model with recovery probability 0.2 and 5 initial infected nodes, on a clustered Holme-Kim graph (N = 3000, m = 3, p_t = 0.9, C = 0.52) and on its degree-preserving randomisation (C = 0.01). 400 runs per point; error bars are one standard error.





At \(\beta = 0.02\) and \(0.03\), close to the threshold, the clustered network has a final size that is 0.4 to 0.5 times that of its degree-preserving randomisation; at \(\beta = 0.04\) the ratio is 0.75. Clustering wastes infection attempts: when two neighbours of an infected node are themselves neighbours, one of them may already have been infected through the other. The effect shrinks as the infection probability grows. The mean-field formula for \(\lambda_c\) has no term for it (Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015).






NoteExercise




Using the table of this page, compute for each data network the ratio between the real transitivity and the transitivity of the degree-preserving null. (b) A student states that “the flights network is clustered like a social network, so triadic closure must be at work”. Evaluate the statement with the two nulls.









TipSolution






Enron: \(0.359/0.114 \approx 3.1\). Flights: \(0.313/0.229 \approx 1.4\). (b) Against \(G(N,E)\) the average clustering of the flights network is 27 times larger, which looks like strong evidence. Against the degree-preserving null the local clustering is only 1.15 times larger (\(0.49\) against \(0.43\)) and the transitivity 1.4 times larger. Most of the apparent clustering is a consequence of the hubs, so the evidence for a triadic-closure mechanism is weak; the Enron network, with a factor of 3 in transitivity, is much stronger evidence. The right null for a statement about a mechanism is the one that keeps everything the mechanism is not supposed to explain.

How many edges are lost? How do the clustering and the largest degree of the simple graph compare with the original?

degs = [d for _, d in flights.degree()]
M = nx.configuration_model(degs, seed=1)
S = nx.Graph(M)
S.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(S))

With seed=1 the simple graph keeps 2293 of the 2781 edges (82%), because self-loops and merged parallel edges are lost, its largest degree is 95 instead of 153, and its average clustering is 0.19 against 0.49 for the original. This is why the degree-preserving swap is the better null for heterogeneous sequences.

title: Configuration Model
text:
What’s Next?
The configuration model is the setting in which the Molloy-Reed criterion and the heterogeneous mean-field threshold hold exactly. SIR and Percolation uses it to connect epidemic outbreaks to the robustness results of Robustness and Percolation.

title: PageRank
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Page et al. (1999), the original description of the algorithm.
Context: the centrality measures of Network Concepts and Centrality in NetworkX.
Degree centrality counts the links that point to a node. It treats every link equally, whether it comes from a hub or from an isolated page. PageRank applies the opposite principle: a node is important if it is linked by important nodes (Page et al. 1999). This looks circular, but it has a precise answer: the importance vector is the stationary distribution of a random walk on the directed graph. This page builds that answer step by step, computes it in three independent ways, and checks it against networkx.

title: PageRank
text:
The random surfer
Take a directed graph with \(n\) nodes (web pages) and an edge \(j \to i\) for each hyperlink from page \(j\) to page \(i\). A surfer sits on page \(j\) and follows one outgoing link chosen uniformly at random. If \(\mathbf{p}^{(t)} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the probability vector of the surfer’s position at step \(t\), then
\[
\mathbf{p}^{(t+1)} = P\,\mathbf{p}^{(t)}, \qquad
P_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1/\text{outdeg}(j) & \text{if } j \to i, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
\tag{1}\]
Each column of \(P\) is the distribution of the next page given the current page, so the columns sum to 1: \(P\) is column-stochastic. If the chain has a stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), it satisfies
\[
\boldsymbol{\pi} = P\,\boldsymbol{\pi}, \qquad
\pi_i = \sum_{j \to i} \frac{\pi_j}{\text{outdeg}(j)} .
\tag{2}\]
The second form is the principle in equations: page \(i\) receives rank from every page \(j\) that links to it, and each page \(j\) shares its own rank equally among its outgoing links. A link from a page with few outgoing links is worth more than a link from a page that links to everyone.

title: PageRank
text:
A five-page example
The graph below is the five-page example: \(A \to B\), \(A \to C\), \(B \to C\), \(C \to A\), \(D \to C\), \(E \to C\) and \(E \to D\). The out-degrees are 2, 1, 1, 1, 2 for \(A, \dots, E\). In NetworkX the function nx.to_numpy_array returns the matrix with \(A_{ij} = 1\) for an edge \(i \to j\), so the matrix of Equation 1 is \(P = A^{\top} D_{\text{out}}^{-1}\).

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

SEED = 7
alpha = 0.85

nodes = list("ABCDE")
G = nx.DiGraph([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("D", "C"), ("E", "C"), ("E", "D")])
n = len(nodes)

A = nx.to_numpy_array(G, nodelist=nodes)          # A[i, j] = 1 if i -> j
outdeg = A.sum(axis=1)
P = (A / outdeg[:, None]).T                        # column-stochastic matrix
print("out-degrees:", {v: int(d) for v, d in zip(nodes, outdeg)})
print("column sums of P:", P.sum(axis=0))

pos = {"A": (0, 1), "B": (1, 1), "D": (0, 0), "C": (1, 0), "E": (0.5, -0.8)}
pr = nx.pagerank(G, alpha=alpha, tol=1e-12)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
sizes = [6000 * pr[v] for v in nodes]
reciprocal = [("A", "C"), ("C", "A")]
nx.draw_networkx_edges(G, pos, ax=ax, edgelist=[("A", "C")], arrowsize=18, node_size=sizes,
                       arrowstyle="<|-|>")   # A -> C and C -> A drawn as one double-headed arrow
nx.draw_networkx_edges(G, pos, ax=ax, edgelist=[e for e in G.edges() if e not in reciprocal],
                       arrowsize=18, node_size=sizes)
nx.draw_networkx_nodes(G, pos, ax=ax, node_size=sizes, node_color="lightsteelblue")
nx.draw_networkx_labels(G, pos, ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print({v: round(pr[v], 4) for v in nodes})

out-degrees: {'A': 2, 'B': 1, 'C': 1, 'D': 1, 'E': 2}
column sums of P: [1. 1. 1. 1. 1.]








Figure 1: The five-page example. Node area is proportional to the PageRank with damping factor 0.85. Page C receives links from four pages and has the largest PageRank. Page A has a single incoming link, but it comes from C. Page E has no incoming links.





{'A': 0.3585, 'B': 0.1823, 'C': 0.3864, 'D': 0.0428, 'E': 0.03}

title: PageRank
text:
Why we need damping
On a real directed graph the chain of Equation 1 can fail in three ways:

Dangling nodes. A page with no outgoing links has a column of zeros in \(P\), so \(P\) is not stochastic: the surfer has nowhere to go.
Reducibility. The graph can contain parts the surfer enters but never leaves, or parts that cannot be reached at all. The stationary distribution is then not unique.
Periodicity. In a directed cycle the surfer’s position rotates forever and \(\mathbf{p}^{(t)}\) never converges.

The remedy is teleportation. With probability \(\alpha\) the surfer follows a link, and with probability \(1 - \alpha\) it jumps to a page chosen uniformly at random. The parameter \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\) is the damping factor, often \(\alpha = 0.85\). The transition matrix becomes
\[
P' = \alpha P + \frac{1-\alpha}{n}\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}, \qquad
P'_{ij} = \alpha P_{ij} + \frac{1-\alpha}{n},
\tag{3}\]
where \(\mathbf{1}\) is the vector of ones. Every entry of \(P'\) is positive, so the chain is irreducible and aperiodic and has a unique stationary distribution. The PageRank vector is the probability vector with \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = P'\boldsymbol{\pi}\) and \(\sum_i \pi_i = 1\).






ImportantDangling nodes need an extra rule



Equation 3 is column-stochastic only if \(P\) is. For a dangling node the standard rule is to replace its zero column by the uniform column \(\mathbf{1}/n\): a surfer stuck on a page teleports at once. NetworkX does this by default. The graph of this page has no dangling nodes, but the exercises and the large example below do.



Three ways to compute \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\)
Eigenvector. \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is the eigenvector of \(P'\) with eigenvalue 1, scaled to sum 1.
Linear system. Since \(\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\pi} = 1\), we have \(\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\pi} = \mathbf{1}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = P'\boldsymbol{\pi}\) becomes
\[
(I - \alpha P)\,\boldsymbol{\pi} = \frac{1-\alpha}{n}\,\mathbf{1}.
\tag{4}\]
The matrix \(I - \alpha P\) is invertible because the eigenvalues of \(\alpha P\) have modulus at most \(\alpha < 1\).
Neumann series. Expanding \((I - \alpha P)^{-1} = \sum_{k \ge 0} \alpha^k P^k\) gives
\[
\boldsymbol{\pi} = (1-\alpha)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \alpha^k P^k\,\frac{\mathbf{1}}{n}.
\tag{5}\]
The term \(P^k \mathbf{1}/n\) is the distribution of a surfer that has followed \(k\) links without teleporting, and the weight \((1-\alpha)\alpha^k\) is the probability that the surfer teleported exactly \(k\) steps ago. So \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) counts walks of all lengths, and \(\alpha^k\) discounts the long ones.

# 1. eigenvector of P'
Pp = alpha * P + (1 - alpha) / n * np.ones((n, n))
w, v = np.linalg.eig(Pp)
i1 = np.argmax(w.real)
pi_eig = np.real(v[:, i1])
pi_eig /= pi_eig.sum()

# 2. linear system
pi_lin = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(n) - alpha * P, (1 - alpha) / n * np.ones(n))

# 3. truncated Neumann series
pi_neu, term = np.zeros(n), np.ones(n) / n
for k in range(200):
    pi_neu += (1 - alpha) * alpha**k * term
    term = P @ term

# 4. NetworkX
pi_nx = np.array([pr[v] for v in nodes])

for name, vec in [("eigenvector", pi_eig), ("linear system", pi_lin), ("Neumann series", pi_neu), ("networkx", pi_nx)]:
    print(f"{name:>15}:", np.round(vec, 5), f" max |difference to eigenvector| = {np.abs(vec - pi_eig).max():.1e}")
print("moduli of the eigenvalues of P':", np.round(np.sort(np.abs(w))[::-1][:3], 4))

    eigenvector: [0.35847 0.18235 0.38643 0.04275 0.03   ]  max |difference to eigenvector| = 0.0e+00
  linear system: [0.35847 0.18235 0.38643 0.04275 0.03   ]  max |difference to eigenvector| = 1.7e-16
 Neumann series: [0.35847 0.18235 0.38643 0.04275 0.03   ]  max |difference to eigenvector| = 3.5e-15
       networkx: [0.35847 0.18235 0.38643 0.04275 0.03   ]  max |difference to eigenvector| = 5.9e-13
moduli of the eigenvalues of P': [1.    0.601 0.601]


All four vectors agree to rounding error. Page \(C\) has the largest PageRank, and page \(E\) has \(\pi_E = (1-\alpha)/n = 0.03\), the minimum possible value: nobody links to it, so it receives only teleportation. Page \(A\) comes second although only one page links to it, because that page is \(C\), which has the largest rank and only one outgoing link. The moduli of the eigenvalues of \(P'\) printed above show that \(1\) is a simple eigenvalue and that all the others are smaller than \(\alpha = 0.85\).






NoteExercise 1: one update by hand



Start from the uniform vector \(\mathbf{p}^{(0)} = \mathbf{1}/5\) and compute one step \(\mathbf{p}^{(1)} = P'\mathbf{p}^{(0)}\) for page \(C\), using the damped formula, \[
p^{(1)}_C = \alpha\left(\frac{p^{(0)}_A}{2} + p^{(0)}_B + p^{(0)}_D + \frac{p^{(0)}_E}{2}\right) + \frac{1-\alpha}{5}.
\] Then compute the other four entries and check them in Python.








TipSolution





For \(C\): \(0.85 \cdot 0.2 \cdot (0.5 + 1 + 1 + 0.5) + 0.03 = 0.51 + 0.03 = 0.54\). The same rule gives \(p^{(1)}_A = 0.85 \cdot 0.2 \cdot 1 + 0.03 = 0.20\) (only \(C\) links to \(A\), with weight 1), \(p^{(1)}_B = 0.85 \cdot 0.2 \cdot 0.5 + 0.03 = 0.115\), \(p^{(1)}_D = 0.85 \cdot 0.2 \cdot 0.5 + 0.03 = 0.115\) and \(p^{(1)}_E = 0.03\). The sum is 1.
p0 = np.ones(5) / 5
p1 = alpha * P @ p0 + (1 - alpha) / 5
print(dict(zip(nodes, p1.round(3))))









NoteExercise 2: equal in-degree, different rank



Pages \(A\), \(B\) and \(D\) each have exactly one incoming link. Explain why their PageRanks differ so much, using Equation 2.








TipSolution





The values are \(\pi_A \approx 0.358\), \(\pi_B \approx 0.182\) and \(\pi_D \approx 0.043\). By Equation 2 with damping, \(\pi_i = \alpha \sum_{j \to i} \pi_j/\text{outdeg}(j) + (1-\alpha)/n\). The link into \(A\) comes from \(C\), which has a large rank and a single outgoing link, so \(A\) receives \(\alpha \pi_C\). The link into \(B\) comes from \(A\), which splits its rank over two links: \(B\) receives \(\alpha \pi_A / 2\). The link into \(D\) comes from \(E\), which has the minimum rank and also splits it over two links: \(D\) receives \(\alpha \pi_E/2\). In-degree sees none of these differences.

title: PageRank
text:
Power iteration
For a web graph the matrix \(P'\) is far too large to diagonalise or to factorise. The practical algorithm is power iteration: start from \(\mathbf{p}^{(0)} = \mathbf{1}/n\) and repeat
\[
\mathbf{p}^{(k+1)} = P'\,\mathbf{p}^{(k)} = \alpha P\,\mathbf{p}^{(k)} + \frac{1-\alpha}{n}\,\mathbf{1}
\tag{6}\]
until \(\lVert \mathbf{p}^{(k+1)} - \mathbf{p}^{(k)} \rVert_1\) is small. The dense matrix \(\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}/n\) is never formed: the teleportation term is a constant vector added after one sparse matrix-vector product. The function below also handles dangling nodes: their total probability mass is spread uniformly.

import scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve


def transition_matrix(G):
    """Sparse column-stochastic matrix P, the node list and a mask of dangling nodes."""
    nodes = list(G.nodes())
    A = nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(G, nodelist=nodes, dtype=float, weight=None)  # A[i, j] = 1 if i -> j
    out = np.asarray(A.sum(axis=1)).ravel()
    dangling = out == 0
    inv = np.where(dangling, 0.0, 1.0 / np.where(dangling, 1.0, out))
    return nodes, sp.csr_array(A.T) @ sp.diags(inv), dangling


def pagerank_power(P, dangling, alpha=0.85, tol=1e-10, max_iter=1000, p0=None):
    """Power iteration for PageRank. Returns the vector and the list of l1 differences."""
    n = P.shape[0]
    p = np.ones(n) / n if p0 is None else p0.copy()
    diffs = []
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        new = alpha * (P @ p + p[dangling].sum() / n) + (1 - alpha) / n
        diffs.append(np.abs(new - p).sum())
        p = new
        if diffs[-1] < tol:
            break
    return p, diffs


nodes5, P5, dang5 = transition_matrix(G)
p_pow, diffs = pagerank_power(P5, dang5, alpha, tol=1e-12)
print("iterations:", len(diffs))
print("max |power iteration - networkx| =", np.abs(p_pow - pi_nx).max())

iterations: 56
max |power iteration - networkx| = 6.710743072346759e-13



How fast does it converge?
The eigenvalues of \(P'\) explain the speed. Because \(\mathbf{1}^{\top} P' = \mathbf{1}^{\top}\), every eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda \neq 1\) satisfies \(\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{v} = 0\). For such a vector \(\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{v} = 0\), hence \(P'\mathbf{v} = \alpha P\mathbf{v}\) and \(\lambda\) is \(\alpha\) times an eigenvalue of \(P\). Since \(P\) is column-stochastic, its eigenvalues have modulus at most 1, and therefore
\[
|\lambda_2(P')| \le \alpha .
\tag{7}\]
The same argument in the \(\ell_1\) norm gives the guarantee \(\lVert \mathbf{p}^{(k)} - \boldsymbol{\pi} \rVert_1 \le 2\alpha^k\). A smaller \(\alpha\) converges faster, but a smaller \(\alpha\) also gives more weight to teleportation and less to the link structure. Figure 2 shows two cases. On a directed cycle the bound is attained, and with \(\alpha = 1\) (no teleportation) the chain never converges, which is the periodicity problem. On a large directed graph with a heavy-tailed degree distribution, the error falls much faster than the bound.

ring = nx.DiGraph([(i, (i + 1) % 6) for i in range(6)])
_, Pr, dr = transition_matrix(ring)
pi_ring = np.ones(6) / 6

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6))
for a_ in (1.0, 0.85):
    p = np.zeros(6)
    p[0] = 1.0
    errs = []
    for _ in range(40):
        p = a_ * (Pr @ p) + (1 - a_) / 6
        errs.append(np.abs(p - pi_ring).sum())
    axes[0].semilogy(errs, "o-", ms=3, label=f"alpha = {a_}")
axes[0].semilogy(2 * (1 - 1 / 6) * 0.85 ** np.arange(1, 41), "k--", lw=1, label="bound, alpha = 0.85")
axes[0].set_xlabel("iteration k")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\|p^{(k)} - \pi\|_1$")
axes[0].set_title("directed cycle")
axes[0].legend()

SF = nx.DiGraph(nx.scale_free_graph(2000, seed=SEED))
SF.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(SF))
nodes_sf, P_sf, dang_sf = transition_matrix(SF)
for a_, c in [(0.5, "C0"), (0.85, "C1"), (0.99, "C2")]:
    pi_ref, _ = pagerank_power(P_sf, dang_sf, a_, tol=1e-14, max_iter=5000)
    p = np.ones(len(nodes_sf)) / len(nodes_sf)
    errs = []
    for _ in range(60):
        p = a_ * (P_sf @ p + p[dang_sf].sum() / len(p)) + (1 - a_) / len(p)
        errs.append(np.abs(p - pi_ref).sum())
    axes[1].semilogy(errs, color=c, label=f"alpha = {a_}")
    axes[1].semilogy(2 * a_ ** np.arange(1, 61), color=c, ls="--", lw=1)
axes[1].set_ylim(1e-14, 3)
axes[1].set_xlabel("iteration k")
axes[1].set_title("scale-free digraph, N = 2000")
axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"dangling nodes in the scale-free digraph: {dang_sf.sum()} of {len(nodes_sf)}")







Figure 2: Distance in the l1 norm between the power iteration and the PageRank vector. Left: directed cycle of 6 nodes, surfer starting on node 0. Without teleportation (alpha = 1) the distance never decreases; with alpha = 0.85 it equals the bound 2(1 - 1/n) alpha^k exactly. Right: directed scale-free graph with 2000 nodes, uniform start; dashed lines are the bound 2 alpha^k.





dangling nodes in the scale-free digraph: 226 of 2000








NoteExercise 3: the damping factor




Predict \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) for \(\alpha \to 0\) and describe what happens to the ranking. (b) Compute the PageRank of the five-page example for \(\alpha = 0.05, 0.5, 0.85, 0.99\) and check your prediction. (c) Which page changes rank most as \(\alpha\) grows?









TipSolution





For \(\alpha \to 0\) the surfer teleports at every step, so \(\boldsymbol{\pi} \to \mathbf{1}/n\) and the links have no influence on the ranking. As \(\alpha \to 1\) the link structure dominates, but \(\alpha = 1\) itself is not allowed in general because of dangling nodes, reducibility and periodicity.
for a_ in (0.05, 0.5, 0.85, 0.99):
    r = nx.pagerank(G, alpha=a_, tol=1e-12)
    print(a_, {v: round(r[v], 3) for v in nodes})
At \(\alpha = 0.05\) every value is within 0.02 of \(0.2\). At \(\alpha = 0.99\) pages \(A\) and \(C\) have about 0.40 each, \(B\) has about 0.20, and \(D\) and \(E\) are below 0.01: the surfer circulates in the loops \(A \to C \to A\) and \(A \to B \to C \to A\), and nobody links to \(E\). The pages that change most are \(E\) and \(D\), which lose almost everything, and \(A\), which gains the most.

title: PageRank
section: Dangling nodes and the normalisation shortcut
text:
Dangling nodes and the normalisation shortcut
If you drop the dangling nodes’ columns, that is, leave them as zero columns in Equation 4, the solution is not a probability vector: its entries add up to less than 1. This still gives the right ranking after normalisation. Let \(D\) be the set of dangling nodes and \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) the PageRank with the uniform rule for \(D\). Then \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) solves \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}} = \alpha P \tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}} + c\,\mathbf{1}/n\) with the scalar \(c = (1-\alpha) + \alpha \sum_{j \in D}\tilde\pi_j\), so \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) is proportional to the solution \(\mathbf{x}\) of Equation 4, and \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}} = \mathbf{x}/\sum_i x_i\). The check below uses a four-page graph in which page \(D\) has no outgoing links.

G_dang = nx.DiGraph([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D")])
nodes_d, P_d, dang_d = transition_matrix(G_dang)
n_d = len(nodes_d)
x = spsolve(sp.eye(n_d, format="csc") - alpha * sp.csc_array(P_d), (1 - alpha) / n_d * np.ones(n_d))
pi_d_nx = nx.pagerank(G_dang, alpha=alpha, tol=1e-14)
print("dangling mask:", dict(zip(nodes_d, dang_d)))
print("solution of (I - alpha P) x = (1-alpha)/n 1:", np.round(x, 4), " sum =", round(x.sum(), 4))
print("x / sum(x)                                :", np.round(x / x.sum(), 4))
print("networkx.pagerank (uniform dangling rule) :", np.round([pi_d_nx[v] for v in nodes_d], 4))

title: PageRank
section: PageRank in practice: beyond the five-page example
text:
PageRank in practice: beyond the five-page example
Figure 3 compares PageRank with in-degree on the directed scale-free graph of the previous figure. The two rankings are strongly correlated and most of the 20 largest nodes coincide. The scatter around the trend shows what in-degree misses: among the nodes with a single incoming link, the largest PageRank is about 20 times the smallest, as in Exercise 2.

from scipy.stats import spearmanr

p_sf, _ = pagerank_power(P_sf, dang_sf, 0.85, tol=1e-12)
indeg = np.array([SF.in_degree(v) for v in nodes_sf])
rho = spearmanr(p_sf, indeg)[0]
top_pr, top_in = set(np.argsort(-p_sf)[:20]), set(np.argsort(-indeg)[:20])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
ax.loglog(indeg + 0.5, p_sf, ".", alpha=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("in-degree (+0.5)")
ax.set_ylabel("PageRank")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"Spearman correlation between PageRank and in-degree: {rho:.3f}")
print(f"nodes in both top-20 lists: {len(top_pr & top_in)} of 20")







Figure 3: PageRank (alpha = 0.85) against in-degree for the directed scale-free graph with 2000 nodes. Each dot is a node; both axes are logarithmic. Nodes with the same in-degree can have PageRanks that differ by a factor of about 20.





Spearman correlation between PageRank and in-degree: 0.994
nodes in both top-20 lists: 15 of 20



Undirected graphs
On an undirected graph every edge is traversed in both directions. The random walk without teleportation then has the stationary distribution \(\pi_i = k_i / 2E\): the walker is found on a node in proportion to its degree. PageRank with damping interpolates between this limit (\(\alpha \to 1\)) and the uniform distribution (\(\alpha \to 0\)), which is why on an undirected network such as the Enron e-mail graph it adds little to degree centrality.

H = nx.Graph(nx.read_edgelist("data/ia-enron-only/ia-enron-only.edges"))
H = H.subgraph(max(nx.connected_components(H), key=len)).copy()
nodes_h, P_h, dang_h = transition_matrix(H.to_directed())
deg_h = np.array([H.degree(v) for v in nodes_h], dtype=float)
stationary = deg_h / deg_h.sum()
print(f"Enron graph (largest component): N = {H.number_of_nodes()}, E = {H.number_of_edges()}")
for a_ in (0.85, 0.99, 0.999):
    p_h, _ = pagerank_power(P_h, dang_h, a_, tol=1e-13, max_iter=100_000)
    print(f"alpha = {a_}: l1 distance to k_i/2E = {np.abs(p_h - stationary).sum():.4f}, "
          f"Spearman with degree = {spearmanr(p_h, deg_h)[0]:.3f}")

alpha = 0.85: l1 distance to k_i/2E = 0.1833, Spearman with degree = 0.936
alpha = 0.99: l1 distance to k_i/2E = 0.0244, Spearman with degree = 0.996
alpha = 0.999: l1 distance to k_i/2E = 0.0026, Spearman with degree = 0.998








NoteExercise 4: PageRank on the networks of this module



Compute the PageRank of the US flights network of Practice: Flights and Other Networks and compare its top 10 airports with the top 10 by degree and by betweenness. Which airports change position, and why can a smaller airport rank higher in PageRank than in degree?








TipSolution





Load the graph as in the practice page (nx.read_graphml("data/openflights/openflights_usa.graphml.gz")), convert it with nx.Graph, call nx.pagerank(G, alpha=0.85) and sort the three dictionaries. On this undirected graph (546 airports) PageRank is close to degree: 9 of the 10 airports coincide. The exception is Anchorage (ANC), which is 40th by degree (34 routes), 10th by PageRank and 1st by betweenness, while Philadelphia (PHL) is in the degree top 10 but not in the PageRank top 10. A neighbour \(j\) passes on \(\pi_j/k_j\), so small airports whose few routes go through Anchorage send it most of their rank: 12 of its 34 neighbours have degree at most 3, against 7 of the 88 neighbours of PHL. Betweenness has a different logic because it counts shortest paths, and it promotes bridges such as Anchorage, Bethel (BET) and Fairbanks (FAI) that connect a region to the rest of the network.

title: PageRank
section: Where PageRank sits in a search engine
text:
Where PageRank sits in a search engine
PageRank sits inside a two-step pipeline. Retrieval finds a candidate set quickly: crawling discovers pages and links, and an inverted index, which maps each word to the list of documents that contain it, returns the candidates in milliseconds. Ranking then orders the candidates by combining text relevance with a link-based authority score such as PageRank. The argument is that on-page signals alone (keyword frequency, meta-tags) are easy to manipulate, while a score that depends on who links to you across the whole graph is harder to fake. PageRank is the ranking signal on this page; real search engines combine it with many other signals.

title: PageRank
text:
Summary

PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links with probability \(\alpha\) and teleports uniformly with probability \(1-\alpha\).
It solves \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = P'\boldsymbol{\pi}\), equivalently \((I - \alpha P)\boldsymbol{\pi} = \frac{1-\alpha}{n}\mathbf{1}\), and equals a discounted count of walks (Equation 5).
Damping removes the three failure modes and makes the solution unique; dangling nodes need a uniform column.
Power iteration converges at least as fast as \(\alpha^k\), and one sparse product per step is enough.

title: PageRank
text:
What’s Next?
The next pages return to models of network growth. The random walk of this page reappears in Epidemic Threshold, where the largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix controls spreading.

title: Small-World Networks
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Watts and Strogatz (1998) (the two-column letter, up to Figure 2).
Recommended: Newman (2003), Section 6.
What the paper did and found: Watts and Strogatz start from a ring lattice with \(n\) vertices and \(k\) edges per vertex and rewire each edge with probability \(p\) to a vertex chosen uniformly at random, forbidding duplicate edges. They work in the regime \(n \gg k \gg \ln n \gg 1\) and find \(L \approx n/2k\) and \(C \approx 3/4\) as \(p \to 0\), against \(L \approx \ln n/\ln k\) and \(C \approx k/n\) as \(p \to 1\). Plotted on a logarithmic axis for \(p\) (Figure 2, averages over 20 realisations, normalised by the values at \(p = 0\)), \(L(p)\) drops rapidly while \(C(p)\) stays almost constant, which defines the small-world regime. Their Table 1 shows that three real networks are small-world: the film-actor graph (\(L = 3.65\) against \(2.99\) for a random graph, \(C = 0.79\) against \(0.00027\)), the western US power grid (\(L = 18.7\) against \(12.4\), \(C = 0.080\) against \(0.005\)) and the neural network of C. elegans (\(L = 2.65\) against \(2.25\), \(C = 0.28\) against \(0.05\)).
A random graph has short paths but almost no clustering. A regular lattice has high clustering but long paths. Watts and Strogatz built a one-parameter model that interpolates between the two (Watts and Strogatz 1998).

title: Small-World Networks
text:
The model

Place \(N\) nodes on a ring and join each node to its \(k\) nearest neighbours (\(k/2\) on each side, \(k\) even).
Visit every edge \((u, v)\). With probability \(p\), replace it by \((u, w)\), where \(w\) is chosen uniformly among the nodes that are not already neighbours of \(u\).

Notation. Some texts call the rewiring probability \(\beta\) and keep \(p\) for the edge probability of the random graph. The original paper uses \(p\) for the rewiring probability, as NetworkX does (nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n, k, p)), and so does this page; read \(p\) here as \(\beta\) in those texts. Rewiring introduces shortcuts that reduce distances while the clustering stays high, and that the result is \(L \sim \log N\). This holds for any fixed \(p > 0\) only once \(N\) is large enough that the shortcuts dominate: for smaller \(N\) the path length is still of the lattice type. Scaling of Path Length and Clustering measures that crossover.
At \(p = 0\) you have the ring lattice. At \(p = 1\) you have a graph close to a random graph with the same number of edges. The degree distribution stays narrow for every \(p\): every node keeps at least \(k/2\) edges.

title: Small-World Networks
text:
Key result
For the ring lattice, the clustering coefficient is \(C(0) = \frac{3(k-2)}{4(k-1)}\), which tends to \(3/4\) for large \(k\), and the average path length grows linearly with \(N\) (Newman 2003, sec. 6.1). Watts and Strogatz found a wide range of small \(p\) in which \(L(p)\) has already dropped close to its random-graph value while \(C(p)\) is still close to \(C(0)\) (Watts and Strogatz 1998). A few random shortcuts are enough to shorten distances across the ring, while they destroy only a few triangles. Networks in this regime are called small-world networks. Watts and Strogatz reported the small-world property in a film actor collaboration network, the power grid of the western United States and the neural network of C. elegans (Watts and Strogatz 1998).
Figure 1 reproduces the shape of their Figure 2 on a smaller graph.








Figure 1: Watts-Strogatz model with N = 300 and k = 6. Average clustering C(p) and average path length L(p), both divided by their values at p = 0, averaged over 3 graphs per value of p.





C(0) = 0.600, formula 3(k-2)/(4(k-1)) = 0.600

title: Small-World Networks
text:
Implementation
In NetworkX, nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n, k, p) generates the model. The variant nx.connected_watts_strogatz_graph retries until the graph is connected, which you need to compute path lengths.

SEED = 7

G_sw = nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n=80, k=6, p=0.08, seed=SEED)
pos = nx.circular_layout(G_sw)
nx.draw(G_sw, pos=pos, node_size=40, node_color="lightblue", edge_color="gray")
plt.title("Watts-Strogatz graph, N = 80, k = 6, p = 0.08")
plt.show()

degrees = [d for _, d in G_sw.degree()]
print("degree range:", min(degrees), "to", max(degrees))
print(f"C = {nx.average_clustering(G_sw):.3f}")








degree range: 4 to 7
C = 0.494


The circular layout keeps the ring visible, so you can spot the rewired shortcuts.






NoteExercise



Compute \(C\) and \(L\) for nx.watts_strogatz_graph(80, 6, p) with \(p = 0\), \(p = 0.08\) and \(p = 1\). Which value of \(p\) gives a small-world network?








TipSolution





for p in [0, 0.08, 1]:
    G = nx.connected_watts_strogatz_graph(80, 6, p, seed=SEED)
    print(p, round(nx.average_clustering(G), 3), round(nx.average_shortest_path_length(G), 2))
At \(p = 0.08\) the clustering is still close to the lattice value (\(C(0) = 0.6\)), while \(L\) has dropped well below its lattice value. At \(p = 1\) both are close to random-graph values.



The model explains short paths together with high clustering. It does not produce hubs: for that you need preferential attachment.
See also: Scaling of Path Length and Clustering for the dependence of \(L\) and \(C\) on \(N\) in the ER, WS and BA models.
In the summary table, the Watts-Strogatz model gets ticks for short paths and for high clustering, and a cross for the degree distribution, which stays narrow. Comparing Graph Models reproduces the whole table.

title: Paths in Directed Graphs
text:
NoteToolkit page



This page is self-study material for the network labs. It continues Paths and Components.
Start with a small directed graph: a food chain where each edge points from prey to predator.
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create a directed graph
D_food_chain = nx.DiGraph()  # food chain (prey -> predator)
D_food_chain.add_edges_from([
    ("grass", "antelope"),
    ("grass", "zebra"),
    ("antelope", "lion"),
    ("antelope", "hyena"),
    ("zebra", "lion"),
    ("zebra", "hyena"),
    ("hyena", "lion"),
])

# Visualize the graph
pos = nx.spring_layout(D_food_chain)
nx.draw(D_food_chain, node_color="lightgreen", with_labels=True, pos=pos)
plt.show()

title: Paths in Directed Graphs
text:
Connectivity in Directed Graphs
Connectivity in directed graphs is more complex than in undirected graphs, because you have to consider the direction of the edges. In a directed graph, you can have strongly connected components and weakly connected components.

Paths in Directed Graphs
In a directed graph, a path must follow the direction of the edges. For example, in the directed food chain graph D_food_chain, is there a path from “grass” to “lion”?

# Draw the graph
pos = nx.spring_layout(D_food_chain)
nx.draw(D_food_chain, node_color="lightgreen", with_labels=True, pos=pos)
plt.show()








You can check for the existence of a path in a directed graph using the same has_path(<graph>, <node1>, <node2>) function:

print("Is there a path from 'grass' to 'lion'?", nx.has_path(D_food_chain, "grass", "lion"))   
print("Is there a path from 'lion' to 'grass'?", nx.has_path(D_food_chain, "lion", "grass"))

Is there a path from 'grass' to 'lion'? True
Is there a path from 'lion' to 'grass'? False




Strongly Connected Components
A strongly connected component is a subgraph in which there is a directed path from any node to any other node. A directed graph is strongly connected if it has only one strongly connected component.

print("Is strongly connected:", nx.is_strongly_connected(D_food_chain))
print("Strongly connected components:", list(nx.strongly_connected_components(D_food_chain)))

Is strongly connected: False
Strongly connected components: [{'lion'}, {'hyena'}, {'antelope'}, {'zebra'}, {'grass'}]




Weakly Connected Components
A weakly connected component is a subgraph in which there is an undirected path from any node to any other node. A directed graph is weakly connected if it has only one weakly connected component.

print("Is weakly connected:", nx.is_weakly_connected(D_food_chain))
print("Weakly connected components:", list(nx.weakly_connected_components(D_food_chain)))

Is weakly connected: True
Weakly connected components: [{'hyena', 'antelope', 'zebra', 'grass', 'lion'}]








NoteExercise



How can you turn D_food_chain into a strongly connected graph? Add as few edges as possible.








TipSolution





To make D_food_chain strongly connected, you need to ensure that there is a directed path from every node to every other node. One way to achieve this is to add edges that create cycles between the nodes. This example is a tough one, as food chains are typically acyclic. Still, you can take note from “The Lion King”:

“When we die, our bodies become the grass, and the antelope eat the grass. And so, we are all connected in the great Circle of Life.” - Mufasa (lion)


# When a predator dies, it returns to the food chain as prey for the grass
D_food_chain.add_edges_from([
    ("lion", "grass"),
])

# Visualize the new graph
pos = nx.spring_layout(D_food_chain)
nx.draw(D_food_chain, node_color="lightgreen", with_labels=True, pos=pos)
plt.show()









print("Is strongly connected:", nx.is_strongly_connected(D_food_chain))
print("Strongly connected components:", list(nx.strongly_connected_components(D_food_chain)))

Is strongly connected: True
Strongly connected components: [{'hyena', 'antelope', 'zebra', 'grass', 'lion'}]







Diameter and Average Path Length in Directed Graphs
The diameter and average path length in directed graphs are calculated based on the shortest paths that follow the direction of the edges. If the graph is not strongly connected, you can only calculate these metrics for the largest strongly connected component.

# Get the largest strongly connected component
largest_scc = max(nx.strongly_connected_components(D_food_chain), key=len)
subgraph = D_food_chain.subgraph(largest_scc)
print("Diameter of the largest strongly connected component:", nx.diameter(subgraph))
print("Average shortest path length of the largest strongly connected component:", nx.average_shortest_path_length(subgraph))

Diameter of the largest strongly connected component: 3
Average shortest path length of the largest strongly connected component: 1.85
