title: Centrality in NetworkX
text:
Centrality (Node Importance)
In many real networks, not all nodes play the same role:

in an airport network, some airports are hubs;
in an email network, some people act as bridges between groups.

These ideas are quantified by centrality measures (Newman 2018).

Degree Centrality
The simplest centrality is based on degree. In an undirected graph with \(N\) nodes, the (normalized) degree centrality is (Newman 2018)
\[
\mathrm{deg\_cent}(i) = \frac{k_i}{N-1}.
\]

deg_cent = nx.degree_centrality(G_foods)
print("Degree centrality:")
for node, c in sorted(deg_cent.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True):
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

Degree centrality:
  chocolate: 0.667
  bread: 0.500
  cured ham: 0.500
  cheese: 0.333
  cookies: 0.333
  milk: 0.333
  watermelon: 0.333


A higher degree centrality means the node is more “important” in terms of connectivity. In the food graph, “chocolate” has the highest degree centrality, while “bread” and “cured ham” are the next most connected nodes.


Closeness Centrality
Closeness measures how close a node is (on average) to all others via shortest paths (Sabidussi 1966). One common definition is
\[
\mathrm{close}(i) = \frac{N-1}{\sum_{j \neq i} d(i,j)},
\]
where \(d(i,j)\) is the shortest-path distance.
A higher closeness centrality means the node can reach other nodes more quickly. In the food graph, “chocolate” has the highest closeness centrality, followed by “bread”.






NoteDisconnected graphs



If a graph is disconnected, some distances are infinite and closeness becomes tricky. In practice you often compute path-based metrics on the largest connected component.



close_cent = nx.closeness_centrality(G_foods)
print("Closeness centrality:")
for node, c in sorted(close_cent.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True):
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

Closeness centrality:
  chocolate: 0.750
  bread: 0.667
  watermelon: 0.600
  cured ham: 0.545
  cheese: 0.500
  cookies: 0.500
  milk: 0.500




Betweenness Centrality
Betweenness identifies bridges: nodes that sit on many shortest paths (Freeman 1977). Formally,
\[
\mathrm{between}(v) = \sum_{s \neq v \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}},
\]
where \(\sigma_{st}\) is the number of shortest paths from \(s\) to \(t\), and \(\sigma_{st}(v)\) is the number of those paths that pass through \(v\).

bc = nx.betweenness_centrality(G_foods)
print("Betweenness centrality:")
for node, c in sorted(bc.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True):
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

Betweenness centrality:
  chocolate: 0.567
  bread: 0.300
  cured ham: 0.100
  watermelon: 0.100
  cheese: 0.000
  cookies: 0.000
  milk: 0.000


Higher betweenness centrality means the node acts as a bridge between different parts of the graph. In the food graph, “chocolate” has the highest betweenness centrality, with “bread” as the second most important bridge.


PageRank (Directed Networks)
For directed networks (like the web), PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random walk (“random surfer”) on the graph (Page et al. 1999).

pr = nx.pagerank(D_food_chain, alpha=0.85)
print("PageRank (directed food chain):")
for node, c in sorted(pr.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True):
    print(f"  {node}: {c:.3f}")

PageRank (directed food chain):
  lion: 0.403
  hyena: 0.218
  antelope: 0.140
  zebra: 0.140
  grass: 0.099








TipPerformance note





On large graphs, exact betweenness can be expensive. NetworkX supports approximation (sample \(k\) sources):
nx.betweenness_centrality(G, k=200, seed=SEED)

title: Centrality in NetworkX
text:
What’s Next?
The Motter-Lai Model uses betweenness as the load of a node in a cascade model.
See also: PageRank, a centrality defined by a random surfer, with a from-scratch power iteration.

title: The Motter-Lai Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Motter and Lai (2002).
What the paper did and found: Motter and Lai define the load of a node as the number of shortest paths through it and the capacity as \(C_j = (1+\alpha)L_j(0)\). They triggered cascades by removing one node, chosen at random or among those with the highest load or degree, on networks with a power-law degree distribution (\(\gamma = 3\), \(5000 \le N \le 5100\), mean degree about 2 in the largest component) and on a homogeneous network with \(N = 5000\) and exactly 3 links per node. For the scale-free networks the largest component stays close to its original size after a random trigger, while a load-based attack with \(\alpha = 0.2\) affects more than 60% of the nodes (more than 3000 of 5000). The homogeneous network showed no cascade for either type of trigger at \(\alpha\) as small as 0.05. For the Internet at the autonomous-system level, an attack on one node disconnected more than 20% of the nodes for \(\alpha \le 0.4\). For the western US power grid (\(N = 4941\), mean degree 2.67), whose degree distribution is close to exponential but whose load distribution is more skewed than that of random networks with the same degrees, a load-based attack on one node reduced the largest component to less than half of its size even at \(\alpha = 1\), while random or degree-based removal triggered no global cascade.
Motter and Lai proposed a minimal model of cascades of overload failures on networks (Motter and Lai 2002). The model has one parameter and one rule. This page states the model. The next page implements it.

title: The Motter-Lai Model
text:
Load
Something travels between every pair of nodes along shortest paths: data packets, goods, or, in a crude picture, power. The load \(L_i\) of node \(i\) is the number of shortest paths between pairs of other nodes that pass through \(i\) (Motter and Lai 2002). When several shortest paths join the same pair, each one counts with equal weight. This is the betweenness centrality of Network Concepts, without normalization:
\[
L_i = \sum_{s \neq i \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(i)}{\sigma_{st}}.
\]

title: The Motter-Lai Model
text:
Capacity
Operators build some spare capacity into each node. Motter and Lai assume that the capacity is proportional to the initial load \(L_i(0)\) of the intact network (Motter and Lai 2002):
\[
C_i = (1 + \alpha)\, L_i(0), \qquad \alpha \ge 0.
\]
The tolerance parameter \(\alpha\) is the same for every node. With \(\alpha = 0\) the network runs at full capacity; with large \(\alpha\) every node has plenty of margin.

title: The Motter-Lai Model
text:
Cascade iteration

Start from the intact network and compute \(L_i(0)\) and \(C_i\) for all nodes.
Remove a trigger node.
Recompute the loads \(L_i\) on the remaining network. The shortest paths change, so the load redistributes.
Remove every node with \(L_i > C_i\).
Repeat steps 3 and 4 until no node is overloaded.

The damage is measured by the relative size of the largest connected component after the cascade (Motter and Lai 2002):
\[
G = \frac{N'}{N},
\]
where \(N\) is the number of nodes of the intact network and \(N'\) the size of its largest component at the end. \(G \approx 1\) means the network survived; \(G \ll 1\) means it broke apart.

title: The Motter-Lai Model
The Motter-Lai Model
text:
A small example
Figure 1 runs one cascade on a Barabási-Albert graph with 40 nodes. The trigger is the node with the largest load and \(\alpha = 0.5\).








Figure 1: One Motter-Lai cascade on a Barabási-Albert graph (N = 40, m = 2, alpha = 0.5). Black: trigger. Red: nodes that fail by overload in the first step. Orange: nodes that fail in the second step. Grey: survivors.





failed per step: [1, 9, 2], G = 0.53


Node size is proportional to the initial load. Most nodes have a small load, and a few hubs carry most shortest paths. Notice that many of the failed nodes had a small initial load: a small load means a small capacity, so a modest increase after the redistribution is enough to overload them.






NoteExercise



In a star graph with \(N\) nodes, what is the load of the centre and of a leaf? What happens to \(G\) if the centre fails? Does \(\alpha\) matter?








TipSolution





Every pair of leaves has exactly one shortest path, through the centre, so the centre has load \(\binom{N-1}{2}\) and each leaf has load 0. If the centre fails, no edges remain and \(G = 1/N\). The value of \(\alpha\) does not matter: the network breaks apart through the removal itself, with no overload step.

title: Practice: Propagation
text:
This page finishes the ungraded practice that starts in Practice: Real Networks. Use the network you characterized there or in Practice: Flights and Other Networks.
Choose one of two options: SIS and SIR (the default), or one propagation model other than SIS and SIR.
In all cases, use the same network for your structural analysis and propagation experiments.
Implementation:
Protocol:

title: Practice: Propagation
text:
SIS and SIR
For the default option, simulate both SIS and SIR on the same graph (as in SIS Simulation and SIR on Networks).

SIS
Report and plot:

mean infected fraction \(\mathbb{E}[I(t)/N]\) over time,
variability: either show a band (e.g., 25 to 75%) or overlay 3 to 5 individual runs.



SIR
Report and plot:

mean curves for \(S(t)/N\), \(I(t)/N\), \(R(t)/N\),
final epidemic size \(R(\infty)/N\) (estimate from your finite simulation horizon).

title: Practice: Propagation
text:
Alternative propagation
For the alternative option, define and simulate one propagation model other than SIS/SIR.
Report and plot at least:

mean fraction of relevant states over time (e.g., spreaders, adopters, skeptics),
variability (band or 3 to 5 individual runs),
one final-outcome metric (e.g., final reach, extinction probability, time-to-peak),
one sensitivity experiment (change one key parameter and compare outcomes).

Your write-up must explicitly explain how both:

the propagation rules (who can influence whom, with what probability/threshold), and
the network structure (hubs, clustering, path lengths, components)

shape the observed dynamics.






TipPractical tip





For large networks, you can simulate on:

the full graph (if it runs fast enough), or
the largest connected component, or
a sampled subgraph (state your sampling method and seed).

The key is that your plots and conclusions must refer to the exact graph you simulated.









NoteDiscuss




Structural: what features suggest “hub-like” propagation vs “cluster-local” propagation?
Rules: how do your propagation rules (infection/recovery/immunity, forwarding/forgetting, thresholds, etc.) change long-run behavior?
Reach: can the process spread to almost all nodes under your parameters? Did you observe it?
Extinction: can the process die out (no active spreaders/infected)? Under what conditions?
Sensitivity: if you increase spreading strength (e.g., \(\beta\) or equivalent) or reduce recovery/forgetting, what changes first: peak height, persistence, or final size?

title: Practice: Propagation
text:
Optional extensions

Remove a high-centrality node and analyze changes in connectivity and epidemic outcome.
Compare two different centrality metrics and discuss differences.
Try a community detection method and summarize results.

Propagation ideas:

Hold the graph fixed (same graph seed) but vary only the dynamics seed to separate “graph randomness” from “process randomness”.
Compare targeted removal (top-degree or top-betweenness) vs random removal and re-run your chosen propagation model.

title: Preferential Attachment
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Barabasi and Albert (1999).
Recommended: Newman (2003), Section 7.2.
What the paper did and found: Barabási and Albert measured the degree distribution of three real networks and found power-law tails \(P(k) \sim k^{-\gamma}\): the film-actor collaboration graph with \(\gamma_{\text{actor}} = 2.3 \pm 0.1\), the World-Wide Web, and the western US power grid, whose distribution they fit with \(\gamma_{\text{power}} \simeq 4\) (the network has only 4941 vertices, so the scaling region is short). Their model combines growth with preferential attachment \(\Pi(k_i) = k_i / \sum_j k_j\), and simulations give \(\gamma_{\text{model}} = 2.9 \pm 0.1\). To show that both ingredients are needed, they studied two variants: model A (growth with uniform attachment) gives an exponential distribution, and model B (a fixed number of vertices and preferential attachment) shows power-law scaling only at early times, because it is not stationary and after \(T \simeq N^2\) steps all vertices are connected.
Neither the random graph nor the small-world model produces hubs. Many real networks have heavy-tailed degree distributions, sometimes close to a power law \(p_k \sim k^{-\gamma}\) (Barabasi and Albert 1999; Newman 2003, sec. 3.3). Barabási and Albert proposed that two ingredients generate such a distribution: growth and preferential attachment (Barabasi and Albert 1999).

title: Preferential Attachment
text:
The Barabási-Albert model

Start with a small network of \(m_0 \ge m\) nodes.
At each step add one new node with \(m\) edges.
Each new edge goes to an existing node \(i\) with probability proportional to its degree, \[
\Pi(k_i) = \frac{k_i}{\sum_j k_j}.
\]
Repeat until the network has \(N\) nodes.

The mean degree tends to \(\langle k \rangle = 2m\).

title: Preferential Attachment
text:
Key results

In the limit of large \(N\), the degree distribution is \[
p_k = \frac{2m(m+1)}{k(k+1)(k+2)} \sim k^{-3}, \qquad k \ge m,
\] so the exponent is \(\gamma = 3\) (Newman 2003, sec. 7.2; Newman 2018).
The degrees of the oldest nodes grow like \(\sqrt{t}\), so the largest degree grows like \(k_{\max} \sim m\sqrt{N}\) (Barabasi and Albert 1999; Newman 2018).
With \(\gamma = 3\) the second moment diverges logarithmically. Summing \(k^2 p_k\) up to \(k_{\max}\) gives \(\langle k^2 \rangle \approx m(m+1)\ln N\) for large \(N\). The degree variance \(\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle^2\) therefore grows without bound as \(N\) grows, even though the mean stays at \(2m\).
The average path length is small, and the clustering is low and decreases with \(N\) (Newman 2003, sec. 7.2).

The divergence of \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) drives two results of this module: the robustness to random failure in Robustness and Percolation and the vanishing epidemic threshold in Epidemic Threshold. Keep in mind that the divergence is slow: at realistic sizes \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) is large but finite.

title: Preferential Attachment
section: Why the exponent is 3: the continuum argument
text:
Why the exponent is 3: the continuum argument
The exponent follows with a continuum (mean-field) argument. Add one node per time step, each with \(m\) edges, so that the total degree at time \(t\) is \(\sum_j k_j = 2mt\). A node \(i\) born at time \(t_i\) receives each of the \(m\) new edges with probability \(\Pi_i = k_i/2mt\), hence
\[
\frac{dk_i}{dt} = m\,\frac{k_i}{2mt} = \frac{k_i}{2t}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k_i(t) = m\left(\frac{t}{t_i}\right)^{1/2}.
\tag{1}\]
Older nodes therefore have larger degree. A node has degree below \(k\) when \(t_i > m^2 t/k^2\), and the nodes are born uniformly in time, so the fraction of nodes with degree at least \(k\) is \(P(K \ge k) \approx m^2/k^2\) and \(p(k) \approx 2m^2/k^3 \sim k^{-3}\).
The argument is an approximation, and it is worth checking how good it is. The chunk compares the degree history of nodes born at different times with Equation 1 and the tail of the degree distribution with \(m^2/k^2\) and with the exact formula \(m(m+1)/\big(k(k+1)\big)\) obtained by summing the exact \(p_k\) above.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

m, N_ba, runs = 3, 10_000, 10
windows = [(20, 40), (100, 200), (500, 1000), (2000, 4000)]
growth = {w: [] for w in windows}
ccdf = []
kmax_grid = np.unique(np.concatenate([np.logspace(np.log10(m), 2.3, 25).astype(int), [20, 40, 80]]))
for s in range(runs):
    G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N_ba, m, seed=s)
    for a, b in windows:
        k_final = G.degree(range(a, b))
        growth[(a, b)].append((np.mean([d for _, d in k_final]), np.mean([m * np.sqrt((N_ba - 1) / i) for i in range(a, b)])))
    deg = np.array([d for _, d in G.degree()])
    ccdf.append([(deg >= k).mean() for k in kmax_grid])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8))
meas = np.array([np.mean(growth[w], axis=0) for w in windows])
axes[0].loglog(meas[:, 1], meas[:, 0], "o", label="simulation")
lim = [meas.min() * 0.8, meas.max() * 1.2]
axes[0].loglog(lim, lim, "k--", lw=1, label="identity")
axes[0].set_xlabel(r"prediction $m\sqrt{t/t_i}$")
axes[0].set_ylabel("mean degree of the cohort")
axes[0].legend()
axes[1].loglog(kmax_grid, np.mean(ccdf, axis=0), "o", ms=4, label="simulation")
axes[1].loglog(kmax_grid, m**2 / kmax_grid**2, "--", label=r"$m^2/k^2$")
axes[1].loglog(kmax_grid, m * (m + 1) / (kmax_grid * (kmax_grid + 1)), "-", label=r"$m(m+1)/(k(k+1))$")
axes[1].set_xlabel("k")
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$P(K \geq k)$")
axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

for w, (obs, pred) in zip(windows, meas):
    print(f"nodes born in {w}: mean degree {obs:.1f}, prediction {pred:.1f}")
for k in (20, 40, 80):
    i = list(kmax_grid).index(k)
    print(f"k = {k}: P(K >= k) = {np.mean(ccdf, axis=0)[i]:.5f}, m^2/k^2 = {m**2 / k**2:.5f}, exact = {m * (m + 1) / (k * (k + 1)):.5f}")







Figure 1: Test of the continuum argument for the Barabási-Albert model (m = 3, N = 10000, averages over 10 graphs). Left: mean degree at the final time of the nodes born in a window of times, against the prediction m sqrt(t / t_i) averaged over the same nodes. Right: complementary cumulative degree distribution, against the continuum approximation m^2 / k^2 and the exact discrete formula m(m+1) / (k(k+1)).





nodes born in (20, 40): mean degree 59.4, prediction 56.1
nodes born in (100, 200): mean degree 25.2, prediction 24.9
nodes born in (500, 1000): mean degree 11.2, prediction 11.1
nodes born in (2000, 4000): mean degree 5.6, prediction 5.6
k = 20: P(K >= k) = 0.02916, m^2/k^2 = 0.02250, exact = 0.02857
k = 40: P(K >= k) = 0.00745, m^2/k^2 = 0.00562, exact = 0.00732
k = 80: P(K >= k) = 0.00204, m^2/k^2 = 0.00141, exact = 0.00185


The growth law holds well: the mean degree of each cohort is within a few per cent of \(m\sqrt{t/t_i}\) (for the oldest cohort the prediction is 5% low), as the printed values show. The tail is a different matter. The continuum prefactor \(m^2\) underestimates the tail probability, by about 20 to 30% at \(m = 3\), while the exact formula with \(m(m+1)\) follows the simulation. The exponent is therefore right, and the amplitude of the continuum argument is only approximate: it replaces \(k(k+1)(k+2)\) by \(k^3\) and \(m(m+1)\) by \(m^2\).

title: Preferential Attachment
text:
Implementation
In NetworkX, nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n, m) adds nodes one at a time, each with m edges attached by preferential attachment.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

SEED = 7

G_sf = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n=200, m=2, seed=SEED)
pos = nx.spring_layout(G_sf, seed=SEED)
size = [5 * d for _, d in G_sf.degree()]
nx.draw(G_sf, pos=pos, node_size=size, node_color="lightgreen", edge_color="gray", alpha=0.8)
plt.title("Barabási-Albert graph, N = 200, m = 2")
plt.show()

title: Preferential Attachment
text:
Degree distribution and second moment
Figure 2 compares the empirical distribution with the exact formula. Use logarithmic bins or the complementary cumulative distribution for real data; here the formula lets you compare point by point.








Figure 2: Left: degree distribution of one Barabási-Albert graph (N = 20000, m = 2) against p_k = 2m(m+1)/(k(k+1)(k+2)). Right: second moment of the degree against N, with the approximation m(m+1) ln N (dashed).





The approximation \(m(m+1)\ln N\) follows the simulated values closely over two decades of \(N\). The small deviations come from the approximations in the sum (the lower limit \(k = m\) and the cutoff at \(k_{\max}\)) and from fluctuations of the largest degrees.






NoteExercise



Compute the mean and the variance of the degree for nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N, 2) with \(N = 10^3\) and \(N = 10^4\). Which one changes?








TipSolution





for N in [1_000, 10_000]:
    k = np.array([d for _, d in nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N, 2, seed=SEED).degree()])
    print(N, k.mean().round(2), k.var().round(1))
The mean stays close to \(2m = 4\). The variance grows with \(N\), as the logarithmic divergence of \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) predicts.









TipOther scale-free generators in NetworkX






nx.powerlaw_cluster_graph(n, m, p, seed=...) adds a triangle-closing step to preferential attachment, which raises the clustering.
nx.scale_free_graph(n, seed=...) returns a directed multigraph.
nx.configuration_model(degree_sequence, seed=...) builds a random graph with any degree sequence you choose.

For this course, nx.barabasi_albert_graph is usually the best starting point.

Compare the three models
Generate the three models of this section with the parameters used in Comparing Graph Models. The readout gives the summary metrics of that page: mean degree, clustering, and the average path length of the largest component.


Erdős–Rényi, \(N = 80\). Lower \(p\) from 0.06 towards 0.01 and watch the size of the largest component. Near which \(p\) does it collapse? Compare with \(\langle k \rangle = (N-1)p = 1\).

With the same two graphs, compare the clustering coefficients. Does preferential attachment produce triangles?

title: Robustness and Percolation
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Albert et al. (2000) (Figures 2 and 3).
Recommended: Newman (2003), Sections 3.4 and 8.1; Molloy and Reed (1995).
What the paper did: Albert, Jeong and Barabási compared an exponential network (Poisson degrees) with a scale-free network with the same number of nodes and links (10,000 nodes in the simulations) and removed nodes either at random or from the highest degree down, following the diameter and the size of the largest cluster. For the scale-free network the diameter did not change under random removal of up to 5% of the nodes, while removing the 5% most connected nodes doubled it; the scale-free network broke apart under attack at a critical fraction of about 0.18, below the value of about 0.28 for the exponential network. They found the same qualitative behaviour in a sample of the Internet at the autonomous-system level and in a sample of the World-Wide Web with 325,729 nodes: for the Internet, random removal of 2.5% of the nodes left the diameter unchanged while attack on the same percentage more than tripled it. The paper is a numerical study; the analytical treatment of the same question came later (Callaway et al. 2000; Cohen et al. 2000).
How much of a network can you remove before it falls apart? You measure the answer with the giant component: the largest connected component, when its size is a finite fraction of \(N\). Let \(S(f)\) be the fraction of the original nodes that stay in the largest component after you remove a fraction \(f\) of the nodes. Removing nodes and asking whether a giant component survives is a site percolation problem (Callaway et al. 2000; Newman 2003, sec. 8.1).

title: Robustness and Percolation
text:
The Molloy-Reed criterion
Consider a random graph with a given degree distribution \(p_k\) and no other structure (the configuration model). Molloy and Reed proved that, as \(N \to \infty\), a giant component exists almost surely when
\[
\sum_k k(k-2)\, p_k > 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \kappa \equiv \frac{\langle k^2 \rangle}{\langle k \rangle} > 2,
\]
and does not exist when the sum is negative (Molloy and Reed 1995). The intuition: follow a random edge to a node. That node has on average \(\kappa - 1\) further edges. The branching process started this way keeps growing when \(\kappa - 1 > 1\).

title: Robustness and Percolation
text:
Random failure
Remove each node independently with probability \(f\). Cohen et al. applied the criterion to the diluted graph and found the critical fraction (Cohen et al. 2000)
\[
f_c = 1 - \frac{1}{\kappa_0 - 1}, \qquad \kappa_0 = \frac{\langle k^2 \rangle}{\langle k \rangle} \text{ of the intact network.}
\]

For an Erdős-Rényi graph, \(p_k\) is Poisson, \(\kappa_0 = \langle k \rangle + 1\), and \(f_c = 1 - 1/\langle k \rangle\).
For a scale-free distribution \(p_k \sim k^{-\gamma}\) with \(2 < \gamma \le 3\), \(\langle k^2 \rangle\) diverges as \(N \to \infty\), so \(f_c \to 1\). An infinite network of this type keeps a giant component under almost any rate of random failure. A finite network has a finite \(\kappa_0\) and a threshold \(f_c < 1\) (Cohen et al. 2000).

title: Robustness and Percolation
text:
Targeted attack
Now remove the nodes with the highest degree first. Albert, Jeong and Barabási showed in simulations that scale-free networks are tolerant to random failure but fragile under this attack: removing a few hubs breaks them apart much faster than an Erdős-Rényi graph with the same \(N\) and \(E\) (Albert et al. 2000). Callaway et al. derived the same behaviour analytically for degree-dependent removal (Callaway et al. 2000).

title: Robustness and Percolation
text:
Generated example
Figure 1 compares a Barabási-Albert graph with an Erdős-Rényi graph that has the same number of nodes and edges. The attack uses the degree ranking of the intact graph.


BA: <k> = 3.99, kappa0 = 11.13, predicted f_c (random) = 0.90
ER: <k> = 3.99, kappa0 = 4.92, predicted f_c (random) = 0.75








Figure 1: Fraction of nodes in the largest component after removing a fraction f of nodes, at random (circles) or by decreasing degree (squares). N = 1000,  close to 4. Dashed lines: the Cohen et al. prediction f_c for random failure, computed from the degree sequence of each graph.





The prediction assumes an uncorrelated configuration model with \(N \to \infty\). Under random failure, the curves of both graphs approach zero close to their dashed lines, but with a tail: for this single BA graph the largest component still holds 4.7% of the nodes at \(f = 0.8\) and 0.8% at \(f = 0.9\), against a predicted \(f_c = 0.90\). Such a tail is expected in a finite graph and is not a failure of the formula. The qualitative result is the one of Albert, Jeong and Barabási (Albert et al. 2000): the BA graph survives random failure about as long as the ER graph (the prediction is even higher, 0.90 against 0.75), but under attack it breaks apart after the removal of about 20% of its nodes, against about 40% for the ER graph.

Which feature of the BA graph explains this?
The BA model differs from a configuration model in two ways: its wiring is not uniformly random given the degrees (it has some degree correlations, and its older nodes are connected among themselves), and its degree sequence is heavy-tailed. To separate the two, we keep the degrees of each BA graph and randomise everything else with \(10E\) double-edge swaps, a degree-preserving null model (see The Configuration Model). If the correlations of the BA model mattered, the randomised graph would behave differently from the original.

from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import connected_components


def giant_curve(G, mode, fractions, rng):
    n = G.number_of_nodes()
    A = nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(G, nodelist=range(n), format="csr")
    if mode == "random":
        order = rng.permutation(n)
    else:
        order = np.argsort(-np.array([G.degree(i) for i in range(n)]), kind="stable")
    out = []
    for f in fractions:
        keep = np.ones(n, bool)
        keep[order[: int(f * n)]] = False
        idx = np.where(keep)[0]
        if idx.size == 0:
            out.append(0.0)
            continue
        _, labels = connected_components(A[idx][:, idx], directed=False)
        out.append(np.bincount(labels).max() / n)
    return np.array(out)


fractions = np.linspace(0, 0.95, 20)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
curves = {(name, mode): [] for name in ("BA", "BA randomised", "ER") for mode in ("random", "attack")}
for s in range(20):
    G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N, 2, seed=s)
    H = G.copy()
    nx.double_edge_swap(H, nswap=10 * G.number_of_edges(), max_tries=10**7, seed=s)
    E = nx.gnm_random_graph(N, G.number_of_edges(), seed=s)
    for name, graph in (("BA", G), ("BA randomised", H), ("ER", E)):
        for mode in ("random", "attack"):
            curves[(name, mode)].append(giant_curve(graph, mode, fractions, rng))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8), sharey=True)
for ax, mode, title in zip(axes, ("random", "attack"), ("random failure", "attack on the highest degrees")):
    for name, style in (("BA", "o-"), ("BA randomised", "s--"), ("ER", "^:")):
        ax.plot(fractions, np.mean(curves[(name, mode)], axis=0), style, ms=4, label=name)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("fraction of removed nodes f")
axes[0].set_ylabel("largest component S")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

for mode in ("random", "attack"):
    ba = np.mean(curves[("BA", mode)], axis=0)
    null = np.mean(curves[("BA randomised", mode)], axis=0)
    er = np.mean(curves[("ER", mode)], axis=0)
    f_half = lambda c: fractions[np.argmax(c < 0.5)]
    f_zero = lambda c: fractions[np.argmax(c < 0.05)]
    print(f"{mode:7s} max |BA - randomised BA| = {np.abs(ba - null).max():.3f};  max |BA - ER| = {np.abs(ba - er).max():.3f};  "
          f"first f with S < 0.05: BA {f_zero(ba):.2f}, randomised {f_zero(null):.2f}, ER {f_zero(er):.2f}")







Figure 2: Largest component S after removing a fraction f of the nodes, for BA graphs (m = 2, N = 1000), the same graphs after degree-preserving randomisation (double-edge swaps) and Erdős-Rényi graphs with the same number of edges. Averages over 20 graphs. Left: random failure. Right: removal by decreasing degree of the intact graph. The BA graph and its randomised version are almost indistinguishable; the ER graph differs under attack.





random  max |BA - randomised BA| = 0.040;  max |BA - ER| = 0.053;  first f with S < 0.05: BA 0.80, randomised 0.80, ER 0.75
attack  max |BA - randomised BA| = 0.061;  max |BA - ER| = 0.672;  first f with S < 0.05: BA 0.20, randomised 0.20, ER 0.40


The measured differences between the BA graphs and their randomised versions are at most 0.04 under random failure and 0.06 under attack, in a quantity that runs from 1 to 0, and both versions fall below \(S = 0.05\) at the same removal fraction (0.80 under random failure and 0.20 under attack). The ER graph, which has the same mean degree but a narrow degree distribution, differs from the BA graph by up to 0.67 under attack. The evidence therefore supports the following reading: the degree sequence alone accounts for the behaviour of the BA graph under both kinds of removal, and the details of its wiring and its degree correlations are at most a small correction at this size (\(N = 1000\), 20 graphs per curve). This test does not show that degree correlations are irrelevant in other networks, and it does not resolve effects smaller than a few per cent.






NoteExercise



Use the formula for \(f_c\) to predict the random-failure threshold of an Erdős-Rényi graph with \(\langle k \rangle = 2\) and with \(\langle k \rangle = 10\).








TipSolution





\(f_c = 1 - 1/\langle k \rangle\) gives \(f_c = 0.5\) for \(\langle k \rangle = 2\) and \(f_c = 0.9\) for \(\langle k \rangle = 10\). A denser random graph survives the removal of a larger fraction of nodes. At \(\langle k \rangle = 1\) the intact graph is already at its percolation threshold.



See also: The Configuration Model, the setting in which the Molloy-Reed criterion holds exactly.

title: Swing Equation
text: The Motter-Lai model has no dynamics. A common next step in power grid modelling describes each node by a phase that obeys the swing equation, a Kuramoto model with inertia (Filatrella et al. 2008; Schäfer et al. 2018). You met the first-order Kuramoto model in The Kuramoto Model.

title: Swing Equation
text:
The model
Each node \(i\) is a generator (\(P_i > 0\)) or a consumer (\(P_i < 0\)). Its phase \(\theta_i\) is measured in a frame that rotates at the grid reference frequency (50 Hz in Europe). The swing equation reads
\[
M \ddot{\theta}_i + D \dot{\theta}_i = P_i + \sum_{j} K_{ij} \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i),
\]
where \(M\) is the inertia, \(D\) the damping and \(K_{ij}\) the capacity of the line between \(i\) and \(j\) (\(K_{ij} = 0\) if there is no line) (Filatrella et al. 2008). The power flow on line \((i,j)\) is \(F_{ij} = K_{ij}\sin(\theta_j - \theta_i)\).

With \(M = 0\) you recover the first-order Kuramoto model, with natural frequencies \(P_i / D\).
A synchronous state has \(\dot{\theta}_i = 0\) for all \(i\) in the rotating frame. It requires \(\sum_i P_i = 0\) (supply equals demand) and lines strong enough to carry the flows.

title: Swing Equation
text:
Dynamical cascades
Schäfer et al. (2018) combine the swing equation with a line-failure rule: a line fails when the magnitude of its flow exceeds a threshold. When one line fails, the flows reroute through a transient that lasts seconds. During the transient a flow can overshoot its new steady-state value and trip a line that a static calculation would call safe. This mechanism is absent from any static model such as Motter-Lai.

title: Swing Equation
text:
A two-node example
Take one generator with \(P_1 = P\) and one consumer with \(P_2 = -P\), joined by one line of capacity \(K\). Subtract the two equations. The phase difference \(\delta = \theta_1 - \theta_2\) obeys
\[
M \ddot{\delta} + D \dot{\delta} = 2P - 2K \sin\delta .
\]
A fixed point needs \(\sin\delta^* = P/K\), so it exists only if \(K \ge P\). The line must be able to carry the power. Figure 1 integrates the equation for \(K\) above and below this bound.








Figure 1: Frequency difference between generator and consumer in the two-node swing equation (M = 1, D = 0.5, P = 1). For K = 1.5 the system settles to a synchronous state. For K = 0.8 there is no fixed point and the phases slip.











NoteExercise



Find the fixed points of the two-node equation for \(K = 2P\) and decide which one is stable.








TipSolution





\(\sin\delta^* = 1/2\) gives \(\delta^* = \pi/6\) and \(\delta^* = 5\pi/6\). Linearize: \(M\ddot{u} + D\dot{u} + 2K\cos(\delta^*)\,u = 0\). At \(\pi/6\) the restoring term is positive, so the fixed point is stable (a damped oscillation). At \(5\pi/6\) it is negative, so the fixed point is a saddle.









TipOptional extension



Build a ring of 6 nodes with alternating \(P_i = \pm 1\) and equal \(K\). Integrate the swing equation with solve_ivp and find numerically the smallest \(K\) for which the ring synchronizes. Then remove one line and repeat.

title: Swing Equation
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



The official report on the Iberian blackout lists voltage control, oscillations and generator disconnections among the interacting factors (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2026). Name one of these factors that the swing equation can represent and one that neither the swing equation nor the Motter-Lai model can represent.








TipSolution





The swing equation describes phase angles and frequency, so it can produce oscillations, such as the damped oscillation around a stable fixed point in the exercise above. Neither model has voltage magnitudes or reactive power, so neither can represent a voltage rise or the overvoltage disconnections that the report describes.

title: The Iberian Blackout
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Motter and Lai (2002).
Recommended: Schäfer et al. (2018).
This lab studies cascading failures with a network model. It starts from a real event so you can see, from the start, how much a simple model leaves out.

title: The Iberian Blackout
text:
What happened on 28 April 2025
The facts below come from the two reports of the Expert Panel set up by ENTSO-E, the European association of transmission system operators: the factual report of 3 October 2025 (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2025) and the final report of 20 March 2026 (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2026). All times are CEST.

At 12:33 the power systems of continental Spain and continental Portugal lost their entire supply. A small area of France near the Spanish border had disruptions for a limited time. The rest of the Continental Europe system had no significant disturbance (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2026, sec. 1.1).
The incident was classified at scale 3, the highest severity level of the ENTSO-E Incident Classification Scale (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2026, sec. 1.1).
In the half hour before the blackout, the grid showed two oscillation episodes: a local oscillation at about 0.63 Hz (12:03 to 12:08) and an inter-area oscillation at about 0.2 Hz (12:19 to 12:22) (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2026, sec. 1.2).
The final report concludes that the blackout resulted from multiple interacting factors. The sequence combined voltage fluctuations and oscillations, widespread generation disconnections in Spain (particularly of inverter-based resources), a cascade of overvoltage disconnections, and the loss of synchronism of the Iberian system with Continental Europe (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2026, sec. 1.9).
The Iberian systems started to lose synchronism with the rest of Europe at 12:33:19. Automatic load shedding and system defence plans activated between 12:33:19 and 12:33:22 but could not prevent the collapse (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2026, sec. 1.3).
The analysis indicates that the blackout originated in Spain, not in Portugal (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2026, sec. 1.4).
Restoration was completed in Portugal by 00:22 on 29 April. In Spain the transmission system was fully restored by 04:00 on 29 April (ENTSO-E ICS Investigation Expert Panel 2026, sec. 1.1).

The reports contain a root cause tree and a long list of recommendations. Read the management summary of the final report if you want the full picture. This page does not try to summarize the causes beyond the points above.

title: The Iberian Blackout
section: What a network model can and cannot say

title: The Iberian Blackout
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



Before you open the next page, write down your answers:

A network has a few hubs that carry most of the shortest paths. Do you expect it to be more fragile when a random node fails or when its most loaded node fails?
Every node gets a capacity 10% above its initial load. Do you expect a small or a large cascade? What about 100%?

You will test both predictions in Cascade Simulation.








TipSolution






When its most loaded node fails. A random node is almost always a node with low load, so little load moves. The most loaded hub sends a large share of all shortest paths to other nodes at once.
With a 10% margin a large cascade is likely, at least when the trigger is a highly loaded node. With a 100% margin most triggers cause only small cascades, but on a network with strong hubs the most loaded node can still do damage. The figure in Cascade Simulation shows both effects.

title: Paths and Components
text:
NoteToolkit page



This page is self-study material for the network labs. It uses the definitions of Network Concepts.
This page measures density, paths, connected components and distances in undirected graphs with networkx (Newman 2018). See NetworkX Basics if you need a refresher on building graphs.
Start by importing the libraries and creating a small undirected graph.
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create an undirected graph
# (foods that go well together)
G_foods = nx.from_edgelist([
    ("bread", "cheese"),
    ("bread", "chocolate"),
    ("bread", "cured ham"),
    ("cheese", "cured ham"),
    ("chocolate", "cookies"),
    ("chocolate", "milk"),
    ("chocolate", "watermelon"),
    ("cookies", "milk"),
    ("cured ham", "watermelon"),
])

# Visualize the graph
pos = nx.circular_layout(G_foods)
nx.draw(G_foods, node_color="lightblue", with_labels=True, pos=pos)
plt.show()

title: Paths and Components
text:
Density
A graph density is the ratio of the number of edges to the number of possible edges. It is a measure of how many edges are present in the graph compared to the maximum possible number of edges. The density of an undirected graph can be calculated as follows:
\[
D = \frac{2|E|}{|V|(|V| - 1)}
\]
where \(|E|\) is the number of edges and \(|V|\) is the number of nodes in the graph.
In a directed graph, there are twice as many possible edges (since each pair of nodes can have two directed edges), so the density is calculated as:
\[
D = \frac{|E|}{|V|(|V| - 1)}
\]
NetworkX provides a built-in function to calculate the density of a graph:

# Density
print("Density:", nx.density(G_foods))

Density: 0.42857142857142855


A graph is sparse when \(D \ll 1\) and dense when \(D \approx 1\). In practice, many real graphs fall in an intermediate range, so density is often better viewed as a spectrum rather than a strict binary label.

# Check if the graph is sparse, intermediate, or dense
D = nx.density(G_foods)
if D < 0.1:
    print("The graph is sparse.")
elif D > 0.6:
    print("The graph is dense.")
else:
    print("The graph has intermediate density.")

The graph has intermediate density.

title: Paths and Components
text:
Connectivity in Undirected Graphs
Connectivity is a fundamental property of graphs that describes how well the nodes are connected to each other. In an undirected graph, a graph is connected if there is a path between any two nodes. If a graph is not connected, it consists of multiple connected components, which are subgraphs in which any two nodes are connected by a path.

Paths in an Undirected Graph
A path in a network is a sequence of edges connecting two nodes.
Take a look at the food graph you created above. Is there a path from “bread” to “watermelon”?

# Draw the graph
pos = nx.circular_layout(G_foods)
nx.draw(G_foods, node_color="lightblue", with_labels=True, pos=pos)
plt.show()








NetworkX provides has_path(<graph>, <node1>, <node2>) to check if there is a path between two nodes:

# Check if there is a path from 'bread' to 'watermelon'
print(
    "Is there a path from 'bread' to 'watermelon'?",
    nx.has_path(G_foods, "bread", "watermelon")
)

Is there a path from 'bread' to 'watermelon'? True


There can be more than one path between two nodes. You can use all_simple_paths(<graph>, <node1>, <node2>) to find all the simple paths between two nodes:

ls_paths = list(nx.all_simple_paths(G_foods, "bread", "watermelon"))
print("All paths from 'bread' to 'watermelon':", ls_paths)

All paths from 'bread' to 'watermelon': [['bread', 'cheese', 'cured ham', 'watermelon'], ['bread', 'chocolate', 'watermelon'], ['bread', 'cured ham', 'watermelon']]




Connected Components in Undirected Graphs
A connected component is a subgraph in which any two nodes are connected by a path. A graph is connected if it has only one connected component.






NoteExercise



How many connected components does G_foods have? Answer from the drawing, then check with nx.connected_components.








TipSolution





G_foods has one connected component, since all nodes are connected to each other through some path.

print("Connected components:", list(nx.connected_components(G_foods)))

Connected components: [{'cookies', 'milk', 'cured ham', 'bread', 'watermelon', 'cheese', 'chocolate'}]







Diameter and Average Path Length
The diameter of a graph is the length of the longest shortest path between any two nodes in the graph. It gives an idea of how “far apart” the nodes are in the graph.

print("Diameter:", nx.diameter(G_foods))

Diameter: 3


The average path length (APL) is the average of the shortest paths between all pairs of nodes.

print("Average shortest path length:", nx.average_shortest_path_length(G_foods))

Average shortest path length: 1.7619047619047619

text:
What’s Next?
The next page repeats these measurements on a directed graph, where paths must follow the direction of the edges.

title: SIR and Percolation
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Pastor-Satorras et al. (2015), the part of the review that maps the SIR model onto bond percolation (transmissibility, Eqs. 59 to 62).
Recommended: Newman (2003), Section 8.2 (epidemiological processes), and Newman (2002), already cited in SIR on Networks.
Context: Robustness and Percolation, Epidemic Threshold and the extension of the SIR model to contact networks in SIR Extensions (Module 1).
The well-mixed SIR model of Module 1 is summarised by the basic reproduction number \(R_0\) and the final size equation. On a network, the same two questions (does an outbreak occur, and how large is it?) have an exact answer in terms of percolation, the problem of Robustness and Percolation. This page states the correspondence, checks it against the simulation code of the lab, and derives from it a network version of the herd immunity threshold of SIR Extensions.

title: SIR and Percolation
text:
Transmissibility
Let the infection pass from an infected node to a susceptible neighbour at rate \(\beta\) along their edge, and let the infected node stay infectious for a time \(\tau\). The transmissibility \(T\) is the probability that the infection crosses a given edge before the infected node recovers. If \(\tau\) is the same for all nodes,
\[
T = 1 - e^{-\beta \tau},
\tag{1}\]
and if the infectious period is exponential with rate \(\mu\), the mean over \(\tau\) gives \(\langle T \rangle = \lambda/(1+\lambda)\) with \(\lambda = \beta/\mu\) (Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015, Eqs. 59 and 61).
For the discrete-time model of the lab, a node that is infectious during \(n\) steps passes the infection to a given neighbour with probability \(1 - (1-\beta)^n\). The number of infectious steps is geometric, \(\mathbb{P}(n) = \mu (1-\mu)^{n-1}\) for \(n \ge 1\), because the node is infectious in the step in which it recovers. Averaging,
\[
T = 1 - \sum_{n \ge 1} \mu(1-\mu)^{n-1}(1-\beta)^n = \frac{\beta}{\beta + \mu - \beta\mu},
\tag{2}\]
which tends to \(\beta/(\beta+\mu) = \lambda/(1+\lambda)\) when \(\beta\) and \(\mu\) are small. For the simplest case, a single edge between two nodes, this can be checked directly.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

from amlab.networks_spreading import random_immunization, run_sir_fast

SEED = 7
beta, mu = 0.3, 0.2
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
K2 = nx.path_graph(2)
# ever-infected fraction is 0.5 if the second node escapes and 1 if it is infected
sizes = np.array([run_sir_fast(K2, beta, mu, initial_infected=1, rng=rng) for _ in range(20_000)])
print(f"simulated T = {np.mean((sizes - 0.5) / 0.5):.3f}, formula T = beta/(beta + mu - beta mu) = {beta / (beta + mu - beta * mu):.3f}")

simulated T = 0.683, formula T = beta/(beta + mu - beta mu) = 0.682

title: SIR and Percolation
text:
The correspondence with percolation
If every infected node stays infectious for the same time, the infections along different edges are independent and happen with probability \(T\). Then the set of nodes reached by an outbreak that starts at one node is exactly the cluster containing that node when each edge is kept with probability \(T\): bond percolation with occupation probability \(T\) (Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015). The giant component of the percolation problem is the epidemic: its existence is the epidemic threshold and its size is the final size. A special case in the lab’s model is the Reed-Frost chain: with recovery probability \(\mu = 1\) every infected node is infectious for exactly one step, so run_sir_fast(G, beta=T, mu=1) is bond percolation with \(T = \beta\).
On a configuration-model network (Configuration Model) with degree distribution \(p_k\), let \(G_0(x) = \sum_k p_k x^k\) and \(G_1(x) = \sum_k k p_k x^{k-1} / \langle k \rangle\). The fraction \(S\) of the network reached by a large outbreak is
\[
S = 1 - G_0(u), \qquad u = 1 - T + T\,G_1(u),
\tag{3}\]
and the transition is at
\[
T_c = \frac{1}{G_1'(1)} = \frac{\langle k \rangle}{\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle} = \frac{1}{\kappa - 1}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{\langle k^2 \rangle}{\langle k \rangle}
\tag{4}\]
(Newman 2003, sec. 8.2, Eq. 87; Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015, Eq. 60). The number \(u\) is the probability that following an edge leads to a finite cluster. For a Poisson distribution \(G_0 = G_1 = e^{\langle k \rangle (x-1)}\), and Equation 3 reduces to \(S = 1 - e^{-\langle k \rangle T S}\), the equation of the giant component of the random graph with \(\langle k \rangle\) replaced by \(\langle k \rangle T\).
When recovery times are random, the infections out of one node are no longer independent: a node that recovers quickly infects few neighbours. The mapping with the mean transmissibility is then only approximate. It still gives the exact threshold and the final size, but not the probability that an outbreak occurs (Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015). We test all this below.

title: SIR and Percolation
text:
Test against simulation
We generate configuration-model graphs with \(N = 4000\) nodes from two degree sequences: Poisson with mean 6, and the degree sequence of a Barabási-Albert graph with \(m = 3\). For each transmissibility, we run the Reed-Frost model from one random node and record the fraction ever infected. A run is a large outbreak if it infects more than 2% of the nodes; we average the size over large outbreaks, which is what Equation 3 predicts. The theory is evaluated with the empirical degree distribution of each graph, so there is no free parameter.

def percolation_S(deg, T, phi=1.0):
    """Fraction of all nodes in the giant cluster for bond occupation T and site occupation phi."""
    p = np.bincount(deg) / len(deg)
    ks = np.arange(len(p))
    mean = (ks * p).sum()
    G0 = lambda x: (p * x**ks).sum()
    G1 = lambda x: (ks[1:] * p[1:] * x ** (ks[1:] - 1)).sum() / mean
    u = 0.5
    for _ in range(20_000):
        u_new = 1 - phi * T + phi * T * G1(u)
        if abs(u_new - u) < 1e-13:
            break
        u = u_new
    return phi * (1 - G0(u))


def simple_configuration_graph(deg, seed):
    G = nx.Graph(nx.configuration_model(list(deg), seed=seed))
    G.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(G))
    return G


N = 4000
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
deg_poisson = rng.poisson(6, N)
deg_poisson[0] += deg_poisson.sum() % 2
deg_ba = np.array([d for _, d in nx.barabasi_albert_graph(N, 3, seed=1).degree()])
nets = {"Poisson": (deg_poisson, "C0"), "Barabási-Albert": (deg_ba, "C1")}

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
n_runs, big = 100, 0.02
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.9))
for name, (deg, colour) in nets.items():
    G = simple_configuration_graph(deg, 1)
    k = deg.astype(float)
    kappa = (k**2).mean() / k.mean()
    Tc = 1 / (kappa - 1)
    # left panel: S against T
    T_fine = np.linspace(0.005, 0.6, 120)
    axes[0].plot(T_fine, [percolation_S(deg, T) for T in T_fine], color=colour, label=f"{name}, theory")
    axes[0].axvline(Tc, color=colour, ls="--", lw=1)
    T_sim = np.array([0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]) * Tc
    means = []
    for T in T_sim:
        s = np.array([run_sir_fast(G, T, 1.0, initial_infected=1, rng=rng) for _ in range(n_runs)])
        means.append(s[s > big].mean() if (s > big).any() else 0.0)
    axes[0].plot(T_sim, means, "o", color=colour, label=f"{name}, simulation")
    # right panel: random immunization at fixed T
    T = 0.4 if name == "Poisson" else 0.2
    R0 = T * (kappa - 1)
    gc = 1 - 1 / R0
    g_fine = np.linspace(0, 0.95, 100)
    axes[1].plot(g_fine, [percolation_S(deg, T, 1 - g) for g in g_fine], color=colour, label=f"{name}, T = {T}")
    axes[1].axvline(gc, color=colour, ls="--", lw=1)
    g_sim = np.array([0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8])
    means = []
    for g in g_sim:
        s = np.array([run_sir_fast(G, T, 1.0, initial_infected=1, immune=random_immunization(G, g, rng), rng=rng)
                      for _ in range(n_runs)])
        means.append(s[s > big].mean() if (s > big).any() else 0.0)
    axes[1].plot(g_sim, means, "o", color=colour)
    g_th = next(g for g in np.linspace(0, 0.99, 991) if percolation_S(deg, T, 1 - g) < 1e-3)
    print(f"{name}: kappa = {kappa:.2f}, T_c = {Tc:.3f};  T = {T}: R0 = {R0:.2f}, g_c = 1 - 1/R0 = {gc:.3f}, "
          f"theory curve falls below 0.001 at g = {g_th:.3f}")
axes[0].set_xlabel("transmissibility T")
axes[0].set_ylabel("fraction reached by a large outbreak")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_xlabel("fraction immunized at random g")
axes[1].set_ylabel("fraction reached by a large outbreak")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Poisson: kappa = 7.01, T_c = 0.166;  T = 0.4: R0 = 2.41, g_c = 1 - 1/R0 = 0.584, theory curve falls below 0.001 at g = 0.584
Barabási-Albert: kappa = 15.63, T_c = 0.068;  T = 0.2: R0 = 2.93, g_c = 1 - 1/R0 = 0.658, theory curve falls below 0.001 at g = 0.654








Figure 1: Final size of SIR outbreaks on configuration-model graphs with N = 4000 and a Poisson degree sequence (ER-like) or a Barabási-Albert degree sequence (m = 3). Left: fraction of nodes reached by a large outbreak against the transmissibility T. Lines: theory of the generating-function equation; dots: Reed-Frost simulation (mean over large outbreaks, 100 runs per point). Vertical dashed lines: T_c = 1/(kappa - 1). Right: the same with a fraction g of the nodes immunized at random, at fixed T; vertical dashed lines: g_c = 1 - 1/R_0 with R_0 = T(kappa - 1).





The simulation follows the theory without adjustment, over the whole range of \(T\) and for both degree distributions: the transition is at \(T_c = 1/(\kappa - 1)\), and the Barabási-Albert sequence, with a larger \(\kappa\), has a transition at a transmissibility 2.4 times smaller than the Poisson one (\(0.068\) against \(0.166\)). The finite size smooths the transition, so the points just above \(T_c\) are slightly different from the curve.

title: SIR and Percolation
section: Random immunization and the herd immunity threshold
text:
Random immunization and the herd immunity threshold
Immunizing a fraction \(g\) of the nodes at random removes each node with probability \(g\). On a configuration-model network this scales the mean number of onward transmissions by \(1 - g\), so an outbreak is possible if
\[
(1-g)\,T\,(\kappa - 1) > 1 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad g < g_c = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0}, \qquad R_0 = T(\kappa - 1).
\tag{5}\]
Here \(R_0 = T(\kappa-1)\) is the mean number of secondary infections caused by a node reached along an edge in the early stage: each of its \(\kappa - 1\) other edges transmits with probability \(T\). This is the formula \(v_c = 1 - 1/R_0\) of SIR Extensions for a well-mixed population, with one difference that matters: the reproduction number now depends on the degree distribution through \(\kappa\). For a Poisson graph \(\kappa - 1 = \langle k \rangle\) and \(R_0 = T\langle k \rangle\), as in the homogeneous model. For a broad distribution \(\kappa - 1\) is large and so is \(g_c\). The right panel of Figure 1 shows the vanishing of the outbreak at the predicted \(g_c\) for both networks; the output above shows that the theory curve falls to zero at the value given by Equation 5.
This is the quantitative content of the first strategy of Vaccination Strategies, random immunization. It also explains why that page finds random vaccination so costly on the Barabási-Albert graph, while targeted vaccination of the hubs, which lowers \(\kappa\), is effective (Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani 2002).






NoteExercise 1: SIR against SIS



For the continuous-time SIR model with exponential recovery, \(\langle T \rangle = \lambda/(1+\lambda)\). Use Equation 4 to show that the SIR threshold in terms of \(\lambda\) is \(\lambda_c^{\text{SIR}} = 1/(\kappa - 2) = \langle k \rangle/(\langle k^2 \rangle - 2\langle k \rangle)\). Evaluate it for a Poisson graph with \(\langle k \rangle = 6\) and compare it with the SIS heterogeneous mean-field threshold \(\lambda_c^{\text{SIS}} = \langle k \rangle/\langle k^2 \rangle\) of Epidemic Threshold.








TipSolution





\(T_c = \lambda_c/(1+\lambda_c) = 1/(\kappa-1)\) gives \(\lambda_c = T_c/(1-T_c) = 1/(\kappa - 2)\), and \(\kappa - 2 = (\langle k^2 \rangle - 2\langle k \rangle)/\langle k \rangle\). For the Poisson distribution \(\langle k^2 \rangle = \langle k \rangle^2 + \langle k \rangle\), so \(\kappa = \langle k \rangle + 1 = 7\) and \(\lambda_c^{\text{SIR}} = 1/5 = 0.2\). The SIS mean-field threshold is \(1/(\langle k \rangle + 1) = 1/7 \approx 0.14\). The SIR threshold is larger: in SIR the infected nodes become immune, so the infection cannot return to a node that has already had it, and a larger spreading rate is needed. The expression for SIR diverges at \(\kappa = 2\), the Molloy-Reed point, below which the network has no giant component at all.









NoteExercise 2: random vaccination in a large scale-free network



A Barabási-Albert graph with \(m = 3\) and \(N = 10^5\) nodes has \(\kappa \approx 22.2\) (compute it with nx.barabasi_albert_graph(100_000, 3, seed=1)). Take \(T = 0.3\). Find \(T_c\) and the fraction \(g_c\) that must be immunized at random, and compare with a Poisson graph of mean degree 6 at the same \(T\).








TipSolution





\(T_c = 1/(\kappa - 1) \approx 0.047\), so \(T = 0.3\) is more than six times the threshold: \(R_0 = T(\kappa - 1) \approx 6.4\) and \(g_c = 1 - 1/R_0 \approx 0.84\). For the Poisson graph, \(R_0 = 0.3 \times 6 = 1.8\) and \(g_c = 1 - 1/1.8 \approx 0.44\). The same transmissibility needs almost twice the coverage on the scale-free network if the vaccinated individuals are chosen at random. The formula is for the configuration model with \(N \to \infty\); the value of \(g_c\) for a finite graph is lower than the one for the infinite network of the same type, but it remains large.









NoteExercise 3: random recovery times



Repeat the test for the discrete-time SIR model with \(\mu = 0.2\) in place of the Reed-Frost chain. Choose \(\beta\) from Equation 2 so that \(T = 1/3\) on the Poisson graph, run 150 simulations, and compare the mean size and the fraction of large outbreaks with the theory.








TipSolution





Invert Equation 2: \(\beta = T\mu/\big(1 - T(1-\mu)\big) \approx 0.0908\) for \(T = 1/3\) and \(\mu = 0.2\).
T, mu = 1 / 3, 0.2
b = T * mu / (1 - T * (1 - mu))
G = simple_configuration_graph(deg_poisson, 1)
s = np.array([run_sir_fast(G, b, mu, initial_infected=1, rng=rng) for _ in range(150)])
print(round(b, 4), (s > 0.02).mean(), s[s > 0.02].mean(), percolation_S(deg_poisson, T))
The mean size of large outbreaks is 0.80 against a theoretical 0.796, so the final size agrees. The fraction of runs that become large outbreaks is lower: in 600 runs it was 0.66 for the geometric recovery times, against 0.78 for the Reed-Frost chain with the same \(T\) (the percolation formula gives 0.80 for the latter). With random recovery times the probability of a large outbreak is not given by the same percolation formula, as the discussion above states. With only 150 runs this fraction fluctuates by several percentage points, so use more runs to see the difference.

title: Comparing Graph Models

The three previous pages built one model each. This page puts them side by side with the same summary metrics, so you can check the properties claimed for each model on a small graph:
The definitions and examples are in Paths and Components and Degree and Clustering.

title: Comparing Graph Models
text:
Helper functions

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx

SEED = 7


def summarize_graph(G, name="G"):
    """Print a small summary of common network statistics."""
    n = G.number_of_nodes()
    m = G.number_of_edges()
    avg_k = 2 * m / n if n > 0 else 0
    density = nx.density(G)

    # Connectivity (undirected)
    is_connected = nx.is_connected(G) if n > 0 else False
    n_components = nx.number_connected_components(G) if n > 0 else 0

    # Work on the largest connected component when disconnected
    if n == 0:
        L = float("nan")
        C = float("nan")
    else:
        C = nx.average_clustering(G)
        if is_connected:
            L = nx.average_shortest_path_length(G)
        else:
            largest_cc = max(nx.connected_components(G), key=len)
            H = G.subgraph(largest_cc).copy()
            L = nx.average_shortest_path_length(H)

    print(f"--- {name} ---")
    print(f"N = {n}, E = {m}, <k> = {avg_k:.2f}, density = {density:.4f}")
    print(f"connected = {is_connected}, components = {n_components}")
    print(f"clustering C = {C:.3f}")
    print(f"avg shortest path L = {L:.3f} (largest CC if disconnected)")


def plot_degree_histogram(G, title="Degree distribution"):
    """Plot a histogram of the node degrees, one bar per degree value."""
    degrees = [deg for _, deg in G.degree()]
    plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3))
    plt.hist(degrees, bins=range(min(degrees), max(degrees) + 2), align="left", rwidth=0.9)
    plt.xlabel("Degree k")
    plt.ylabel("Count")
    plt.title(title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

title: Comparing Graph Models
text:
Summary
The comparison organises the three models around three empirical features of real networks: short paths, high clustering and heavy-tailed degrees. With \(L\) for the average path length, \(C\) for the average clustering and \(p(k)\) for the degree distribution, the comparison reads:









Network
\(L\)
\(C\)
\(p(k)\)




Real networks
small
high
heavy tail


Erdős-Rényi
\(\sim \log N\) (yes)
low, \(C \approx \langle k \rangle / N\) (no)
Poisson (no)


Watts-Strogatz
small (yes)
high (yes)
narrow (no)


Barabási-Albert
very small (yes)
low (no)
\(\sim k^{-3}\) (yes)


Preferential attachment with triadic closure (Holme-Kim)
small (yes)
high (yes)
\(\sim k^{-3}\) (yes)



None of the first three models has all three properties; the last row is the idea of combining preferential attachment with triadic closure, which is the subject of Triadic Closure. The numbers behind each cell are in Scaling of Path Length and Clustering. A caution that applies to every row: \(L\), \(C\) and \(p(k)\) are only some features of real networks. Degree correlations, community structure, links that appear and disappear, and edge weights need further models, and The Configuration Model shows that matching the degree sequence alone does not reproduce clustering.

import numpy as np

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



Mandelbrot’s stable model predicts \(\alpha < 2\) (Mandelbrot 1963). A Gaussian has no power-law tail at all. Which value do you expect for your series? Write it down before you estimate it.








TipSolution





For market returns expect a value between 2 and 5, often close to 3 (Cont 2001; Gopikrishnan et al. 1998). That is heavier than a Gaussian but lighter than a stable law. Compare your estimate with this range in the Interpretation section.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
The Hill estimator
Sort the positive data in decreasing order, \(X_{(1)} \ge X_{(2)} \ge \dots\). Using only the \(k\) largest values,
\[
\hat{\alpha}_k = \left[ \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \ln \frac{X_{(i)}}{X_{(k+1)}} \right]^{-1}
\tag{1}\]
(Hill 1975). This is the power-law maximum likelihood estimator of Power Laws with \(x_{\min} = X_{(k+1)}\), written for the CCDF exponent \(\alpha = \alpha_{\text{pdf}} - 1\). For i.i.d. data with an exact power-law tail its standard error is approximately \(\hat{\alpha}_k / \sqrt{k}\).
The choice of \(k\) is a trade-off. Small \(k\) uses few points and gives a noisy estimate. Large \(k\) reaches into the centre of the distribution, where the power law does not hold, and biases the estimate. The usual tool is the Hill plot, \(\hat{\alpha}_k\) against \(k\): you look for a range of \(k\) where it is roughly flat. Clauset et al. (2009) note that reading the plateau by eye is subjective and sensitive to noise in the tail, and that a common practice in quantitative finance is to use only the largest \(\sqrt{n}\) or \(n/10\) observations. They propose to choose the threshold by minimizing a Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance and to check the fit with a goodness-of-fit test; Fitting Power Laws Properly implements this.
