def hill(x, k):
    """Hill estimate of the tail index from the k largest values of x > 0."""
    xs = np.sort(x)[::-1]
    return 1.0 / np.mean(np.log(xs[:k] / xs[k]))


print(f"k = 100: alpha = {hill(a, 100):.2f}")

k = 100: alpha = 3.28


A vectorized version that accepts an array of k values is amlab.finance.hill_estimator.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Validation on known tails
Before you trust the estimator on returns, apply it to samples whose tail index you know. A Student-t variable with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom has \(\Pr(|X| > x) \sim C x^{-\nu}\).

from amlab.finance import hill_estimator

rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
for nu in [2, 3, 4]:
    x = np.abs(rng.standard_t(nu, size=a.size))
    print(f"Student-t nu = {nu}: Hill (k = 100) = {hill_estimator(x, 100):.2f}")

Student-t nu = 2: Hill (k = 100) = 2.31
Student-t nu = 3: Hill (k = 100) = 3.01
Student-t nu = 4: Hill (k = 100) = 3.20


The estimates are close to \(\nu\) but not equal. The Student-t tail is a power law only asymptotically, and the deviation grows with \(\nu\). Keep this bias in mind when you read the value for returns.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Experiment: Hill plot

ks = np.arange(20, a.size // 5)
alpha_r = hill_estimator(a, ks)
gauss = np.abs(rng.normal(0.0, a.std(), a.size))
alpha_g = hill_estimator(gauss, ks)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.plot(ks, alpha_r, label="returns")
ax.fill_between(ks, alpha_r * (1 - 1 / np.sqrt(ks)), alpha_r * (1 + 1 / np.sqrt(ks)), alpha=0.2)
ax.plot(ks, alpha_g, label="Gaussian sample")
ax.axhspan(2, 5, color="grey", alpha=0.1, label="range in Cont (2001)")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("number of upper order statistics $k$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\hat{\alpha}_k$")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Hill plot of the absolute log returns and of a Gaussian sample of the same size and standard deviation. The shaded band is plus or minus one standard error \(\hat{\alpha}_k/\sqrt{k}\) for the returns.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Interpretation
For heavy-tailed data the Hill plot has a plateau at small to intermediate \(k\). For the Gaussian sample \(\hat{\alpha}_k\) keeps growing as \(k\) shrinks, because the true tail index is infinite: the estimator always returns a finite number, so the shape of the Hill plot matters more than any single value.
For market returns Cont (2001) reports tail indices between 2 and 5, and Gopikrishnan et al. (1998) report values close to 3 for US stocks. A value above 2 means finite variance. Such a tail is heavy, but it is not the tail of a Lévy stable law with \(\alpha < 2\).

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Limitations

The standard error \(\hat{\alpha}_k/\sqrt{k}\) assumes i.i.d. data. Volatility clustering makes the effective sample size smaller, so the real uncertainty is larger (Cont 2001).
A power law holds only asymptotically. A slowly varying correction, such as a logarithm, changes the estimate at every finite \(k\) (Cont 2001).
There is no automatic rule for \(k\) in this lab. Report the range of \(k\) you used and show the Hill plot. The KS-based choice of the threshold in Fitting Power Laws Properly is more objective, but it makes the same assumption of independent observations.

title: Tail Exponent
text:
Optional extension






NoteExercise



Estimate the tail index separately for losses (\(r < 0\)) and gains (\(r > 0\)). Is there evidence for the gain/loss asymmetry listed by Cont (2001)? Use the standard errors to judge whether the difference is larger than the noise.








TipSolution





Use the same \(k\) for both tails. The standard error of the difference of two independent estimates is \(\sqrt{s_1^2 + s_2^2}\). A smaller \(\alpha\) for losses means a heavier loss tail. Call the asymmetry real only if the difference is about two standard errors or more, and check that it holds over a range of \(k\).
rc = r - r.mean()
losses, gains = -rc[rc < 0], rc[rc > 0]
k = 100
a_loss, a_gain = hill_estimator(losses, k), hill_estimator(gains, k)
se = np.hypot(a_loss / np.sqrt(k), a_gain / np.sqrt(k))
print(f"losses {a_loss:.2f}, gains {a_gain:.2f}, difference {a_loss - a_gain:.2f} +/- {se:.2f}")

title: Stable Distributions
text: The Gaussian is the limit of sums with finite variance. Sums of variables with power-law tails and infinite variance also converge, but to a different family: the Lévy stable laws (Gnedenko and Kolmogorov 1954; Mantegna and Stanley 2000, chap. 4).

title: Stable Distributions
text:
Definition
A random variable \(X\) is stable if a sum of independent copies has the same shape as \(X\) itself: for every \(n\) there are constants \(a_n > 0\) and \(b_n\) with
\[
X_1 + \dots + X_n \overset{d}{=} a_n X + b_n .
\]
The scale factor is always \(a_n = n^{1/\alpha}\) for some index \(0 < \alpha \le 2\) (Gnedenko and Kolmogorov 1954). A stable law has no closed-form density in general. It is defined through its characteristic function. For the symmetric case centred at zero,
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{ikX}\right] = \exp\left(-|c k|^{\alpha}\right),
\tag{1}\]
with scale \(c > 0\). The general family adds a skewness parameter \(\beta \in [-1, 1]\) and a location (Mantegna and Stanley 2000, chap. 4).

title: Stable Distributions
text:
Key properties

\(\alpha = 2\) gives the Gaussian with variance \(2c^2\). \(\alpha = 1\) gives the Cauchy law, with density \(c / [\pi (c^2 + x^2)]\).
For \(\alpha < 2\) the tails are power laws, \(\Pr(|X| > x) \sim C x^{-\alpha}\) as \(x \to \infty\). The variance is infinite. For \(\alpha \le 1\) the mean does not exist either (Mantegna and Stanley 2000, chap. 4).
Generalized central limit theorem. If i.i.d. variables have tails \(\Pr(|X| > x) \sim C x^{-\alpha}\) with \(0 < \alpha < 2\), their suitably centred sums divided by \(n^{1/\alpha}\) converge to a stable law with the same \(\alpha\). If the variance is finite, the limit is Gaussian (Gnedenko and Kolmogorov 1954).
In the power-law notation of Power Laws, where the density decays as \(x^{-\alpha_{\text{pdf}}}\), the stable index is \(\alpha = \alpha_{\text{pdf}} - 1\). Only \(\alpha_{\text{pdf}} < 3\) leads to a non-Gaussian limit.

You can sample symmetric stable variables with the method of Chambers et al. (1976), implemented in amlab.random_walks.sample_symmetric_stable and in scipy.stats.levy_stable (Virtanen et al. 2020).

title: Stable Distributions
text:
Cauchy against normal sample means
For Gaussian data the sample mean of \(n\) values has width \(\propto n^{-1/2}\). For Cauchy data, \(\alpha = 1\) and \(a_n = n\), so the sample mean \(S_n / n\) has exactly the same Cauchy law as a single observation. Averaging does not help.








Figure 1: Running sample mean of 10000 draws for five independent sequences. Left: standard normal. Right: standard Cauchy (\(\alpha = 1\)). The normal means settle at 0; the Cauchy means keep jumping whenever a very large value arrives.











NoteExercise



Check the scaling \(a_n = n^{1/\alpha}\) for \(\alpha = 1.5\). Draw 10000 sums of \(n\) symmetric stable variables for \(n = 1, 10, 100, 1000\), and compute the interquartile range (IQR) of each set of sums. Fit the slope of \(\log \text{IQR}\) against \(\log n\). Why do you use the IQR and not the standard deviation?








TipSolution






rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
ns = np.array([1, 10, 100, 1000])
iqr = []
for m in ns:
    s = sample_symmetric_stable(1.5, (10000, m), rng=rng).sum(axis=1)
    q75, q25 = np.percentile(s, [75, 25])
    iqr.append(q75 - q25)
slope = np.polyfit(np.log(ns), np.log(iqr), 1)[0]
print(f"slope {slope:.3f}, theory 1/alpha = {1 / 1.5:.3f}")

slope 0.670, theory 1/alpha = 0.667


The standard deviation is infinite for \(\alpha < 2\), so its sample value is dominated by the largest draw and does not converge. Quantiles exist for every stable law.

title: Normality Tests
text:
The Gaussian random walk model predicts normal log returns. On this page you test that prediction graphically and with the Jarque-Bera test. On the next page, Calibrated KS Test, you add a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test with a correctly computed p-value. You continue from Loading Prices and Computing Returns.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

from amlab.finance import load_prices, log_returns

r = log_returns(load_prices()["close"])
z = (r - r.mean()) / r.std(ddof=1)  # standardized returns
n = r.size

WARNING: data/finance/prices.csv not found. Using a SYNTHETIC GARCH(1,1) series with Student-t innovations (seed 2026). These are not market data. See data/finance/README.md.

title: Normality Tests
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



If returns were normal, what fraction of days would have \(|z| > 4\)? Write the number down. Then count them in the data.








TipSolution





For a standard normal, \(\Pr(|Z| > 4) = 2\,\Pr(Z > 4) \approx 6 \times 10^{-5}\), about one day in 16 000. Real returns exceed this by a large factor.

print(f"normal prediction: {2 * stats.norm.sf(4):.1e}")
print(f"observed:          {np.mean(np.abs(z) > 4):.1e}")

normal prediction: 6.3e-05
observed:          5.8e-03

title: Normality Tests
section: Graphical checks: histogram and Q-Q plot
text:
Graphical checks: histogram and Q-Q plot
A histogram on a logarithmic density axis shows the tails. A quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot shows the sorted standardized returns against the quantiles of the standard normal at probabilities \((i - 0.5)/n\). Normal data lie on the diagonal.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.8))
grid = np.linspace(-8, 8, 400)
axes[0].hist(z, bins=80, range=(-8, 8), density=True, alpha=0.6)
axes[0].semilogy(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid), "k-")
axes[0].set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("standardized return")
axes[0].set_ylabel("density")

theoretical = stats.norm.ppf((np.arange(1, n + 1) - 0.5) / n)
axes[1].plot(theoretical, np.sort(z), ".", ms=2)
axes[1].plot([-4, 4], [-4, 4], "k--")
axes[1].set_xlabel("normal quantile")
axes[1].set_ylabel("sample quantile")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Left: histogram of standardized log returns with the standard normal density, on a log scale. Right: normal Q-Q plot. Points above the diagonal on the right and below it on the left indicate heavier tails than the normal.

title: Normality Tests
text:
The Jarque-Bera test
With sample skewness \(S\) and sample excess kurtosis \(K\), the Jarque-Bera statistic is
\[
JB = \frac{n}{6} \left( S^2 + \frac{K^2}{4} \right),
\]
which is asymptotically \(\chi^2\) with 2 degrees of freedom under normality (Jarque and Bera 1980).

jb = stats.jarque_bera(r)
print(f"skewness {stats.skew(r):.2f}, excess kurtosis {stats.kurtosis(r):.2f}")
print(f"JB = {jb.statistic:.1f}, p-value = {jb.pvalue:.2e}")

skewness -0.33, excess kurtosis 11.97
JB = 29942.3, p-value = 0.00e+00


The test depends on the fourth moment. For heavy-tailed returns the sample kurtosis fluctuates wildly between samples (Cont 2001), so read \(K\) as “far from 0”, not as a precise number.

title: Normality Tests
text:
Interpretation so far
The Q-Q plot shows how the data depart from the normal, which a p-value does not. The Jarque-Bera test gives a p-value but relies on moments that may not exist for heavy tails. Next you build a test based on the whole distribution function: Calibrated KS Test.

title: Returns and Efficient Markets
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Mantegna and Stanley (2000), Chapters 1 to 3.
Recommended: Mandelbrot (1963); Mantegna and Stanley (1995).
The first random walk model of prices is older than Einstein’s theory of Brownian motion. Bachelier modelled price changes on the Paris exchange as independent Gaussian increments in his 1900 thesis (Bachelier 1900). This page asks how well that model describes real markets.

title: Returns and Efficient Markets
text:
Prices and returns
Let \(P_t\) be the closing price on day \(t\). The simple return and the log return are
\[
R_t = \frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}}, \qquad r_t = \ln \frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}} = \ln(1 + R_t).
\tag{1}\]
For daily data \(|R_t|\) is usually small and \(r_t \approx R_t\). Log returns have one property that makes them the natural variable for modelling: they add over time. The log return over \(\Delta t\) days is
\[
r_t(\Delta t) = \ln \frac{P_t}{P_{t - \Delta t}} = \sum_{i=0}^{\Delta t - 1} r_{t-i} .
\tag{2}\]
So \(\ln P_t\) is a random walk whose steps are the daily log returns, and everything from The Random Walk and Stable Distributions applies to it.

title: Returns and Efficient Markets
text:
The random walk hypothesis
The simplest model assumes that daily log returns are independent and identically distributed, often Gaussian with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\):
\[
\ln P_t = \ln P_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t} r_i, \qquad r_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2).
\tag{3}\]
Then \(\operatorname{Var}[r_t(\Delta t)] = \sigma^2 \Delta t\), the financial version of \(\mathrm{MSD} = 2Dt\). Bachelier’s original model used price changes instead of log returns (Bachelier 1900).

title: Returns and Efficient Markets
text:
Efficient markets
Fama (1970) calls a market efficient when prices “fully reflect” the available information. He distinguishes three forms by the information set: past prices (weak form), all public information (semi-strong form), and all information, including private information (strong form). Fama also notes that the independence assumed in Equation 3 is stronger than what efficiency requires. In a “fair game” model the deviations of returns from their expected values cannot be predicted from the information set, but they need not be independent or identically distributed (Fama 1970).
The practical consequence you test in the lab: under weak-form efficiency, past returns should carry no linear information about future returns.








Figure 1: Five simulated price paths from the geometric random walk with \(P_0 = 100\), \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 0.01\) per day over 1000 days. All paths come from the same model; the apparent trends are chance.











NoteExercise



A price goes from 100 to 150 and then back to 100. Compute the two simple returns and the two log returns. Which of them sum to the total return over the two days?








TipSolution






p = np.array([100.0, 150.0, 100.0])
R = np.diff(p) / p[:-1]
r = np.diff(np.log(p))
print("simple returns:", R, "sum", R.sum())
print("log returns:   ", r.round(4), "sum", r.sum().round(12))

simple returns: [ 0.5        -0.33333333] sum 0.16666666666666669
log returns:    [ 0.4055 -0.4055] sum 0.0


The simple returns are \(+50\%\) and \(-33.3\%\); their sum, \(+16.7\%\), is not the true total return of \(0\). The log returns are \(\pm 0.405\) and sum to exactly \(0\).

title: Scaling of Returns
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Mantegna and Stanley (1995), the whole letter (four pages).
Recommended: Mantegna and Stanley (1994), on the truncated Lévy flight.
If log returns are independent draws from one stable law, their distribution at every time horizon is a rescaled copy of the one-step distribution. Mantegna and Stanley (1995) tested this idea on the S&P 500 index. This page states the prediction and their result.

title: Scaling of Returns
text:
The scaling prediction
Let the one-step log returns be i.i.d. symmetric stable with index \(\alpha\) and density \(p_1\). By Stable Distributions, the return over \(\Delta t\) steps, \(r(\Delta t)\), is stable with the same \(\alpha\) and a scale multiplied by \(\Delta t^{1/\alpha}\). Its density is
\[
p_{\Delta t}(x) = \Delta t^{-1/\alpha}\, p_1\!\left( x\, \Delta t^{-1/\alpha} \right).
\tag{1}\]
At \(x = 0\) this gives the probability of return to the origin
\[
p_{\Delta t}(0) = p_1(0)\, \Delta t^{-1/\alpha} .
\tag{2}\]
On log-log axes \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) against \(\Delta t\) is a straight line with slope \(-1/\alpha\). For Gaussian returns \(\alpha = 2\) and the slope is \(-1/2\). The peak of the distribution is well sampled, so Equation 2 is easier to measure than the tail.
Mantegna and Stanley (1995) write the symmetric stable law as \(L_\alpha(Z, \Delta t) = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\infty \exp(-\gamma \Delta t\, q^{\alpha}) \cos(qZ)\, dq\), so that their scale factor is \(\gamma = c^{\alpha}\) in the notation of Stable Distributions. The probability of return then has the closed form
\[
p_{\Delta t}(0) = \frac{\Gamma(1/\alpha)}{\pi\,\alpha\,(\gamma\,\Delta t)^{1/\alpha}} .
\tag{3}\]
The check below compares this expression with the density at zero of scipy.stats.levy_stable.

import numpy as np
from scipy import special, stats

c = 0.7  # scale in the convention of the Stable Distributions page, gamma = c**alpha
for alpha in [1.0, 1.4, 1.8, 2.0]:
    formula = special.gamma(1 / alpha) / (np.pi * alpha * (c**alpha) ** (1 / alpha))
    scipy_pdf0 = stats.levy_stable(alpha, 0, scale=c).pdf(0.0)
    print(f"alpha = {alpha}: formula {formula:.6f}, scipy {scipy_pdf0:.6f}")

alpha = 1.0: formula 0.454728, scipy 0.454728
alpha = 1.4: formula 0.414450, scipy 0.414450
alpha = 1.8: formula 0.404384, scipy 0.404384
alpha = 2.0: formula 0.402993, scipy 0.402993

title: Scaling of Returns
section: What Mantegna and Stanley did and found
text:
What Mantegna and Stanley did and found
Mantegna and Stanley (1995) analysed the S&P 500 cash index from January 1984 to December 1989. The data are 1,447,514 records from the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. The records are not equally spaced: the mean gap was close to one minute in 1984 and 1985 and close to 15 seconds from 1986 to 1989. The authors join the trading sessions into one continuous “trading time”, select non-overlapping records separated by \(\Delta t\) (within a small tolerance), and study the index variations \(Z = y(t) - y(t - \Delta t)\), that is, differences of the index and not log returns. They report that returns give similar properties at high frequency and that the overnight difference does not change the scaling. The number of samples falls from 493,545 at \(\Delta t = 1\) minute to 562 at \(\Delta t = 1000\) minutes.
Their results are:

\(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) follows Equation 2 for \(\Delta t\) from 1 to 1000 minutes, three orders of magnitude. The slope of the log-log fit is \(-0.712 \pm 0.025\), against \(-0.5\) for a Gaussian. Inverting the slope gives \(\alpha = 1.40 \pm 0.05\); the error follows from \(\delta\alpha = \alpha^2\,\delta(\text{slope})\).
The distributions at different \(\Delta t\), rescaled with Equation 1 and \(\alpha = 1.40\), collapse onto the one-minute distribution. The scale factor of the Lévy law is not fitted to the shape: it is computed from the measured \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\). The one-minute distribution agrees with the symmetric Lévy law over almost three orders of magnitude of probability for \(|Z|/\sigma \lesssim 6\), where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation.
For \(|Z|/\sigma \gtrsim 6\) the tails fall off approximately exponentially, faster than the Lévy law. The variance is therefore finite, which the authors present as the resolution of the problem of the infinite variance of a stable law.
The exponent is roughly constant from year to year: the yearly curves of \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) are parallel to the curve for the whole period, and a monthly analysis gives \(\alpha = 1.38 \pm 0.14\). The scale factor varies with the volatility.
Using the Berry-Esseen theorem with the measured third absolute moment and second moment at one minute, the authors estimate that the time needed to approach a Gaussian process is of the order of one month, and they point to an independent study of daily, weekly and monthly returns, which shows a gradual convergence to a Gaussian. I did not reproduce this estimate: it depends on the numerical constant used in the Berry-Esseen bound.
A GARCH(1,1) process with parameters chosen to mimic their one-minute distribution gives a slope of \(-0.531 \pm 0.025\), hence \(\alpha \approx 1.88 \pm 0.09\), about 43 % above the value found in the data. GARCH reproduces fat tails, but not this scaling.

The exponentially truncated tails fit the idea of a truncated Lévy flight, a Lévy flight whose largest steps are cut off. Mantegna and Stanley (1994) had introduced it a year earlier, and the 1995 letter cites it for the point that a process with finite variance can show Lévy scaling over a long range of \(n\) before it converges to a Gaussian. The exercise below shows this crossover. Later work on the tails of individual US stocks found a power-law tail exponent close to 3, outside the stable range \(0 < \alpha \le 2\) (Gopikrishnan et al. 1998). This is consistent with the heavy-tail and aggregational Gaussianity facts of Stylized Facts of Returns.

title: Scaling of Returns
text:
A simulated check
The figure applies the \(p_{\Delta t}(0)\) method to two synthetic series of \(10^6\) i.i.d. returns: symmetric stable with \(\alpha = 1.4\) and Gaussian. The density at zero is estimated, as one simple choice, as the fraction of aggregated returns in a window \(|r| < \varepsilon/2\) divided by \(\varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon\) equal to one tenth of the interquartile range at that horizon.








Figure 1: Estimated probability of return to the origin against horizon for i.i.d. stable (\(\alpha = 1.4\)) and Gaussian returns. Lines have slopes \(-1/1.4\) and \(-1/2\).











NoteExercise



Fit the slope of \(\log p_{\Delta t}(0)\) against \(\log \Delta t\) for both series and convert it to an estimate of \(\alpha\). Then repeat the fit for the stable series using only \(\Delta t \ge 100\). Why does the estimate get noisier?








TipSolution






for label, r in series.items():
    p0 = np.array([p_zero(aggregate_returns(r, h)) for h in horizons])
    s_all = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons), np.log(p0), 1)[0]
    big = horizons >= 100
    s_big = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons[big]), np.log(p0[big]), 1)[0]
    name = label.replace("$", "").replace("\\alpha", "alpha")
    print(f"{name:18s} alpha (all) = {-1 / s_all:.2f}, alpha (dt >= 100) = {-1 / s_big:.2f}")

stable, alpha = 1.4 alpha (all) = 1.37, alpha (dt >= 100) = 1.15
Gaussian           alpha (all) = 2.08, alpha (dt >= 100) = 2.52


With \(10^6\) returns there are only 2000 non-overlapping blocks at \(\Delta t = 500\), and few of them fall inside the small window around zero. Long horizons cost data, which is why Mantegna and Stanley (1995) needed more than a million intraday records to span three decades of \(\Delta t\).









NoteExercise



Build a truncated Lévy flight: draw symmetric stable steps with \(\alpha = 1.4\) and discard those with \(|x| > 50\) in units of the scale. Estimate the local slope of \(\log p_{\Delta t}(0)\) against \(\log \Delta t\) for short horizons (\(\Delta t \le 10\)) and for long horizons (\(100 \le \Delta t \le 500\)). What do you expect, and what does it say about reading \(\alpha\) off a scaling window?








TipSolution





Truncated steps have finite variance, so for very long horizons the aggregated returns approach a Gaussian and the slope tends to \(-1/2\). For short horizons the truncation is not felt and the slope stays close to \(-1/1.4 \approx -0.71\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
raw = sample_symmetric_stable(1.4, 3 * 10**6, rng=rng)
steps = raw[np.abs(raw) < 50.0][: 2 * 10**6]
print(f"fraction of steps kept: {np.mean(np.abs(raw) < 50.0):.4f}")
for lo, hi in [(1, 10), (100, 500)]:
    sel = (horizons >= lo) & (horizons <= hi)
    p0_steps = np.array([p_zero(aggregate_returns(steps, h)) for h in horizons[sel]])
    slope = np.polyfit(np.log(horizons[sel]), np.log(p0_steps), 1)[0]
    print(f"dt in [{lo}, {hi}]: slope {slope:.2f}, effective alpha {-1 / slope:.2f}")

fraction of steps kept: 0.9981
dt in [1, 10]: slope -0.71, effective alpha 1.41
dt in [100, 500]: slope -0.55, effective alpha 1.83


Only about 0.2 % of the steps are removed, yet the apparent index moves from about 1.4 at short horizons towards 2 at long horizons. A straight line over a limited window therefore gives an effective index that depends on the window, and a Lévy-like scaling over a finite range does not prove infinite variance.

title: The Diffusion Equation
text: A single walker is unpredictable. The density of many walkers obeys a deterministic partial differential equation. This page derives it from the lattice walk, following the idea of Berg (1993, chap. 2).

title: The Diffusion Equation
section: From the walk to a PDE
text:
From the walk to a PDE
Let \(P(x, t)\) be the probability that a walker is at site \(x\) at time \(t\). An unbiased walker at \(x\) at time \(t + \tau\) came from \(x - \delta\) or from \(x + \delta\), each with probability \(1/2\):
\[
P(x, t + \tau) = \tfrac{1}{2} P(x - \delta, t) + \tfrac{1}{2} P(x + \delta, t).
\]
Expand the left side to first order in \(\tau\) and the right side to second order in \(\delta\):
\[
\tau \frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = \frac{\delta^2}{2} \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x^2} + O(\delta^4) + O(\tau^2).
\]
Now let \(\delta \to 0\) and \(\tau \to 0\) while the ratio \(D = \delta^2 / (2\tau)\) stays fixed. The result is the diffusion equation
\[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = D \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x^2} .
\tag{1}\]
The limit only makes sense with \(\delta^2 \propto \tau\). If you scale \(\delta \propto \tau\) instead, the right side vanishes and nothing spreads. This is the continuum version of the \(\sqrt{t}\) law from Mean Squared Displacement. The same equation, written for a concentration, is Fick’s second law (Berg 1993, chap. 2).

title: The Diffusion Equation
text:
The heat kernel
For walkers that all start at \(x = 0\), \(P(x, 0) = \delta_{\text{Dirac}}(x)\), the solution on the whole line is
\[
P(x, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi D t}} \exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{4Dt}\right),
\tag{2}\]
a Gaussian with mean zero and variance \(2Dt\) (Berg 1993, Eq. 1.22). Its variance reproduces \(\langle x^2 \rangle = 2Dt\). The same Gaussian also follows from the binomial distribution of the walk when the number of steps is large, which is a special case of the central limit theorem.








Figure 1: Positions of 20000 lattice walkers (\(\delta = \tau = 1\), so \(D = 1/2\)) after 25, 100 and 400 steps, compared with the heat kernel. Bins have width \(2\delta\) because a walker after \(n\) steps sits only on sites with the parity of \(n\).

title: The Diffusion Equation
text:
Assumptions to remember
Equation 1 needs independent steps with finite variance and no bias. A bias adds a drift term, which gives diffusion with drift (Berg 1993, chap. 4). If the step variance is infinite, the limit is not a Gaussian at all; see Stable Distributions. In Module 4 the same Laplacian term appears in reaction-diffusion models.






NoteExercise



Check numerically that Equation 2 solves Equation 1. Evaluate heat_kernel on a grid at \(t = 10\) with \(D = 0.5\), approximate \(\partial_t P\) with a centred difference in time and \(\partial_{xx} P\) with the three-point stencil, and report the largest difference between the two sides.








TipSolution






from amlab.random_walks import heat_kernel

D, t, h, dt = 0.5, 10.0, 0.01, 1e-4
xg = np.arange(-10, 10, h)
dPdt = (heat_kernel(xg, t + dt, D) - heat_kernel(xg, t - dt, D)) / (2 * dt)
P = heat_kernel(xg, t, D)
d2Pdx2 = (P[2:] - 2 * P[1:-1] + P[:-2]) / h**2
print(f"max |dP/dt - D d2P/dx2| = {np.max(np.abs(dPdt[1:-1] - D * d2Pdx2)):.2e}")
print(f"max |dP/dt| = {np.max(np.abs(dPdt)):.2e}")

max |dP/dt - D d2P/dx2| = 1.58e-08
max |dP/dt| = 6.31e-03


The residual is several orders of magnitude smaller than the terms themselves, as expected from discretization error alone.

title: Module 3: Modelling with Randomness
text:
This module adds randomness to your models. You start from the random walk and derive diffusion, the law behind the spread of molecules in a cell. You then see what happens when rare, very large steps dominate: fat tails, stable laws and Lévy flights. Finally you apply these ideas to financial prices and test the random walk model on a daily price series in the laboratory. Reusable code is in amlab.random_walks and amlab.finance.

Session Structure
Session 15: From random walks to diffusion
The Random Walk Mean Squared Displacement The Diffusion Equation Diffusion in Biology
Session 16: When the bell curve fails: fat tails and anomalous diffusion
The Central Limit Theorem Power Laws Stable Distributions Lévy Flights Lévy Foraging
Session 17: Modelling financial markets
Returns and Efficient Markets Stylized Facts of Returns Scaling of Returns
Session 18: Laboratory: financial time series
Loading Prices and Computing Returns Normality Tests Calibrated KS Test Tail Exponent Fitting Power Laws Properly Scaling of Returns in Data



Learning Goals
After this module you can:

Derive the mean and variance of a lattice random walk and the relation \(\langle x^2 \rangle = 2Dt\).
Obtain the diffusion equation as the continuum limit of a random walk, with \(D = \delta^2 / (2\tau)\).
State the central limit theorem, its assumptions, and the generalized version for infinite variance.
Estimate a power-law exponent by maximum likelihood and explain why a least-squares fit on a log-log histogram is biased.
Describe stable laws with index \(0 < \alpha \le 2\) and simulate Lévy flights.
Explain when a Lévy-flight search strategy is optimal (sparse, revisitable targets) and when it is not.
Apply the full procedure of Clauset, Shalizi and Newman to a heavy-tailed sample: maximum likelihood fit, KS choice of the lower cutoff, bootstrap goodness of fit and a likelihood-ratio comparison with alternatives.
Compute log returns, test them for normality with a correctly calibrated Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, and estimate their tail index.
Compare real or synthetic return data with the random walk model and with the stylized facts of financial markets.

title: Diffusion in Biology
text: The relation \(\langle x^2 \rangle = 2Dt\) has a direct consequence for living cells: diffusion is fast over short distances and very slow over long ones. The numbers on this page come from Berg (1993, chap. 1).

title: Diffusion in Biology
text:
Time to diffuse a distance
Invert \(\langle x^2 \rangle = 2Dt\) from Mean Squared Displacement to get the typical time to cover a distance \(x\) along one axis:
\[
t \approx \frac{x^2}{2D}.
\]
Berg (1993, chap. 1) uses \(D = 10^{-5}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\) for a small molecule in water at room temperature. The code below reproduces his two examples: the width of a bacterium (\(10^{-4}\) cm) and the width of a test tube (1 cm).

D = 1e-5  # cm^2/s, small molecule in water (Berg 1993, Chapter 1)

for label, x_cm in [("bacterium, 1 micrometre", 1e-4), ("test tube, 1 cm", 1.0)]:
    t = x_cm**2 / (2 * D)
    print(f"{label:25s} t = {t:9.2e} s = {t / 3600:8.2e} h")

bacterium, 1 micrometre   t =  5.00e-04 s = 1.39e-07 h
test tube, 1 cm           t =  5.00e+04 s = 1.39e+01 h


The first time is about half a millisecond and the second about 14 hours, as in Berg (1993, chap. 1). The distance grew by \(10^4\) and the time by \(10^8\).

title: Diffusion in Biology
text:
Consequences

There is no “diffusion velocity”. The ratio \(\sqrt{\langle x^2 \rangle}/t = \sqrt{2D/t}\) depends on the observation time (Berg 1993, chap. 1).
Over micrometres diffusion moves small molecules within milliseconds. Over centimetres it takes hours, so transport over large distances needs flow or active mechanisms. Berg’s example is perfume: with \(D \approx 10^{-1}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\) in air, diffusion alone would take about a month to cross a crowded room, so convection does the work (Berg 1993, chap. 1).
A random walker explores a small region thoroughly and returns to the same points many times before it wanders off (Berg 1993, chap. 1). Chapter 3 of the same book computes how fast molecules diffuse to a receptor or a cell (“diffusion to capture”).
Swimming bacteria are self-propelled random walkers. Their motion is treated in Berg (1993, chap. 6).

Britton (2003, chap. 5) covers biological motion from the modelling side, including taxis and travelling waves.






NoteExercise



A protein such as lysozyme has \(D \approx 10^{-6}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\) in water (Berg 1993, chap. 1). Estimate the time it needs to cross a cell of diameter \(10\ \mu\text{m}\) and to travel along a nerve axon of length 1 m. What does the second number tell you about how neurons must transport proteins?








TipSolution






D = 1e-6  # cm^2/s
for label, x_cm in [("cell, 10 micrometres", 1e-3), ("axon, 1 m", 100.0)]:
    t = x_cm**2 / (2 * D)
    print(f"{label:22s} t = {t:9.2e} s = {t / (3600 * 24 * 365):8.2e} years")

cell, 10 micrometres   t =  5.00e-01 s = 1.59e-08 years
axon, 1 m              t =  5.00e+09 s = 1.59e+02 years


Crossing the cell takes about half a second. Diffusing along a 1 m axon would take over a century, so axons must use active transport. This is an order-of-magnitude argument; it ignores crowding and binding, which slow diffusion further.

title: The Random Walk
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Berg (1993), Chapters 1 and 2.
Recommended: Britton (2003), Chapter 5 (Biological Motion).
A random walk is a sequence of positions in which each step is random and independent of the previous ones. Karl Pearson named the problem in a letter to Nature (Pearson 1905). In the same year Einstein’s theory of Brownian motion described a suspended particle through many independent displacements (Einstein 1905). In this module you use random walks to model diffusing molecules, heavy-tailed fluctuations and prices.

title: The Random Walk
text:
The one-dimensional lattice walk
Follow Berg (1993, chap. 1). A particle starts at \(x = 0\) at time \(t = 0\) and obeys three rules:

Every \(\tau\) seconds it steps a distance \(\delta\) to the right or to the left.
It steps right with probability \(p\) and left with probability \(q = 1 - p\), independently of earlier steps.
Different particles move independently of each other.

After \(n\) steps the position is a sum of independent steps \(\xi_i \in \{+\delta, -\delta\}\):
\[
x(n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \xi_i .
\tag{1}\]

title: The Random Walk
text:
Mean and variance
Each step has mean \((p - q)\delta\) and variance \(4pq\,\delta^2\). Means and variances of independent variables add, so
\[
\langle x(n) \rangle = n (p - q)\,\delta, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}[x(n)] = 4 n p q\, \delta^2 .
\tag{2}\]
This agrees with the binomial derivation in Berg (1993, Eqs. 1.15 to 1.20). For the unbiased walk, \(p = q = 1/2\), the mean stays at zero and \(\langle x^2(n) \rangle = n\delta^2\). The typical distance from the origin grows as \(\sqrt{n}\), not as \(n\).








Figure 1: Twenty unbiased lattice walks with \(\delta = 1\). The dashed curves are \(\pm\sqrt{n}\), one standard deviation of \(x(n)\).











NoteExercise



Simulate 5000 walkers for 400 steps with \(p = 0.6\) and \(\delta = 1\) using simulate_lattice_walk. Compare the sample mean and variance of \(x(400)\) with Equation 2.








TipSolution





The theory gives \(\langle x \rangle = 400 \cdot 0.2 = 80\) and \(\operatorname{Var} = 4 \cdot 400 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.4 = 384\).

from amlab.random_walks import simulate_lattice_walk

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = simulate_lattice_walk(5000, 400, p=0.6, rng=rng)
print(f"mean     {x[:, -1].mean():7.2f}  (theory 80)")
print(f"variance {x[:, -1].var():7.2f}  (theory 384)")

mean       79.92  (theory 80)
variance  394.05  (theory 384)

title: The Random Walk
text:
What the model leaves out
The lattice walk ignores inertia: successive steps are uncorrelated. Berg (1993, chap. 1) estimates that a protein such as lysozyme in water takes about \(10^{12}\) such steps per second, so the memory of each step is lost almost at once. Walks with memory or with long jumps behave differently; you meet one kind in Lévy flights.

title: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity
text:
NoteReading




Recommended: Hethcote (2000), the sections on vaccination and on SEIR and SIRS models.
Background: Keeling and Rohani (2008).
The SIR model rests on several assumptions: all individuals start susceptible, vaccinated individuals are fully protected, infection makes people infectious at once, immunity is permanent and the population is closed and well mixed. This page follows a simple rule: break one assumption at a time and change the model as little as possible. Each change gives a new behaviour and often a new mathematical object, such as a higher-dimensional system of ODEs, a PDE or a network.
We use the normalized SIR model of Compartmental Models with \(S + I + R = 1\),
\[
\dot S = -\beta S I, \qquad \dot I = \beta S I - \gamma I, \qquad \dot R = \gamma I,
\qquad R_0 = \frac{\beta}{\gamma}.
\]
crumbs: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity

title: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity
text:
Vaccination with a perfect vaccine
Suppose a fraction \(v\) of the population is vaccinated and fully protected at \(t = 0\). The equations do not change; only the initial condition does,
\[
S(0) = 1 - v - I_0, \qquad I(0) = I_0, \qquad R(0) = v .
\]
An outbreak grows if \(\beta S(0) > \gamma\), that is if the effective reproduction number \(R_{\text{eff}}(0) = R_0(1 - v)\) exceeds \(1\). The herd immunity threshold is
\[
v_c = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0},
\tag{1}\]
the same expression as the herd immunity formula in The Reproduction Number. Two points are easy to misread:

\(v_c\) is a threshold for growth. Above \(v_c\) an introduced case does not start an epidemic in the deterministic model, but a few cases can still occur.
It assumes homogeneous mixing and a vaccine that gives complete protection.
crumbs: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity

title: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity
section: How large is the threshold for real diseases?
text:
How large is the threshold for real diseases?
Equation 1 grows quickly with \(R_0\). The table uses typical \(R_0\) ranges, published estimates vary between studies and populations, so treat the ranges as orders of magnitude. The thresholds are computed from Equation 1.



Disease
Typical \(R_0\)
\(v_c = 1 - 1/R_0\)




Seasonal influenza
1.2 to 1.6
0.17 to 0.38


COVID-19 (original strain)
2 to 3
0.50 to 0.67


Smallpox
5 to 7
0.80 to 0.86


Polio
5 to 7
0.80 to 0.86


Measles
12 to 18
0.92 to 0.94



For measles, a drop of a few percentage points in coverage below about 94% is enough for epidemics to be possible again, which is why measles elimination is fragile.
crumbs: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity

title: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity
text:
An imperfect (“leaky”) vaccine
Now relax the assumption that vaccinated people are fully protected. A leaky vaccine reduces susceptibility by a factor \(\varepsilon\) with \(0 \le \varepsilon \le 1\). Split the susceptibles into unvaccinated \(S_u\) and vaccinated-but-still-susceptible \(S_v\):
\[
\dot S_u = -\beta S_u I, \qquad
\dot S_v = -\varepsilon \beta S_v I, \qquad
\dot I = \beta (S_u + \varepsilon S_v) I - \gamma I, \qquad
\dot R = \gamma I .
\tag{2}\]
With coverage \(v\), we have \(S_u(0) \approx 1 - v\) and \(S_v(0) \approx v\), so \(R_{\text{eff}}(0) = R_0\,(1 - v + \varepsilon v)\). Setting this below \(1\) gives
\[
v_c^{\text{leaky}} = \frac{1 - 1/R_0}{1 - \varepsilon} .
\tag{3}\]
For \(\varepsilon = 0\) we recover Equation 1. For \(\varepsilon > 0\) the threshold is higher, and if \(\varepsilon > 1/R_0\) then \(v_c^{\text{leaky}} > 1\): even vaccinating everyone does not prevent an epidemic. Coverage and efficacy are two separate quantities.
Figure 1 integrates Equation 2 with \(R_0 = 3\) and checks Equation 3. The fraction ever infected falls to zero at the predicted thresholds.








Figure 1: Fraction of the population ever infected as a function of vaccine coverage v, for R0 = 3. Dashed lines mark the thresholds from the formula. With eps = 0.6 the threshold is above 1, so vaccination alone cannot prevent an epidemic.
crumbs: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity

title: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity
text:
Why smallpox could be eradicated
Smallpox is the standard case where the SIR assumptions hold well. It has no animal reservoir, so transmission is only between humans. Infection and vaccination both give long-lasting immunity, and the disease is easy to recognize. With \(R_0\) about 5 to 7 the threshold is about 80 to 86%. The WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980, after the last natural case in 1977.
Other diseases break one or more assumptions, so the SIR model is not enough for them:







Disease
Why the plain SIR model fails or is fragile




Measles
SIR-like, but a very high \(R_0\) means a threshold above 90%.


Influenza
Waning immunity, antigenic drift and animal reservoirs.


Tuberculosis
Long latent periods, partial immunity and chronic infection.



In modelling terms, eradication requires the disease-free equilibrium to be reachable and globally stable, not merely locally stable.
crumbs: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity

title: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity
text:
A menu of extensions
Each row breaks one assumption and gives the smallest model change that does so. You have already seen the first rows above.








Assumption broken
Model change
New behaviour




All start susceptible
\(S(0) = 1 - v\)
Herd immunity threshold \(v_c\).


Vaccine fully protective
Two susceptible classes, factor \(\varepsilon\) (Equation 2)
Higher threshold, coverage separated from efficacy.


Infection means infectious at once
Add an exposed class \(E\) with latent period \(1/\sigma\) (SEIR)
Delay between infection and cases, later and lower peak.


Immunity is permanent
Waning at rate \(\omega\) (SIRS)
Endemic equilibrium in a closed population, possible recurrent outbreaks.


Closed population
Births and deaths at rate \(\mu\)
Endemic equilibria, vaccination as a steady-state control problem.


Homogeneous mixing
Groups with a contact matrix \(\beta_{ij}\)
\(R_0\) is the spectral radius of a next-generation matrix, targeted vaccination.


Space is irrelevant
Diffusion terms (reaction-diffusion SIR, a PDE)
Spatial waves and hotspots.


A single population
Patches coupled by a mobility matrix
Importation, exportation and staggered regional waves.


Risk depends only on fractions
Contacts on a network (Module 5)
Superspreading, different thresholds, targeted vaccination of high-degree nodes.


Constant infectiousness
Infectiousness depending on time since infection (renewal equation)
Direct link to generation-interval data.


Constant \(\beta\)
\(\beta(t)\) or \(\beta(I) = \beta_0/(1 + kI)\)
Multiple waves without waning immunity.


We observe infections directly
Observation model: reported cases \(\approx \rho\, i(t - \tau)\)
Explains mismatches between model and reported data.



The last row connects to Fitting an Epidemic to Data and Predicting the Peak, where reporting noise is the reason the peak is hard to predict.

Two extensions in simulation
The SEIR model adds one equation and one time scale,
\[
\dot S = -\beta S I, \quad \dot E = \beta S I - \sigma E, \quad \dot I = \sigma E - \gamma I, \quad \dot R = \gamma I,
\]
and the SIRS model returns recovered individuals to the susceptible class,
\[
\dot S = -\beta S I + \omega R, \quad \dot I = \beta S I - \gamma I, \quad \dot R = \gamma I - \omega R .
\]
In SIRS, the endemic equilibrium has \(S^* = 1/R_0\) and \(I^* = \dfrac{\omega}{\gamma + \omega}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{R_0}\right)\), which exists for \(R_0 > 1\).








Figure 2: Left: SIR and SEIR with the same beta, gamma and initial infectious fraction 0.001 (sigma = 0.2 per day). The latent period delays and lowers the peak. Right: SIRS with omega = 0.01 per day settles to the endemic level given by the formula.
crumbs: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity

title: SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity
text:
Choosing the right model
Extend the SIR model only as far as the question and the data require. More realism is not more truth: every extension adds parameters and uncertainty. Use these models to understand mechanisms and thresholds and to compare intervention scenarios, not to produce a perfect forecast.






NoteExercise 1



For measles with \(R_0 = 15\), compute the herd immunity threshold. A vaccine reduces susceptibility by a factor \(\varepsilon = 0.05\) (95% efficacy). What coverage is needed?








TipSolution





\(v_c = 1 - 1/15 \approx 0.933\). With a leaky vaccine, Equation 3 gives \(v_c^{\text{leaky}} = 0.933/(1 - 0.05) \approx 0.98\). Almost the whole population must be vaccinated, which shows why measles elimination is fragile.









NoteExercise 2



Use Figure 2 as a starting point. Increase the latent period (reduce \(\sigma\)) and describe how the peak time and the height of the peak change. Does the final size change?








TipSolution





A longer latent period delays the peak and lowers it. The final size does not change, because it depends only on \(R_0\) and the initial condition.









NoteOptional project



Consider a hypothetical human-only disease with \(R_0\) between 5 and 7 and fatality ratio about 0.3, with outbreaks starting in five regions at once. Choose a model structure (SEIR, single population or metapopulation), model a vaccination campaign with a start delay and a daily dose capacity, estimate cumulative infections and deaths until you declare control, and identify the two or three assumptions that most affect your estimate.

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text: An SIR epidemic always ends with some susceptibles left. How many people are infected in total can be computed without solving the ODE in time (Kermack and McKendrick 1927; Hethcote 2000).

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
The final size relation
Divide \(\dot S = -\beta S I\) by \(\dot R = \gamma I\):
\[
\frac{dS}{dR} = -R_0 S \quad \Longrightarrow \quad S(t) = S(0)\, e^{-R_0 (R(t) - R(0))} .
\]
As \(t \to \infty\), \(I \to 0\). With \(R(0) = 0\) and \(R(\infty) = 1 - S(\infty)\) you get
\[
\ln\frac{S(0)}{S(\infty)} = R_0 \bigl(1 - S(\infty)\bigr) .
\tag{1}\]
For a small initial seed, \(S(0) \to 1\), and the fraction ever infected, \(z = 1 - S(\infty)\), satisfies
\[
z = 1 - e^{-R_0 z} .
\tag{2}\]
For \(R_0 \le 1\) the only solution in \([0, 1]\) is \(z = 0\). For \(R_0 > 1\) there is a unique positive solution, and it is the final size (Hethcote 2000).

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
Solving it numerically
Equation 2 has no closed-form solution in elementary functions, but a root finder solves it instantly.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

for r0 in [1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0]:
    z = brentq(lambda z: z - 1 + np.exp(-r0 * z), 1e-9, 1.0)
    print(f"R0 = {r0}: final size z = {z:.3f}, herd immunity threshold = {1 - 1 / r0:.3f}")

R0 = 1.5: final size z = 0.583, herd immunity threshold = 0.333
R0 = 2.0: final size z = 0.797, herd immunity threshold = 0.500
R0 = 3.0: final size z = 0.940, herd immunity threshold = 0.667
R0 = 5.0: final size z = 0.993, herd immunity threshold = 0.800


The final size is larger than the herd immunity threshold \(1 - 1/R_0\). The epidemic overshoots: when \(S\) reaches \(1/R_0\) the number of infectious people is at its maximum, and they still cause many infections on the way down.

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
Peak prevalence
The same trick gives the maximum of \(I\). From \(dI/dS = -1 + 1/(R_0 S)\),
\[
I_{\max} = I(0) + S(0) - \frac{1}{R_0} - \frac{1}{R_0}\ln\bigl(R_0 S(0)\bigr),
\]
valid when \(R_0 S(0) > 1\) (Hethcote 2000). amlab.epidemics.peak_prevalence implements this formula.






NoteExercise



Check the final size relation against a simulation for \(R_0 = 3\) (\(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\)) with \(I(0) = 10^{-4}\).








TipSolution






from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from amlab.epidemics import final_size, sir_rhs

sol = solve_ivp(sir_rhs, (0, 400), [1 - 1e-4, 1e-4, 0.0], args=(0.3, 0.1), rtol=1e-9)
print(f"Simulated: {1 - sol.y[0, -1]:.4f}")
print(f"Relation:  {final_size(3.0, s0=1 - 1e-4) + 1e-4:.4f}")

Simulated: 0.9405
Relation:  0.9405


The simulated fraction \(1 - S(\infty)\) matches Equation 1 including the initial seed.

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
Extensions
The SIR model is the starting point of a large family. Each extension relaxes one assumption from Compartmental Models. The page SIR Extensions: Vaccination and Herd Immunity develops vaccination, leaky vaccines, SEIR and SIRS and lists the others.

SEIR: an exposed class \(E\) for people infected but not yet infectious. It changes the timing of the epidemic but, in the simplest case, not \(R_0\) (Hethcote 2000; Keeling and Rohani 2008).
Vital dynamics: births and deaths allow endemic equilibria and recurrent epidemics (Hethcote 2000).
Age structure: contact rates that depend on age (Hethcote 2000; Keeling and Rohani 2008).
Spatial structure and networks: contacts limited to neighbours or to a contact network. Module 5 studies epidemics on networks (Pastor-Satorras et al. 2015).
Stochastic models: needed when the number of cases is small, for example to compute the probability that an outbreak dies out by chance (Keeling and Rohani 2008).

title: The Final Size of an Epidemic
text:
Next
Simulating the SIR Model implements these models, and Fitting an Epidemic to Data fits them to data.

title: Reproducible Code
text: A result is reproducible when someone else can run your code and obtain the same numbers and figures. You will need this for the assignments and the group project. The practices below follow Sandve et al. (2013).

title: Reproducible Code
text:
Pin the environment
Record the exact package versions you used. The course repository does this in requirements.txt:
matplotlib==3.10.8
numpy==2.2.5
scipy==1.14.1
streamlit==1.53.0
Create a clean environment and install from the file:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
After adding a package, write the versions back with pip freeze > requirements.txt and remove the lines you do not need.

title: Reproducible Code
text:
Fix the random seed
Any simulation with randomness must set a seed, and the seed must appear in the code, not only in your notes. Use a local generator instead of the global state:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
print(rng.normal(size=3))
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
print(rng.normal(size=3))  # identical

[ 0.30471708 -1.03998411  0.7504512 ]
[ 0.30471708 -1.03998411  0.7504512 ]


Deterministic ODE solvers such as solve_ivp give the same output for the same input, but results still depend on rtol, atol and method. Write these values explicitly in your code.

title: Reproducible Code
section: Scripts that run from start to finish
text:
Scripts that run from start to finish

One script (or notebook) produces each figure, from raw data to the saved file.
Run it in a fresh session before you submit. Notebooks run out of order hide bugs.
Avoid manual steps such as editing a figure by hand.
Use relative paths from the project root, never paths on your own computer such as C:\Users\....

title: Reproducible Code
text:
Freeze the data

Keep a copy of the raw data you used, with its source and download date, for example in data/ with a README.md.
Never overwrite raw data. Write processed data to a separate file.
If the data came from an online source that changes, record the date and version.

title: Reproducible Code
text:
Validation






NoteExercise



A classmate sends you analysis.py that reads C:/Users/ana/Desktop/cases.csv, uses np.random.rand without a seed, and imports streamlit which is not in requirements.txt. List the three changes needed to make it reproducible.

title: Reproducible Code
text:
Exit question






NoteExercise



You run the same budworm simulation twice with solve_ivp and get identical numbers, but a classmate with a different SciPy version gets values that differ in the fourth decimal. Is your result reproducible?








TipSolution





Your result is repeatable on your machine but not fully reproducible. Different library versions can change default settings or internal algorithms. Pin the version in requirements.txt and set rtol and atol explicitly. Differences below the solver tolerance do not change any conclusion, so you should also report the tolerance you used.

title: Reproducible Code
text:

Hysteresis returns to the budworm with this code.

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
In the SIS model recovered individuals become susceptible again (Hethcote 2000). With \(S = 1 - I\),
\[
\dot I = \beta I (1 - I) - \gamma I .
\tag{1}\]

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Prediction
From The Reproduction Number: for \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma > 1\) the solution should approach the endemic level \(I^* = 1 - 1/R_0\); for \(R_0 < 1\) it should decay to 0.






NoteExercise



Sketch \(\dot I\) against \(I\) for \(R_0 = 2\) and mark the fixed points, as you did for the budworm.








TipSolution





\(\dot I = I\bigl(\beta(1 - I) - \gamma\bigr)\) is a downward parabola with zeros at \(I = 0\) and \(I^* = 1 - \gamma/\beta = 0.5\). It is positive between them and negative for \(I > 0.5\). So \(I = 0\) is unstable (slope \(\beta - \gamma > 0\)) and \(I^* = 0.5\) is stable (slope \(-(\beta - \gamma) < 0\)).

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Implementation






NoteExercise



Write the right-hand side of Equation 1 in the form solve_ivp expects. The state i arrives as an array with one element.
def sis_model(t, i, beta, gamma):
    didt = # TODO: right-hand side of the SIS equation
    return [didt]








TipSolution





def sis_model(t, i, beta, gamma):
    return [beta * i[0] * (1 - i[0]) - gamma * i[0]]
The reference version is amlab.epidemics.sis_rhs.

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Validation

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from amlab.epidemics import sis_endemic_level, sis_rhs

gamma = 0.1
t = np.linspace(0, 200, 800)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for r0, color in [(0.8, "tab:gray"), (1.5, "tab:blue"), (3.0, "tab:red")]:
    sol = solve_ivp(sis_rhs, (0, 200), [0.01], args=(r0 * gamma, gamma), t_eval=t)
    ax.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0], color=color, label=f"R0 = {r0}")
    ax.axhline(sis_endemic_level(r0), color=color, ls=":")
    print(f"R0 = {r0}: I(200) = {sol.y[0, -1]:.4f}, 1 - 1/R0 = {sis_endemic_level(r0):.4f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (days)")
ax.set_ylabel("I")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

R0 = 1.5: I(200) = 0.3328, 1 - 1/R0 = 0.3333
R0 = 3.0: I(200) = 0.6664, 1 - 1/R0 = 0.6667








Figure 1: SIS model with gamma = 0.1 and three values of R0. Dotted lines: endemic level 1 - 1/R0.

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Experiment






NoteExercise




Start from \(I(0) = 0.9\) with \(R_0 = 1.5\). Does the solution approach the same level from above?
Take \(R_0\) close to 1, for example 1.05. How long does it take to get close to \(I^*\)? Relate the time scale to the linearization \(f'(I^*) = -(\beta - \gamma)\).









TipSolution





The endemic equilibrium attracts every \(I(0) > 0\), from above or below. Near it, perturbations decay like \(e^{-(\beta - \gamma)t}\). For \(R_0 = 1.05\) and \(\gamma = 0.1\), \(\beta - \gamma = 0.005\) per day, so the relaxation time is about 200 days.

title: Simulating the SIS Model
text:
Interpretation and limitations
The SIS model has no epidemic peak followed by extinction: the disease settles at a constant endemic level. In a finite population the deterministic endemic state hides random fluctuations, and the infection can go extinct by chance when the number of infected individuals is small (Keeling and Rohani 2008).






TipOptional extension



The SIS equation is a logistic equation. Solve it analytically and compare the formula with the numerical solution.

title: Saddle-Node Bifurcation
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Strogatz (2024), Section 3.7.
Recommended: Murray (2002), Chapter 1 (continuous population models for single species).
A bifurcation is a qualitative change in the dynamics as a parameter crosses a critical value: fixed points appear, disappear or change stability. In one dimension, the basic way to create or destroy fixed points is the saddle-node bifurcation (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.1).

title: Saddle-Node Bifurcation
text:
Normal form
The prototype is
\[
\dot x = \mu + x^2 .
\tag{1}\]

\(\mu < 0\): two fixed points \(x^* = \pm\sqrt{-\mu}\). The negative one is stable, the positive one unstable.
\(\mu = 0\): one half-stable fixed point at \(x^* = 0\).
\(\mu > 0\): no fixed points.

As \(\mu\) increases through 0, the two fixed points approach each other, collide and annihilate. Near any saddle-node bifurcation of a smooth 1D system, a Taylor expansion reduces the dynamics to Equation 1, which is why it is called a normal form (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.1).

title: Saddle-Node Bifurcation
text:
Explore the normal forms
Saddle-node is not the only way a fixed point can change in one dimension. The figure shows the four normal forms of Strogatz (2024), Chapter 3. Left: the flow \(\dot x = f(x; \mu)\) with its fixed points (filled: stable, hollow: unstable) and the direction of motion on the \(x\)-axis. Right: the bifurcation diagram.


With the saddle-node form, move \(\mu\) from \(-1\) towards 0. The two fixed points approach each other. At which \(\mu\) do they collide, and what is left for \(\mu > 0\)?
Read the decay time \(1/|f'(x^*)|\) of the stable point at \(\mu = -0.25\) and at \(\mu = -0.01\). By what factor does it grow? This is critical slowing down.
Switch to the transcritical form and cross \(\mu = 0\). The fixed points do not disappear. What happens to them instead?
Compare the two pitchforks at \(\mu = 0.5\). In which one does a trajectory that leaves the origin find another stable state to settle on?



Build this in Python. In the lab you compute bifurcation diagrams in code, starting with the budworm: Budworm: Integration and Time Series asks you to locate its equilibria and their saddle-node curves as \(r\) and \(k\) change.

title: Saddle-Node Bifurcation
text:
Conditions
At a saddle-node bifurcation of \(\dot x = f(x; \mu)\), a fixed point is also a point of tangency:
\[
f(x^*; \mu_c) = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x^*; \mu_c) = 0 .
\tag{2}\]
The linearization gives no information at \(\mu_c\): the decay rate \(|f'(x^*)|\) goes to zero, and perturbations relax more and more slowly as \(\mu \to \mu_c\). This is called critical slowing down.

title: Saddle-Node Bifurcation
text:
Bifurcation diagram of the budworm
Apply Equation 2 to the budworm model with \(k\) as the control parameter and \(r = 0.56\) fixed. Figure 1 plots the positive fixed points against \(k\).








Figure 1: Bifurcation diagram of the budworm model for r = 0.56. Solid: stable fixed points. Dashed: unstable. Saddle-node bifurcations occur near k = 6.45 and k = 9.94.





The diagram has an S shape. The middle branch is unstable. At each fold, a stable branch meets the unstable branch in a saddle-node bifurcation.
You can find the folds numerically by checking where the number of equilibria changes:

counts = [len(budworm_equilibria(0.56, k)) for k in np.linspace(2, 16, 1400)]
k_grid = np.linspace(2, 16, 1400)
changes = k_grid[1:][np.diff(counts) != 0]
print("Number of equilibria changes near k =", np.round(changes, 2))

Number of equilibria changes near k = [6.45 9.94]








NoteExercise



Show that the saddle-node conditions Equation 2 for \(f(x) = rx(1 - x/k) - x^2/(1+x^2)\) can be solved for \(r\) and \(k\) in terms of the double root \(x\).








TipSolution





For \(x \neq 0\) divide \(f = 0\) by \(x\): \(r(1 - x/k) = x/(1+x^2)\). Tangency of the two curves means equal slopes: \(-r/k = (1 - x^2)/(1 + x^2)^2\). Substituting \(r/k\) into the first equation gives
\[
r = \frac{2x^3}{(1 + x^2)^2}, \qquad k = \frac{2x^3}{x^2 - 1}, \qquad x > 1,
\]
as in Strogatz (2024), Section 3.7. These curves are used on the next page.

title: Compartmental Models: SIR and SIS
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Britton (2003), chapter on epidemic models.
Recommended: Murray (2002), chapter on the dynamics of infectious diseases.
Compartmental models divide a population into groups according to infection status and describe the flows between them. The SIR model goes back to Kermack and McKendrick (Kermack and McKendrick 1927); Hethcote (2000) and Keeling and Rohani (2008) review the family.

title: Compartmental Models: SIR and SIS
text:
The SIR model
Let \(S\), \(I\), \(R\) be the fractions of the population that are susceptible, infectious and removed (recovered and immune, or dead). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot S &= -\beta S I,\\
\dot I &= \beta S I - \gamma I,\\
\dot R &= \gamma I .
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

\(\beta\) is the transmission rate: a susceptible person meets infectious people at a rate proportional to \(I\), and each contact transmits with a fixed probability.
\(\gamma\) is the recovery rate. The infectious period is exponentially distributed with mean \(1/\gamma\).
\(S + I + R = 1\) is conserved, so only two equations are independent.

The SIR model describes a single outbreak of a disease that gives lasting immunity, such as measles in a population without vaccination (Hethcote 2000).

title: Compartmental Models: SIR and SIS
text:
The SIS model
If recovery gives no immunity, recovered individuals return to \(S\):
\[
\dot S = -\beta S I + \gamma I, \qquad \dot I = \beta S I - \gamma I .
\tag{2}\]
With \(S = 1 - I\) this reduces to one equation, \(\dot I = \beta I (1 - I) - \gamma I\), which is a logistic equation for \(I\). Its long-run state is a disease-free equilibrium or an endemic equilibrium (Hethcote 2000). SIS models are used for some bacterial infections and sexually transmitted diseases that do not confer immunity (Keeling and Rohani 2008).

title: Compartmental Models: SIR and SIS
text:
Assumptions
Each assumption is a simplification you should be able to defend or replace.

Well mixed. Every individual is equally likely to meet every other. Real contacts are structured by households, schools, age and geography.
Constant rates. \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) do not change in time. Seasons, behaviour change and interventions all change \(\beta\).
Closed population. No births, deaths or migration during the outbreak. This is reasonable for a short epidemic, not for an endemic disease over decades.
Exponential infectious period. Recovery happens at a constant rate, so some people recover almost immediately and others stay infectious for a long time.
Deterministic and continuous. Fractions change smoothly. This fails at the start of an outbreak, when there are only a few cases and chance matters.







NoteExercise



In Equation 1, show that \(S(t)\) is decreasing and \(R(t)\) is increasing for all \(t\). Can \(I(t)\) increase?








TipSolution





\(\dot S = -\beta S I \le 0\) and \(\dot R = \gamma I \ge 0\) because \(S, I \ge 0\). \(\dot I = I(\beta S - \gamma)\) is positive when \(S > \gamma/\beta\). So \(I\) grows while the susceptible fraction is above \(\gamma/\beta\), then decreases. This threshold is the subject of the next page.

title: Bistability
text: For some values of \(r\) and \(k\) the budworm model has two stable fixed points separated by an unstable one. The system is then bistable: the long-run state depends on where you start (Strogatz 2024, sec. 3.7).

title: Bistability
text:
Two stable states
With \(r = 0.5\) and \(k = 10\) the positive fixed points are \(x_a \approx 0.683\), \(x_b = 2\) and \(x_c \approx 7.317\) (see Fixed Points and Stability).

\(x_a\) is stable. Strogatz calls it the refuge level: predation keeps the budworm scarce.
\(x_c\) is stable. It is the outbreak level: the budworm is limited by food, not by predators.
\(x_b\) is unstable. It is the threshold between the two.

Ludwig et al. describe the same two regimes as limitation by predators and limitation by food (Ludwig et al. 1978, 320).

title: Bistability
text:
Basins of attraction
The basin of attraction of a stable fixed point is the set of initial conditions whose trajectories approach it. In one dimension trajectories cannot cross fixed points, so the basins here are intervals:

\(0 < x_0 < 2\) converges to the refuge \(x_a\);
\(x_0 > 2\) converges to the outbreak \(x_c\).









Figure 1: Trajectories of the budworm model for r = 0.5, k = 10 from several initial conditions. The dotted line is the unstable threshold x = 2.





Two features of Figure 1 deserve attention.

Trajectories that start near \(x = 2\) take a long time to leave it, because \(|f'(2)| = 0.14\) is small.
Trajectories never overshoot. In a one-dimensional autonomous ODE, solutions are monotonic in time, so oscillations are impossible (Strogatz 2024, sec. 2.6).

title: Bistability
text:
Explore the basins
The figure below solves the same equation in your browser. The left panel is the rate \(f(x)\) with its fixed points (filled: stable, hollow: unstable) and the direction of the flow on the \(x\)-axis. Click on it to choose an initial condition; the trajectory appears on the right.


With \(r = 0.5\) and \(k = 10\), click just left of \(x = 2\) and then just right of it. Where does each trajectory end?
Click very close to \(x = 2\). Why does the trajectory wait so long before leaving? Relate it to \(|f'(2)| = 0.14\).
Press Fan of starts, keep \(k = 10\) fixed and drag \(r\) slowly up towards \(0.6\). The refuge and the threshold move towards each other. What happens to the blue trajectories once they meet?
Now fix \(r = 0.5\) and lower \(k\). Use the readout to find the value of \(k\) at which the system stops being bistable. Which two fixed points collide there?



Build this in Python. In the lab you write the code behind this figure: the rate plot in Budworm: the Model in Code and the trajectories in Budworm: Integration and Time Series, both with solve_ivp.

title: Bistability
text:
Ecological interpretation
Bistability means that the same forest conditions (\(r\) and \(k\) fixed) can support two very different budworm densities. Which one you observe depends on history: a large enough immigration or a good year for the insect can push the population across the threshold, and it will then grow to the outbreak level without any change in the parameters.
The model also shows what it cannot do. With \(r\) and \(k\) constant, an outbreak never ends. The observed cycles of outbreak and collapse require the forest to change, which is the subject of Budworm and Forest: Fast and Slow.
Bistability with a threshold is common in ecological models of sudden regime shifts in lakes, forests and other systems (Scheffer et al. 2001).






NoteExercise



For \(r = 0.5\) and \(k = 10\), the population sits at the refuge \(x_a \approx 0.68\). What is the smallest instantaneous increase \(\Delta x\) that triggers an outbreak?








TipSolution





The population must cross the unstable fixed point \(x_b = 2\), so \(\Delta x > 2 - 0.683 \approx 1.32\) in dimensionless units, that is about \(1.32A\) in larvae per acre.

title: Bistability
text:
Next
The budworm model in code turns this analysis into code.

title: The Phase Plane
text:
A planar system
\[
\dot x = f(x, y), \qquad \dot y = g(x, y)
\tag{1}\]
defines a vector field on the \((x, y)\) plane. Each point is a state, and trajectories follow the arrows. You can often understand the whole dynamics from a few geometric objects: nullclines, fixed points and closed orbits (Strogatz 2024, chap. 6 and 7).

title: The Phase Plane
text:
Nullclines
The \(x\)-nullcline is the curve \(f(x, y) = 0\), where the flow is vertical. The \(y\)-nullcline is \(g(x, y) = 0\), where the flow is horizontal. The nullclines divide the plane into regions in which the signs of \(\dot x\) and \(\dot y\) are fixed, so you can sketch the direction of the flow in each region (Strogatz 2024, sec. 6.1).

title: The Phase Plane
text:
Fixed points and the Jacobian
Fixed points are the intersections of the two nullclines. To find their type, linearize: with \(\mathbf u = (x - x^*, y - y^*)\), \(\dot{\mathbf u} \approx J\mathbf u\) with the Jacobian
\[
J = \begin{pmatrix} \partial f/\partial x & \partial f/\partial y \\ \partial g/\partial x & \partial g/\partial y \end{pmatrix}_{(x^*, y^*)} .
\]
Then classify \(J\) by its trace and determinant as in Linear Systems in the Plane. If no eigenvalue has zero real part (a hyperbolic fixed point), the linearization predicts the local phase portrait correctly (Strogatz 2024, sec. 6.3).

title: The Phase Plane
text:
Limit cycles
A limit cycle is an isolated closed trajectory. Nearby trajectories spiral towards it (stable limit cycle) or away from it (unstable). A stable limit cycle is a self-sustained oscillation: its amplitude and period are set by the system, not by the initial condition, and the system returns to it after a small perturbation (Strogatz 2024, chap. 7). Linear systems cannot have limit cycles: their closed orbits, when they exist, come in continuous families.








Figure 1: Phase plane of the Van der Pol oscillator (mu = 1, Lienard form) with nullclines. Two trajectories, one starting inside and one outside, approach the same limit cycle.

title: The Phase Plane
section: Explore the Van der Pol phase plane
text:
Explore the Van der Pol phase plane


Click once close to the origin and once far from it. Both trajectories approach the same closed curve. Is its amplitude set by the initial condition?
Read the type of the fixed point at the origin in the readout. Check it by hand: here \(\operatorname{tr} J = \mu\) and \(\det J = 1\).
Increase \(\mu\) slowly. At which value does the origin change from an unstable spiral to an unstable node? Compare with \(\operatorname{tr}^2 J = 4 \det J\).
Set \(\mu = 5\). Where does the trajectory move slowly and where does it jump? Look at the time series on the right: this is a relaxation oscillation.
Set \(\mu = 0.1\). Why does it take so long to reach the cycle, and why is the cycle almost a circle?



Build this in Python. In the lab you write the code behind this figure: Van der Pol Oscillator implements the vector field, plots the nullclines and integrates trajectories onto the limit cycle.

title: The Phase Plane
text:
The Poincaré-Bendixson theorem
In the plane, the long-run behaviour of a bounded trajectory is limited.






NoteTheorem (Poincaré-Bendixson)



Let \(R\) be a closed, bounded region of the plane, and let the vector field be continuously differentiable on an open set containing \(R\). If \(R\) contains no fixed points and there is a trajectory that starts in \(R\) and stays in \(R\) for all future time, then that trajectory is a closed orbit or spirals towards a closed orbit as \(t \to \infty\) (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.3).


In practice you look for a trapping region: a region on whose boundary the vector field points inwards. If you remove a small disc around an unstable fixed point, the remaining annulus contains no fixed point, and the theorem guarantees a closed orbit. A consequence is that chaos is impossible in autonomous planar systems; it requires at least three dimensions, as in the Lorenz system (Strogatz 2024, sec. 7.3).






NoteExercise



For the Van der Pol system in the form \(\dot x = \mu(y - x^3/3 + x)\), \(\dot y = -x/\mu\), find the fixed point and its type for \(\mu = 1\).








TipSolution





The nullclines \(y = x^3/3 - x\) and \(x = 0\) meet only at the origin. The Jacobian there is \(\begin{pmatrix} \mu & \mu \\ -1/\mu & 0\end{pmatrix}\), with \(\tau = \mu = 1\) and \(\Delta = 1\). Since \(\tau^2 - 4\Delta = -3 < 0\) and \(\tau > 0\), the origin is an unstable spiral. Trajectories leave it and approach the limit cycle in Figure 1.

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Castro et al. (2020).
Course material: Compartmental Models, The Reproduction Number, The Final Size of an Epidemic.
The SIR model is a small system of three ODEs (Kermack and McKendrick 1927; Keeling and Rohani 2008). The solve_ivp workflow from Solving Initial Value Problems applies unchanged: the state is now a vector.
\[
\dot S = -\beta SI, \qquad \dot I = \beta SI - \gamma I, \qquad \dot R = \gamma I .
\]
The state has three components, but \(S + I + R = 1\) is conserved, so only two are independent.

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



For \(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\), \(S(0) = 0.99\), \(I(0) = 0.01\), use the formulas from The Reproduction Number and The Final Size of an Epidemic to predict the peak prevalence \(I_{\max}\) and the final size before you simulate.








TipSolution





Here \(R_0 = 3\). The peak prevalence is \(I_{\max} = I_0 + S_0 - \frac{1}{R_0}\bigl(1 + \ln(R_0 S_0)\bigr) \approx 0.304\), reached when \(S = 1/R_0 \approx 0.333\). The final size relation \(\ln(S_0/S_\infty) = R_0 (1 - S_\infty)\) gives \(S_\infty \approx 0.059\), so about 93% of the susceptibles are infected and \(R_\infty \approx 0.94\).

from amlab.epidemics import final_size, peak_prevalence

print(f"I_max = {peak_prevalence(3.0, 0.99, 0.01):.3f}")
print(f"final size = {final_size(3.0, 0.99):.3f}")

I_max = 0.304
final size = 0.931

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Implementation






NoteExercise



Complete the right-hand side of the SIR model. The solver only needs one function that returns the three derivatives.
def sir_model(t, y, beta, gamma):
    s, i, r = y
    dsdt = # TODO
    didt = # TODO
    drdt = # TODO
    return [dsdt, didt, drdt]








TipSolution





def sir_model(t, y, beta, gamma):
    s, i, r = y
    dsdt = -beta * s * i
    didt = beta * s * i - gamma * i
    drdt = gamma * i
    return [dsdt, didt, drdt]



The solver call follows the usual pattern:
solution = solve_ivp(
    sir_model,
    t_span=(0, 160),
    y0=[0.99, 0.01, 0.0],
    args=(0.3, 0.1),
    t_eval=np.linspace(0, 160, 1000),
)
The reference implementation amlab/odes_1d/sir_model.py provides sir_model and the plotting helper plot_sir_model.








Figure 1: SIR dynamics for beta = 0.3, gamma = 0.1 (R0 = 3), S(0) = 0.99, I(0) = 0.01.

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Validation
Check three facts against the theory: \(S + I + R\) stays equal to 1, the peak of \(I\) matches the formula, and the peak happens when \(S = 1/R_0\).

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from amlab.epidemics import peak_prevalence
from amlab.odes_1d.sir_model import sir_model

sol = solve_ivp(sir_model, (0, 160), [0.99, 0.01, 0.0], args=(0.3, 0.1),
                t_eval=np.linspace(0, 160, 4001), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12)
s, i, r = sol.y
print(f"max |S+I+R-1| = {np.max(np.abs(s + i + r - 1)):.1e}")
print(f"I_max simulated = {i.max():.4f}, formula = {peak_prevalence(3.0, 0.99, 0.01):.4f}")
print(f"S at the peak = {s[i.argmax()]:.4f}, 1/R0 = {1 / 3:.4f}")

max |S+I+R-1| = 6.7e-16
I_max simulated = 0.3038, formula = 0.3038
S at the peak = 0.3331, 1/R0 = 0.3333

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
What to look for

The susceptible fraction decreases monotonically.
The infected fraction rises, peaks and then falls.
The recovered fraction grows monotonically.
Changing \(\beta\) mostly affects how fast the outbreak grows.
Changing \(\gamma\) mostly affects how quickly the outbreak resolves.

title: Simulating the SIR Model
text:
Experiment






NoteExercise



Start from \(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\), \(I(0) = 0.01\) and change one thing at a time.

Increase \(\beta\) with \(\gamma\) fixed. What happens to the height and the time of the peak?
Increase \(\gamma\) with \(\beta\) fixed. Does the epidemic end sooner? Is it smaller?
Change \(I(0)\) from \(10^{-2}\) to \(10^{-5}\). Which quantities change: peak height, peak time, final size?









TipSolution





With \(\beta = 0.45\) (\(R_0 = 4.5\)) the peak rises from 0.30 to 0.45 and comes earlier, near day 17 instead of day 27. With \(\gamma = 0.15\) (\(R_0 = 2\)) the peak drops to 0.16 and the final size to 0.80; the epidemic is smaller, and it dies out a little sooner. With \(I(0) = 10^{-5}\) the peak height (0.30) and the final size (0.94) barely change, but the peak moves from day 27 to about day 61.

for beta, gamma, i0 in [(0.3, 0.1, 1e-2), (0.45, 0.1, 1e-2), (0.3, 0.15, 1e-2), (0.3, 0.1, 1e-5)]:
    run = solve_ivp(sir_model, (0, 300), [1 - i0, i0, 0.0], args=(beta, gamma),
                    t_eval=np.linspace(0, 300, 30001), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12)
    i_run = run.y[1]
    print(f"beta={beta}, gamma={gamma}, I0={i0:.0e}: peak {i_run.max():.2f} "
          f"on day {run.t[i_run.argmax()]:.0f}, final R {run.y[2, -1]:.2f}")
