Live cells after 200 generations: 8


The outcome depends on the relative position and phase of the gliders: they can annihilate, leave a still life or oscillators, or produce new gliders. Shift one glider by one cell and compare.

title: Cellular Automata
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Boccara (2010), Chapter 6.
Recommended: Wolfram (1983).
A cellular automaton (CA) is a dynamical system in which space, time and state are all discrete. Each cell of a lattice holds one of finitely many states, and all cells update at the same time with the same local rule (Wolfram 1983; Boccara 2010).

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Definition
A cellular automaton has four ingredients:

a lattice of cells, here \(\mathbb{Z}\) or a ring of \(N\) cells;
a finite state set, here \(\{0, 1\}\);
a neighbourhood, the cells whose states determine the next state of a cell;
a local rule \(f\) that maps each neighbourhood configuration to a new state.

For a one-dimensional CA with radius \(r\), the update is
\[
x_i^{t+1} = f\big(x_{i-r}^t, \ldots, x_i^t, \ldots, x_{i+r}^t\big),
\]
applied to every \(i\) at the same time. This synchronous update is what separates a CA from a model where cells change one at a time.

title: Cellular Automata
text:
From fields to cells
In Module 4 you updated each grid point of a reaction-diffusion model with a local stencil and explicit time stepping (Laplacian in 2D). A CA keeps the same local-update mindset, but changes the mathematical object:

A field value becomes a discrete state, usually 0 or 1.
A finite-difference stencil becomes a lookup rule on a small neighbourhood.
A PDE time step becomes one synchronous rule application across the whole lattice.

The main idea stays the same. Local interactions create global structure.

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Neighbourhoods

One dimension, radius 1: the cell and its two nearest neighbours. These are the elementary cellular automata (Wolfram 1983).
Two dimensions, von Neumann neighbourhood: the cell and its four orthogonal neighbours.
Two dimensions, Moore neighbourhood: the cell and its eight surrounding cells. The Game of Life uses it (Gardner 1970).

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Rule numbering
An elementary rule assigns a new state to each of the \(2^3 = 8\) neighbourhoods. So there are \(2^8 = 256\) elementary rules. Wolfram lists the neighbourhoods from 111 down to 000, writes the eight outputs as a binary number, and uses its decimal value as the rule number (Wolfram 1983).



Table 1: Rule table of Rule 30. The outputs, read from left to right, form 00011110 in binary, which is 30.





Neighbourhood
111
110
101
100
011
010
001
000




New state
0
0
0
1
1
1
1
0












NoteExercise



Write the rule table of Rule 90. Then show that Rule 90 sets the new state of a cell to the sum of its two neighbours modulo 2.








TipSolution





\(90 = 01011010_2\), so the outputs for 111, 110, 101, 100, 011, 010, 001, 000 are 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0. The output is 1 exactly when the left and right cells differ, whatever the centre cell is. So \(x_i^{t+1} = (x_{i-1}^t + x_{i+1}^t) \bmod 2\).



Reflection (swap left and right) and complement (swap 0 and 1) map rules to rules with the same behaviour up to symmetry. The chunk below counts the resulting equivalence classes.

from amlab.cellular_automata.elementary import equivalence_class

classes = {min(equivalence_class(rule)) for rule in range(256)}
print("Inequivalent elementary rules:", len(classes))
print("Rule 110 is equivalent to", sorted(equivalence_class(110)))

Inequivalent elementary rules: 88
Rule 110 is equivalent to [110, 124, 137, 193]

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Initial conditions
Two initial conditions are standard (Wolfram 1983):

a single seed, one cell in state 1 and all others 0, which shows how a local perturbation grows;
a random row, each cell 1 with probability \(1/2\), which shows the typical long-run behaviour of the rule.

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Boundary conditions
A computer can only store a finite lattice, so you must decide what happens at the edges.

Periodic: cell \(N\) is the left neighbour of cell \(1\), and the lattice is a ring.
Fixed: ghost cells beyond the edges hold a constant state, usually 0.

On a finite lattice with periodic boundaries there are only \(2^N\) configurations. Every orbit is therefore eventually periodic. The lab page Boundary Conditions measures this.

title: Cellular Automata
text:
Why no ODE solver
A cellular automaton is not a discretization of a differential equation. It is defined directly by the local rule, so you do not need scipy.integrate.solve_ivp or any other ODE solver. The numerical method is exact: a loop over time steps that applies \(f\) to every cell.

title: Wolfram Classes
text: Wolfram studied the long-run behaviour of one-dimensional cellular automata started from random initial rows. He proposed that almost all rules fall into four qualitative classes (Wolfram 1984).

title: Wolfram Classes
text:
The four classes

Class 1. Evolution leads to a homogeneous state, for example all cells 0.
Class 2. Evolution leads to a set of separated simple structures that are stable or periodic.
Class 3. Evolution leads to an aperiodic, chaotic pattern.
Class 4. Evolution leads to complex localized structures, sometimes long-lived.

Wolfram related the first three classes to limit points, limit cycles and chaotic attractors of continuous dynamical systems, and conjectured that class 4 rules can support universal computation (Wolfram 1984).








Figure 1: Space-time diagrams of one representative rule per class, started from the same random row (200 cells, periodic boundaries, time runs downward). Rule 32 (class 1), rule 108 (class 2), rule 30 (class 3) and rule 110 (class 4).

title: Wolfram Classes
text:
How to read the diagrams

In rule 32 every cell is 0 after a few steps.
In rule 108 isolated stripes remain fixed or blink with a short period. A change in the initial row only affects nearby stripes.
In rule 30 the pattern looks random, and a single-cell change in the initial row spreads through a growing region.
In rule 110 moving localized structures travel over a periodic background and collide.

title: Wolfram Classes
text:
Explore the rule space
The figure below implements the same convention as amlab.cellular_automata.elementary: bit \(n\) of the rule number is the new state of the neighbourhood with value \(n = 4\,\text{left} + 2\,\text{centre} + \text{right}\). The rule table is drawn from 111 down to 000, as on Cellular Automata.


Use the quick buttons for rules 32, 108, 30 and 110 and match each diagram with its class in the list above.
Switch the start to single cell and compare rule 90 with rule 30. Which one is symmetric, and why? Check your answer against the rule table of rule 90.
Starting from rule 0, click outputs in the rule table until you have built rule 90 \(= 01011010_2\).
Press Flip the centre cell for rules 108 and 30. The red cells are those where the two runs differ. How does the damage grow in each case?
Use rule 184 with densities 0.3 and 0.7 to answer the exercise at the end of this page.



Build this in Python. In the lab you write the code behind this figure: 1D Cellular Automata for the rule table and the update, and Rule Exploration for space-time diagrams of many rules side by side.

title: Wolfram Classes
text:
Sensitivity to a single flip
A quantitative way to separate class 2 from class 3 is to flip one cell of the initial row and track the Hamming distance, the number of cells in which the two runs differ.








Figure 2: Number of cells that differ between two runs whose initial rows differ in one cell (400 cells, periodic boundaries).





For rule 30 the distance grows roughly linearly, because the perturbed region spreads at a finite speed of at most one cell per step on each side.

title: Wolfram Classes
text:
Limits of the classification
The classes are defined by visual inspection of typical runs, not by a formal test. Some rules show different behaviour for different initial conditions, and later work proposed measures such as Langton’s \(\lambda\) to organize the rule space (Langton 1990). Treat the classes as a first vocabulary, not as a theorem.






NoteExercise



Run rule 184 from a random row with density \(0.3\) and with density \(0.7\). Which class would you assign? Does your answer depend on the density?








TipSolution






fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3), sharey=True)
for ax, rho in zip(axes, (0.3, 0.7)):
    ax.imshow(simulate_eca(random_row(200, rho, seed=1), 184, 100), cmap="binary", aspect="auto")
    ax.set_title(f"Rule 184, density {rho}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Rule 184 conserves the number of 1s. At density \(0.3\) all particles end up moving freely to the right; at \(0.7\) the holes move freely to the left. Both look like class 2 after a short transient, so the answer does not depend on the density here. You will meet rule 184 again as the simplest traffic model.

title: Traffic Model
text:
NoteReading




Compulsory: Nagel and Schreckenberg (1992), Section 2 (the model) and Section 3 (the ring).
Guide to the paper: What Nagel and Schreckenberg Did.
Traffic flow is a natural agent-based model. Each car moves according to simple local rules, but repeated interactions create stop-and-go waves, jams, and a transition between free flow and congestion (Nagel and Schreckenberg 1992). The rules are on the page The Nagel-Schreckenberg Model. In this lab you implement them.

title: Traffic Model
text:
Prediction






NoteExercise



With \(v_{\max} = 5\) and \(p = 0\), below which density should every car end up moving at \(v_{\max}\)? What changes in the space-time diagram when you switch on \(p = 0.3\)?








TipSolution





A car at \(v_{\max} = 5\) needs 5 empty cells ahead, so each car uses 6 cells. Below \(\rho = 1/(v_{\max}+1) = 1/6 \approx 0.17\) there is room for every car, and with \(p = 0\) all cars reach \(v_{\max}\) after a transient. With \(p = 0.3\) random slowdowns start jams even below that density. In the diagram they appear as dense streaks that are almost vertical, because a stopped car stays in the same cell, and that lean slightly to the left, against the traffic.

title: Traffic Model
text:
What you need

numpy stores the occupancy pattern, the speed of each car and the experimental results.
matplotlib.pyplot plots space-time diagrams and flow-density curves.







TipScripts or notebooks?



Use a notebook for density sweeps, repeated trials and parameter scans. Use a script if you want a faster interactive visualization or plan to add widgets later.










Figure 1: Traffic CA space-time diagram (cars as black pixels).

title: Traffic Model
text:
Represent the road state
We store the system with two arrays of length length:

occupied[i] tells us whether cell i contains a car.
speeds[i] stores the speed of that car, measured in cells per step.

This lets the road stay discrete while each agent still has its own internal state.

title: Traffic Model
text:
Initialize the agents
The initialization function samples an occupancy pattern and assigns a random speed to each occupied cell.
occupied, speeds = initialize_road(length=100, density=0.2, vmax=5)
The density is
\[
\rho = \frac{\text{number of cars}}{\text{road length}}.
\]

title: Traffic Model
text:
Implement one synchronous update
At each time step, every car follows the same four rules:

Accelerate up to \(v_{\max}\).
Brake so it does not collide with the next car.
Slow down randomly with probability \(p_{\text{slow}}\).
Move forward by its new speed.

The key point is that all cars update synchronously.






NoteExercise



Complete step(). It returns the new occupancy and speed arrays after one synchronous update of all cars on a periodic road.
def step(occupied, speeds, vmax=5, p_slow=0.3, rng=None):
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng()

    # TODO: accelerate
    # TODO: brake to avoid collisions
    # TODO: random slowdown
    # TODO: move cars
    return new_occupied, new_speeds








TipHint





Work with the car positions positions = np.where(occupied)[0], which are sorted along the road. The gap of a car is the number of empty cells up to the next car, (next_pos - pos - 1) % length. The next car of the last car in the list is the first car, because the road is a ring. Write all new speeds first and move the cars only at the end, so that every car sees the old configuration.









TipSolution





def step(occupied, speeds, vmax=5, p_slow=0.3, rng=None):
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng()

    length = len(occupied)
    positions = np.where(occupied)[0]
    speeds_new = speeds.copy()

    speeds_new[positions] = np.minimum(speeds_new[positions] + 1, vmax)

    gaps = np.zeros_like(positions)
    for idx, pos in enumerate(positions):
        next_pos = positions[(idx + 1) % len(positions)]
        gaps[idx] = (next_pos - pos - 1) % length
    speeds_new[positions] = np.minimum(speeds_new[positions], gaps)

    slow_mask = rng.random(len(positions)) < p_slow
    speeds_new[positions[slow_mask]] = np.maximum(
        speeds_new[positions[slow_mask]] - 1, 0
    )

    new_occupied = np.zeros_like(occupied)
    new_speeds = np.zeros_like(speeds)
    new_positions = (positions + speeds_new[positions]) % length
    new_occupied[new_positions] = True
    new_speeds[new_positions] = speeds_new[positions]

    return new_occupied, new_speeds

title: Traffic Model
text:
Validation
Three checks catch most bugs:

the number of cars stays constant;
no two cars ever occupy the same cell (the occupancy array keeps the same number of True entries);
for \(p = 0\) and density below \(1/(v_{\max}+1)\), every car reaches \(v_{\max}\) after a transient.


import numpy as np
from amlab.cellular_automata.traffic import initialize_road, step

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
occupied, speeds = initialize_road(length=120, density=0.1, vmax=5, rng=rng)
n_cars = occupied.sum()
for t in range(200):
    occupied, speeds = step(occupied, speeds, vmax=5, p_slow=0.0, rng=rng)
    assert occupied.sum() == n_cars, "a car was lost or two cars collided"
print("Cars:", n_cars, "| speeds after 200 steps:", np.unique(speeds[occupied]))

Cars: 15 | speeds after 200 steps: [5]

title: Traffic Model
text:
Simulate a full run
Wrap the update in a loop and save the occupancy pattern at every time step.
grid = simulate(steps=200, length=100, density=0.2, vmax=5, p_slow=0.3, seed=1)

title: Traffic Model
text:
Plot the space-time diagram
plt.imshow(grid, cmap="binary", interpolation="nearest", aspect="auto")
plt.xlabel("Road position")
plt.ylabel("Time")
plt.show()

title: Traffic Model
text:
What the dark bands mean
In the diagram, black cells are occupied sites and time runs downward. A car that is stopped or slow stays in the same cell or moves only a little from one row to the next, so it draws a nearly vertical line, and a jam is a dense group of such lines. A car that moves freely advances several cells per row and draws a line that leans strongly to the right. A sparse pattern of such lines means free flow.

title: Traffic Model
text:
Interpretation
A jam is not imposed externally. It emerges from repeated local braking and stochastic slowdown. Jams in the diagram drift to the left while cars move to the right: the jam front moves against the traffic.

title: Traffic Model
text:
Limitations

The road is a ring with one lane, identical cars and identical drivers.
The cell-based loop over cars in step() is slow for long roads. The vectorized version in amlab/cellular_automata/traffic_models.py stores only the car positions.

Full reference: amlab/cellular_automata/traffic.py.
